hade-001.title: A dying star seeds the Sun's birth cloud
hade-001.text: A supernova, the explosion of a dying star, blasted a dense corner of the Milky Way and seeded it with heavy elements later built into Earth. Its shock wave may also have triggered the collapse of the solar nebula, the gas cloud that became the Solar System, and set it spinning.

hade-002.title: The Sun ignites and the Solar System begins
hade-002.text: About 25,000 light years from the center of the Milky Way, a cloud of hydrogen collapsed and gave birth to the Sun. The spinning cloud flattened into a protoplanetary disk, a pancake of gas and dust that held the raw material of Earth. Its first solids, tiny calcium–aluminum-rich inclusions, date to 4,567.3 million years ago, and their age marks the start of both the Solar System and the Hadean. Within 10 million years, the young Sun's wind had cleared away the disk's leftover gas.

hade-003.title: Molten iron plunges inward and Earth gets a core
hade-003.text: Radioactive decay and heat left over from the planet's assembly melted the young Earth enough for its metal to move. Dense iron and nickel sank to the center, releasing energy that fed a runaway process called the iron catastrophe. The result was a metal core beneath a rocky mantle, and its spinning molten metal set up the magnetic field that still shields life from the solar wind. Sources disagree on timing: one puts the event just 10 million years after Earth began to form, another about 500 million years in.

hade-004.title: A restless mantle and a debate over early plates
hade-004.text: Scientists still debate whether the hard-churning Hadean mantle drove plate tectonics, the drifting and diving of crustal slabs, or lay under a rigid lid. Early loss of atmospheric carbon dioxide hints at Hadean plates, but one study argues global plate tectonics began in the Archean, about 3.0 billion years ago.

hade-005.title: Dust and rubble come together to build Earth
hade-005.text: In a runaway process called accretion, dust and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies until they built Earth. The proto-Earth took shape at the cool outer edge of the habitable zone, where liquid water can exist, and grew through a series of giant impacts. Most of the work was done within 10–20 million years, though 2023 evidence suggests it may have taken only about three million. The newborn planet spun fast: a day lasted only about six hours.

hade-006.title: An ocean of magma swallows the surface
hade-006.text: Giant impacts and the heat of core formation melted Earth's outer layers into a magma ocean, a global sea of molten rock about 200 km deep. There were probably several, and the last, raised by the Moon-forming impact, may have reached 2,000 km down. The first one solidified within about 5 million years, and the hot gases it left behind built a heavy carbon dioxide atmosphere. The case is weaker than on the Moon, and sources disagree: one cites chemical traces, while another finds no evidence that Earth ever had a magma ocean.

hade-007.title: Under a faint young Sun, Earth somehow stays warm
hade-007.text: The young Sun shone with only about 70% of today's output, so early Earth should have frozen solid. Yet it seems to have kept liquid water, and how it stayed warm remains an unsolved problem. In greenhouse models, staying above freezing took at least 0.1 bar of carbon dioxide, a tenth of today's air pressure, with 10 bar a plausible upper limit. Scientists still debate how much there was, and some point instead to a darker, less reflective surface or to a young Sun that lost mass.

hade-008.title: Theia strikes, and the Moon is born
hade-008.text: In the explanation most astronomers favor, a Mars-sized protoplanet called Theia slammed into the young Earth some 20–100 million years after the Solar System formed. The blow probably vaporized much of Earth's crust and upper mantle, wrapping the planet in rock vapor and disrupting any water already present. Debris flung into orbit circled as rings for a few million years, then gathered into the Moon, whose rocks date to 4.53 billion years. The Moon's pull later steadied Earth's wobbling axis, which made the climate more regular.

hade-009.title: Floating crystals build the Moon's pale crust
hade-009.text: About 100 million years after the Moon formed, light plagioclase crystals floated up through its magma ocean, then 200–300 km thick. They formed the Moon's first crust, anorthosite, which still makes the pale highlands covering about 80% of its surface.

hade-010.title: Steam condenses and a global ocean fills
hade-010.text: By 4.404 billion years ago, zircon crystals record liquid water and an atmosphere, very soon after Earth formed. As the surface cooled, water vapor condensed into a superocean that covered nearly the whole planet. The seas stayed liquid despite the heat because the air pressed down about 27 times harder than it does today. Most of the water probably seeped out of the mantle rather than arriving on comets, and dissolved carbon dioxide made the seas slightly acidic.

hade-011.title: A grain of zircon, the oldest mineral on Earth
hade-011.text: A single zircon crystal from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, 4.404 billion years old, is the oldest dated mineral on Earth. It lies in a conglomerate, a rock of cemented pebbles, within the Narryer Gneiss terrane, a block of banded rock remade by heat and pressure. Most zircons there are only 3.6–3.8 billion years old, and the oldest consistently dated ones cluster near 4.35 billion, making the record grain a slight outlier. Their chemistry hints that crust was already forming much as it does today, though later recycling of that crust has made Hadean zircon rare.

hade-012.title: Carbon dioxide replaces Earth's first atmosphere
hade-012.text: After the Moon-forming impact stripped away Earth's first atmosphere, rich in hydrogen compounds, gases from the cooling magma ocean built a second one by 4,404 million years ago. This new air was mostly carbon dioxide, at about 230 °C and more than 27 times today's pressure.

hade-014.title: A solid crust hardens over the cooling planet
hade-014.text: Zircons that formed 4.4 billion years ago show that Earth had a solid crust about 100 million years after the planet formed. This first crust probably formed much like the Moon's, as similar materials separated out of the cooling magma. Hafnium isotopes, forms of the element that differ slightly in weight, fit crust forming from 4.5 billion years ago onward, possibly an early reservoir like continental crust. Only mineral grains survive from this Hadean crust; the oldest intact rock formations are Archean.

hade-013.title: Cool early Earth: a hypothesis at odds with zircons
hade-013.text: The cool early Earth hypothesis holds that between about 4.4 and 4.0 billion years ago, temperatures were cold enough to freeze water. The idea remains unsettled, since zircons show liquid water by 4.404 billion years ago, a clash one source calls a paradox.

hade-015.title: The last impact big enough to boil the oceans
hade-015.text: About 4.3 billion years ago, the last impact large enough to vaporize the oceans struck Earth, and life probably emerged only after it. Later Hadean impacts came thousands to millions of years apart, yet any young life stayed vulnerable to the biggest ones.

hade-016.title: Possible microfossils from an ancient Quebec seabed
hade-016.text: Seafloor hot-spring deposits in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq Belt, dated anywhere from 3.77 to 4.28 billion years old, hold tiny structures that may be fossil microbes. If real and 4.28 billion years old, they would be the oldest record of life, but non-living chemistry can mimic such shapes and the rocks' age is disputed.

hade-017.title: Light carbon in Jack Hills zircons hints at life
hade-017.text: Tiny flecks of diamond and graphite inside 4.25-billion-year-old Jack Hills zircons hold unusually light carbon, rich in the lighter isotope that living things favor. Studies in 2005, 2006 and 2009 found no such light carbon, so whether the signal exists, let alone comes from life, is unresolved.

hade-018.title: Guyana's younger rocks hide Hadean zircon cores
hade-018.text: Zircon cores from southern Guyana's Iwokrama Formation date back 4.22 billion years, and eastern Brazil has yielded uranium-rich, once-molten material just as old. Hadean grains inside younger rock show that the rock formed on older crust and swallowed pieces of it.

hade-020.title: Hadean granite hidden inside Canada's Acasta rocks
hade-020.text: In Canada's Slave Craton, one of the ancient, stable blocks at the heart of continents, 3.94-billion-year-old gneisses hold zircons from granite that crystallized 4.2 billion years ago. Hadean crust was already being melted and remade, and these grains, like those of Western Australia, may record early continental crust.

hade-021.title: LUCA: a genetic date for life's common ancestor
hade-021.text: Every living thing descends from LUCA, the last universal common ancestor, and a 2024 study placed it at about 4.2 billion years ago. That figure comes from a molecular clock, which counts genetic changes to date branches in the tree of life, not from any fossil. If correct, only about 100–200 million years separated the origin of life from LUCA. Other studies range from about 4.5 to 3.5 billion years ago, though most agree LUCA existed by 3.5 billion years ago.

hade-019.title: How much land? Models clash over the first continents
hade-019.text: Models clash over the Hadean's continents: one has crust reaching today's volume by 4.2–4.0 billion years ago, another only 25% of today's area by the eon's end. Small proto-continents probably existed, and some may have risen in the mid-Hadean only to vanish beneath a deep ocean.

hade-022.title: Nuvvuagittuq, a contender for Earth's oldest rock
hade-022.text: A 4,157-million-year-old dike, a sheet of once-molten rock, cuts through Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq Belt, so the dark rocks it crosses are at least that old. A 2012 study gave 4,321 million years, which would make the belt Earth's oldest known rock, but other studies accept only a minimum of 3.75 billion.

hade-024.title: The origin of life: when and where remain open
hade-024.text: No one knows when life began, and sources call the evidence for Hadean life controversial. The geologic record puts life's emergence most likely between 4.32 and 3.48 billion years ago, with geochemical hints as early as 4.1 billion. Hot springs on volcanic land may have let RNA, a molecule that carries genetic information, form and copy itself. Alternatively, life may have begun in deep hydrothermal vents, shielded from impacts and ultraviolet light, perhaps as early as 4.4 billion years ago.

hade-025.title: A carbon speck in zircon, maybe the oldest life
hade-025.text: Carbon locked in a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon from Western Australia may be a chemical fossil of living things, possibly the oldest trace of life on Earth. The evidence is preliminary, and the carbon may not be biological at all.

hade-023.title: Late Heavy Bombardment: spike or slow decline?
hade-023.text: Crater counts suggest a storm of impacts struck the Moon from about 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, and by inference Earth, Mercury, Venus and Mars. The key evidence is a cluster of ages in impact-melted rock brought back by Apollo astronauts, mostly from near the Moon's Imbrium Basin. Scientists now argue whether it was a real spike or a long, gradual decline, because the cluster could be debris from one large impact. Whatever its shape, life either arose afterward or, more likely, survived the barrage.

arch-001.title: Canada's Acasta Gneiss, the oldest intact rock
arch-001.text: In Canada's Northwest Territories, zircons in the Acasta Gneiss crystallized about 4.03 billion years ago, making it the oldest known felsic crust, the pale, silica-rich rock of continents. Geologists use that age, 4,031 million years, to mark the start of the Archean Eon. Its tonalites, granite-like rocks that rose as lighter melt during partial melting, are among the first sizable pieces of continental crust. The complex records more than a billion years of melting and remaking, from over 4.0 to 2.9 billion years ago.

arch-002.title: The carbon cycle settles into its basic pattern
arch-002.text: Early carbon isotope ratios closely match today's, a sign that the carbon cycle's fundamental features were already in place about 4 billion years ago. Much of the early atmosphere's carbon dioxide dissolved in water, reacted with calcium and magnesium from weathered rock and built carbonate sediments, or limy deposits.

arch-003.title: DNA takes over from RNA as life's genetic store
arch-003.text: Early life probably kept its genes in RNA and only later adopted DNA, a more chemically stable store, which LUCA most likely already had. The 4-billion-year date rests on one proposal, from virologist Luis Villarreal, that viruses ferried RNA genes into DNA genomes; the timeline remains open.

arch-004.title: The Napier orogeny raises early Antarctic mountains
arch-004.text: An orogeny, an episode of mountain building, raised the Napier range of East Antarctica about 4 billion years ago, give or take 200 million years. Its folding and faulting may have produced some of Earth's first metamorphic rocks, rocks remade by heat and pressure.

arch-005.title: The final phase of a debated bombardment
arch-005.text: The final phase of the Late Heavy Bombardment is placed at about 3,920–3,850 million years ago, though impacts stayed frequent into the early Archean. Lunar melt ages cluster near 3.9 billion years, but scientists still argue whether that marks one cataclysm or several smaller episodes stretching to about 3.5 billion years ago.

arch-006.title: Contested carbon on Greenland's Akilia Island
arch-006.text: Graphite in rock at least 3.85 billion years old on Akilia Island, Greenland, is low in carbon-13, which may mark organic matter made by living things. Whether the rock was ever sediment, how old it really is and whether its carbon is biological are all disputed.

arch-007.title: The first rocks of the East European Craton
arch-007.text: The oldest rocks of the Ukrainian Shield and Voronezh Massif formed around 3.8 billion years ago, the first pieces of what became the East European Craton. This Archean crust, 3.2 to 3.8 billion years old, now lies in the craton's southwest and east.

arch-008.title: Granite blocks gather into the first cratons
arch-008.text: Around 3.8 billion years ago, blocks of granite began to gather into the first cratons, the first complete continental masses. These deep-rooted cores of continents are old and stable, and most of them formed in the Archean. On the eastern edge of the Antarctic craton, light, silica-rich magma rose as a great continental mass began to gather. Antarctic zircons suggest that recycling within the crust was key to building cratons, and about 39% of today's continental crust formed in the Archean.

arch-010.title: Isua holds the oldest banded iron formations
arch-010.text: The oldest known banded iron formations, rocks of thin alternating iron-rich and silica-rich layers, formed at Isua in Greenland about 3,800–3,700 million years ago. Their iron isotopes point to almost no oxygen, with iron oxidized by anoxygenic photosynthesis, a form of photosynthesis that releases no oxygen.

arch-009.title: Isua's pillow lavas record water 3.8 billion years ago
arch-009.text: The Isua Greenstone Belt, a band of ancient lavas and sediments tinted green by heat and pressure, is Earth's largest exposure of Eoarchean surface rock. Its pillow basalts, lava that erupted underwater and cooled into rounded blobs, show that liquid water existed 3.8 billion years ago.

arch-012.title: China's Yangtze Block takes shape
arch-012.text: The Yangtze Block, the northwestern part of the South China Craton, is thought to have formed 3.8–3.2 billion years ago. Its Kongling Complex holds China's oldest rocks, with zircons 3.3–2.9 billion years old.

arch-011.title: The Pilbara Craton, a window on early Earth
arch-011.text: Western Australia's Pilbara Craton holds crust up to 3.8 billion years old, laced with granite domes and greenstone belts of 3.5–3.2 billion years. Along with South Africa's Kaapvaal Craton, it is one of only two pristine Archean crusts left on Earth. Zircon grains worn from older rock show that crust was already eroding 300 million years before the oldest rocks that survive. The craton stabilized around 3.6 billion years ago, and by 2.97 billion years its western and eastern blocks had collided and joined.

arch-013.title: Microbes harvest sunlight without making oxygen
arch-013.text: From about 3.7 billion years ago, microbes that lived without oxygen appear, including some that fed on chemicals and some that ran on sunlight. Their simpler photosynthesis released no oxygen, because it used hydrogen sulfide, sulfur or iron in place of water. These bacteria made ATP, the cell's energy currency, by running protons across a membrane, a trick nearly every later organism still uses.

arch-014.title: Greenland rocks reveal an early magnetic shield
arch-014.text: Rocks from Greenland, described in 2024, show that Earth had a magnetic field by 3.7 billion years ago. Earlier studies of magnetism frozen into Australian lava and South African pebble beds had traced the field back to at least about 3,450 million years ago. Earth makes its field from electrically conducting fluid in motion, the churning molten metal of the core that formed in the Hadean.

arch-015.title: Isua's disputed traces of life
arch-015.text: Graphite in 3.7-billion-year-old sediments at Isua, Greenland, holds carbon that hints at life, the earliest such sign from a whole rock rather than one mineral grain. In 2016 a team reported domed stromatolites 1–4 cm high, 220 million years older than those of Australia's Dresser Formation. A 2018 study, joined by one of the original proponents, argued that the shapes came from rock deformation instead. Both the carbon and the stromatolites remain disputed, and the earliest undisputed evidence of life is about 3.5–3.48 billion years old.

arch-016.title: Granite thickens South Africa's Kaapvaal Craton
arch-016.text: Between 3.7 and 2.6 billion years ago, batholiths, huge bodies of granite that cooled underground, thickened South Africa's Kaapvaal Craton and made it stable. Its oldest core is gneiss of about 3.6–3.7 billion years, later joined by granite and greenstone terranes, slivers of crust that dock against a larger block. From 3.0 to 2.7 billion years ago, collisions with chains of volcanic islands built basins that filled with thick piles of lava and sediment. Today its granite lies exposed in the heart of the Vredefort impact structure.

arch-019.title: The Wyoming Craton takes root
arch-019.text: The Wyoming Craton began as a 100,000 km² block of crust with gneisses 3.6–3.0 billion years old, and zircon grains in it reach back 4.0 billion years. Late Archean magma and plate movements reworked it, and its three subprovinces had joined by the end of the eon.

arch-018.title: Vaalbara, a possible first supercontinent
arch-018.text: South Africa's Kaapvaal and Australia's Pilbara cratons may have merged into Vaalbara, an early supercontinent, perhaps as far back as 3.6 billion years ago. The two share strikingly similar rock sequences from 3.5 to 2.7 billion years ago, including the same layers of impact debris. By 2.78 billion years ago they lay 30 degrees of latitude apart, so any union had broken up by about 2.8 billion. Some scientists doubt Vaalbara existed, blaming the shared features on global processes, and it competes with the largely incompatible Ur hypothesis.

arch-017.title: India's Dharwar Craton takes shape
arch-017.text: India's Dharwar Craton, the oldest part of the Indian peninsula, formed between 3.6 and 2.5 billion years ago as sinking ocean crust melted into light, granite-like rock. Its three blocks joined between 2,560 and 2,500 million years ago, closing all its subduction zones, places where one plate dives beneath another.

arch-020.title: Lavas and sediments build the Barberton Greenstone Belt
arch-020.text: The Barberton Greenstone Belt of South Africa and Eswatini built up from lavas and sediments between 3.5 and 3.2 billion years ago, as terranes docked in two episodes. Its Makhonjwa Mountains are among the oldest in Africa, and its rocks hold some of the oldest traces of life.

arch-021.title: Glassy beads record the oldest known impacts
arch-021.text: Eight layers of spherules, tiny glassy beads of rock melted and hurled out by impacts, lie in the Barberton belt and record at least four big strikes. Spherules 3.5 billion years old in South Africa and Western Australia are the oldest known products of impacts on Earth. A 2024 review counts 36 such layers in two windows of time, which it reads as a tail of the Late Heavy Bombardment. Some of the objects that made them were up to 100 km wide.

arch-022.title: Dresser stromatolites, the earliest undisputed life
arch-022.text: In the Dresser Formation of Australia's Pilbara Craton, stromatolites laid down about 3,483–3,479 million years ago are the earliest direct evidence of life. Textures pressed into the same sediments record microbial mats, and the nearby North Pole chert, a glassy silica rock, holds microfossils and chemical signs of heat-loving microbes. Most of these mounds grew in a shallow lagoon or flooded caldera, a collapsed volcanic crater, where seawater mixed with hot fluids from below. Some older sources put the first uncontroversial life later, at 3,000 or even 2,700 million years ago.

arch-023.title: Life may already gain a foothold on land
arch-023.text: Geyserite, a mineral crust left by hot springs, in the Pilbara's Dresser Formation holds possible traces of microbes living on land by 3.48 billion years ago. Such springs offered elements life needs, including phosphorus, boron, nitrogen and sulfur. Fossil mats show that life was firmly established on land by 3.22 billion years ago. By at least 2.7 billion years ago, microbes had built whole land ecosystems, with organic-rich soils and ponds.

arch-024.title: Apex chert: fossils or mineral mimics?
arch-024.text: The 3.465-billion-year-old Apex chert of the Pilbara may hold microorganisms turned to stone, possibly the earliest direct fossils of life. Once likened to cyanobacteria, microbes that make oxygen by photosynthesis, the structures remain contested and may not be biological at all.

arch-025.title: Strelley Pool stromatolites show microbes adapting
arch-025.text: Stromatolites in Western Australia's 3.43-billion-year-old Strelley Pool Formation change shape in ways that suggest microbial communities reacting to shifting conditions. They imply that some form of photosynthesis was under way by then, and the rocks also hold a variety of microfossil shapes.

arch-026.title: Possible methane microbes beneath Barberton's seafloor
arch-026.text: About 3.42 billion years ago, threadlike microbes, possibly ones that made or ate methane, may have lived in mineral veins beneath the seafloor at Barberton. Nearby cherts hold fossil microbial mats, and some Barberton microbes show they reproduced by splitting in two.

arch-027.title: Nitrogen fills a stable sky with almost no oxygen
arch-027.text: By about 3.4 billion years ago, nitrogen dominated a stable second atmosphere laced with methane, carbon dioxide, water vapor and sulfur gases. Volcanoes vented these gases, with extra supplies from huge asteroids of the Late Heavy Bombardment. Oxygen stayed around or below 0.001% of today's level until about 2.4 billion years ago, as iron, sulfur and methane swallowed whatever early photosynthesis made. Unusual sulfur-isotope signals, which rarely form when oxygen is plentiful, rule out significant oxygen before about 2.45 billion years ago.

arch-028.title: Granite-like magma builds the Johannesburg Dome
arch-028.text: Tonalite and related granite-like magma forced its way into dark greenstone in the central Kaapvaal Craton, forming South Africa's Johannesburg Dome. Zircons date this phase, the oldest yet found there, to 3,340 million years, and younger intrusions suggest the craton grew piece by piece, in spurts.

arch-029.title: Two blocks fuse into the Zimbabwe Craton
arch-029.text: About 3.3 billion years ago, the Zimbabwe Craton stabilized as two smaller blocks, with rocks up to 3.46 billion years old, fused together. Together with the Kaapvaal Craton and Limpopo Belt, it sits on a buoyant mantle root about 250 km thick that yields diamonds.

arch-030.title: Fig Tree microfossils from 3.26 billion years ago
arch-030.text: South Africa's Fig Tree Formation, laid down about 3.28–3.22 billion years ago, holds stromatolites and fossils of microscopic life about 3.26 billion years old. Among them are forms named Archaeosphaeroides barbertonensis and Eobacterium.

arch-031.title: A giant asteroid strikes and boils the ocean surface
arch-031.text: Around 3.26 billion years ago, an asteroid 37–58 km wide slammed into Earth and left the S2 spherule layer in the Barberton Greenstone Belt. Its crater may have been almost 480 km across, two and a half times the diameter of the Chicxulub crater. The blow probably shook the whole planet with strong earthquakes and raised megatsunamis thousands of meters high. Its heat boiled the ocean surface, evaporating tens of meters of water from the global ocean.

arch-032.title: Microbial mats carpet the Moodies tidal flats
arch-032.text: The Moodies Group of South Africa and Eswatini, laid down about 3.22 billion years ago, holds Earth's oldest well-preserved tidal deposits of sand and mud. Microbial mats flourished on its tidal flats, and its microfossils are among the few Archean examples that scientists accept.

arch-034.title: Cyanobacteria begin splitting water and releasing oxygen
arch-034.text: Around 3.2 billion years ago, evidence appears for photosynthesis that makes oxygen, with pockets of free oxygen around stromatolites on shallow carbonate platforms. Cyanobacteria split water and released oxygen as waste, which first reacted with iron dissolved in the oceans to form iron ore. Oxygen built up only slowly, poisoning many bacteria, and after the Archean it triggered the Great Oxygenation Event, the first lasting buildup of oxygen in the air. The timing is fiercely debated: claims reach back to 3.5 billion years, genetic work favors 2.9–3 billion, and certain evidence dates only from about 2.4 billion.

arch-033.title: A hot world under a methane greenhouse
arch-033.text: Oxygen isotopes in Mesoarchean cherts suggest oceans as hot as 55–85 °C, though studies of weathering point to averages below 50 °C. Either way, the climate was at least temperate, probably thanks to high levels of methane and carbon dioxide. Volcanoes supplied the carbon dioxide and early microbes the methane, which lasted longer in air that held no oxygen. Nitrogen levels were probably close to today's, so nitrogen did little to warm the planet.

arch-036.title: Ur, a small and hypothetical early supercontinent
arch-036.text: Ur is a hypothetical supercontinent, built from rocks now in India, western Australia and southern Africa, that may have formed around 3.1 billion years ago. It would have covered just 12–16% of today's continental crust. The main argument is that cratons stable by about 3 billion years ago all sat in one region of Pangaea, a far later supercontinent. Ur is controversial, and its layout largely conflicts with the rival Vaalbara hypothesis.

arch-035.title: The Saamian orogeny builds Fennoscandia's ancient core
arch-035.text: Between 3.1 and 2.9 billion years ago, the Saamian orogeny built a broad expanse of granite-like crust in the Kola Peninsula, Karelia and northeastern Finland. This crust of the Baltic Shield later became the core of Kenorland, a proposed supercontinent.

arch-037.title: Miralga, an impact scar with three different ages
arch-037.text: Shatter cones near Marble Bar in the Pilbara, cone-shaped fractures made by an impact's shock, reveal the Miralga impact structure, whose crater may have topped 100 km. A March 2025 study dated it to 3,470 million years ago, which would make it the oldest known impact structure by over a billion years. Months later, another study found shatter cones in rocks younger than 2.71 billion years, putting the impact sometime between then and 400 million years ago. A 2026 study dated zircon recrystallized by the impact to about 3.024 billion years ago, but the age remains disputed.

arch-038.title: Maniitsoq, a proposed impact that may never have happened
arch-038.text: A structure at Maniitsoq in West Greenland was proposed as an ancient impact site, dated to about 3,000.9 million years ago. The impact evidence is highly contentious, and magma bodies there that formed 3,013 million years ago are too old to have been made by the supposed impact.

arch-039.title: Modern-style plate tectonics may begin
arch-039.text: Around 3 billion years ago, plate tectonics may have begun working much as it does today, though its timing is still debated. The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction, including a chain of ocean volcanoes at a Pilbara plate boundary about 3.12 billion years ago. Minerals trapped in ancient diamonds suggest that the supercontinent cycle, the repeated gathering and breakup of continents, began roughly then. Other estimates range from more than 4 billion years ago, in the Hadean, to 2.2 billion, or just 800 million years ago for fully modern tectonics.

arch-040.title: Continents grow fast in the late Archean
arch-040.text: Before 3.7 billion years ago, continents held less than 10% of today's continental crust. By 3.0 billion years ago that share had reached roughly 20–25%, and widespread melting of the mantle pushed it to about 60% by 2.6 billion. Only the last fifth of today's continental crust formed during the past 2.5 billion years. The oldest rocks survive inside cratons, the cores of continents, which escape the recycling that destroys ocean crust.

arch-041.title: Pongola, Earth's oldest known ice age
arch-041.text: Between about 2.985 and 2.837 billion years ago, ice spread across part of the planet in the Pongola glaciation, the oldest known on Earth. Its traces are diamictites, jumbled mixes of boulders and mud dropped by glaciers, in the Mozaan Formation of KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini. Ice reached a latitude of 48 degrees, interrupting a climate kept mild by methane and carbon dioxide, though no one knows whether it reached the tropics. Sulfur isotopes hint that the cold may be tied to a brief, early rise in atmospheric oxygen.

arch-042.title: A brief first whiff of oxygen
arch-042.text: Around 2,980–2,960 million years ago, oxygen rose briefly in an atmosphere that otherwise held almost none, and oases of relatively oxygen-rich water formed in some shallow coastal seas. Sulfur isotopes link this episode to the Pongola glaciation of the same age.

arch-043.title: Rivers pour gold into the Witwatersrand Basin
arch-043.text: Rivers and a sea laid 5–7 km of sediment in the Witwatersrand Basin, and braided river deltas on its wide coastal plain concentrated gold, pyrite and uraninite. The basin holds the world's largest known gold reserves: over 40,000 metric tons mined, about 22% of all gold above ground.

arch-044.title: Terranes collide to build the North Atlantic Craton
arch-044.text: The North Atlantic Craton, now found in West Greenland, Labrador and northwest Scotland, grew as terranes collided in a series of orogenies. Magma, deformation and metamorphism then reworked and stabilized it.

arch-045.title: The Yilgarn Craton assembles from older pieces
arch-045.text: Western Australia's Yilgarn Craton was pieced together from many older terranes, including the Narryer Gneiss, home of the Jack Hills zircons. Most of its gold was deposited 2,650–2,630 million years ago.

arch-046.title: The vast Abitibi greenstone belt forms
arch-046.text: The Abitibi greenstone belt of Ontario and Quebec, one of the world's largest Archean greenstone belts, formed between 2,800 and 2,600 million years ago. Mostly volcanic, it is a stack of crustal slices pushed over one another, and it contains the huge Blake River Megacaldera Complex.

arch-047.title: The Limpopo Belt welds two cratons together
arch-047.text: About 2.8–2.5 billion years ago, heat and pressure welded the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe cratons together along the 250 km wide Limpopo Belt. Once the two cratons had stabilized as one, the intense metamorphism in the belt stopped.

arch-048.title: North China's basement crust forms in two pulses
arch-048.text: About 85% of the North China Craton's basement, its deep foundation rock, formed in two Neoarchean pulses, 2.8–2.7 and 2.6–2.5 billion years ago. Geologists still debate whether its blocks joined about 2.5 billion years ago or only at 1.85 billion.

arch-049.title: Fortescue and Hamersley basins open on the Pilbara
arch-049.text: From about 2.78 to 2.42 billion years ago, a thick pile of sedimentary and volcanic rock filled the Fortescue, Hamersley and Turee Creek basins on the Pilbara. Uranium–lead dating puts the base of this pile, the Mount Bruce Supergroup, at 2,768 million years ago.

arch-050.title: The Slave Craton's deep root settles
arch-050.text: The Slave Craton stabilized mainly about 2.75 billion years ago, a time recorded by abundant peridotite, a dense mantle rock, in its deep root. Its oldest diamonds, 3.5–3.3 billion years old, imply that a thick root existed far earlier.

arch-051.title: Stromatolites and puzzling microfossils in the Tumbiana lakes
arch-051.text: Western Australia's Tumbiana Formation records the oldest known carbonate-rich lake system, and its limestones hold stromatolites and some of the few accepted Archean microfossils. Their size and protrusions resemble those of eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, but such features are not unique to eukaryotes, so what they were remains unclear.

arch-052.title: Kenorland, a proposed supercontinent, comes together
arch-052.text: Kenorland, a hypothetical supercontinent, may have formed about 2.72 billion years ago as Neoarchean cratons and new continental crust gathered together. Its core was the Baltic Shield of Fennoscandia, and its final assembly was finished by about 2,600–2,550 million years ago. It broke up sometime after 2.45–2.1 billion years ago into pieces that included the forerunners of Laurentia and Baltica. Some geologists argue instead that the cratons formed separate clusters, called Superia and Sclavia, rather than one supercontinent.

arch-053.title: Ventersdorp lavas halt the Witwatersrand gold deposits
arch-053.text: Around 2.715 billion years ago, vast outpourings of lava, the Ventersdorp lavas, abruptly ended deposition of the Witwatersrand's gold-rich Central Rand Group. Their cause is speculative: one source ties them to a collision with the Zimbabwe Craton, another to rifting, when the crust stretches and splits.

arch-054.title: Blake River, a supervolcano of the Precambrian
arch-054.text: About 2,707 million years ago, the Blake River Megacaldera Complex of Ontario and Quebec, the first known Precambrian supervolcano, began to form. Its first caldera, Misema, stretches 80 km long and 40 km wide, and later phases piled up 7–9 km of erupted rock.

arch-055.title: Komatiite floods hint at a churning mantle
arch-055.text: A major, possibly global eruption of komatiite, an extremely hot lava made when 30–40% of mantle rock melts, may mark an overturn of the mantle. Komatiite lava erupted at up to about 1,600 °C and formed almost only in the Archean, when the mantle may have run 100–250 °C hotter.

arch-058.title: A pulse of oxygen around 2.7 billion years ago
arch-058.text: Around 2.7 billion years ago, oxygen rose again, and some researchers see this pulse as a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event. Skewed sulfur isotopes in pyrite, a shiny iron sulfide mineral, record a small rise in atmospheric oxygen at this time. Cyanobacteria had appeared by then at the latest, and an atmosphere containing oxygen began to develop late in the Archean. Most scholars, however, still place the start of the Great Oxygenation Event at about 2,400 million years ago, in the Paleoproterozoic.

arch-059.title: The Stillwater complex intrudes Montana's ancient gneiss
arch-059.text: About 2.7 billion years ago, magma pushed into older gneisses in southern Montana and cooled in layers, forming the Stillwater complex. About 5,500 m of its layers lie exposed along the Beartooth Mountains, rich in chromium and platinum-group metals such as palladium.

arch-060.title: Stromatolite reefs spread through shallow seas
arch-060.text: Stromatolites appear throughout the Archean, but from about 2.7 billion years ago they become a major part of the fossil record. The earliest ones of confirmed microbial origin, by one account, date to 2.724 billion years ago. In Zimbabwe, stromatolites of the Bulawayo series built the first verified reef community on Earth. One timeline puts the rise of stromatolites as reef builders earlier, at about 3 billion years ago.

arch-061.title: Sturgeon Lake Caldera erupts in Ontario
arch-061.text: Explosive eruptions and lava domes on the seafloor filled the Sturgeon Lake Caldera of northwestern Ontario with nearly 3,000 m of rock. It remains one of the world's best-preserved calderas rich in metal ores.

arch-062.title: Raindrops and lava bubbles weigh the ancient air
arch-062.text: Fossil raindrop prints in South African volcanic ash show the air was less than twice as dense as today's, and gas bubbles in lava suggest only 0.23 bar. Both results undercut ideas that very high carbon dioxide or nitrogen kept the Archean warm under the faint young Sun.

arch-056.title: The Algoman orogeny stitches the Superior Craton together
arch-056.text: In the Algoman, or Kenoran, orogeny, repeated collisions and subduction crumpled terranes together along a belt from South Dakota to Sudbury, Ontario. Between 2,720 and 2,680 million years ago, a run of these collisions stitched together the Superior Craton, the largest Archean craton. Dates of about 2,700 million years from near Rainy Lake, Ontario, favor a model in which moving plates drove the docking. The orogeny closed out the Archean about 2,500 million years ago, by which time continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick.

arch-057.title: A nickel famine hits the methane makers
arch-057.text: From 2.7 to 2.4 billion years ago, nickel deposition in the oceans fell steadily from 400 times today's level. Methane-making microbes need nickel, so as volcanic nickel dwindled, oxygen producers began to outcompete them.

arch-063.title: Stromatolites build carbonate platforms in the Transvaal
arch-063.text: Stromatolites built two successive carbonate platforms, thick shelves of limy rock in shallow water, in the Transvaal Basin on the Kaapvaal craton. The oldest known giant carbonate platform dates from about 2,600 million years ago, and a rising sea flooded tidal flats around 2.550 billion years ago.

arch-064.title: The Great Dyke slices across Zimbabwe
arch-064.text: Magma forced its way across the Zimbabwe Craton and cooled into the Great Dyke, a layered band of rock 550 km long and 3–12 km wide. It has stayed undeformed ever since, proof that the craton was already stable, and it is one of the world's three most significant platinum sources.

arch-065.title: Arctica, a hypothetical continent, assembles
arch-065.text: Arctica, a hypothetical continent, formed about 2.565 billion years ago from the Siberian, Slave, Wyoming, Superior and North Atlantic cratons. The Algoman, or Kenoran, orogeny built it by joining the Canadian Shield to the Siberian craton.

arch-066.title: First evidence of microbes that live on sulfur
arch-066.text: The earliest evidence of microbes oxidizing sulfur to extract energy comes from South Africa's Gamohaan Formation, about 2.52 billion years ago. It shows that sulfur-oxidizing bacteria evolved before the Great Oxygenation Event.

arch-067.title: An oxygen pulse closes the Archean
arch-067.text: Around 2,501 million years ago, a pulse of higher oxygen appeared, and some researchers see it as a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event. Studies from 2016–2022 place the first oxygenation of the air anywhere from 2.7 to 2.3 billion years ago.

arch-068.title: Continents rise above the sea at last
arch-068.text: For most of the Archean, continental crust lay drowned beneath a superocean deeper than today's oceans. Only as the eon closed did the continents likely rise above the waves, with crust by then about 40 km thick. As land emerged, weathering of the continents increased and pushed the oxygen isotopes of seawater toward modern values.

prot-003.title: Iron settles out of the sea in banded layers
prot-003.text: Across most continents, iron settled out of seawater as massive banded iron formations, striped rocks whose red layers are oxidized iron. Deposition peaked around 2.5 billion years ago, when most of the world's banded iron was laid down. Australia's Hamersley Range holds the thickest and most extensive deposits, more than 900 meters of rock laid down between 2,470 and 2,450 million years ago. Some sources place most banded iron slightly earlier, in the late Archean.

prot-002.title: Oxygen sparks an explosion of new minerals
prot-002.text: Oxygen from the Great Oxidation Event combined with many elements near the surface, and about 2,500 new minerals pushed the total past 4,000. Oxidized uraninite, a uranium ore, alone gave rise to over 200 new minerals, and more than two-thirds of mineral species owe their existence to life.

prot-004.title: Kenorland, a possible supercontinent, splits apart
prot-004.text: Between 2.48 and 2.45 billion years ago, plumes of hot mantle rock began to rift apart Kenorland, a single giant landmass, or supercontinent, at low latitudes. The breakup dragged on for hundreds of millions of years, ending with great swarms of dikes across North America 2.2 to 2.1 billion years ago. Its fragments seeded later continents such as Baltica and Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, and the breakup is linked to the era's glaciations. Kenorland itself is hypothetical, though, and some geologists argue the land instead formed two large blocks called Superia and Sclavia.

prot-005.title: Dike swarms crack the Superior Craton
prot-005.text: Around 2,470 million years ago, the Mistassini and then the Matachewan dike swarms cut the Superior Craton, the latter across at least 300,000 square kilometers. Each is a large igneous province, a vast outpouring of magma, read as rifting above a hotspot near Sudbury, Ontario, as Kenorland began to break up.

prot-006.title: The Great Oxidation Event: oxygen enters the air
prot-006.text: For the first time, free oxygen built up in the air and shallow seas, turning a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, and the change never reversed. Cyanobacteria get most of the credit, but oxygen could accumulate only once the iron, sulfur and methane at the surface that react with it had been used up. Between 2,410 and 2,320 million years ago, the pressure of oxygen rose from about two millionths of a bar to at least two thousandths. Rust-red soils appear by 2.3 billion years ago, and by the event's end oxygen had reached as much as 10 percent of today's level.

prot-007.title: Oxygen poisons the microbial world
prot-007.text: To a biosphere made mostly of anaerobes, microbes that live without oxygen, the new gas was toxic. It may have wiped out many early organisms, mostly colonies of archaea, an ancient group of single-celled microbes, in what is called the first known mass extinction. It might even have been the worst ever, but early life is too poorly known to compare it with the Big Five extinctions of later eons. It is also the only well-documented extinction before the Phanerozoic, the eon of abundant animal life, because earlier life was microbial or soft-bodied.

prot-008.title: Australia's Turee Creek chert keeps ancient microbes
prot-008.text: Black chert, a hard silica rock, in Australia's Turee Creek Group preserves microfossils 2,450 million years old, some read as iron-oxidizing bacteria. The group also holds the Kazput Reef Complex, 2,400 to 2,300 million years old and the oldest reef complex known from the Proterozoic.

prot-010.title: The Sleaford orogeny forges the Gawler Craton
prot-010.text: From 2,440 to 2,420 million years ago, the Sleaford orogeny, a slow collision that crumples crust into mountains, deformed the Gawler Craton of South Australia. The craton formed about then and remained a set of active mountain belts until about 1,550 million years ago.

prot-009.title: An impact scars India's Bundelkhand craton
prot-009.text: An impact struck the Bundelkhand craton and left the largest impact structure in India. Its size is uncertain, estimated at 3 kilometers across by some sources and 11 by others, and its age is poorly constrained.

prot-011.title: Dike swarms slice through Scotland and Western Australia
prot-011.text: The Scourie dike swarm cut Scotland's Lewisian gneisses, ancient banded rocks, at about the same time as a phase of crustal deformation called the Inverian. Around 2,410 million years ago, the Widgiemooltha swarm intruded the Yilgarn Craton of Western Australia, close in time to the Sebanga Poort dike in Zimbabwe.

prot-012.title: Possible fungi grow in cracks of South African basalt
prot-012.text: Filaments that grew in cracks and gas cavities of basalt in South Africa's Ongeluk Formation may be fossils of fungus-like organisms. Bottom-dwelling, multicellular and built of threads that could fuse, they are the earliest fossils with typical fungal features, and Ukraine's much younger Volyn biota is cited in support.

prot-013.title: The Huronian ice age chills an oxygenated world
prot-013.text: Rising oxygen destroyed methane, cutting it from 300 to 4 parts per million and weakening the greenhouse that kept Earth warm. Average global temperatures fell below 0 °C, and ice spread in pulses that left diamictite, a jumble of boulders and mud dropped by glaciers, near Lake Huron. Glacial beds turn up on six cratons, including Wyoming, Kaapvaal and Karelia-Kola, with three pulses dated between about 2,440 and 2,310 million years ago. This is the earliest well-established ice age, with ice on land; only the Pongola glaciation is older.

prot-015.title: Makganyene: a possible snowball Earth in South Africa
prot-015.text: South Africa's Makganyene glaciation has been proposed as a snowball Earth, a near-total freeze of the planet's surface, set off by the evolution of cyanobacteria. Its glacial sediments, slightly younger than the Huronian beds, may have formed in the tropics. Magnetic signals locked in the rocks place South African glacial deposits of 2.2 billion years ago near the equator. Above them sit cap carbonates, layers of limestone or dolomite laid down on top of glacial deposits.

prot-014.title: Buried carbon leaves the largest isotope swing on record
prot-014.text: Marine carbonate rocks record the largest and longest-lasting positive carbon isotope excursion known, a swing toward heavy carbon reaching values of +5 to +30 parts per thousand. To produce it, the burial of organic carbon would have had to double or triple for millions of years. The excursion went hand in hand with a surge in oxygen, an expansion of life and more organic matter buried in sediments. Oxygen then fell around 2.1 billion years ago in the Shunga-Francevillian event, and organic-rich black shales piled up; if global, the excursion lasted 128 to 249 million years.

prot-016.title: Yarrabubba: a giant impact of disputed age
prot-016.text: An impactor about 7 kilometers wide hit Western Australia's Yilgarn craton, perhaps through a 2-kilometer ice sheet, and left a crater 30 to 70 kilometers across. Its date of 2,229 million years ago falls near the Huronian glaciation's end, but a later study challenged it and suggested a much younger impact.

prot-017.title: West Africa is welded together in the Eburnean orogeny
prot-017.text: A long series of collisions, intruding magma and metamorphism, the remaking of rock by heat and pressure, reshaped what is now West Africa. It built the Eglab and Man shields of the West African Craton and gave its Birimian domain its structure. Together with the Transamazonian orogeny, it welded South American and West African cratons, an early step toward the supercontinent Columbia. Around 2,070 million years ago, hot mantle welled up beneath the region and released a large volume of magma after the mountain building.

prot-018.title: The first red beds rust on land
prot-018.text: Iron in weathered sandstone rusted to hematite, a red iron oxide, as it met oxygen in the air, staining the first continental red beds. Iron in ancient soils shows oxygen reaching 5 to 18 percent of present levels around 2,200 million years ago.

prot-019.title: The first eukaryotes: an archaeon takes in a bacterium
prot-019.text: Eukaryotes are thought to have arisen in this period when an Asgard archaeon, a kind of single-celled microbe, took in an alphaproteobacterium. Sexual reproduction probably appeared then too, and the earliest known eukaryotic acritarchs, organic-walled microfossils, date from 2,150 to 1,950 million years ago. Yet the timing is debated: claimed eukaryote fossils from 2.1 billion years ago are considered questionable, and another view puts the earliest evidence at 1.85 billion years. The oldest remains that are unmistakably eukaryotic come from China and are 1.8 to 1.6 billion years old.

prot-020.title: South America's old cores collide in the Transamazonian orogeny
prot-020.text: Two small Archean proto-continents, the Gavião and Jequié blocks, collided, shaping what are now the São Francisco Craton and the Guiana Shield. With West Africa's Eburnean orogeny, this collision marks the start of Columbia's assembly.

prot-022.title: Gabon's mysterious disks: early life or mineral mimics?
prot-022.text: Black shales in Gabon's Francevillian B Formation hold flattened, disk-shaped structures up to 17 centimeters across. Some authors read them as the earliest multicellular life and the earliest eukaryotes, and a 2023 zinc isotope study found a signal that could reflect eukaryotic metabolism. Recent reviews lean the other way, however. A 2017 review called their biological origin questionable, and a 2023 review suggested they are artifacts of diagenesis, the chemical changes that turn sediment into rock.

prot-021.title: The supercontinent Columbia, or Nuna, comes together
prot-021.text: Collisions across the globe gathered almost all of Earth's continental blocks into the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna. Orogenies such as the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China stitched together the future cores of Laurentia, Baltica, Amazonia, Australia and others. Zircons, tough crystals that record when they formed, reveal a great high range, the Nuna Supermountains, between 2.0 and 1.8 billion years ago. Modern plate tectonics may have emerged with the supercontinent, by at least 2.2 billion years ago, and final assembly came about 1.82 billion years ago.

prot-023.title: A Karelian lagoon's mud turns to oil and shungite
prot-023.text: As the crust rifted in what is now Russian Karelia, organic-rich mud settled in a brackish lagoon, where volcanic nutrients may have boosted life. Heat and pressure later cooked the mud into shungite deposits holding over 250 gigatonnes of carbon, veined with petroleum of confirmed biological origin.

prot-025.title: Bushveld magma builds Earth's largest layered intrusion
prot-025.text: Magma from the mantle rose through long cracks in the Kaapvaal craton and cooled underground into the largest layered igneous intrusion in Earth's crust. Like a cake, it formed in layers, including three platinum-bearing bands called reefs. It holds the world's largest reserves of platinum-group metals, along with vast amounts of iron, tin, chromium, titanium and vanadium. About 30 million years later, the Vredefort asteroid struck nearby.

prot-026.title: Vredefort: the largest verified impact on Earth
prot-026.text: An asteroid struck the Kaapvaal craton in today's South Africa; it was first put at 10 to 15 kilometers wide and, in 2022, at 20 to 25. It blasted a crater 170 to 300 kilometers across, the largest verified impact structure on Earth and possibly bigger than Chicxulub. Erosion has since stripped away 7 to 11 kilometers of rock, leaving the rebounded central uplift, a 70-kilometer ring of hills called the Vredefort Dome. By dropping the Witwatersrand rocks down, the impact also saved rich gold deposits from being eroded away.

prot-028.title: Pilbara and Glenburgh crash into the Yilgarn
prot-028.text: In the Glenburgh orogeny, the Pilbara Craton and the Glenburgh Terrane, a block of crust with its own geological history, collided with the Yilgarn craton in Western Australia. The collision brought abundant granite magma and intense deformation and metamorphism to the Glenburgh Terrane.

prot-029.title: Atlantica joins West Africa and South America
prot-029.text: Cratons now in West Africa and eastern South America joined to form the continent Atlantica, which included Amazonia and the Congo, West Africa and North Africa cratons. Geologists do not generally count it as a supercontinent.

prot-032.title: Svecofennian mountains rise across Sweden and Finland
prot-032.text: Mountain building affected what are now Sweden, Finland and Russia, joining the cratons of Baltica within Columbia. Subduction closed an ocean basin and, about 1,950 million years ago, emplaced the Jormua and Outokumpu ophiolites, slices of ocean floor pushed onto land. Full collision between continents lasted from 1,870 to 1,790 million years ago, even as the crust farther south stretched. The mountains then collapsed under their own weight between 1,790 and 1,770 million years ago.

prot-034.title: The Trans-Hudson orogeny forges North America's core
prot-034.text: The largest Paleoproterozoic mountain belt in the world, the Trans-Hudson orogen sutured the Hearne-Rae, Superior and Wyoming cratons into North America's core, forming the Canadian Shield. Old cratons, ocean deposits and island arcs, curved chains of volcanoes above sinking plates, were folded, thrust and metamorphosed, then invaded by hundreds of huge granite bodies. The Manikewan Ocean finally closed around 1.83 billion years ago, and metamorphism peaked about 1.82 to 1.8 billion years ago. Following the Wopmay orogeny, it capped the assembly of Laurentia from six or seven Archean fragments.

prot-030.title: Three blocks merge into Baltica
prot-030.text: Baltica formed from the collision of three blocks: Fennoscandia, Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia. Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia joined first, as Proto-Baltica, around 2.0 billion years ago. Proto-Baltica then collided with Fennoscandia 1.8 to 1.7 billion years ago. One account dates the meeting of Sarmatia and Fennoscandia a little earlier, to 1.84 to 1.82 billion years ago, after a quiet spell that followed subduction.

prot-031.title: The early Ruker orogeny begins building Antarctica
prot-031.text: The early Ruker orogeny was a key event in the assembly of Antarctica, joining East Antarctica to an unknown continental block as Columbia formed.

prot-035.title: Greenland crumples in the Nagssugtoqidian orogeny
prot-035.text: Mountain building in Greenland formed the northern edge of the mainly Archean North Atlantic craton, one of the collisions that sutured Laurentia's blocks within Columbia. Island-arc terranes and two possible sutures, seams where colliding plates joined, record subduction zones that have since vanished.

prot-036.title: Magma rings the Superior craton in a geological instant
prot-036.text: Between 1,884 and 1,870 million years ago, as the Trans-Hudson, New Quebec and Penokean orogenies closed in, dark, iron-rich magma flooded the Superior craton's margin. In an extremely short geological time, dikes, flat sheets of magma called sills, and lavas built the Circum-Superior Belt, a large igneous province. Its cause remains unclear, with proposals ranging from rifting behind an island arc to mantle plumes and the breakup of a microcontinent. Stretching more than 3,400 kilometers from Manitoba to Labrador, it now hosts major copper, nickel and platinum-group deposits, including Manitoba's Thompson nickel belt.

prot-037.title: The Wopmay orogeny shows plate tectonics at work
prot-037.text: The Hottah terrane, a continental volcanic arc, collided with the Archean Slave Craton in northern Canada, closing the Coronation Ocean and raising a belt about 500 kilometers long. Its oceanic crust, island arcs and colliding continents show that modern plate-tectonic forces were already at work in the early Proterozoic.

prot-038.title: Gunflint chert preserves a world of microbes
prot-038.text: Black chert layers in banded iron formation on Lake Superior's north shore preserve microfossils of microbes like cyanobacteria. The rock is built of stromatolites, layered mounds made by microbial colonies, and in Ontario some of the colonies have turned to jasper. These microbes show that photosynthesis was under way and that the air held enough oxygen to sustain microbial life. Uranium–lead dating gives a consensus age of about 1.878 billion years, though older methods once gave 2.08 and 2.11 billion.

prot-039.title: Grypania: a coiled ribbon of uncertain identity
prot-039.text: Grypania, a coiled tube over a centimeter long, is among the commonest large Proterozoic fossils, probably ranging from about 1,870 million years ago into the Ediacaran. Scientists still argue whether it was a giant bacterium, a bacterial colony or an alga; only an alga would mean eukaryotes with organelles already existed.

prot-040.title: Penokean collision folds the Lake Superior region
prot-040.text: Around Lake Superior, two crustal domains collided on the Superior Craton's southern margin, thrusting and folding rocks northward and reawakening the Great Lakes tectonic zone. It was one of the orogens of 1.9 to 1.8 billion years ago that stitched Laurentia's blocks together as Columbia assembled.

prot-041.title: Viruses that infect bacteria appear
prot-041.text: Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, had emerged by at least 1.85 billion years ago. They arose before, or soon after, the split between the lineages of prokaryotes, cells without a nucleus, and eukaryotes.

prot-042.title: Banded iron vanishes as the deep sea gains oxygen
prot-042.text: After 1.85 billion years ago, banded iron formations largely vanish from the rock record worldwide. Geologists read their end as the oxygenation of the deep ocean, once the iron dissolved in seawater had been oxidized. Until then the ocean had been persistently rich in iron, with possible spells of sulfidic, oxygen-free water. A 10-kilometer asteroid struck water about 1,000 meters deep 1.849 billion years ago, at the same time as a pause in iron deposition.

prot-043.title: North China's two halves collide, but when?
prot-043.text: The Eastern and Western Blocks of the North China Craton collided to form the Trans-North China Orogen, which Zhao ties to Columbia's assembly about 1.85 billion years ago. Kusky disagrees, placing the merger 2.5 to 2.3 billion years ago and reading the 1.85-billion-year event as a collision with Columbia; the dispute is unresolved.

prot-044.title: The Sudbury impact strikes the supercontinent Nuna
prot-044.text: Near the end of the Orosirian, a stony asteroid 10 to 15 kilometers wide struck the supercontinent Nuna in what is now Ontario, Canada. It left one of the oldest and largest known impact structures and would have scattered debris across the globe. The Sudbury Igneous Complex formed at the same time, and its ores hold nickel, copper, platinum-group metals, gold and silver. Some researchers propose that the impact mixed the layered ocean through tsunamis, vaporized seawater and runoff from wrecked continental margins.

prot-045.title: Capricorn mountain building reworks Western Australia
prot-045.text: Once the Pilbara Craton and Glenburgh Terrane had joined the Yilgarn craton, the Capricorn orogeny reworked the crust within the continent. Chief of four orogenies to shape the Gascoyne Complex, it brought vast Moorarie granites and, around 1,830 million years ago, flood basalts in the Yerrida Basin.

prot-046.title: Columbia keeps growing at its edges
prot-046.text: After its final assembly about 1.82 billion years ago, Columbia kept growing until 1.5 billion years ago, as subduction fed magma and added new crust at its margins. A great belt of magma formed along what are now the southern margins of North America, Greenland and Baltica. Similar belts grew around Amazonia, the North Australia and Gawler cratons, and North China. Widespread magmatism about 1,750 million years ago in Baltica, Sarmatia, Siberia, Laurentia and West Africa shows these cratons were linked.

prot-049.title: The oldest sand seas form on several cratons
prot-049.text: Around 1.8 billion years ago, the oldest known ergs, vast seas of wind-blown sand, developed on several cratons.

prot-050.title: The Boring Billion: Earth's long, quiet middle age
prot-050.text: From about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, Earth passed through the Boring Billion, or Earth's Middle Ages, a span of tectonic stability, steady climate and slow evolution. Oxygen stayed very low and no glaciations occurred, though one Scottish lake of 1 billion years ago froze over in winter. The oceans may have been oxygen-poor, sulfidic and starved of nutrients, ruled by purple bacteria that used hydrogen sulfide instead of water, a so-called Canfield ocean. The span ended with Rodinia's breakup, a second rise in oxygen and the Snowball Earth glaciations of the Cryogenian.

prot-051.title: The Yavapai arc collides with proto-North America
prot-051.text: The Yavapai island arc collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona, one of several arcs added to Laurentia's 1,800-million-year-old core. Similar collisions of island arcs with the mainland formed the Grand Canyon's Vishnu basement schists, flaky metamorphic rocks, 1.75 to 1.73 billion years ago.

prot-052.title: Natural nuclear reactors switch on in Gabon
prot-052.text: In what is now Oklo, Gabon, concentrated uranium deposits began sustaining nuclear fission after groundwater flooded them. These natural reactors ran on and off, probably never producing more than 100 kilowatts.

prot-054.title: The Mazatzal arc extends southern Laurentia
prot-054.text: The Mazatzal island arc collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona, the next pulse of growth after the Yavapai orogeny. Between the two collisions, short-lived basins opened as the crust stretched, filling with quartz sand, now quartzite, and volcanic rhyolite.

prot-055.title: The first sure multicellular eukaryotes appear in China
prot-055.text: The Chuanlinggou Formation of North China's Yan Mountains preserves the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes: Qingshania, Tawuia and Changchengia. Qingshania seems to consist of nearly identical cells, but organisms whose cells took on specialized jobs began to appear around 1.7 billion years ago. Multicellular eukaryotes probably evolved from colonies of single cells somewhere between 2 and 1.4 billion years ago. Such finds show that life in the following Mesoproterozoic was not purely microbial, as once thought.

prot-056.title: Shoemaker crater: an impact of uncertain age
prot-056.text: An impact in the Mid West of Western Australia left a structure at least 30 kilometers across, with shatter cones and shocked quartz, both forged by impact shock. Its most cited age, about 1,630 million years, records a reheating of the granite that may date the impact or merely a regional tectonic event.

prot-057.title: India's Chitrakoot rocks hold the oldest red algae
prot-057.text: The Chitrakoot Formation in India's Vindhya Range preserves the earliest known red algae, Rafatazmia and Ramathallus. Algae are eukaryotes that make their own food by photosynthesis, and these red algal mats, about 1.6 billion years old, are the oldest of their kind.

prot-059.title: Mount Isa's metal ores form amid the Isan orogeny
prot-059.text: The Isan orogeny, a major bout of mountain building, struck Queensland's Mount Isa Block as huge deposits of lead, silver, copper and zinc formed. The ores sit in the 1,000 m thick Urquhart Shale, with copper above lead, zinc and silver, on one flank of a faulted fold.

prot-058.title: Eukaryotes capture cyanobacteria and become algae
prot-058.text: Around 1.6 billion years ago, some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria as endosymbionts, partners living inside their cells, and gained oxygen-producing photosynthesis through organelles called plastids. These cells became the algae, which eventually overtook cyanobacteria as the dominant primary producers, the organisms that make food at the base of the food web. North China's Gaoyuzhuang Formation, about 1,589 million years old, preserves some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia and Grandilingulata. Rocks dated between 1.5 and 1.4 billion years hold a diverse collection of fossil algae.

prot-061.title: Oxygen pulses briefly in the middle of the Boring Billion
prot-061.text: Between 1.59 and 1.36 billion years ago, oxygen may have pulsed briefly to about 4 percent of present levels, though how widely is unclear. North China's Gaoyuzhuang rocks suggest a rise near 1.57 billion years ago; rocks from Australia, Russia and North China mark another near 1.4 billion. Early in the Ectasian period, 50 to 80 percent of the seafloor was oxidized, a share that later declined. Otherwise oxygen in the Boring Billion may have stayed below 0.1 to 1 percent of modern levels, stalling complex life.

prot-064.title: Volyn microbes fill cavities in Ukrainian igneous rock
prot-064.text: Exceptionally preserved microfossils formed in cavities of igneous rock in what is now Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, about 1.5 billion years ago. They include filaments of varied shapes and fungus-like organisms, possibly among the first fossils of the deep biosphere, the life that dwells within rock.

prot-063.title: The supercontinent Columbia splits apart
prot-063.text: Columbia began to fragment about 1.5 to 1.35 billion years ago, as rifts opened along the margins of Laurentia, India, Baltica, Siberia, southern Africa and North China. Magma rose far from any mountain belt, forming suites of anorthosite, granite and related rocks across North America, Baltica, Amazonia and North China. Atlantica split away, and North China broke off along the Zhaertai–Bayan Obo rift, where sills of dark rock record the event. Final breakup came about 1.3 to 1.2 billion years ago, marked in North America by the Mackenzie and Sudbury dike swarms, and the fragments later regathered as Rodinia.

prot-065.title: Horodyskia, a string of beads of unknown nature
prot-065.text: Horodyskia, a string of beads joined by a fine thread, is one of the oldest known structurally complex eukaryotes, with fossils spanning 1,480 to 550 million years ago. Its identity is unsettled: it may have been an early animal, or a colony of foraminifera, single-celled organisms that build shells.

prot-066.title: Belt Basin mud becomes Glacier National Park's peaks
prot-066.text: In a rift basin on Laurentia's edge, probably closed off like a lake, mud, silt and sand piled up more than 15 km thick. These layers, the Belt Supergroup, hold stromatolites and rich ores of lead, zinc and silver, and they now form the mountains of Glacier National Park.

prot-067.title: The Picuris orogeny and the great 1.4-billion-year granites
prot-067.text: From 1.43 to 1.3 billion years ago, mountain building struck what is now the southwestern United States. Its batholiths, huge bodies of once-molten rock about 1,400 million years old, make up over 20 percent of exposed Precambrian rock in New Mexico and the Rocky Mountains.

prot-068.title: Kibaran collisions fuse Africa's Tanzanian and Congo cratons
prot-068.text: From about 1,400 million years ago, a series of Kibaran mountain-building events fused Africa's Tanzanian and Congo cratons, continuing until Rodinia assembled about 1,000 million years ago. In a narrower sense, the name covers an event about 1,375 million years ago that formed the Karagwe-Ankolean belt.

prot-069.title: A great magma pulse marks Columbia's breakup
prot-069.text: As Columbia, or Nuna, broke up about 1,380 million years ago, a major large igneous province formed, linking today's Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia, Congo and West Africa. Rocks of 1.37 to 1.35 billion years ago suggest that a superplume, a giant upwelling of hot mantle, helped split Columbia apart.

prot-070.title: The Mackenzie eruptions flood the Canadian Shield
prot-070.text: Starting about 1,270 million years ago, a massive igneous event spread across the Canadian Shield, from Arctic Nunavut to the Great Lakes. Its province covers 2.7 million square kilometers, built from about 3 million cubic kilometers of magma. That magma formed the Muskox layered intrusion, the Coppermine River flood basalts and the huge Mackenzie dike swarm. Linked to the Mackenzie hotspot, its dikes mark the final breakup of Columbia.

prot-071.title: Rodinia: Columbia's scattered pieces regather
prot-071.text: Between 1.26 and 0.90 billion years ago, the fragments of Columbia collided again to form Rodinia, the largest landmass yet, with Laurentia at its core. It joined North American, East European, Amazonian, West African, Antarctic, Australian and Chinese blocks, ringed by a global superocean called Mirovia. Baltica and Amazonia collided with Laurentia in the Grenville, Sveconorwegian and Sunsás orogenies of 1.1 to 0.9 billion years ago. Rodinia's shape and history remain far less understood than those of later supercontinents.

prot-073.title: Stromatolites reach their peak, then begin to fade
prot-073.text: Stromatolites reached their greatest abundance and diversity about 1.25 billion years ago, when colonies and reefs of cyanobacteria ruled the tidal zones. After that they declined steeply, perhaps as predators began grazing on stromatolites and acritarchs. The decline sped up around 1 billion years ago, and grazing by more complex organisms is the most widely supported explanation. By the start of the Cambrian, they had fallen to 20 percent of their peak.

prot-072.title: The Grenville orogeny raises mountains from Labrador to Mexico
prot-072.text: As Rodinia assembled, a long-lived collision raised a mountain belt from Labrador to Mexico and on to Scotland. Laurentia collided with other blocks, notably Amazonia, beginning the construction of what are now the Appalachian Mountains. The main pulses came 1,240 to 1,220, 1,090 to 1,020 and 1,010 to 980 million years ago, named the Elzevirian, Ottawan and Rigolet. Crust of this age turns up worldwide, where the same events go by other names, such as Kibaran in Africa and Sunsás in Brazil.

prot-074.title: Three orogenies shape Australia's Musgrave Province
prot-074.text: Between 1.22 and 1.12 billion years ago, three orogenic events shaped the Musgrave Province of central Australia, a region of 220,000 square kilometers formed by a magma plume. The Musgravian orogeny, about 1,200 million years ago, melted the lower crust and produced great volumes of Kulgera granite.

prot-077.title: Stac Fada: impact debris without a crater
prot-077.text: Rocks of the Stac Fada Member record an impact about 1.2 billion years ago, but the crater, inferred to be about 40 kilometers wide, has never been found.

prot-075.title: The Grand Canyon Supergroup piles up in an ancient sea
prot-075.text: Between 1.2 billion and 740 million years ago, a sea deposited the Grand Canyon Supergroup's nine formations; the oldest holds the canyon's earliest fossils, stromatolites. About 800 million years ago, the Grand Canyon orogeny tilted the layers 15 degrees and broke them into fault blocks.

prot-078.title: Scandinavia's crust thickens in the Sveconorwegian orogeny
prot-078.text: Mountain building reshaped southwestern Sweden and southern Norway from 1,140 to 960 million years ago, thickening and metamorphosing the crust most from 1,050 to 980 million. A collision between Amazonia and Baltica may have caused it, and it is grouped with the Grenville orogens that assembled Rodinia.

prot-080.title: A 2,000-kilometer rift nearly splits North America
prot-080.text: About 1.1 billion years ago, the core of North America began to split apart, opening a rift 2,000 kilometers long through the middle of the continent. Lava poured from cracks along the rift valley, which Lake Superior now fills where its western and eastern arms meet. Then the rift failed, leaving thick layers of igneous rock in the deepest failed rift on Earth. Magmatism of about the same age struck Africa, India and South America.

prot-082.title: A rift lake preserves freshwater microbes
prot-082.text: An oxygenated lake in the Midcontinent Rift preserved freshwater microbes exceptionally well in what is now Michigan. Its shale, siltstone and sandstone, 150 to 210 meters thick, extend from Michigan and Wisconsin to Iowa.

prot-083.title: The Warakurna magma province spreads across central Australia
prot-083.text: In central Australia, the Warakurna large igneous province intruded the Giles Complex and Winburn granites and erupted the volcanic rocks of the Bentley Supergroup. A link to a 1,110-million-year-old magmatic event in Africa, India and Amazonia is possible but unlikely.

prot-084.title: Bangiomorpha, the first known organism to have sex
prot-084.text: A multicellular red alga from Somerset Island, Canada, Bangiomorpha pubescens closely resembles the living red alga Bangia. Its specialized reproductive cells are the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction and meiosis, the cell division that makes sex cells. It is also the earliest organism known for certain to have differentiated cells, and the oldest belonging to a living phylum, one of life's major branches. Sex raised genetic variation, speeding the evolution and diversification of eukaryotes; earlier studies dated the fossil to 1.2 billion years ago.

prot-085.title: Lakhanda: a bacterial community with a food web
prot-085.text: Rocks of the Lakhanda Group in Russia's Uchur-Maya Depression preserve a community dominated by anaerobic bacteria, with evidence of interactions in an early food web.

prot-086.title: Ourasphaira, the earliest known fungus
prot-086.text: Shale of the Grassy Bay Formation in the Canadian Arctic preserves Ourasphaira giraldae, multicellular organic-walled microfossils that make it the earliest known fungus. Older fossils from 1.43 billion years ago have also been read as multicellular fungi with differentiated cells.

prot-087.title: Acritarchs boom as the first predators appear
prot-087.text: Eukaryotes, long inconspicuous, diversified rapidly around 1 billion years ago. Acritarchs boomed in number, variety, size and shape in their first large radiation, growing more and longer spines. The first dinoflagellates, single-celled organisms with whip-like tails, may have been the first predators, since some ate prey, pushing acritarchs into an arms race of defenses. After this, species lasted only about 100 million years, perhaps because early protists, single-celled eukaryotes, grazed more heavily.

prot-088.title: Eukaryotes take over fresh water
prot-088.text: By 1 billion years ago, eukaryotes, including multicellular forms, dominated habitats away from the sea, judging from abundant microfossils in Scotland's freshwater Torridon Group. Nutrients washed off the continents probably favored them near land. Phosphatic microfossils from Scotland's Diabaig Formation, about 994 million years old, rank among the oldest known non-marine eukaryotes. Molecular clocks, which estimate timing from genetic differences, suggest photosynthetic multicellular eukaryotes and fungi had moved onto land by 1,000 million years ago.

prot-089.title: Proterocladus: green algae go multicellular
prot-089.text: Proterocladus antiquus, about 1 billion years old, is the first known preserved case of multicellularity in green algae. Around this time the first multicellular plants emerged, probably green algae, though the line between a colony of cells and a multicellular organism is blurred.

prot-090.title: The Nimrod orogeny may have begun the Gamburtsev range
prot-090.text: Around 1 billion years ago, a mountain-building event called the late Ruker, or Nimrod, orogeny struck Antarctica. It may have begun the Gamburtsev mountain range and the Vostok Subglacial Highlands.

prot-091.title: Proto-India and Antarctica collide in the Rayner orogeny
prot-091.text: In the Rayner orogeny, proto-India collided with Antarctica, and rocks of East Antarctica's Rayner Complex form an extension of India's Eastern Ghats. They belong to a Grenville-age belt along the coast, read as the seam where East Antarctica joined southern Africa, India and western Australia.

prot-093.title: Bitter Springs chert freezes microbes in silica
prot-093.text: Cherts of Australia's Bitter Springs Group preserve stromatolites and cyanobacteria exceptionally well in silica, a style of preservation that ended once silica-secreting organisms appeared late in the era. Some fossils with ghostly internal structures, such as Glenobotrydion, have been read as green algae among the earliest plants, but that claim is debated.

prot-094.title: Sponge-like fossils hint at the first animals
prot-094.text: Sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 million years old may be the oldest animals, but their identity is highly debated. Otavia, about 800 million years old, has been described as a primitive sponge. Molecular studies place the root of the animal family tree in the Tonian, yet physical evidence for such early animals is lacking. If sponges did emerge this early, they survived the ice ages that followed, though some researchers argue the oldest sponge fossils are Cryogenian instead.

prot-095.title: Island arcs start building the Arabian-Nubian Shield
prot-095.text: From 870 million years ago, island arcs built the Arabian-Nubian Shield as the Mozambique Ocean closed; they collided from 780, and assembly ended by 550. Almost all the gold mined in antiquity in Egypt and Sudan comes from its rocks.

prot-096.title: A second great oxidation transforms air and sea
prot-096.text: Often called the second Great Oxidation Event, a rise in oxygen swept the air and oceans about 850 to 540 million years ago, globally or in regional pulses. Between 900 and 815 million years ago, oxygen climbed from under 0.1 percent of present levels to over 13 percent. Air trapped in rock salt 813 million years old holds 10.9 percent oxygen, yet the deep ocean stayed oxygen-free and iron-rich as late as 580 million years ago. The surge drove rapid evolution of multicellular life, and some authors credit it with letting the oxygen-hungry Ediacaran biota spread.

prot-099.title: Worm-shaped creatures mark a step in evolution at Huainan
prot-099.text: Near Huainan City in China's Anhui province, small worm-shaped organisms visible to the naked eye record a transitional stage in evolution. A similar biota about 1 billion years old has been found on Russia's Timan Ridge.

prot-100.title: The Adelaide Rift opens as Laurentia pulls away
