prot-100.text: Sediment began filling the Adelaide Superbasin just before 830 million years ago, as Laurentia began rifting away from Australia. Developing until about 550 million years ago, its basins record Rodinia's breakup, two great Cryogenian glaciations, the Neoproterozoic oxygenation and the Ediacaran fauna.

prot-102.title: Eukaryotes grow more complex and armor up
prot-102.text: Around 800 million years ago, eukaryote fossils grew notably more complex and numerous as sulfide in the oceans declined. By about 750 million years ago some small algae wore mineral armor, probably against single-celled predators, though persistent oxygen-free, sulfidic water kept overall diversity low.

prot-104.title: Cyanobacteria start drifting as ocean plankton
prot-104.text: About 800 million years ago, cyanobacteria descended from seafloor and freshwater ancestors began drifting as plankton in the sea, helping to oxygenate the oceans. Their spread is thought to have sped oxygenation and the removal of carbon dioxide, which may help explain the severe Cryogenian ice ages.

prot-105.title: A new ocean, the Pharusian, opens beside West Africa
prot-105.text: About 800 million years ago, rifting along the eastern edge of the West African craton during Rodinia's breakup opened the Pharusian Ocean. It began to close about 730 million years ago, as the Tilemsi arc was subducted eastward against the Hoggar region.

prot-101.title: The East African Orogeny begins to forge Gondwana
prot-101.text: Gondwana, the great southern supercontinent, began to form as India and Madagascar collided with East Africa in the East African Orogeny. This was the main stage in joining East and West Gondwana along the Mozambique Belt, uniting Africa, India and Arabia. The Mozambique Ocean, which separated Madagascar and India from the Congo–Tanzania craton, began closing between 700 and 580 million years ago. In one model, arc collisions became a full continental collision when a block called Azania struck the Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block around 640 million years ago.

prot-109.title: The Kaigas glaciation that never was
prot-109.text: Kaigas Formation conglomerates, rocks of cemented pebbles, on the Kalahari Craton once suggested a Snowball Earth glaciation about 750 million years ago, before the Sturtian. The formation turned out not to be glacial at all, leaving no evidence for any Neoproterozoic glaciation before the Sturtian.

prot-108.title: Rodinia breaks apart and new oceans open
prot-108.text: Rifting began as early as 850 to 800 million years ago, perhaps driven by a superplume. Most geologists agree the breakup proper began about 750 million years ago, with eruptions on most continents. As Rodinia split into Proto-Laurasia, the Congo craton and Proto-Gondwana, new oceans such as the Adamastor and the proto-Pacific Panthalassa opened while Mirovia closed. The breakup may have triggered the Cryogenian Snowball Earth and the rapid evolution of life that followed.

prot-110.title: Franklin lavas flood the Arctic, and ice follows
prot-110.text: In about two million years, magma flooded more than 1.1 million square kilometers of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland. Uranium–lead dating pins this rapid outpouring, one of the largest in Earth's history, between about 719.9 and 718.6 million years ago. Together with the Irkutsk province, it marks the rifting of Siberia away from Laurentia. As the fresh basalt weathered, it drew down carbon dioxide, and glaciation began just 0.9 to 1.6 million years later.

prot-112.title: Sturtian ice grips the planet for 57 million years
prot-112.text: The first of the Cryogenian's great ice ages lasted from about 717 to 660 million years ago, some 57 million years. It began just 0.9 to 1.6 million years after the Franklin eruptions, perhaps as weathering basalt absorbed carbon dioxide and ocean ridges released less of it. With Rodinia near the equator, glacial ice reached sea level, evidence that the glaciation was global. Scientists still debate whether ice sealed the whole ocean, a Snowball Earth averaging about −50 °C, or left open water, a Slushball; some see several regional glaciations instead.

prot-111.title: Snowball Earth: did ice cover the whole planet?
prot-111.text: The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that Earth's surface froze almost completely, usually during the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations, when glaciers reached sea level near the equator. Whether the planet became a full snowball or a slushball, with a band of open tropical water, is still disputed. Either way, thick ice blocking sunlight would have badly hindered primary production in shallow seas. Rodinia's breakup is thought to have triggered the cooling and the burst of evolution that followed in the Ediacaran and Cambrian.

prot-113.title: Shelled amoebae appear in the icy Cryogenian
prot-113.text: Fossils of testate amoebae, single-celled organisms that live inside shells, first appear around 700 million years ago, during the Cryogenian.

prot-115.title: A warm pause between two ice ages
prot-115.text: Between the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations came a relatively warm interval of rising seas, oxygen-free oceans and very low biodiversity. Oxygen may have reached about 50 percent of present levels, though chromium isotopes suggest oxygenation was slow and subdued.

prot-114.title: The Cadomian orogeny builds Gondwana's northern edge
prot-114.text: As the Sturtian glaciers retreated, island arcs began colliding along the margin of the future Gondwana, laying down the terranes of Avalonia, Armorica and Iberia. An Andes-like volcanic arc rose 650 to 600 million years ago; a basin behind it opened 590 to 560 million years ago and closed 545 to 540.

prot-116.title: Algae take over the ocean's plankton
prot-116.text: About 659 to 645 million years ago, red and green algae replaced cyanobacteria as the main phytoplankton, the sea's drifting photosynthesizers. They kept that role until the Permian extinction. Single-celled algae diversified rapidly, and their numbers rose a hundred- to thousandfold. Late in the Cryogenian, plankton appeared that fed on algae and prokaryotes, ending the dominance of bacteria in the oceans.

prot-117.title: Demosponges and the disputed first animals
prot-117.text: Demosponges, sponges with skeletons of tiny needles called spicules made of spongin protein and silica, appear around 650 million years ago. Some researchers argue that the oldest sponge fossils, and so the oldest animal fossils, are Cryogenian, but these may be proto-sponges or microbial structures instead. Even the oldest sponge spicules, about 580 million years old from China's Doushantuo Formation and Mongolia, are challenged. Clearly recognizable sponges, such as Helicolocellus, which lacked a mineral skeleton, appear only in the latest Ediacaran.

prot-118.title: Seaweeds grow during a pause in the Marinoan ice
prot-118.text: Around 650 million years ago, during a short break in the Marinoan glaciation, large seaweeds of the Songluo Biota grew in South China. It is the only known biota of large fossils from the Cryogenian, the first large carbon-rich fossils in rocks of that age.

prot-119.title: The Marinoan glaciation, the Cryogenian's last great freeze
prot-119.text: Late in the Cryogenian, the Marinoan glaciation, also called the Varanger or Elatina, spread ice across the globe. Its timing is poorly constrained; a 2025 study dates it to 639 to 635 million years ago. Often described as the most significant snowball Earth event, it ended as volcanic carbon dioxide built up and clathrates, ice-like deposits holding methane, dissolved. Later ice ages never again covered so much of the planet.

prot-120.title: Cap carbonates seal the last great glaciation
prot-120.text: The Ediacaran begins at a cap carbonate, the Nuccaleena Formation, which sits directly on Elatina glacial deposits in South Australia's Flinders Ranges. Neoproterozoic glacial beds are commonly topped by a sharp layer of limestone or dolomite, meters to tens of meters thick. A favored explanation holds that after a snowball, acid rain loaded with carbon dioxide weathered rock and washed calcium into the sea, where it formed carbonate layers. Their glacial link is questioned, though: some caps are too thick for a rapid thaw, and many glacial sequences lack them.

prot-121.title: Large ornamented acritarchs replace the old plankton
prot-121.text: As the Ediacaran began, much of the long-stable acritarch plankton died out, and larger, ornamented species, usually over 100 micrometers across, dominated until about 575 million years ago. They largely vanished before 560 million years ago, about when the Ediacara biota arose; if they were animal resting stages, they fit a sea often short of oxygen.

prot-122.title: Antarctic mountains rise in the Beardmore orogeny
prot-122.text: From about 633 to 620 million years ago, the Beardmore orogeny built mountains in Antarctica as Rodinia's last fragments began moving back together toward Pannotia, a proposed supercontinent.

prot-123.title: The Petermann orogeny thrusts up the rocks of Uluru
prot-123.text: Between 630 and 520 million years ago, mountain building inside central Australia formed an unusual east–west belt, suggesting India struck Western Australia from the northwest. It thrust up the rocks that now form Uluru, sediments laid down around 550 to 530 million years ago.

prot-124.title: Tide-laid layers record a 21.9-hour day
prot-124.text: Tidal rhythmites, bands of sand and silt laid down by strong tides off estuaries, record a 21.9-hour day and a year of about 400 days. Tides slow Earth's spin as the Moon recedes; since then it has moved away at an average 2.17 cm a year, about half today's rate.

prot-125.title: The Timanide orogeny, the Precambrian's last big collision
prot-125.text: The Timanide orogeny, called the Precambrian's last major mountain-building event, deformed the northern Baltic Shield from about 620 to 550 million years ago. Around 555 million years ago Baltica's northern margin turned active, adding the Timan-Pechora Basin, the northern Urals and Novaya Zemlya.

prot-126.title: Weng'an embryos preserved in three dimensions
prot-126.text: In China's Doushantuo Formation, the Weng'an biota preserves three-dimensional embryo-like animals in calcium phosphate from 609 to 570 million years ago. Its richest layer postdates the Gaskiers glaciation, and Caveasphaera, a 609-million-year-old multicellular organism, may record one of the earliest steps in animal evolution.

prot-127.title: The Lantian biota: early large, complex fossils
prot-127.text: South China's Lantian Biota, about 602 million years old, holds some of the oldest large, complex fossils, including seaweeds and possible cnidarians, the jellyfish and coral group. Even older large fossils, the Ancanping assemblage of about 620 to 610 million years ago, occur in the Doushantuo Formation.

prot-128.title: The Iapetus Ocean opens between Laurentia and Baltica
prot-128.text: A mantle plume, the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province, forced Laurentia and Baltica apart and opened the Iapetus Ocean between them. Rifting began with Norway's Egersund dike swarm around 650 million years ago; from 600 million years ago the continents rotated up to 180 degrees. The eastern Iapetus opened around 590 million years ago, and its southern arm, between Laurentia and South America, about 550 million years ago. In the Southern Hemisphere, the ocean lasted until about 425 million years ago, bordered by Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and other continents.

prot-129.title: Enough oxygen gathers to form an ozone layer
prot-129.text: By about 600 million years ago, enough oxygen had built up to form an ozone layer, a high band of three-atom oxygen molecules that screens out ultraviolet light. Before then, any life on land probably needed other chemicals to block ultraviolet radiation. Atmospheric oxygen, between 1 and 18 percent of present levels 800 million years ago, began rising more significantly around 600 million years ago.

prot-130.title: The Pan-African orogeny assembles Gondwana
prot-130.text: The Pan-African orogeny, a series of major mountain-building events, built Gondwana and the proposed supercontinent Pannotia. It began around 635 million years ago when the West African and Saharan cratons collided, closing the Pharusian Ocean. By about 600 million years ago most of western Gondwana had joined, while Australia and East Antarctica remained separate. All African cratons were assembled by about 550 million years ago, and Gondwana endured until the later supercontinent Pangaea broke up in the Early Jurassic.

prot-131.title: Pannotia: a supercontinent that may never have been whole
prot-131.text: Pannotia, also called Greater Gondwana, is a proposed supercontinent that may have formed during the Pan-African orogeny around 600 million years ago. If it existed, it lasted only some 50 million years, breaking apart about 560 million years ago as the Iapetus Ocean opened. A 2022 paper argues it never fully existed, because it began to break up before it was fully assembled. Its breakup coincided with rising seas, dramatic shifts in climate and ocean chemistry, and rapid animal diversification.

prot-132.title: The Acraman impact showers South Australia with debris
prot-132.text: About 590 million years ago, a stony asteroid struck what is now the Gawler Ranges of South Australia; the date comes from its debris in nearby basins. Estimates of the eroded crater's original width run from 35–40 kilometers to 85–90 kilometers; the larger implies 5.2 million megatons of TNT. The ejecta layer, holding shocked minerals and a spike of the rare metal iridium, lies in Flinders Ranges rocks at least 300 kilometers to the east. Just above it, a radiation of acritarchs begins, and some authors suspect a link.

prot-134.title: The first widely accepted animals: cnidarians
prot-134.text: The earliest widely accepted animal fossils are modern-looking cnidarians, possibly about 580 million years old, though the Doushantuo fossils are only roughly dated. Their presence implies that the lineages of cnidarians and bilaterians, animals with a left and a right side, split well before 580 million years ago. Even older microfossils, from 632.5 million years ago, just after the Cryogenian ice, may be embryonic resting stages of the earliest known animals.

prot-133.title: The Damara orogeny closes the Adamastor Ocean
prot-133.text: Between 580 and 550 million years ago, the Damara orogeny stitched the Congo–São Francisco and Río de la Plata cratons together, forming northern Gondwana with India. Meanwhile the Adamastor Ocean closed southward, from the Araçuaí Belt to the Kaoko Belt.

prot-135.title: The Gaskiers glaciation: a short, sharp freeze
prot-135.text: Over about 250,000 years, from 579.88 to 579.63 million years ago, glacial deposits formed on eight ancient continents, some lying just 10 to 30 degrees from the equator. It was the shortest of at least three Neoproterozoic ice ages and probably not a Snowball Earth. As the last major glacial event of the Proterozoic, it lies just below some of the oldest Ediacaran fossils, though a 9-million-year gap separates them.

prot-136.title: The Avalon explosion: the Ediacaran biota bursts forth
prot-136.text: About 575 million years ago, a proposed burst of evolution, named for fossils on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, is thought to have produced the Ediacaran biota. These large, mostly soft-bodied tube- and frond-shaped organisms are the earliest known complex multicellular life, and most vanished in the end-Ediacaran extinction about 539 million years ago. Their place in the tree of life is unclear, and it is not even certain that most were animals. The 2008 study of body shapes that defined the explosion has also been disputed, though the biota itself is not.

prot-137.title: The Shuram excursion: the deepest carbon plunge on record
prot-137.text: The Shuram excursion is an Ediacaran shift in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12, first noticed in South Australia's Wonoka Formation. It is the largest negative carbon-13 excursion in Earth history, with a recovery lasting 50 million years, though chemical changes after burial may exaggerate it. Its timing is debated: it began around 573 million years ago and ended around 562 or 551 million, and its cause is unknown. The oxygen-using Ediacaran biota radiated during it, and it may have helped spark the rise of animals that led to the Cambrian explosion.

prot-138.title: Charnia, the first recognized Precambrian fossil
prot-138.text: Charnia, a frond with leaf-like ridges branching alternately from a zigzag midline, lived on deep seafloors 570 to 550 million years ago. The first fossil ever recognized as Precambrian, from England's Charnwood Forest, it is still among the hardest Ediacaran forms to place in the tree of life.

prot-139.title: Animals begin to crawl and burrow
prot-139.text: From about 575 to 560 million years ago, mobile organisms left the earliest trails, moving on and just beneath the microbial mats. These traces are simple, near-horizontal feeding trails, and the first widely accepted burrows come from the lower Blueflower Formation, about 567.3 million years old. Bilaterians were present by 555 million years ago. By 551 million years ago, an animal with leg-like appendages was leaving tracks in mud.

prot-140.title: Mistaken Point: a deep-sea community buried in ash
prot-140.text: Volcanic ash beds at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, date its fossils to about 565 million years ago and preserve them in fine detail. One of the most diverse and best-preserved Precambrian collections, the site defines the deep-water Avalon assemblage, the oldest locality rich in Ediacaran fossils.

prot-141.title: Earth's magnetic field grows strangely weak
prot-141.text: Rocks about 565 million years old record an unusually weak, frequently reversing magnetic field, hinting that the solid inner core was only beginning to form. The inner core's age is unresolved, though, with estimates from 0.5 to 2 billion years, so an Ediacaran start remains only one hypothesis.

prot-142.title: The earliest possible arthropods
prot-142.text: The earliest arthropods, the group of insects and crabs, are placed around 560 million years ago, and some read Ediacaran Spriggina, Parvancorina and Yilingia as arthropods. That reading is debated, though embryos 543 million years old suggest parts of arthropod development arose before the Proterozoic ended.

prot-143.title: The White Sea biota reaches peak Ediacaran diversity
prot-143.text: Named for Russia's White Sea coast, the White Sea biota flourished 560 to 550 million years ago; one bed holds the highest Ediacaran diversity yet found. South Australia's Ediacara Hills, the period's namesake, preserve abundant fossils about 555 million years old, like a community of the same age in Sonora, Mexico.

prot-144.title: Dickinsonia, a slow-moving quilted disc
prot-144.text: Dickinsonia, a large, slow-moving, quilted disc, first appears about 558 million years ago, its fossils often lying at the end of trails that match its shape. Cholesterol found in its fossils in 2018 was taken as evidence that it was an animal, though the molecule may instead point to fungi or red algae.

prot-145.title: Kimberella scrapes a living from the seafloor
prot-145.text: Kimberella, about 555 million years old, was almost certainly a bilaterian; if mollusk-like, as some argue, major animal lineages split well before 550 million years ago. Scratch marks, perhaps from a rasping tongue called a radula, and its grazing trail show that it crawled across the seafloor and fed there.

prot-146.title: Dengying fossils capture the Ediacaran's last moments
prot-146.text: Several sites in China's Dengying Formation, dated 551 to 543 million years ago, preserve life just before the Phanerozoic. The Jiangchuan biota holds giant thallophytes, simple plant-like organisms, while at Gaojiashan fossils replaced by pyrite record how Cloudina built its tubes.

prot-147.title: Cloudina and its kin grow early mineral skeletons
prot-147.text: Between 549 and 542 million years ago, Cloudina, Namacalathus and about a dozen other organisms built mineralized tubes, preserved in carbonate rocks, among the earliest small shelly fossils. Rising oxygen lowered ocean acidity and raised seawater calcium near the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary, possibly prompting the move to skeletons. Cloudina tubes often bear holes bored by predators, so predation existed in the Ediacaran at least. The cloudinids, an early animal family, died out at the base of the Cambrian.

prot-150.title: Proto-Tethys takes shape between Gondwana and the north
prot-150.text: The Proto-Tethys Ocean lay between Baltica and Laurentia to the north and Gondwana to the south from about 550 million years ago until the Carboniferous. After the Cadomian mountain building, it formed the eastern part of an ocean system sinking beneath Gondwana's northern margin.

prot-151.title: A supermountain sheds a vast fan of sediment
prot-151.text: The East African Orogeny raised the Transgondwanan Supermountain, a range more than 8,000 kilometers long and 1,000 kilometers wide. Its erosion built the Gondwana Super-fan, over 100 million cubic kilometers of sediment laid down over 260 million years. That flood of sediment coincided with the Cambrian explosion and probably helped early animals diversify. By the Ordovician, the range had been worn down to a plain in what is now Ethiopia.

prot-149.title: The Nama assemblage, the Ediacaran's final act
prot-149.text: The Nama assemblage, the last Ediacaran community, about 550 to 539 million years ago, was impoverished, never regaining the diversity lost as the White Sea biota gave way. By the period's end, no more than a dozen of 92 possible ways of life were occupied.

prot-148.title: India joins Africa in the Malagasy orogeny
prot-148.text: India collided with the already joined Azania and Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block about 550 to 515 million years ago. The collision affected Madagascar, eastern East Africa and southern India.

prot-153.title: The Baykonurian glaciation, a late Ediacaran chill
prot-153.text: Late in the Ediacaran, from about 547 to 540 million years ago, the Baykonurian glaciation left deposits in Asia and Africa and apparently affected both hemispheres. It has been proposed as one contributor to the Cambrian explosion.

prot-154.title: Trail-makers grow longer and keener-sensed
prot-154.text: Ediacaran trail-makers grew steadily longer, and by the period's end their bodies were over eight times longer than wide. Their trails looped more tightly and accurately, and around 540 million years ago their sensing range grew from millimeters or centimeters to decimeters.

prot-155.title: Flood basalts fill the Southern Oklahoma rift
prot-155.text: As Laurentia rifted 550 to 525 million years ago, the Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen became a failed rift arm; two sister arms opened the young Iapetus Ocean. Its flood basalts began or peaked around 540 million years ago, covering about 40,000 square kilometers with roughly 250,000 cubic kilometers of magma.

prot-156.title: The end-Ediacaran extinction closes the Proterozoic
prot-156.text: Near the end of the Ediacaran, a mass extinction called the Kotlin Crisis wiped out the soft-bodied Ediacaran biota and shelled Cloudina and Namacalathus. Both groups vanish abruptly 538.8 million years ago, so their loss cannot simply reflect fossils ceasing to be preserved. A major negative swing in carbon isotopes marks the boundary; in Oman it coincides with the last Namacalathus and Cloudina. Acritarch diversity also fell sharply, and very few organisms crossed into the Cambrian, where new animals radiated into the vacant niches.

camb-001.title: Newfoundland burrows mark the start of the Cambrian
camb-001.text: A rock section at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, marks the formal start of the Cambrian, the Paleozoic Era and the Phanerozoic Eon. Geologists trace the boundary worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum, a trace fossil, or burrow, linked to early priapulid worms. Radiometric dating puts the boundary at 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago, an age revised in 2022 from 541 million years ago. Several chemical markers show that the environment changed drastically at about the same time.

camb-002.title: The Cambrian explosion: most animal body plans appear
camb-002.text: Within about 20–25 million years, complex life produced the first members of most modern animal phyla, the major branches of the animal family tree. Animals grew mineralized skeletons, more complex bodies and new behaviors, and their burrowing churned the seafloor and opened new ecosystems. Molybdenum isotopes tie the rising diversity to the spread of oxygenated bottom waters, pointing to oxygen as a driver. No later burst among marine animals matches its pace, though scientists still debate how explosive it truly was.

camb-007.title: Orthid brachiopods begin a long career
camb-007.text: On Early Cambrian seafloors, orthid brachiopods, shelled animals that look a little like clams, made their debut and began to branch out late in the epoch. By the late Cambrian they came in many forms 2–5 cm wide, and they went on to become very diverse in Ordovician shelf seas.

camb-010.title: Tiny shells chart an orderly rise of animal groups
camb-010.text: Small shelly fossils, mineralized tubes, plates and needle-like spicules often only millimeters long, run almost unbroken from the latest Ediacaran to the end of the Early Cambrian. Graham Budd's scheme moves from a Tube world, 550 to 536 million years ago, to a Sclerite world of halkieriids, tommotiids and hyoliths. The record shows phyla appearing in a rapid but orderly sequence, and marks of selective attacks suggest predators helped drive new species. Most were thought to have died out in the end-Botomian extinction, though their disappearance may partly reflect the loss of phosphate preservation.

camb-004.title: The sea floods over the Great Unconformity
camb-004.text: A marine transgression, a slow advance of the sea over land, began with the Cambrian and became the second-greatest sustained sea-level rise of the Phanerozoic. As the climate warmed, shallow seas spread across flat, eroded surfaces such as the sub-Cambrian peneplain and the Great Unconformity, burying them in marine sediment. Seas covered Baltica and much of Antarctica, and marine invertebrates flourished in the shallow water. In North America, this Sauk transgression got going in earnest only in the middle Cambrian.

camb-013.title: An asteroid blasts the Neugrund crater in Estonia
camb-013.text: An asteroid about 1 km across hit what is now the Gulf of Finland, in Estonia, leaving a crater measured at 8 or about 20 km wide. It was once dated to around 470 million years ago, in the Ordovician, before newer research gave it a Cambrian age.

camb-014.title: The Pampean orogeny raises Gondwana's western edge
camb-014.text: The Pampean orogeny, an episode of mountain building, raised ranges on Gondwana's western margin between about 535 and 520 million years ago. It partly involved an exotic terrane, a block of crust from elsewhere, docking on the proto-Pacific margin long before the Andes formed.

camb-016.title: Cuyania splits from ancient North America
camb-016.text: Around 530 million years ago, Cuyania, a block now part of Argentina, split away from Laurentia and opened a new ocean that widened into the Early Ordovician. Magnetic signals locked in its rocks support this Laurentian origin, and the block later joined Gondwana.

camb-017.title: Animals may leave the first footprints on land
camb-017.text: Footprints from about 530 million years ago are the oldest known on land, though no one has confirmed that jointed-legged arthropods walked ashore so early. Early Cambrian trace fossils suggest that mollusc-like animals could already spend at least 15 minutes out of the water. Tracks from about 490 million years ago, at the Cambrian's close, probably record large amphibious arthropods, perhaps euthycarcinoids, crossing coastal dunes.

camb-018.title: Final collisions weld southern Gondwana together
camb-018.text: The Kalahari and Mawson cratons, old and stable cores of continents, collided around 530 million years ago in the Kuunga–Damara orogeny, completing southern Gondwana. Collisions in East Antarctica's Lützow-Holm and Prydz belts climaxed at the same time, and deformation in the Damara belt peaked between 530 and 500 million years ago. In West Gondwana, Amazonia closed the narrow ocean beside it and, by the mid-Cambrian, collided with the São Francisco–Congo and Río de la Plata blocks. These last stages of assembly overlapped with the Cambrian explosion.

camb-020.title: A carbon swing and two molluscs mark Stage 2
camb-020.text: Around 529 million years ago, a positive carbon isotope excursion called the ZHUCE lines up with the first appearances of the molluscs Watsonella crosbyi and Aldanella attleborensis. Together these markers reliably flag the boundary between the Fortunian and Cambrian Stage 2.

camb-019.title: Oxygen pulses open up more of the seafloor
camb-019.text: In Cambrian Stages 2 and 3, productive but anoxic, or oxygen-free, seafloor waters buried vast amounts of organic carbon and pyrite, or fool's gold. Oxygen-rich water then spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas, extending the habitable seafloor. These pulses match the burst of small shelly fossils and CARE, an isotope signal tied to the radiation of arthropods, the jointed-legged animals. Each pulse cut burial rates, anoxia returned, and the cycle repeated several times in the early Cambrian.

camb-022.title: Baltica and Arctida collide to raise the Timanides
camb-022.text: Between 528 and 510 million years ago, Baltica, the ancient core of northern Europe, collided with Arctida and raised the Timanide mountain belt. Erosion began wearing it down in the Cambrian and grew stronger in the Ordovician.

camb-021.title: India's Ramgarh crater: an impact of uncertain age
camb-021.text: Uranium–lead dating places the impact that made India's Ramgarh crater somewhere between 528 and 395 million years ago, a very wide window. Other studies propose a younger age.

camb-023.title: Archaeocyath sponges build the first animal reefs
camb-023.text: East Siberia yields the first archaeocyaths, cup-shaped sponges anchored to the seafloor, at the start of the Tommotian, 525 million years ago. With porous limy skeletons, they joined cyanobacteria, sun-powered microbes, to build reefs in warm tropical seas. These early Cambrian reefs are the oldest known large-scale structures made by animals. The sponges diversified rapidly in Stage 3, then declined sharply in Stage 4.

camb-025.title: Greenland's Sirius Passet preserves an early fauna
camb-025.text: At Sirius Passet in Greenland, rocks of the Buen Formation preserve an animal community much like that of China's Maotianshan Shales. A microbial mat most likely sealed the carcasses like a death mask. Alongside the Burgess Shale and the Maotianshan Shales, it ranks among the Cambrian's major Lagerstätten.

camb-028.title: Trilobites appear with calcite shells and crystal eyes
camb-028.text: Around 521 million years ago, trilobites evolved hard outer skeletons of calcite, and their body fossils appear for the first time. Even the earliest had complex compound eyes with lenses made of calcite. They quickly split into the classic Cambrian orders, Redlichiida, Ptychopariida, Agnostida and Corynexochida, and became the most diverse animals of the early Cambrian. Tracks called Rusophycus and Cruziana, claimed as trilobite trails, turn up much earlier, from about 537 million years ago.

camb-026.title: Eocrinoids, the first stalked echinoderms, appear
camb-026.text: Cambrian Stage 3 brought the eocrinoids, an extinct class of echinoderms, the spiny-skinned group that includes starfish and sea urchins. The earliest known stalked echinoderms with brachioles, small feeding arms, they became the commonest echinoderms of the Cambrian and lasted into the Silurian.

camb-027.title: Radiodonts grow into the giants of Cambrian seas
camb-027.text: Giants entered the oceans in Cambrian Series 2 with the radiodonts, early offshoots of the arthropod family tree that thrived worldwide for the rest of the period. Most dwarfed their neighbors, with large species typically 30–50 cm long. The biggest, Anomalocaris, reached up to 2 m, the largest animal in Cambrian seas.

camb-030.title: A small impact scars Ritland in Norway
camb-030.text: About 520 ± 20 million years ago, an impact at Ritland, in Norway, left a confirmed crater about 2 km across.

camb-031.title: The Ross orogeny lifts the Transantarctic Mountains
camb-031.text: After early Cambrian rifting, when the crust stretched and split, Antarctica deformed and the Transantarctic Mountains rose in the mid-Cambrian. Between about 520 and 450 million years ago, Cambrian sediments there were uplifted, folded, altered by heat and pressure, and invaded by great masses of granite.

camb-033.title: Chengjiang captures the explosion in soft-bodied detail
camb-033.text: The Maotianshan Shales of Chengjiang, in Yunnan, preserve an extremely diverse early Cambrian fauna, soft tissues and all, laid down no earlier than 518 million years ago. They hold the Phanerozoic's oldest diverse animal community and the best record of the Cambrian explosion. Chengjiang has every animal group found in the Burgess Shale yet is about ten million years older, implying that animals diversified earlier or faster. Its chordates, the group that includes vertebrates, feature early fish such as Haikouichthys, and about one in eight of its animals defy classification.

camb-034.title: Backbones arrive with the first vertebrates
camb-034.text: Backbones enter the fossil record with the earliest known vertebrates, in China's Chengjiang biota of about 518 million years ago. Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia already had fins, gills and vertebrate muscles, and Haikouichthys had distinct vertebrae. Fish are thought to have begun evolving around 530 million years ago, and Cambrian chordates lived as mid-sized suspension feeders, sieving food from the water. Despite their later abundance, early vertebrates remain rare in the Cambrian record.

camb-037.title: Crustaceans appear, hinting at a hidden radiation
camb-037.text: Crustaceans had appeared by 517 million years ago, when relatives of living lineages turn up in the Chengjiang biota. One of them, Sunella, may be an early relative of ostracods, or seed shrimp, suggesting that modern pancrustaceans, which unite crustaceans and insects, already existed. Their Cambrian fossils are sparse, despite signs of an early and largely hidden diversification. Even so, most major groups, from branchiopods and maxillopods to malacostracans, appear before the period ends.

camb-039.title: Ediacaran-style fronds make a disputed last stand
camb-039.text: Petalonamids, frond-like animals typical of the Ediacaran, are dated from about 635 to 516 million years ago, and the group may include Cambrian forms such as Stromatoveris. Whether any truly outlived the Ediacaran is disputed: rare possible survivors appear as late as 510–500 million years ago, but no Cambrian report is widely accepted.

camb-042.title: Emu Bay Shale keeps the oldest phosphatized muscle
camb-042.text: South Australia's Emu Bay Shale, about 514–512 million years old, preserves soft tissue turned to apatite, a phosphate mineral, or to calcium carbonate. It holds the oldest phosphatized muscle tissue known and is younger than the Chengjiang and Sirius Passet Lagerstätten.

camb-041.title: The Delamerian orogeny buckles Australia's eastern margin
camb-041.text: From about 514 to 490 million years ago, the Delamerian orogeny ended deposition in the Adelaide Superbasin and folded and deformed its rocks. Australia's eastern margin became a subduction zone, where the Paleo-Pacific seafloor sank beneath the continent.

camb-046.title: The Sinsk Event: the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction
camb-046.text: About 513.5 million years ago, the Sinsk Event began the end-Botomian crisis, the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction, which removed over 60% of animal species. A major transgression spread anoxic deep water and black shales over the continental shelves, while the nearly simultaneous Kalkarindji eruptions probably drove warming and oxygen loss. The crisis devastated reefs, above all the archaeocyath sponges that dominated them, along with halkieriids and much of the small shelly fauna. Mobile animals such as trilobites recovered fast, but diversity stayed low into the early Ordovician.

camb-048.title: Kalkarindji lavas flood ancient Australia
camb-048.text: Around 511 million years ago, flood basalts of the Kalkarindji large igneous province, a vast outpouring of lava, began erupting in what is now Australia. They covered over 2,100,000 km², making Kalkarindji the earliest large igneous province of the Phanerozoic and one of the largest. The eruptions released carbon dioxide, methane and sulfur dioxide, warming the seas and leaving three large, rapid carbon isotope excursions. Their timing suggests they helped cause the early to middle Cambrian mass extinction.

camb-050.title: Tracks of animals leaving the sea at Blackberry Hill
camb-050.text: At Blackberry Hill in Wisconsin, large molluscs and euthycarcinoid arthropods left some of the oldest evidence of animals walking out of the sea. Protichnites trackways come from here and from Quebec's Potsdam Sandstone, and Climactichnites, the largest Cambrian trace fossil, formed on sandy tidal flats.

camb-053.title: The Glikson impact scars Western Australia
camb-053.text: The Glikson crater in Western Australia, about 19 km across, formed no earlier than about 508 million years ago. Nearby dolerite, a dark rock formed from magma, dated to 508 ± 5 million years suggests the impact is younger, probably still within the Paleozoic.

camb-052.title: The Burgess Shale records Cambrian life in carbon
camb-052.text: In British Columbia, the Burgess Shale preserves soft-bodied animals from about 508–505 million years ago as thin, dark films of carbon. One of the best-known Cambrian Lagerstätten, it holds a key record of the Cambrian explosion. Its cast includes strange arthropods like Opabinia, the giant radiodont Anomalocaris, the first great apex predator, and bell-shaped medusa jellyfish such as Burgessomedusa. Metaspriggina, an early vertebrate with prominent eyes and gills, also turns up there.

camb-062.title: The first great trilobite extinction strikes
camb-062.text: At the boundary between Series 2 and the Miaolingian, the first major trilobite extinction wiped out the olenellids, the eodiscids and most redlichiids. A carbon isotope event called ROECE marks the boundary and coincides with the main phase of the Kalkarindji eruptions. Spain's Murero Lagerstätte records this crisis, known as the Valdemiedes event, in fine detail. Surviving trilobites evolved larger tails and thicker cuticles, or outer coverings, that better resisted predators.

camb-058.title: Conodonts begin a 300-million-year run
camb-058.text: From the Middle Cambrian on, the seas held conodonts, eel-like jawless animals known mostly from their tooth elements. They lasted more than 300 million years, until the start of the Jurassic. One of them, Iapetognathus fluctivagus, would later mark the base of the Ordovician.

camb-060.title: The Paleo-Tethys Ocean begins to open
camb-060.text: Along Gondwana's northern margin, the Paleo-Tethys Ocean began to open in the Middle Cambrian. It grew through the Paleozoic and did not close until the Late Triassic.

camb-061.title: Paradoxides, the biggest Cambrian trilobites, spread worldwide
camb-061.text: Paradoxides, a genus of large to very large trilobites, lived in seas throughout the world in the Middle Cambrian. No Cambrian trilobites grew bigger.

camb-064.title: Rising anoxic water stalls the reefs' recovery
camb-064.text: About 504.5 million years ago, anoxic deep water rose into shallower seas, leaving a carbon isotope signal, DICE, that marks the start of the Drumian. It hampered the recovery of reef ecosystems already battered by the early and middle Cambrian mass extinctions.

camb-068.title: The Dresbachian extinction adds another Cambrian crisis
camb-068.text: The Dresbachian extinction, about 502 million years ago, was one of several Cambrian crises; one account ranks it the second severe one, after the end-Botomian. Carbonate rocks such as those of the North China Craton record these crises, including the biomeres, rock units bounded by extinctions.

camb-070.title: A meteorite splashes into a shallow sea at Gardnos
camb-070.text: About 500 ± 10 million years ago, a meteorite 200–300 m across hit a shallow sea at Buskerud, Norway, blasting the 5 km Gardnos crater. When the crater rim was breached, rock avalanches and debris flows poured in.

camb-071.title: An impact leaves the Mizarai crater in Lithuania
camb-071.text: Lithuania's 5 km Mizarai crater formed in an impact about 500 ± 20 million years ago.

camb-072.title: The Newporte impact structure forms in North Dakota
camb-072.text: The 3.2 km Newporte impact structure in North Dakota formed no earlier than about 500 million years ago, and possibly somewhat later.

camb-073.title: Sweden's Orsten preserves microscopic seafloor animals
camb-073.text: Sweden's Kinnekulle Orsten and Alum Shale hold the oldest well-documented seafloor meiofauna, animals so small they live among grains of sediment. They include microscopic arthropods such as free-living pentastomids.

camb-074.title: An impact carves the Presqu'île crater in Quebec
camb-074.text: The 24 km Presqu'île crater in Quebec is estimated to be less than 500 million years old, so the impact came no earlier than that.

camb-077.title: Plankton launch the Great Ordovician Biodiversification
camb-077.text: One Paleozoic-wide study dates the start of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, or GOBE, to 497.05 million years ago, in the late Cambrian. Its first phase centered on plankton, drifting life, as invertebrate lineages invaded open water and started new food chains.

camb-079.title: The End-Marjuman extinction culls shallow-water trilobites
camb-079.text: Beginning in the mid-Guzhangian, an extinction cut species diversity by 45% over about 3 million years, ending early in the Furongian. The likely culprit was gradual ocean deoxygenation linked to the SPICE event, as spreading anoxia killed off the marjumiid and damesellid trilobites. Deep-water olenimorph trilobites replaced the shallow-water polymerids. In South China the losses came in two phases, a slight decline and then a sharper one, and the extinction's second wave matches the onset of SPICE.

camb-084.title: The SPICE event buries carbon, then oxygen rises
camb-084.text: The Steptoean positive carbon isotope excursion, or SPICE, was a global event between about 497 and 494 million years ago. Erosion of Gondwana's mountains pushed seawater strontium ratios to a peak, while spreading seafloor anoxia boosted the burial of organic matter and pyrite. Sea-level change, cooling surface waters and extinctions of trilobites and brachiopods all accompany it, and its end matches the End-Steptoean biomere extinction. The oxygen rise that followed opened niches for photosynthetic plankton and helped drive their radiation.

camb-080.title: The first cephalopods build chambered shells
camb-080.text: Plectronoceras, from the Late Cambrian, is the earliest undisputed cephalopod, the group that includes today's squid and octopus. Its shell already had septa, inner walls dividing it into chambers, and a siphuncle, a tube running through them. Nautiloids arose in the same epoch and were already diverse in the warm, shallow sea of northeastern China's Fengshan Formation. Most early nautiloids carried the siphuncle along the underside, as later ammonites would.

camb-085.title: Ollo de Sapo magma wells up in future Iberia
camb-085.text: From the Furongian to the end of the Early Ordovician, about 495–470 million years ago, a mantle plume fed magma into northwestern Gondwana. The plume, a rising column of hot rock from deep inside Earth, struck crust that now forms the Iberian Peninsula.

camb-087.title: The Jiangshanian extinction cuts diversity again
camb-087.text: Diversity had rebounded from the End-Marjuman extinction at the very start of the Jiangshanian, but a new crisis then cut species diversity by 55.2%. Smaller swings in species richness followed and lasted until shortly after the Ordovician began.

camb-091.title: The Famatinian arc rises along western South America
camb-091.text: The Famatinian orogeny ran from the Late Cambrian to at least the Late Devonian, with mountain building peaking about 490–460 million years ago. Its climax came when Cuyania, the block that had split from Laurentia, collided with Pampia in the Ordovician. A chain of volcanoes, the Famatinian magmatic arc, rose in what is now western South America. From 480 to 435 million years ago, rocks of the Cordillera Oriental buckled as the arc developed.

camb-090.title: Closing Iapetus starts the Caledonian mountain building
camb-090.text: The Caledonian orogeny, roughly 490 to 390 million years ago, gathers the mountain-building events that unfolded as Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collided. Its mountains now survive in northern Britain and Ireland, Scandinavia, Svalbard, East Greenland and north-central Europe. The Iapetus Ocean between them, widest in the Late Cambrian and Early Ordovician, had begun closing by subduction between 500 and 488 million years ago. Some studies date the orogeny's onset to about 500 million years ago, in the Late Cambrian.

camb-092.title: The first brittle stars appear
camb-092.text: Just before the Cambrian ends, about 488 million years ago, the earliest brittle stars, or ophiuroids, slender-armed echinoderms, enter the fossil record.

camb-093.title: A disputed extinction closes the Cambrian
camb-093.text: An extinction at the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary eliminated many brachiopods and conodonts and severely cut the number of trilobite species. Almost all Redlichiida and most Late Cambrian trilobite stocks died out, and agnostid diversity fell sharply. Some suggest volcanism, especially from large igneous provinces, as the cause, while others argue the extinction is an artifact of a gap in the rock record. Either way, a new radiation followed and established the animals that dominated the rest of the Paleozoic.

ordo-009.title: Marine life multiplies in the Great Ordovician Biodiversification
ordo-009.text: Through the Ordovician, marine animals radiated so widely that global diversity rose severalfold, as each phylum filled out with new classes and lower groups. A fauna rich in suspension feeders and swimmers replaced the Cambrian one and fixed the ecological template for the rest of the Paleozoic. The rise was neither global nor instantaneous: different groups diversified at different times, from the Late Cambrian to the Middle Ordovician. Proposed drivers include rising ocean oxygen, nutrients eroded from the Taconic mountains, global cooling and a meteorite shower.

ordo-010.title: The Iapetus Ocean narrows as continents converge
ordo-010.text: At the start of the Ordovician, the Iapetus Ocean between Gondwana, Laurentia and Baltica was over 4,000 km wide. Baltica drifted toward Laurentia, while island arcs, curved chains of volcanic islands, and microcontinents such as Ganderia were added to Laurentia and Avalonia. As the gap shrank, seafloor brachiopods and trilobites spread between continents, though ostracods and fishes stayed isolated. Some sources say Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia had merged into Euramerica by the period's end; others place the final Laurentia–Baltica collision in the Silurian.

ordo-012.title: Nautiloids reach their peak variety
ordo-012.text: Nautiloids reached their peak variety in the Ordovician, with straight, curved and coiled shells living side by side. They spread from shallow waters into open-ocean niches at all latitudes, joined by new orders such as Bisonocerida and Ascocerida.

ordo-013.title: A conodont at Green Point opens the Ordovician
ordo-013.text: The Ordovician begins with the first appearance of the conodont Iapetognathus fluctivagus, in the cliffs at Green Point in western Newfoundland. That rock section is the period's global reference point, or GSSP, dated at 486.85 million years ago. The period lasts about 43.75 million years, until the Silurian begins at 443.1 million years ago. Its name honors the Ordovices, a Celtic tribe of north Wales, where its rocks were first identified.

ordo-001.title: Rising seas drown North America's Transcontinental Arch
ordo-001.text: Sea level rose more or less continuously through the Early Ordovician before leveling off around mid-period. Shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana, and on flooded Laurentia, warm shallow waters became a haven for shelled sea life. Even North America's Transcontinental Arch, a long spine of higher ground, went under water, not to reappear until the Devonian.

ordo-004.title: Phacopid trilobites join a new Ordovician fauna
ordo-004.text: Nine trilobite orders had arisen in the Cambrian; a tenth, Phacopida, probably first appears in the early Ordovician. Trilobites with schizochroal eyes, built from separate large lenses, appear suddenly at this time, part of a new fauna that replaced the old Cambrian one.

ordo-005.title: The first true starfish join Ordovician seas
ordo-005.text: Echinoderm diversity climbed in the Early Ordovician as new classes appeared, including the first true starfish and the diploporitans. Starfish lived alongside brittle stars, but their fossil record is sparse because their bodies fall apart after death.

ordo-006.title: Stromatoporoid sponges take up reef building
ordo-006.text: Reefs gained new builders in the stromatoporoids, extinct sponges that first appear unambiguously in the Tremadocian and grew reefs in South China as the Ordovician began. Their first order, Labechiida, spread worldwide in the Middle Ordovician and diversified abruptly in the mid-to-late Darriwilian.

ordo-007.title: The oceans switch to calcite seas
ordo-007.text: The mixed aragonite–calcite seas of the Cambrian gave way to fully calcite seas by the early Ordovician. Aragonite and calcite are two crystal forms of calcium carbonate, the mineral of shells and limestone.

ordo-014.title: The plankton revolution fills the open sea
ordo-014.text: The GOBE's first phase, built on plankton, lasted until late in the Early Ordovician. As more plankton filled the open sea, suspension feeders on the seafloor and swimmers above them multiplied. Chitinozoans, tiny flask-shaped fossils, diversified explosively in the Tremadocian, the first age of the Ordovician, and later became key markers for dating rocks. Acritarchs, mostly tiny marine algae, went on to reach their greatest variety of species and shapes in the Middle Ordovician.

ordo-016.title: Corals revive reefs after a long Cambrian lull
ordo-016.text: Ever since the archaeocyath sponges died out, reefs had been rare. Then new reef-building corals diversified, and Early Ordovician reefs included the earliest known octocorals, corals whose polyps have eight tentacles. By the middle of the Tremadocian, reefs built by microbes and sponges occupied deeper water, as in South Korea's Dumugol Formation.

ordo-017.title: The Sauk Sea drains from North America
ordo-017.text: A marine regression, a retreat of the sea, ended North America's Sauk sequence, the layers laid down by the Sauk Sea, early in the Ordovician. At its peak that shallow sea had covered most of the continent, and the next sequence, the Tippecanoe, followed later in the period.

ordo-018.title: Strophomenid brachiopods flourish on Ordovician shelves
ordo-018.text: Brachiopods hit a high point as strophomenids, an order that lasted from the Early Ordovician to the mid Carboniferous, became among the period's most diverse and abundant. Orthids, which had appeared in the Cambrian, peaked alongside them, but the Late Ordovician mass extinction later hit the strophomenids hard.

ordo-019.title: Tumblagooda trackways: the first land animals, perhaps
ordo-019.text: Some researchers read trackways in Western Australia's Tumblagooda Sandstone as the earliest evidence of fully land-dwelling animals, though both that reading and the age are uncertain. Conodonts in overlying beds suggest an early Ordovician age, not the once-favored Silurian, but the dating is too loose to show whether plants reached land first.

ordo-021.title: Morocco's Fezouata Shale bridges two great radiations
ordo-021.text: Morocco's Fezouata Shale preserves exceptional soft-bodied fossils from the Early Ordovician. Its more than 1,500 specimens of 50 taxa, or kinds of organism, resemble Burgess Shale-type biotas, linking the Cambrian explosion to the GOBE. Among them is Aegirocassis, a filter-feeding arthropod over 2 m long that outsized even Anomalocaris and was the largest animal of its time.

ordo-022.title: Jawless fish build the first true bone
ordo-022.text: Around 485 million years ago, jawless fishes became the first vertebrates with true bone. Armored jawless fish, called ostracoderms, rose to prominence and remained the main vertebrates until the Devonian. Early fishes lived mainly near shore, in intertidal zones between the tides and in shallow lagoons. Some accounts place the first small armored ostracoderms, such as a plated Laurentian group, as early as the late Cambrian.

ordo-020.title: A super-greenhouse bakes the Early Ordovician
ordo-020.text: The Early Ordovician was extremely hot, with very high carbon dioxide and sea surface temperatures comparable to those of the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. One set of estimates falls from 43.9 °C to 37.1 °C between 485 and 470 million years ago. Even the cooler figure roughly matches the heat of the human body. This long-lasting warmth shaped the biodiversification that followed in the Middle Ordovician.

ordo-024.title: Avalonia breaks away and opens the Rheic Ocean
ordo-024.text: Around 480 million years ago, the microcontinent Avalonia, including parts of future Newfoundland, southern Britain and New England, broke free from Gondwana. The rift between them grew into a mid-ocean ridge, a seam where new seafloor forms, opening the Rheic Ocean. As Avalonia drifted north, it narrowed the Iapetus Ocean ahead of it and widened the Rheic behind it. Carolina, Armorica and other terranes also broke away during the Ordovician, and Ganderia had probably left near the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary.

ordo-025.title: The Damara orogeny's thrusting comes to an end
ordo-025.text: In the Damara orogeny, thrusting, the shoving of rock slabs over one another, continued onto the Kalahari Craton until 480 million years ago. The wider Damara–Kuunga orogeny, under way since the Cambrian, marked the final joining of northern and southern Gondwana.

ordo-026.title: Sea lilies appear and begin their first radiation
ordo-026.text: The earliest unequivocal crinoids, or sea lilies, date to about 480 million years ago, in the middle Tremadocian. During the Ordovician they went through the first of their two great adaptive radiations, bursts of evolution into new ways of life.

ordo-027.title: Sea scorpions make their first appearance
ordo-027.text: Eurypterids, the sea scorpions, enter the record in the Tremadocian, about 480 million years ago, and several lineages existed by the Middle Ordovician, hinting at Cambrian roots. Laurentia's megalograptids became the first truly successful eurypterids in the Late Ordovician, though most groups appear only in the Silurian.

ordo-028.title: Horseshoe crabs first appear in Morocco
ordo-028.text: Horseshoe crabs, or xiphosurans, first appear around 480 million years ago, in still-undescribed fossils from the Fezouata Formation of Morocco. The oldest named early relative, Lunataspis, lived in what is now Canada about 445 million years ago.

ordo-029.title: Gene-based estimates date the origin of insects
ordo-029.text: A 2014 molecular study, based on DNA differences, dates the origin of insects to about 480 million years ago, around when land plants appeared. It allows an origin as early as the Cambrian, and has insects' early radiation happening no later than 479 million years ago, in marine or coastal settings.

ordo-030.title: Island arcs ram Laurentia in the Taconic orogeny
ordo-030.text: Volcanic island arcs rammed into Laurentia, raising a great mountain chain from eastern Canada down the east of today's United States. A change in plate motions in the middle Ordovician led to this first Paleozoic mountain building in North America, which affected most of New England. Erosion of the new mountains fed iron and phosphorus to the oceans, a proposed driver of the GOBE. Later, weathering of the rising Appalachians and Caledonides drew carbon dioxide out of the Late Ordovician air.

ordo-031.title: Ordovician seas cool from greenhouse toward icehouse
ordo-031.text: Oxygen isotopes in conodont fossils show the climate began turning from greenhouse to icehouse at the end of the Early Ordovician. A sharp rise in carbon isotope ratios during the Floian age may record cooling through the burial of organic carbon, a proposed trigger for the GOBE. By the end of the Middle Ordovician, low-latitude seas had cooled to today's equatorial temperatures, and biodiversity climbed in step with the cooling. Graptolite ranges suggest Earth was in a mild icehouse by about 460 million years ago.

ordo-033.title: A 200-meter meteor strikes Decorah, Iowa
ordo-033.text: Around 470 million years ago, a meteor about 200 m wide struck what is now Decorah, Iowa, with the energy of 1,000 megatons of TNT. The possible crater, about 5.6 km across and now buried under the Winneshiek Shale, may belong to the Ordovician meteor event.

ordo-034.title: Moss-like plants begin to green the land
ordo-034.text: Cryptospores, the spores of the first land plants, appear about 470 million years ago and dominate plant fossils for some 60 million years. These pioneers evolved from green algae and resembled mosses and liverworts. By burying organic carbon, they began drawing down carbon dioxide and transforming land environments and the global climate. Without deep roots, though, they did little to break rock into soil.

ordo-032.title: Clearwater East: the older of two Quebec craters
ordo-032.text: Between 470 and 460 million years ago, an impact created Quebec's 26 km Clearwater East crater, whose central peak now hides under lake water and sediment. Its neighbor Clearwater West formed much later, in the Early Permian, and different meteorite signatures show the two are not twins.

ordo-035.title: Oxygen climbs in the Paleozoic Oxidation Event
ordo-035.text: Atmospheric oxygen rose between 470 and 400 million years ago, in what is called the Paleozoic Oxidation Event. Spreading from about 470 to 445 million years ago, the first land plants buried organic carbon in sediments, removing material that would otherwise use up oxygen. Oxygen later reached and then passed today's level of about 21% in the early Carboniferous.

ordo-037.title: A shattered asteroid showers Earth with meteorites
ordo-037.text: When the parent body of the L-chondrites, a common type of stony meteorite, broke apart in space, its fragments swung into orbits that crossed Earth's. For millions of years, about 100 times as many meteorites hit Earth each year as today. Shock ages in L-chondrites still falling today, and helium-3 in seafloor sediments, back the event; Oklahoma's 16 km Ames crater may be one of its scars. It was once thought to have sparked the GOBE, but other evidence puts it about 600,000 years after the Darriwilian diversity burst.

ordo-038.title: The first sea urchins appear
ordo-038.text: The earliest sea urchins, or echinoids, date to the Middle Ordovician, around 465 million years ago. Shallow-water limestones of Estonia, from the Ordovician and Silurian, are famous for their echinoid fossils.

ordo-041.title: The Decorah crater fills with exquisite fossils
ordo-041.text: Sediments that filled the Decorah crater preserve conodonts, bivalved arthropods and some of the earliest eurypterids in exceptional detail.

ordo-040.title: The Early Paleozoic Ice Age grips Gondwana
ordo-040.text: A long ice age, also called the Andean-Saharan glaciation, lasted from about 460 to 420 million years ago. Glaciers were probably on Gondwana by the Sandbian, and the ice centered on the Sahara before shifting to South America in the Silurian. Gondwana's position over the South Pole may explain how ice could form despite high carbon dioxide levels. As ice caps grew and melted, sea level rose and fell.

ordo-043.title: The Hunic terranes split away from Gondwana
ordo-043.text: In the Late Ordovician, back-arc spreading, the stretching of crust behind a volcanic arc, split the Hunic terranes from Gondwana and opened the Paleo-Tethys Ocean. The terranes then began moving north toward Euramerica.

ordo-044.title: Kazakh island arcs gather into Kazakhstania
ordo-044.text: The Kazakh terranes, an equatorial archipelago of island arcs and microcontinents, merged as part of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt. Crust was added to paleo-Kazakhstan through the Ordovician and Silurian, and one account places the final assembly of Kazakhstania in the late Silurian.

ordo-045.title: The last agnostid trilobites die out
ordo-045.text: Agnostid trilobites had declined sharply across the Cambrian–Ordovician transition, and the last of them died out in the Late Ordovician. The Ordovician mass extinction finished them off, along with the once-successful Telephinidae.

ordo-046.title: Siberian islands strike Baltica as the Ural Ocean forms
ordo-046.text: The Ural Ocean formed when large islands from Siberia collided with Baltica.

ordo-047.title: Twin asteroids may have struck Sweden at Lockne
ordo-047.text: Chitinozoan microfossils date the impact to about 458 million years ago, when an asteroid about 600 m across blasted the 7.5 km Lockne crater in northern Sweden. The smaller Målingen crater, 16 km away, may be its twin, made by a body about 250 m across.

ordo-048.title: A meteorite carves the Kärdla crater in Estonia
ordo-048.text: About 455 million years ago, a meteorite impact carved the 4 km Kärdla crater in what is now Estonia.

ordo-049.title: Super-eruptions blanket Laurentia in ash
ordo-049.text: During the Taconic orogeny, huge eruptions, probably from a volcanic arc, spread ash over Laurentia. That ash survives as the Deicke and Millbrig bentonites, clay layers formed from altered volcanic ash. The Millbrig ash fall, about 454 million years ago, was the largest in the last 590 million years. Each eruption left an ash layer larger in volume than that of the Toba eruption.

ordo-052.title: The Guttenberg carbon excursion flags the Katian's start
ordo-052.text: The Guttenberg carbon isotope excursion began soon after the start of the Katian, the Ordovician's next-to-last age. With the first appearance of the graptolite Diplacanthograptus caudatus, its onset helps fix the Katian boundary at Black Knob Ridge, Oklahoma.

ordo-050.title: The Boda Event briefly warms the Katian world
ordo-050.text: Early in the Katian, global temperatures rose briefly in the Boda Event, which built reef mounds and spread animal communities across Europe.

ordo-051.title: Extinction rates climb well before the Hirnantian ice
ordo-051.text: Extinction rates rose significantly in the early or middle Katian, several million years before the Hirnantian glaciation. This early phase is linked to the Boda Event and to eruptions of a large igneous province, possibly the Alborz province of northern Iran.

ordo-054.title: Arthropods make the first clear move onto land
ordo-054.text: The oldest clear evidence of animals on land comes from arthropods around 450 million years ago. Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods, the groups of millipedes, spiders and insects, began colonizing land at least from the Ordovician. They may have thrived on the food supplied by early land plants. Late Ordovician trace fossils, a little over 445 million years old, probably record invertebrates living on land.

ordo-055.title: Avalonia docks with Baltica, closing the Tornquist Sea
ordo-055.text: Eastern Avalonia collided with Baltica at about 30°S, closing the Tornquist Sea between them. The collision formed the northwestern Trans-European Suture Zone, the seam where the plates joined, and coincided with the Shelveian orogeny of western England and Wales. It also stopped the Rheic Ocean from widening south of Avalonia. Avalonian magmatism peaked between 457 and 449 million years ago, while a gigantic ash fall struck Baltica.

ordo-056.title: A stony meteorite gouges Charlevoix, Quebec
ordo-056.text: A stony meteorite struck what is now Charlevoix, Quebec, leaving a structure about 54 km across. Its age, 450 ± 20 million years, could place it anywhere from the Ordovician to the Silurian.

ordo-053.title: The Alice Springs Orogeny begins squeezing central Australia
ordo-053.text: From about 450 to 300 million years ago, the Alice Springs Orogeny squeezed central Australia from north to south, far from any plate edge. It shortened the crust by under 100 km, raised the MacDonnell Ranges and may have tilted Uluru's sandstone layers to near vertical.

ordo-061.title: Deniliquin's buried rings hint at a disputed impact
ordo-061.text: A deeply buried multiple-ring structure at Deniliquin, in southeastern Australia, dates to around the start of the first extinction pulse but is not a confirmed impact crater. A 2023 paper proposed that its impact winter triggered the Hirnantian glaciation and extinction, an idea that remains untested.

ordo-058.title: A carbon isotope spike marks the Hirnantian
ordo-058.text: A positive carbon isotope excursion, the HICE, ran through the Hirnantian alongside its short but severe glaciation. Scientists still debate its cause, but it is a key marker for defining the Ordovician–Silurian boundary worldwide. Its exact age is uncertain, because the Hirnantian is short and dating errors are comparatively large.

ordo-059.title: Hirnantian ice caps spread across Gondwana
ordo-059.text: A sudden cooling at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary rapidly expanded the glaciers in one of the most severe glaciations of the Phanerozoic. Ice caps covered Gondwana's polar lands in today's Africa and South America, in cold probably harsher than the height of the last ice age. Oxygen isotope ratios jumped by 2–4 parts per thousand and carbon dioxide dropped sharply, while sea level fell from about 220 m above today's to 141 m. Then the ice retreated abruptly, and Earth returned to a much warmer climate in the Rhuddanian, the first age of the Silurian.

ordo-060.title: Black shales spread as the ice melts
ordo-060.text: As the glaciers retreated, black shales, mud laid down in oxygen-starved water, spread from isolated basins to every latitude and depth, marking a global anoxic event. Repeated spells of anoxia mark the Ordovician–Silurian boundary, and this episode may be one of the longest in geologic time, though its cause is uncertain. Anoxia is the most common suspect for the extinction's second pulse. Sudden volcanism may have supplied sulfur dioxide that favored euxinia, water both oxygen-free and rich in toxic hydrogen sulfide.

ordo-062.title: Beecher's Trilobite Bed turns soft parts to pyrite
ordo-062.text: In Oneida County, New York, a thin shale bed preserves trilobites such as Triarthrus eatoni with their soft tissues replaced by pyrite. It ranks among the world's finest examples of near-perfect fossil preservation.

ordo-063.title: Jawed fish may make their first appearance
ordo-063.text: The first jawed vertebrates, which arose from among the ostracoderms, may have appeared in the Late Ordovician, about 445 million years ago. The earliest evidence is a scatter of scale microfossils, possibly from acanthodians, the so-called spiny sharks. Jawed fish became common only in the Devonian, the 'Age of Fishes'.

ordo-064.title: The first of the Big Five mass extinctions strikes
ordo-064.text: The first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions, second only to the end-Permian, struck in two pulses, at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary and later in the Hirnantian. The first pulse is tied to the sudden glaciation, the second to warming and spreading anoxia as the ice retreated. Estimates range from about 60% of marine genera, groups of related species, to 85% of marine species; trilobites lost about 70% of their genera. Many brachiopods, bryozoans and corals also vanished, yet the extinction changed ecosystem structure little, and diversity rebounded quickly in the Silurian.

silu-001.title: Armorica breaks away from Gondwana
silu-001.text: The Armorican terranes, fragments of crust with their own geologic histories, split from Gondwana, probably breaking free completely near the end of the Silurian. They drifted toward Laurussia through the Devonian and struck it late in the Carboniferous, in the Variscan orogeny, a slow collision that pushed up mountains.

silu-002.title: Armored jawless fishes reach their peak
silu-002.text: By the Late Silurian, the ostracoderms, armored fishes without jaws, had reached the high point of their evolution. Anaspids appeared early in the period, osteostracans followed in the Llandovery or Wenlock, and thelodont scales turned up worldwide. Heterostracans of the order Traquairaspidiformes joined them in the Late Silurian. Even so, the rise of jawed fishes coincided with a sharp decline among other jawless animals, such as the conodonts, eel-like creatures known mainly from tooth-like fossils.

silu-003.title: The asaphid trilobites disappear
silu-003.text: Asaphida, a large and varied order of trilobites, the hard-shelled sea arthropods of the Paleozoic, had lived since the Middle Cambrian but died out in the Silurian. Its last members, the Trinucleioidea, vanished before the period ended.

silu-004.title: The Clinton Ironstones fill the Appalachian basin
silu-004.text: From New York to Alabama, the Appalachian basin filled with shale, mudstone, sandstone and the iron-rich beds known as the Clinton Ironstones. These Clinton Group rocks preserve a rich record of early Silurian sea life, yet they are best known for their iron ore.

silu-009.title: Jawed fishes branch out in Silurian seas
silu-009.text: The great milestone of Silurian seas was the spread of fishes with jaws: armored placoderms, acanthodians or 'spiny sharks', and bony fishes. By about 419 million years ago, jawed fishes had split into three branches: placoderms, bony fishes, and spiny sharks together with cartilaginous fishes, the lineage of sharks. Cartilaginous and bony fishes, the two jawed groups still alive today, had both appeared by the late Silurian. Lobe-finned fishes also emerged in the Silurian and early Devonian, though every one of them still lived in water.

silu-011.title: Straight-shelled dissidocerids make their exit
silu-011.text: Dissidocerida, an order of straight-shelled cephalopods, the group that includes squid and octopus, makes its last appearance in the Early Silurian. The order had lived since the Early Ordovician.

silu-012.title: The last eocrinoids vanish
silu-012.text: Eocrinoids, early stalked echinoderms, relatives of starfish and sea urchins, make their last appearance in the Silurian. They had lived since Cambrian Stage 3.

silu-013.title: Trilobite-like nektaspids make their last appearance
silu-013.text: Nektaspids, trilobite-like arthropods whose shells never hardened with minerals, last appear in upper Silurian rocks. Their lineage stretched back to the early Cambrian.

silu-014.title: Paracrinoids fade from the shallow seas
silu-014.text: Paracrinoids, echinoderms of shallow seas, had lived since the Early Ordovician. Their last fossils come from the Early Silurian.

silu-016.title: Reef-building stromatoporoid sponges branch out
silu-016.text: Most orders of stromatoporoids, sponges with stony skeletons that helped build reefs, originated in the Silurian, among them Stromatoporida and Amphiporida, first recorded in the Ludlow. Clathrodictyids and actinostromatids diversified strongly, while labechiids declined.

silu-017.title: Nematophytes tower over Silurian land plants
silu-017.text: Nematophytes, a loose group of land organisms that included some plants and algae, appear in the Silurian and last into the Early Devonian. They towered over even the largest land plants, and no plant grew bigger until the Early Carboniferous.

silu-019.title: The Rheic Ocean stretches to 4,000 kilometers
silu-019.text: As the Avalonia–Carolina block drifted north from Gondwana, the Rheic Ocean opened to its greatest width in the Silurian, about 4,000 km. It separated Laurussia to the north from Gondwana to the south.

silu-020.title: Graptolites at Dob's Linn mark the Silurian's start
silu-020.text: Dob's Linn, a small valley in southern Scotland, holds the rock layers chosen to mark the start of the Silurian. In its Birkhill Shale, the boundary falls where two graptolites, Parakidograptus acuminatus and Akidograptus ascensus, first appear after the end-Ordovician extinctions.

silu-015.title: Survivors restock the seas as the ice melts
silu-015.text: As melting ice raised sea level and flooded the continental shelves again, life rebounded within the surviving orders. Many 'Lazarus taxa', groups missing from the latest Ordovician rocks, reappeared, showing that small populations had survived in refuges. Sponges dominated South China's oxygen-poor seafloors early in the Rhuddanian, the first age of the Silurian. Trilobites and atrypid brachiopods, shelled seafloor animals, began recovering then too, but pentamerid brachiopods lagged until the following age, the Aeronian.

silu-006.title: The first placoderms bring jaws and armor
silu-006.text: The first identifiable placoderms, armored fishes with jaws, appear in rocks from the late Llandovery. The vertebrate jaw probably evolved during the Silurian and appeared in placoderms, which went on to diversify further in the Devonian. Their Silurian record is patchy, probably because they lived where fossils rarely formed. One rare near-complete find is Silurolepis, an antiarch placoderm from Ludlow rocks in Yunnan, China.

silu-010.title: Early plants spread over much of Earth's land
silu-010.text: Shifts in mercury isotopes show that land plants had spread across much of Earth's land surface by the Early Silurian. Eohostimella, probably a land plant, comes from rocks about 440 to 430 million years old. Spores and other plant microfossils of this age turn up in China and Pennsylvania. Silurian land floras looked broadly alike around the globe, with little regional difference.

silu-018.title: Barrier reefs spread, even into high latitudes
silu-018.text: Widespread reef building began in the Llandovery and carried on into the Devonian. Barrier reefs covered far more seafloor than reefs do today, and they grew even at high latitudes. Tabulate corals, an extinct group that grew in colonies, raised prominent mounds. Corals may have begun teaming up with sunlight-harvesting partners in the Llandovery, and such photosymbiotic corals appear by the Middle Silurian.

silu-024.title: The Taconic orogeny comes to an end
silu-024.text: About 440 million years ago, the Taconic orogeny ended: subduction, where one plate sinks beneath another, stopped, and the Iapetus Terrane was welded onto eastern North America. As the New England mountains wore down through the Silurian and Devonian, their sediment spread over the Appalachians and the North American midcontinent.

silu-023.title: Smaller ice ages shift to South America
silu-023.text: Milder glaciations with smaller ice caps followed the Hirnantian ice age through the Silurian, and their center moved from the Sahara to South America. Later Silurian rocks lack tillites, the rubble glaciers leave behind, so ice cannot easily explain the period's climate swings.

silu-025.title: Qianodus and Fanjingshania, the oldest sure jawed fishes
silu-025.text: Remains from Aeronian rocks in Guizhou, China, about 439 million years old, belong to Qianodus and Fanjingshania, the oldest unambiguous jawed vertebrates. Both were acanthodians, or 'spiny sharks', early relatives of the cartilaginous fishes. Acanthodians arose about 50 million years before the first true sharks. Older Ordovician records may exist, but unambiguous jawed fossils appear only by the early Silurian and become abundant in the Devonian.

silu-026.title: Chongqing's rocks preserve the earliest whole jawed fishes
silu-026.text: Near Chongqing, China, the Huixingshao Formation preserves complete fossils of the earliest jawed vertebrates, about 436 million years old. The site also holds jawless galeaspids and eurypterids, or sea scorpions, while Shenacanthus, a fish of the same age, wore placoderm-like chest armor.

silu-027.title: Bony fishes appear, with pouches that became lungs
silu-027.text: The oldest known bony-fish fossils, about 436 million years old, have teeth arranged midway between those of sharks and true bony fishes. These early bony fishes still had mostly cartilage skeletons; their real novelty was pouches off the foregut that later became swim bladders and lungs. Guiyu oneiros, about 425 million years old from Yunnan, China, is one of the earliest bony fishes found with its skeleton still joined. One branch of the bony fishes, the lobe-finned fishes, would later give rise to every land vertebrate.

silu-029.title: Baltica rams Laurentia and the Caledonian mountains rise
silu-029.text: From about 435 to 410 million years ago, Baltica and Laurentia collided in the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny. Avalonia joined them near the equator, and the three began to form Euramerica. The collision folded long-accumulated coastal sediments into mountains that ran from New York State through Greenland and Britain to Norway. Around 429 million years ago, Baltica's margin was buried about 120 km deep, deep enough to form micro-diamonds.

silu-031.title: Cooksonia sprouts: the oldest known vascular plants
silu-031.text: In the middle of the Silurian, Cooksonia appears: the oldest known vascular plant, one with internal tissues that carry water. It remained an important part of the flora until the end of the Early Devonian, from 433 to 393 million years ago. Most rocks bearing Cooksonia are marine, but the plants probably grew along rivers and streams. Slightly later, more complex Gondwanan plants such as Baragwanathia hint that vascular plants began earlier, perhaps in the early Silurian.

silu-032.title: The Ireviken extinction sweeps up from the deep
silu-032.text: At the boundary between the Llandovery and Wenlock, the Ireviken event, first of three Silurian extinctions, unfolded over about 200,000 years. It began in the deep ocean and spread to the shelf seas, killing over half of trilobite species at Ireviken on Gotland and 80% of conodont species worldwide. Graptolites suffered badly too, but shallow reefs were barely touched. Linked to global cooling, the die-off came in eight steps that appear to track Milankovitch cycles, regular rhythms in Earth's orbit.

silu-033.title: Bisonocerid nautiloids disappear
