silu-033.text: Bisonocerida, an order of nautiloids, cephalopods with external shells, makes its last appearance in the Wenlock. The order dated back to the Tremadocian, the first age of the Ordovician.

silu-035.title: Carbon isotopes spike after the Ireviken crisis
silu-035.text: After the first Ireviken extinctions, the carbon-isotope ratio δ13C rose from +1.4‰ to +4.5‰, and the oxygen ratio δ18O climbed from −5.6‰ to −5.0‰. This excursion, about 431 million years ago, resembles the Cambrian SPICE event, one of many swings that give the Silurian more isotope excursions than any other period.

silu-036.title: The Lundgreni event hits graptolites hard
silu-036.text: The Lundgreni event, or Mid-Homerian Biotic Crisis, hit graptolites, seafloor animals and microscopic plankton hardest, driving graptolite diversity to a global low and wiping out the cyrtograptids. Scientists blame eutrophication, an overload of nutrients, and anoxia, a loss of oxygen in the water, and a double-peaked carbon isotope excursion began with the crisis.

silu-038.title: Scorpions appear in Silurian Scotland
silu-038.text: Scorpions date back about 430 million years; the oldest known, Dolichophonus loudonensis, lived in what is now Scotland. Whether early scorpions lived in water or on land is still debated, though early forms such as Eramoscorpius had book lungs, stacked folds for breathing air.

silu-039.title: The Great Glen Fault shapes the Scottish Highlands
silu-039.text: Late in the Caledonian orogeny, as Laurentia and Baltica collided, the Great Glen Fault formed, probably between 430 and 390 million years ago. This fault, a fracture along which rock slides past rock, helped shape the Scottish Highlands.

silu-041.title: Plants pump oxygen toward modern levels
silu-041.text: From about 428 to 359 million years ago, oxygen climbed in steps to modern levels and beyond, keeping pace with the spread of vascular plants. Oxygen was still low in the early Silurian, but by the Devonian it was approaching today's level. Land plants, with their higher photosynthetic yield, likely drove the rise, and organic carbon buried in rocks could no longer consume oxygen. As carbon was locked away, carbon dioxide fell too, cooling the climate.

silu-042.title: The Terrestrial Revolution turns the land green
silu-042.text: From 428 to 359 million years ago, plants and fungi colonized dry land and diversified rapidly, most critically in the Late Silurian and Early Devonian. Vascular plants arose from simpler ones, new fungi spread, and arachnids, myriapods such as millipedes, and six-legged hexapods became fully terrestrial. The rise in plant diversity has been compared with the Cambrian explosion of animals, especially among tall, woody plants that later formed canopies. The new vegetation reshaped the water cycle, the climate and ocean nutrients, likely feeding plankton blooms tied to the Late Devonian extinction.

silu-043.title: The Mulde event, a second Silurian crisis
silu-043.text: About 427 million years ago, the Mulde event, an episode of oxygen-starved seas, was the second of three relatively minor Silurian mass extinctions. It coincided with a global drop in sea level and was soon followed by an isotope excursion. Carbon isotopes suggest a sustained fall in carbon dioxide at the time. Some apparent conodont losses, however, may reflect changing sediments rather than real extinction.

silu-048.title: Baragwanathia and the first lycophytes
silu-048.text: Lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving lineages of vascular plants, date back about 425 million years. Baragwanathia, a clubmoss known from Australia, Canada and China, was advanced for its age, with branching stems and needle-like leaves 10–20 cm long. Its leaves alone outstripped most Middle Silurian plants, which stood under 10 cm tall.

silu-052.title: Kerrera's millipedes, among the first animals ashore
silu-052.text: At Kerrera in Scotland, Kampecaris obanensis and Archidesmus left the oldest definite millipede fossils, about 425 million years old. Millipedes are among the oldest known land animals and among the first to colonize land. Air-breathing arthropods from Kerrera and from Ludlow, about 420 million years old, both predate Pneumodesmus as dated by zircon crystals. Still, land animals made little mark on Earth until they diversified in the Devonian.

silu-049.title: Palaeoscolecid worms make their final appearance
silu-049.text: Palaeoscolecid worms, known since the late Early Cambrian, make their last appearance in the Ludfordian. The Lau extinction event may have finished them off.

silu-051.title: Ludfordian ice lowers the sea and bares new land
silu-051.text: In the Ludfordian, the Early Paleozoic Ice Age delivered its last major glaciation, associated with the Lau event. Ice growth in the middle Ludfordian caused a major regression, a retreat of the sea from the land, exposing vast new ground. Plants and mats of cyanobacteria, microbes that live by photosynthesis, quickly colonized the bare surfaces, pushing plant diversification further.

silu-054.title: The Lau event strikes conodonts and remakes communities
silu-054.text: The Lau event, last of three Silurian extinctions, began at the start of the late Ludfordian and takes its name from Lau parish on Gotland. It struck conodonts hardest, while graptolites suffered in the Kozlowskii event, which came just after and may even have been simultaneous. It coincided with a glacially driven low in global sea level, and most major groups saw extinction rates rise. Rated 6.2 in severity, it changed communities for good: microbial mats and stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbes, spread as after the end-Ordovician and end-Permian extinctions.

silu-055.title: Sea scorpions reach their peak
silu-055.text: Eurypterids, the sea scorpions, were major players in Silurian seas and peaked in diversity in the Pridoli, 423 to 419.2 million years ago. Most eurypterid groups first appear in Silurian rocks, and in most beds one group, the eurypterines, makes up 90% of specimens. Late in the Silurian came the large pterygotids, with rudder-like tails and big pincers; one, Acutiramus, reached about 2 m long. The most abundant, Eurypterus, lived from about 432 million years ago to the Pridoli's end, and Pennsylvania's Tonoloway Formation holds a mass assemblage.

silu-056.title: Ascomycete fungi make their first appearance
silu-056.text: The earliest known ascomycete fungi, the sac fungi, a group that today includes yeasts, date from 423 to 419 million years ago. They belong to the dikaryan fungi, which began expanding and diversifying during the Silurian.

silu-059.title: The first wildfires leave the oldest charcoal
silu-059.text: In the Pridoli, oxygen rose high enough for wildfires, and the first charcoal appears in the fossil record. That Silurian charcoal shows oxygen had crossed about 15%, enough to sustain fire for the first time.

silu-062.title: The Šilalė event thins out the conodonts
silu-062.text: Early in the Pridoli, the Šilalė event cut down conodonts and left a negative carbon isotope excursion, traced from Lithuanian cores to North America's Appalachian Basin. Brachiopods, meanwhile, flourished, and the event fell during the Pridoli's weakest 405,000-year cycle of orbital eccentricity, the stretching of Earth's orbit.

silu-061.title: Pneumodesmus, an early air breather of disputed age
silu-061.text: Pneumodesmus newmani, a millipede-like myriapod from Scotland, is among the oldest creatures known to have lived on land. Openings in its cuticle are read as spiracles, or breathing holes, making it the earliest known arthropod with a tracheal system, a network of air tubes. Its age is disputed. A 2023 study argued for the late Wenlock, about 430 million years ago, but zircon dates and a 2025 study favor about 414 million years.

silu-063.title: Centipedes and early arachnids join millipedes on land
silu-063.text: By about 420 million years ago, millipedes shared the land with centipedes and trigonotarbids, an early group of arachnids. Land scorpions appear in the record at about the same time. Some of these animals were predators, which implies simple food webs built on prey that ate plants or detritus, dead organic matter. Together they show myriapods and arachnids becoming fully terrestrial during the Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution.

silu-064.title: Andreolepis, perhaps the first ray-finned fish
silu-064.text: The earliest known ray-finned fish may be Andreolepis hedei, about 420 million years old, found in Russia, Sweden and Estonia. Ray-finned fishes now make up the vast majority of living fish. Yet their crown group, the branch holding every living ray-finned fish, arose much later, near the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary.

silu-065.title: The Iapetus Ocean closes and Laurussia is born
silu-065.text: By the end of the Silurian, about 420 million years ago, the Iapetus Ocean had closed entirely, leaving a seam called the Iapetus Suture. Avalonia and Baltica fused with Laurentia in the Caledonian orogeny, forming Laurussia, later the northern part of the supercontinent Pangaea. Subduction of the Iapetus had stopped by then, and the thrust sheets of Scandinavia reached peak metamorphism, their greatest heat and pressure, about 420 million years ago.

silu-066.title: Ascocerid nautiloids vanish at the Silurian's close
silu-066.text: Ascocerid cephalopods, cut back by the end-Ordovician extinction, recovered during the Silurian. Then, at the very end of the period, they died out abruptly.

silu-067.title: Falling seas leave the thick Salina salts
silu-067.text: At the Silurian's close, sea level fell again and the young mountains eroded rapidly. In a shallow inland basin under a warm, arid climate, drying water left the Salina Group's evaporites, salt-rich layers 120 to 800 m thick.

devo-001.title: Jawed fishes multiply in the Age of Fishes
devo-001.text: Jawed vertebrates, which may have appeared as early as the late Ordovician, became common in the Devonian, popularly called the Age of Fishes. Fish variety soared, especially among ostracoderms, placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks. Cartilaginous and bony fishes both diversified and played a large role in Devonian seas. Among the bony fishes, lobe-finned forms such as coelacanths and lungfish were the most diverse of the period.

devo-003.title: The Chaitenia island arc docks with Patagonia
devo-003.text: Chaitenia, an island arc, or curved chain of volcanic islands, was welded onto Patagonia in what is now south-central Chile. Patagonia's margin had turned convergent, with plates pushing together, leading toward a collision that began in the mid-Carboniferous.

devo-006.title: Alkaline magma builds Russia's Kola province
devo-006.text: Devonian magma on Russia's Kola Peninsula built an estimated 15,000 cubic km of alkaline rock, rich in sodium and potassium, including the Khibiny and Lovozero massifs. This huge outpouring, the Kola large igneous province, erupted about when the Viluy and Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets provinces did and is a suggested trigger of the Hangenberg extinction.

devo-007.title: Spreading plants pull carbon dioxide from the air
devo-007.text: Carbon dioxide fell steeply through the Devonian as land plants spread. Their roots increased silicate weathering, a chemical breakdown of rock that consumes carbon dioxide, as carbonates formed in ancient soils reveal. Anoxic events in the oceans grew longer during the period, and the growing plant life probably helped steady carbon dioxide levels. Over the long run, falling carbon dioxide and rising oxygen led on to the late Paleozoic icehouse, a cold world with ice sheets near the poles.

devo-009.title: Oxygen climbs toward modern levels
devo-009.text: Early in the Devonian, oxygen was still fairly scarce, possibly about half of modern values. Over the period it rose to near-modern levels, as land plants spreading across the continents buried more organic carbon in sediments. That rise may have favored vertebrates able to breathe air, helping push tetrapods, the four-limbed vertebrates, onto land.

devo-011.title: Armored placoderms dominate Devonian waters
devo-011.text: After a patchy Silurian record, placoderms appear with seemingly sudden diversity at the very start of the Devonian. They went on to dominate almost every known aquatic ecosystem, in fresh water and salt water alike. One 419-million-year-old placoderm, Entelognathus, already had a bony mouth skeleton like a bony fish's. Giants such as Dunkleosteus grew up to seven meters long.

devo-002.title: The Caledonian mountains begin to collapse
devo-002.text: Once Baltica's margin had been dragged down and buried under thrust sheets, the Caledonian mountains began a long collapse, with crust stretching and sinking across Scandinavia. Rocks in Norway's Western Gneiss Region record burial peaking about 410 million years ago and a return to the surface about 400 to 385 million years ago.

devo-005.title: Jawless fishes peak, then fade for good
devo-005.text: Armored jawless fishes and thelodonts peaked in diversity in the Early Devonian, when Cephalaspis, the most advanced jawless fish, appeared about 415 million years ago. By the Middle Devonian, jawed fishes were thriving while the ostracoderms dwindled, never to recover.

devo-008.title: Schinderhannes, the last of Anomalocaris's kin
devo-008.text: Radiodonts, the group of Cambrian predators that includes Anomalocaris, make their last appearance in the Early Devonian. One late survivor, Schinderhannes bartelsi, lived in what is now Germany.

devo-010.title: Asian blocks break from Gondwana, opening the Paleo-Tethys
devo-010.text: North China, South China and Tarim rifted, or pulled away, from Gondwana's northern edge, opening the Paleo-Tethys Ocean behind them. For South China and Indochina, the split began as early as the Silurian, and as they moved north the Proto-Tethys shrank ahead of them. The blocks stayed close enough to Gondwana that their Devonian fossils look more like Australian species than north Asian ones. South China and Annamia, now Southeast Asia, later collided in the Carboniferous.

devo-012.title: The Rheic Ocean starts to close
devo-012.text: The Rheic Ocean, wide at the start of the Devonian, began to close in the Early Devonian as Gondwana moved toward Euramerica. Its ocean floor was consumed by subduction as the gap narrowed. Near the end of the Early Devonian, Franconia and Saxothuringia struck Laurussia, pinching out the eastern part of the ocean. Closure finished in the Mississippian, the early Carboniferous, when Gondwana and Laurentia collided to form Pangaea.

devo-013.title: The Old Red Sandstone spreads across Laurussia
devo-013.text: From around 419 million years ago, the sediments of the Old Red Sandstone piled up across Britain, Ireland, Norway, northeastern North America, Greenland and Svalbard. Its red beds were so abundant that Laurussia earned the name Old Red Sandstone Continent. In Scotland, uplifted Silurian rocks wore down into fresh water, probably large river deltas, between 408 and 370 million years ago. At Siccar Point, around 370 million years ago, rainy-season rivers near the equator laid iron-rich sands that winds reworked into dunes.

devo-014.title: Lobe-finned fishes appear and split in two
devo-014.text: The first lobe-finned fishes, about 418 million years ago, closely resembled spiny sharks. Between 416 and 397 million years ago they split into two main lineages, the coelacanths and the rhipidistians. While placoderms dominated the seas, some lobe-finned fishes moved into fresh water between 416 and 385 million years ago. Coelacanths had their heyday later, in the Late Devonian and Carboniferous, from 385 to 299 million years ago.

devo-015.title: Arthropods spread over coasts, floodplains and new soils
devo-015.text: By about 415 million years ago, many arthropods lived along coasts and on river floodplains, and some of them ate plants. Early rooted plants had built the first stable soils, which sheltered mites, scorpions, trigonotarbids and myriapods.

devo-020.title: Nautilids, the nautilus lineage, first appear
devo-020.text: The first nautilids, the order of the living nautilus, appear about 410 million years ago, led by Rutocerina, whose shell resembled those of its likely oncocerid ancestors. By the Middle Devonian, nautilids had grown to about 22 genera, even as other nautiloids declined.

devo-022.title: Hot springs petrify an early land ecosystem at Rhynie
devo-022.text: About 410 million years ago, silica-rich water from volcanic hot springs in Scotland petrified plants, fungi, lichens and animals almost instantly, right where they lived. The resulting Rhynie chert, a hard silica rock, preserves one of the first known fully terrestrial ecosystems, from an early stage of land colonization. Its animals include arachnids and hexapods, and Rhyniognatha, possibly the oldest insect, is known from its mandibles, or jaws. Fungi among its rootless, leafless plants suggest that fungi played a large role in plants' move onto land.

devo-023.title: Trimerophytes and the first euphyllophytes appear
devo-023.text: Trimerophytes, a class of early vascular plants known only from the Devonian, appear about 410 million years ago. They are among the early euphyllophytes, the plant lineage that also includes ferns and seed plants.

devo-019.title: Coiled ammonoids appear in the Emsian
devo-019.text: The first ammonoids, cephalopods with coiled shells, appeared in the Emsian, around 410 to 408 million years ago. They arose from straight-shelled bactritids, and transitional fossils show the shell coiling step by step. Bactritids also first appear in the Early Devonian, and their radiation alongside ammonoids may reflect falling oxygen in deeper water. Ammonoids later grew abundant in the Mesozoic and vanished around the end-Cretaceous extinction.

devo-024.title: Tungsenia, the oldest fish on the tetrapod line
devo-024.text: The oldest known tetrapodomorph, a fish on the lineage leading to four-limbed animals, is Tungsenia from China, about 409 million years old. Tetrapods have their roots among these early Devonian fishes. Kenichthys, a small Chinese lobe-fin from about 395 million years ago, shows the internal nostril, or choana, caught mid-evolution. Relatives of these fishes became the most numerous bony fishes in Devonian and Carboniferous waterways.

devo-025.title: Jaekelopterus, the largest arthropod ever known
devo-025.text: A giant claw from Germany's Klerf Formation, about 45.5 cm long when complete, shows that the sea scorpion Jaekelopterus rhenaniae was the largest arthropod ever known. Even so, eurypterines, the most common sea scorpions, lost over half their diversity within 10 million years in the Early Devonian.

devo-026.title: Hunsrück Slate fossils wrapped in fool's gold
devo-026.text: Germany's Hunsrück Slate, from the latest Pragian to the early Emsian, is one of the few marine Devonian Lagerstätten, fossil beds that preserve soft tissue. Many of its fossils wear a coat of pyrite, or fool's gold, and its fauna includes the trilobite Chotecops and the puzzling placoderm Stensioella.

devo-028.title: Rhyniognatha, a contested first insect
devo-028.text: The oldest proposed insect fossil, Rhyniognatha hirsti, is about 400 million years old and known only from its jaws. Whether it really was an insect remains contested. The first possible insect fossils appear around 416 million years ago. Early Devonian rocks of about 400 million years ago preserve only a few kinds of flightless insects.

devo-031.title: Laurussia comes together near the Tropic of Capricorn
devo-031.text: By about 400 million years ago, the Caledonian collisions had welded Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and smaller terranes into Laurussia, also called Euramerica. The new continent sat in the dry belt along the Tropic of Capricorn, then drifted north while rotating counterclockwise. The collision raised a string of mountain ranges along its southeastern coast. Low seas in the Early Devonian split its seafloor animals into separate provinces, which merged again by the Middle Devonian.

devo-032.title: Lungfish appear and evolve at speed
devo-032.text: Lungfish appeared about 400 million years ago and evolved so rapidly through the Devonian that the burst is called the 'dipnoan renaissance'. By the Middle Devonian, 397 to 385 million years ago, they had proto-lungs and proto-limbs for spells out of water.

devo-033.title: Sharks and their kin take shape
devo-033.text: By about 395 million years ago, cartilaginous fishes, the sharks, rays and chimaeras, had evolved from acanthodians. Their oldest unambiguous fossils are Middle Devonian, though shark-like scales go back to the Ordovician. They went on to become diverse and important in Devonian seas.

devo-036.title: Cladoxylopsid trees grow Earth's first forests
devo-036.text: In the Eifelian, fern-like cladoxylopsid trees formed the first forests in Earth's history. Trees more than eight meters tall had appeared by the Middle Devonian, and the oldest known fossil forest dates from the Eifelian. By the late Givetian, cladoxylalean ferns, lycopsids and progymnosperms had all evolved tree-like forms. Over the Devonian, plant heights rose from about 30 cm to 30 m.

devo-041.title: Sponges and corals build the Devonian's great reefs
devo-041.text: After a strong recovery, stromatoporoid sponges peaked in diversity in the Eifelian, building reefs alongside tabulate corals and rugose, or horn, corals. Microbes built the other kind of Devonian reef, thriving in warm periods, while corals and stromatoporoids dominated in cooler times. One barrier reef in Australia's Kimberley region stretched 350 km along the coast of a Devonian continent. Reefs also fringed Laurussia's southeast coast, in what are now southern England and Belgium.

devo-038.title: Young forests may have cooled the planet
devo-038.text: Newly evolved forests drew carbon from the air and buried it in sediments. That drawdown may show up as a Middle Devonian cooling of around 5 °C.

devo-039.title: Progymnosperms take root in the Middle Devonian
devo-039.text: Progymnosperms first appear in the Middle Devonian, and the group lasts into the Lopingian, the late Permian. Their order Archaeopteridales, home of the tree Archaeopteris, spans the Middle and Late Devonian.

devo-040.title: The Variscan collision begins to build mountains
devo-040.text: Variscan mountain building began in the Middle Devonian and continued into the early Permian. Drifting north from Gondwana, the Armorican terranes closed the Rheic Ocean ahead of them and began colliding with southeastern Laurussia. The collision deformed crust from Iberia and Ireland to France, Germany and the Czech Republic. By the end of the Devonian, every Armorican terrane had joined Laurussia.

devo-035.title: The Catskill Delta spreads west from the Acadian Mountains
devo-035.text: Rivers and marshes carried sediment from the eroding Acadian Mountains west into the inland Kaskaskia Sea, building the Catskill Delta, up to 3,000 m thick. It preserves many early tetrapodomorph fishes and land plants, key evidence for how vertebrates moved onto land.

devo-042.title: Zachełmie footprints, perhaps the oldest tetrapod tracks
devo-042.text: Trackways at Zachełmie, Poland, left in shallow Eifelian lagoons, may be the oldest evidence of tetrapods, and some prints even show digits. They predate the oldest tetrapod body fossils by about 18 million years and support the idea that land vertebrates first emerged along tidal shores. Some researchers, however, read the marks as fish feeding traces, so the case remains open. If the tracks are genuine, Tiktaalik-like elpistostegids were late-surviving relics.

devo-043.title: Rising, oxygen-starved seas bring the Kačák event
devo-043.text: Near the Eifelian's end, the Kačák event raised global sea level and spread anoxia, laying down black shales over perhaps 200,000 to 700,000 years. Strong sunlight probably warmed the oceans, raising sea level as the water expanded, and fed stronger monsoons that filled Scotland's Achanarras lake, the Orcadian Basin's deepest. Open-ocean animals suffered most, and warming devastated the cool-water Malvinoxhosan Realm off Gondwana. Estimates put the loss at about 24% to 32% of marine genera, milder than the Late Devonian extinctions to come.

devo-044.title: Oxygen loss drives the Taghanic extinction
devo-044.text: The Taghanic event, an extinction in the Givetian, struck when an anoxic event drained oxygen from the oceans. It sharply cut trilobite diversity, especially in shallow water, and wiped out the trilobite order Lichida. One study ranks this crisis as the eighth most ecologically severe mass extinction. Another account places it at the Givetian–Frasnian boundary and credits it with killing about half of coral genera.

devo-046.title: The first wetlands take shape
devo-046.text: Modern-style land ecosystems appeared only in the Late Devonian, as land plants stabilized freshwater habitats and the first wetlands developed, with ever more complex food webs. These wetlands later gave way to the coal forests of the Early Carboniferous.

devo-048.title: The Chilenia terrane docks against the Precordillera
devo-048.text: Continued subduction carried the Chilenia terrane into the western border of the Precordillera, where it collided and stuck fast, becoming part of the continent.

devo-051.title: Mountains rise across the Canadian Arctic
devo-051.text: From the Late Devonian into the early Carboniferous, the Innuitian, or Ellesmere, orogeny raised mountain ranges across the Canadian Arctic and northernmost Greenland. When these mountains later collapsed, the Sverdrup Basin opened on Laurussia's northern margin.

devo-052.title: The Late Devonian warms without more carbon dioxide
devo-052.text: The Late Devonian warmed back to Early Devonian levels, as increased continental weathering and the distribution of plants show, though carbon dioxide did not rise to match. Arid climates shrank, and temperate ones became more common.

devo-047.title: Oxygen-starved seafloors bury the makings of oil
devo-047.text: Anoxia during the Late Devonian extinctions halted decay, so organic matter survived to make Devonian rocks oil-rich, especially in Canada and the United States. The Bakken shales, partly laid down in oxygen-free, sulfide-rich water, underlie about 520,000 square km of the Williston Basin and are a prolific source of oil.

devo-053.title: Siberia's Viluy Traps pour out flood basalts
devo-053.text: Rifting and deep mantle plumes fed the Viluy Traps, flood basalts that erupted along a triple-junction rift, where three rifts meet, at the edge of the Siberian Platform. The main eruptions ran from about 381 to 366 million years ago, give or take 5 million years, with a later pulse toward the end of the Devonian. Dating finds two volcanic phases, the first matching the age of the Kellwasser event. Yet the main eruptions seem to predate the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, so their role in it is still debated.

devo-054.title: The Antler orogeny stirs western North America
devo-054.text: Subduction of Panthalassic ocean floor along Laurussia's western margin drove the Antler orogeny in the ancestral Sierra Nevada region. Most sources date its start to the Late Devonian, but others place it just after the period ended.

devo-055.title: The deep ocean finally holds its oxygen
devo-055.text: Only after 380 million years ago did oxygen in the deep sea, sporadic and variable before, settle near modern levels.

devo-056.title: Gogo fossils and the oldest live birth
devo-056.text: Western Australia's Gogo Formation, about 380 million years old, preserves soft tissues in three dimensions, down to nerves and embryos with umbilical cords. More than fifty fish species have been described from it, along with arthropods. The 380-million-year-old placoderms Materpiscis, Incisoscutum and Austroptyctodus are the oldest known examples of live birth. Gogonasus, one of the earliest tetrapodomorphs, dates from the same time.

devo-057.title: An impact scars Russia's Kaluga region
devo-057.text: About 380 million years ago, an impact in what is now Kaluga Oblast, Russia, blasted a crater 15 km across. The crater now lies buried under about 800 m of sediment, hidden from the surface.

devo-059.title: The Ilyinets crater forms in Ukraine
devo-059.text: An impact about 378 million years ago left the Ilyinets crater in Ukraine, 8.5 km across.

devo-058.title: The Alamo impact hits shallow Nevada seas
devo-058.text: Some 377 to 378 million years ago, one or more hypervelocity objects slammed into shallow seas in what is now southeastern Nevada, perhaps dislodging huge slide blocks. Among the best-exposed and most accurately dated impacts, it struck about 5.9 million years before the Frasnian-Famennian extinctions and probably did not affect them.

devo-060.title: Siljan, Europe's largest impact scar, forms in Sweden
devo-060.text: A meteorite struck what is now Dalarna in central Sweden, leaving the Siljan Ring, about 52 km across and the largest impact structure in Europe. The impact is dated to 376.8 ± 1.7 million years ago, or 377 ± 2 million years ago, in the Frasnian. Scientists once proposed it as a cause of the Kellwasser extinction, but that event has since been dated later, to 371.93–371.78 million years ago.

devo-061.title: The Acadian orogeny raises mountains along the Atlantic edge
devo-061.text: Beginning roughly 375 million years ago, the Acadian orogeny built mountains along North America's Atlantic seaboard for about 50 million years, into the early Mississippian. Collisions with Avalonian crust broken from Gondwana closed the southern Iapetus Ocean and raised a high mountain belt between 375 and 359 million years ago. Volcanoes and uplift in New England shed sediment into an inland sea, and the Catskill Delta filled the basin at the mountains' foot. In the British Isles, Acadian sideways squeezing between 404 and 394 million years ago joined the landmasses into the islands as they are now.

devo-062.title: Tiktaalik bridges fishes and four-legged animals
devo-062.text: Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish with many tetrapod-like features, lived about 375 million years ago; its fossils come from Frasnian rocks in Nunavut, Canada. It bridges fishes such as Panderichthys, about 380 million years old, and early tetrapods such as Acanthostega. Its group, the elpistostegalians, disappeared at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary. If the older Zachełmie tracks were made by tetrapods, Tiktaalik's lineage was an evolutionary dead end.

devo-063.title: The Cerberean Caldera blows in a supereruption
devo-063.text: The Cerberean Caldera, a giant volcanic collapse crater in what is now Victoria, Australia, is thought to have produced a supereruption about 374 million years ago. Some researchers suggest it was an overlooked contributor to the Kellwasser extinction.

devo-067.title: The Kellwasser event, one of the Big Five extinctions
devo-067.text: At the Frasnian-Famennian boundary, the Kellwasser event, named for Germany's Kellwassertal, struck as one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions. The wider Late Devonian crisis came in pulses from the mid-Givetian to the end of the Famennian and killed about 70% of species. Warm-water reef builders such as stromatoporoid sponges and corals were hit hardest, most remaining jawless fishes died, and every Frasnian tetrapod vanished. Proposed causes include anoxia spread by rising seas, global cooling and nutrient runoff from tree roots, but volcanism is debated and no cause is settled.

devo-064.title: A mantle plume fires up the Dnieper-Donets rift
devo-064.text: A mantle plume drove magmatism in the East European Platform's Dnieper-Donets rift from the late Frasnian, peaking in the Famennian along with the rifting. This Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets igneous province has been linked to the Frasnian-Famennian extinction.

devo-065.title: Seeds appear, freeing plants from the riverbanks
devo-065.text: Seed plants first appear in the Famennian, the last age of the Devonian, and diversified substantially; the earliest seed ferns were Late Devonian lyginopterids. A 385-million-year-old seed-plant precursor from Belgium predates them by about 20 million years. Seeds sped the spread of plants and let them exploit uplands away from river edges. Pollen also first appears in the Late Devonian, though it still looks no different from spores.

devo-066.title: Hyneria, a lobe-finned giant, hunts in murky water
devo-066.text: Hyneria, a predatory lobe-finned fish, hunted the murky fresh waters of the Famennian, finding prey with large sensory canals. Hyneria lindae, the largest and most common lobe-fin of Pennsylvania's Red Hill Shale, reached about 2.5 to 3 m, possibly 3.5 m.

devo-068.title: Big wildfires become a regular event
devo-068.text: By the late Famennian, oxygen had risen high enough for regular, large-scale wildfires for the first time. The first charcoal had appeared back in the Silurian; now fire became a routine part of the landscape.

devo-069.title: Archaeopteris forests spread and cool the planet
devo-069.text: Archaeopteris forests spread rapidly in the Late Devonian, reaching even the coasts of Gondwana. These trees grew to 30 m, and giant Archaeopteris dominated a fairly uniform, low-diversity flora in the Famennian. The trees drew down carbon dioxide, cooling the climate toward the later ice age, part of what is called the 'Late Devonian wood crisis'. Their deepening roots boosted weathering and nutrient runoff, feeding algal blooms that stripped oxygen from deeper waters.

devo-070.title: Cladoselache, the first common shark
devo-070.text: Cladoselache, an early shark, appears about 370 million years ago as the first abundant genus of cartilaginous fish.

devo-072.title: Tree roots turn braided rivers into meanders
devo-072.text: By 370 million years ago, trees such as Archaeopteris bound soils so firmly that rivers changed their form. Rivers that had mostly braided, splitting into many shifting channels, now mostly meandered, flowing in single looping bends.

devo-075.title: Acanthostega and Ichthyostega: fins become legs
devo-075.text: By about 365 million years ago, bony, jointed fins had become legs, and Acanthostega and Ichthyostega were among the earliest vertebrates able to walk. Acanthostega, though, still had gills as well as lungs, and its limbs were too weak to carry it on land. The oldest Late Devonian tetrapod fossils come from Greenland, yet by the period's end tetrapods lived worldwide, even in high-latitude Gondwana. The Late Devonian extinctions squeezed these early tetrapods through two bottlenecks, weeding out the most aquatic forms.

devo-076.title: Tadpole shrimp appear and barely change
devo-076.text: The oldest known notostracan, or tadpole shrimp, is Strudops goldenbergi from Famennian rocks in Belgium, about 365 million years old. Its living relatives Triops and Lepidurus are 'living fossils', with similar forms since the end of the Devonian.

devo-077.title: The Woodleigh impact strikes Western Australia
devo-077.text: The Woodleigh impact structure in Western Australia, 60 to 160 km across, is dated to 364 ± 8 million years ago, between the Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous. Its age roughly matches the Late Devonian extinction.

devo-078.title: Flynn Creek crater forms in a Tennessee sea
devo-078.text: About 360 million years ago, an impactor perhaps 90 to 190 m wide hit a shallow sea in what is now Tennessee. Buried by Chattanooga Sea shales within a few million years, its crater, 3.8 km across and 150 m deep, is among the best-preserved ancient impact structures.

devo-081.title: The Late Paleozoic Ice Age begins
devo-081.text: The Late Paleozoic Ice Age spread large ice sheets over land from the Late Devonian into the Late Permian, roughly 360 to 255 million years ago. Its first glacial episodes came in the late Famennian and the Tournaisian, the first Carboniferous age, as greenhouse gave way to icehouse in steps. Late Devonian glacial deposits lie in Brazil's Solimoes, Amazonas and Paranaiba basins and in Bolivia, then near the South Pole. Carbon buried by plants, together with the uplift of Gondwana, tipped Earth into an icehouse that lasted through the Carboniferous and Permian.

devo-082.title: Waterloo Farm preserves a polar Devonian coast
devo-082.text: Waterloo Farm, near Makhanda in South Africa, holds Famennian fossils about 360 million years old and is southern Gondwana's most important Late Devonian site. The only record of a near-polar coastal ecosystem from the latest Devonian, it has overturned assumptions about life at high latitudes.

devo-080.title: Twin Warburton impacts: proposed, not proven
devo-080.text: Two asteroids about 10 km wide may have struck Australia's West and East Warburton Basins, leaving a 400-km impact zone. The basins have been linked to the Late Devonian extinction, but the craters remain hypothetical.

devo-083.title: The placoderms vanish in the Hangenberg event
devo-083.text: All placoderms died out in the end-Devonian Hangenberg event, and no species is confirmed from the Carboniferous. Already weakened by the Kellwasser event, the last arthrodires, antiarchs, phyllolepids and ptychodontids disappeared abruptly. Their loss opened niches for bony and cartilaginous fishes, which radiated in the Carboniferous.

devo-084.title: The Hangenberg event closes the Devonian
devo-084.text: The Hangenberg event, or end-Devonian extinction, closed the Famennian about 358.9 million years ago, dated by Polish ash beds that bracket its black shale. Most marine and freshwater groups died out or dwindled to a few lineages; one estimate ranks it the fourth-deadliest extinction, though plants were spared. The last placoderms and stromatoporoid sponges vanished, Proetida became the only trilobite order, and the ammonoids barely survived. Severe cooling and glaciation, as the Late Paleozoic Ice Age began, may have driven it, though anoxia, volcanism, ozone loss and even a nearby supernova are also suspects.

devo-086.title: The last armored jawless fishes disappear
devo-086.text: Osteostracans, galeaspids and heterostracans had vanished by the end of the Frasnian, and thelodonts survived barely into the Famennian. The last armored jawless fishes, the ostracoderms, died out at the end of the Devonian.

devo-087.title: Chitinozoans drop out of the record
devo-087.text: Chitinozoans, tiny filter-feeding organisms of the open ocean known only as microfossils, appear to have died out at the end of the Devonian. Rare later finds may be older specimens eroded and redeposited in younger rocks.

carb-006.title: Cordaitales trees crowd into the coal swamps
carb-006.text: Cordaitales, an order of gymnosperms, seed plants with naked seeds, grew in the coal swamps as tall trees, shrubs and mangrove-like thickets. Their lineage lasted from the Carboniferous into the Permian.

carb-007.title: Giant lobe-finned fish rule rivers and lakes
carb-007.text: Lobe-finned fish, named for their fleshy, limb-like fins, were the dominant predators of Carboniferous and Permian fresh waters. The largest known, Rhizodus hibberti from Great Britain, grew up to 6 m long.

carb-008.title: A Scottish shrimp bed preserves a conodont's body
carb-008.text: Conodonts, eel-like animals known mostly from their tiny teeth, rarely fossilize whole. Scotland's Granton Shrimp Bed preserves Clydagnathus windsorensis, one of only three conodont species known with its trunk.

carb-009.title: Siberia rams Kazakhstania and raises the Altai
carb-009.text: Siberia, an independent continent since the early Paleozoic, collided with Kazakhstania and pushed up the Altai Mountains, while the closing Turkestan Ocean shoved northern Tarim against Kazakhstania. With Kazakhstania joined to Laurussia, Siberia was effectively part of Pangaea by 310 Ma, though the blocks kept sliding past each other into the Permian.

carb-002.title: A tiny conodont marks where the Carboniferous begins
carb-002.text: Geologists fix the start of the Carboniferous at La Serre in Montagne Noire, southern France, where the conodont Siphonodella sulcata first appears. Later study found that species below the boundary too, which weakens the marker.

carb-004.title: Tetrapods split into two lines and settle on land
carb-004.text: By the very start of the Carboniferous, four-limbed vertebrates, or tetrapods, had split into two lines with living descendants. One led to modern amphibians; the other led to amniotes, animals whose eggs can survive on dry land. The earliest confirmed land-dwelling tetrapods come from early Carboniferous rocks, some 20 million years after the first Devonian forms. Lineages with extra digits died out, fixing hands and feet at five digits or fewer, and the survivors became the dominant land animals of the Carboniferous and Permian.

carb-012.title: Romer's gap: a missing chapter in the tetrapod story
carb-012.text: After the Hangenberg extinction closed the Devonian, tetrapod fossils grow strikingly scarce from the Tournaisian into the early Visean, a stretch called Romer's gap. Finds at Blue Beach, Nova Scotia, and in Scotland now show stem tetrapods and amphibians recovering and diversifying rapidly in that hidden interval.

carb-014.title: Tropical seas build the limestone of Britain and Ireland
carb-014.text: Warm, shallow tropical seas laid down limestone across Britain and Ireland, built from corals, clam-like brachiopods and crinoids, or sea lilies, set in carbonate mud. Uplifted long afterward, the rock now forms karst, a landscape of caves and gorges dissolved out of limestone, in the Mendips and the Yorkshire Dales.

carb-003.title: Sea lilies carpet the Mississippian sea floor
carb-003.text: Camerate crinoids, stalked sea lilies related to starfish, peaked in diversity in the Mississippian, and some limestones near Clitheroe, England, consist almost entirely of their remains. Their variety fell from the Middle Mississippian onward as shell-crushing fish and sharks multiplied.

carb-010.title: The last cladoxylopsid trees fall
carb-010.text: Cladoxylopsids, large trees on the ancestral line of ferns, make their last appearance in the Early Carboniferous. Their lineage, including the order Pseudosporochnales, had stood since the Devonian.

carb-013.title: Sharks and ray-finned fish take over the seas
carb-013.text: After the Hangenberg extinction closed the Devonian, sharks and their kin and ray-finned fish took over the oceans in both diversity and abundance. Few Devonian species of either group survived, and no placoderm, the armored fish of the Devonian, is confirmed in the Carboniferous. Cartilaginous fish radiated, especially holocephalans such as the stethacanthids, and helicoprionids appeared with a single circular whorl of teeth in the lower jaw. The first large sharks, ratfishes and hagfish show up around 350 Ma.

carb-015.title: A warm spell follows the Devonian's final chill
carb-015.text: After a brief glaciation at the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary, the climate warmed in the Early Tournaisian Warm Interval. Global average temperature was about 22 °C, with the tropics near 30 °C and the poles at a chilly 1.5 °C.

carb-016.title: Glaciers creep back into South American basins
carb-016.text: By about 350 Ma, glacial layers were building up in basins of Bolivia, Argentina and Paraguay, and a mid-Tournaisian glaciation left species-poor frozen tundra in western Argentina. These short, minor glaciations were early steps in a slow shift from greenhouse to icehouse.

carb-017.title: Temnospondyls arrive to rule the Age of Amphibians
carb-017.text: Temnospondyls, often seen as primitive amphibians, left their first traces as footprints about 350 million years ago. Their oldest body fossils, such as Balanerpeton, date to around 330 Ma, and they went on to flourish worldwide through the Carboniferous, Permian and Triassic. All their branches except the stereospondylomorphs, from edopoids to dissorophoids, appeared during the Carboniferous. Their rise as the dominant land vertebrates gave the period its nickname, the Age of Amphibians.

carb-021.title: Lepidodendron, the giant scale tree, takes root
carb-021.text: Lepidodendron, a massive tree lycophyte and a giant relative of today's club mosses, first appeared near the Tournaisian–Visean boundary. With Sigillaria, it went on to dominate the coal swamps, while horsetails and seed ferns, fern-like plants that bore seeds, grew between the giants. Its order, the Lepidodendrales, lasted from the Carboniferous to the Late Permian.

carb-018.title: Seawater chemistry tips into aragonite seas
carb-018.text: From the early Carboniferous, the ratio of magnesium to calcium in seawater climbed. By the Middle Mississippian, aragonite seas, which favor shells built of the mineral aragonite, had replaced calcite seas. Aragonite reef builders, including algae and sponges, followed in the Pennsylvanian.

carb-020.title: Insects grow wings and take to the sky
carb-020.text: The oldest known winged insects appear in mid-Mississippian rocks, though flight may have evolved even earlier, in the Late Devonian. Across the Carboniferous, winged insects went through a major radiation, dominated by sap-sucking palaeodictyopteroids. By the Pennsylvanian, cockroach relatives had become the most successful insects of all. Neoptera, insects that can fold their wings back, appeared then too, and Miomoptera show the earliest evidence of complete metamorphosis, the passage from larva through pupa to adult.

carb-022.title: Glaciers nearly vanish in the Visean warmth
carb-022.text: During the Visean Warm Interval, glaciers almost disappeared from the planet. They clung on only in the proto-Andes of Bolivia and Argentina and in the highlands of Brazil and southwest Africa.

carb-019.title: Ocean life booms as Pangaea splits the seas
carb-019.text: Beginning in the Visean, alongside the main phase of the ice age, marine life began a long radiation called the Carboniferous–Earliest Permian Biodiversification Event. Fusulinids, shell-building single-celled foraminifera, led it with brachiopods; they diversified extremely fast, and some later grew giant and hosted photosynthetic algae. The closing Rheic Ocean, falling sea level and Pangaea's assembly split the oceans into isolated regions, which may have driven the boom. Bryozoans, tiny colonial filter feeders, also peaked in the Visean, while cephalopods and swimming conodonts declined.

carb-023.title: East Kirkton opens a window on early land life
carb-023.text: The East Kirkton quarry in Scotland preserves dozens of early tetrapods from about 341 Ma, among them the temnospondyl Balanerpeton and the proto-amniote Westlothiana, nicknamed 'Lizzie'. Scorpions and eurypterids, or sea scorpions, lived alongside them, and the mostly land-dwelling fauna reflects a wider Carboniferous shift away from amphibious life.

carb-024.title: Gondwana rams Laurussia in the Variscan collision
carb-024.text: Gondwana and a fringe of smaller crustal blocks struck Laurussia at an angle, crumpling, heating and melting rock along the join; full collision came around 340 Ma. Geologists call this mountain-building collision, or orogeny, the Variscan in Europe and the Alleghanian in North America, but it was a single continental crash. Its main squeeze, from about 330 to 320 Ma, drove Hercynian granites into central Europe. Together the two raised the Central Pangean Mountains, which reached their greatest height by about 295 Ma.

carb-025.title: The continents fuse into Pangaea
carb-025.text: Around 335 million years ago, Gondwana, Euramerica and Siberia came together as the supercontinent Pangaea, and the Rheic Ocean that divided Gondwana from Laurussia closed. Plate motions sped up as it assembled, and Pangaea endured about 160 million years, until its breakup began around 175 Ma. Its glacial deposits, scattered from South America to Australia, later helped prove that continents drift. Some sources date Pangaea's full assembly closer to 300 million years ago.

carb-026.title: Reptiliomorphs branch off toward the amniotes
carb-026.text: The first reptiliomorphs, tetrapods on the branch that leads to amniotes, appear between 335 and 325 Ma. By the Visean, early tetrapods had already split into at least three or four main branches, and the reptile-like Westlothiana lived then.

carb-027.title: Ice sheets kilometers thick bury southern Gondwana
carb-027.text: In the late Visean, as the climate cooled and carbon dioxide fell, the main phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age began, dropping sea level worldwide. Ice spread from up to 30 centers across Gondwana, and around 330 Ma a sheet kilometers thick buried much of Africa over the South Pole. Glacial periods millions of years long alternated with warmer spells, and the harshest phase came late in the Pennsylvanian. The ice left deposits 1,000 m thick in southern Africa's Dwyka Formation and 1,400 m thick in Brazil's Itararé Group.

carb-031.title: Gondwana's South American edge raises the Ouachitas
carb-031.text: Beginning in the Late Mississippian, the South American part of Gondwana struck the southern margin of Laurussia at an angle in the Ouachita orogeny. The uplifted Ouachita Mountains created foreland basins, troughs that sink in front of a rising range, such as the Delaware Basin. Rivers draining the new mountains carried their sediment through the Pennsylvanian and Permian.

carb-032.title: Chilled seas bring the Serpukhovian extinction
carb-032.text: Early in the Serpukhovian, the largest extinction of the Carboniferous wiped out about 31% of marine genera. A major glaciation at the Visean–Serpukhovian boundary chilled the seas and picked off species adapted to narrow tropical temperature ranges. Rich crinoid and coral communities gave way to species-poor ones spread worldwide, and the long-term ecological damage may have exceeded that of the end-Ordovician extinction. Its severity is still debated: a 2026 study finds it weaker in North America, and sources disagree over whether diversity then stagnated or surged.

carb-030.title: Deltas spread the Millstone Grit across northern England
carb-030.text: With Britain near the equator, rivers carried sand and mud into the Pennine Basin, and when growing southern ice caps lowered the sea, deltas advanced across the region. Their thick sandstones, the Millstone Grit, now form the edges and moors of the Pennines and the Peak District.

carb-029.title: Avion yields the earliest known thrips
carb-029.text: The Avion fossil site in Pas-de-Calais, France, preserves the earliest known thrips, tiny plant-feeding insects, along with the earliest titanopterans, an extinct order of insects.

carb-033.title: Amniotes evolve an egg that survives on dry land
carb-033.text: One tetrapod lineage wrapped its embryos in protective membranes, so its eggs could survive on dry land: the amniotes. Timelines place the first amniotes around 330 Ma, with Paleothyris among the earliest, but their true origin is disputed. Clawed footprints from Australia's Snowy Plains Formation, claimed as amniote tracks, would push it back to the start of the Carboniferous or even earlier. Amphibians ruled until the mid-Carboniferous, when climate change cut their diversity and amniotes took over.

carb-034.title: Patagonia first nudges against Gondwana
carb-034.text: Igneous rocks of 330–320 Ma under the North Patagonian Massif show that subduction, one plate sinking beneath another, began there in the early Carboniferous. Subduction lasted about 20 million years, and the Patagonian landmass first touched Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous, though the broader collision came in the early Permian.

carb-036.title: Glasgow's Fossil Grove: a forest buried standing
carb-036.text: About 325 Ma, sediment buried a stand of Lepidodendron trees in what is now Glasgow while they were still upright. Scotland then lay in the tropics, near the equator.

carb-035.title: Africa and North America collide to build the Appalachians
carb-035.text: Starting about 325 Ma, Africa, then part of Gondwana, ground into North America in at least five separate bouts of deformation. The collision built the Appalachian and Allegheny Mountains, a wide, high chain along today's eastern seaboard, and lasted some 65 million years, into the Permian. The crash helped weld Pangaea together, and sediment from the rising peaks filled basins such as the Black Warrior Basin. When West Africa struck in the Late Pennsylvanian, the same grinding raised the Little Atlas range around 300 Ma.

carb-037.title: Montana's Bear Gulch teems with shark relatives
carb-037.text: The Bear Gulch Limestone of central Montana preserves an unusually diverse fauna of cartilaginous fish, relatives of sharks, rays and chimaeras. Brachiopods, ray-finned fish, arthropods and the puzzling Typhloesus, possibly a mollusk, lived there too.

carb-040.title: Arrow Canyon, Nevada, marks the Pennsylvanian's start
carb-040.text: The base of the Pennsylvanian and its first stage, the Bashkirian, is fixed at Arrow Canyon, Nevada. The marker is the first appearance of the conodont Declinognathodus noduliferus.

carb-050.title: The first great glacial maximum drops sea level worldwide
carb-050.text: From the Serpukhovian to the Moscovian, ice sheets spread from cores in southern Africa and South America in the ice age's first major glacial period. In the Bashkirian, a worldwide fall in sea level marked its first great glacial maximum, matched by glacial deposits across southern Gondwana. The low seas left an unconformity, a gap in the rock record, that separates the Mississippian from the Pennsylvanian in North America. Early in the Bashkirian, the closing gateway between the Rheic and Tethys oceans changed ocean circulation and added to the cooling.

carb-038.title: Every modern class of fungi is in place
carb-038.text: By the late Carboniferous, all the modern classes of fungi had appeared, as rocks of Pennsylvanian age show.

carb-039.title: Coal forests pump the air full of oxygen
carb-039.text: Every model shows oxygen climbing from 15–20% of the air at the start of the Carboniferous to highs of 25–30%, well above today's 21%. Records from pyrite, the mineral called fool's gold, suggest over 25% in the Pennsylvanian before a drop below 20% near the period's end. The coal forests drove the rise, releasing oxygen as they grew and burying carbon as peat, while charcoal from wildfires grew more common. How far the oxygen-rich air let arthropods and other life grow large is still debated.

carb-041.title: Carbon dioxide crashes to one of its lowest levels ever
carb-041.text: In the Pennsylvanian and early Permian, atmospheric carbon dioxide fell below 300 parts per million (ppm), one of its lowest levels ever. Buried organic matter, oxygen-starved oceans, fast-growing coal forests and the weathering of the rising Central Pangean Mountains all drew it down, cooling the climate and spreading glaciers. Near the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, erosion of iron- and magnesium-rich mountain rock pushed it as low as 175 ppm, and it stayed under 400 ppm for 10 million years. From a record low about 298 million years ago, carbon dioxide then rose fourfold by 294 million years ago.

carb-042.title: The Central Pangean Mountains summon monsoon rains
carb-042.text: The Central Pangean Mountains set up a year-round monsoon over today's Europe and eastern North America, keeping them swampy while the Colorado Plateau stayed dry. Climate models suggest the range helped lay down vast coal deposits.

carb-043.title: Cimmerian blocks start to tear away from Gondwana
carb-043.text: Rifting between India and the Cimmerian blocks began in the Early Carboniferous, and late in the period these crustal slivers started leaving Gondwana's northern edge. Their departure would open the Neo-Tethys Ocean in the early Permian, and they would dock with Asia in the Triassic and Jurassic.

carb-044.title: Swamp forests bury the carbon that becomes coal
carb-044.text: Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land in the late Carboniferous, and their towering lycopsids marked the high point of Paleozoic land plants. Their buried peat became coal: about 90% of all coal beds formed in the Carboniferous and Permian, just 2% of Earth's history. Glacial sea-level falls exposed wide shelves where peat mires spread, and rising seas between glaciations buried them. Why coal peaked is debated: either fungi that digest wood's lignin had yet to evolve, or equatorial land, high productivity and sinking wet basins combined uniquely.

carb-045.title: Cyclothems record the pulse of distant ice sheets
carb-045.text: Across tropical Laurussia and the China blocks, shallow seas laid down cyclothems, repeating stacks of sediment that each record a sea-level fall and rise over about 100,000 years. Gondwana's ice sheets grew slowly and melted fast on a Milankovitch cycle, set by regular shifts in Earth's orbit, swinging sea level by up to 120 m.

carb-046.title: The heart of Pangaea begins to dry out
carb-046.text: Toward the end of the Carboniferous, Pangaea's equatorial belt grew drier, beginning a trend that would last into the Triassic. After about 318 Ma, seasons swung often between humid and arid, and from the late Moscovian a cycle of drying brought abrupt changes in animal life. Late Pennsylvanian soils record drier, better-drained and more stable landscapes. Across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, falling carbon dioxide and low-latitude aridity made the shift to seasonally dry woodland permanent.

carb-047.title: Conifers and cycads claim the drier uplands
carb-047.text: Cycads, Voltziales conifers and Callistophytales seed ferns appeared in the late Carboniferous, and ginkgophytes also arose in the period. Early conifers such as Walchia favored higher, drier ground, and the oldest probable cycad leaves, such as Crossozamia from South Korea and China, date to around 300 Ma.

carb-049.title: Arthropleura and Meganeura: the age of giant arthropods
carb-049.text: Arachnids, myriapods such as millipedes, and above all flying insects went through a major radiation in the late Carboniferous. The millipede-like Arthropleura, up to 2.6 m long, was the largest land invertebrate of all time. The griffinfly Meganeura, with a wingspan of about 75 cm, was the largest flying insect ever and dominated the skies around 305 Ma. These giants thrived while tetrapods stayed small, until the rainforest collapse; high oxygen may explain their size, though that idea is debated.

carb-051.title: The crust tears open at the Oslo Rift
carb-051.text: Around today's Oslo, the crust began to tear apart in the late Carboniferous, in the last phase of the Variscan orogeny. The rifting coincided with the rainforest collapse and culminated in heavy volcanism, piling rhomb porphyry lavas about 3,000 m thick in Vestfold.

carb-052.title: The Ural Mountains begin to rise
carb-052.text: About 323 Ma, as the Ural Ocean began to close, Kazakhstania started colliding with Laurussia and the Uralian orogeny began. Siberia, Kazakhstania and Baltica eventually merged into Laurasia, the foundation of most of present-day Eurasia. Deformation and granite intrusions carried on into the Permian, and around 300 Ma the Urals rose as Pangaea was finally stitched together. One source dates the orogeny's start to the Late Devonian, when the Magnitogorsk island arc, a chain of volcanic islands, was already colliding with Baltica.

carb-053.title: Amniotes split into the mammal and reptile lines
carb-053.text: Amniotes divided into two great lines: synapsids, which would lead to mammals, and sauropsids, which would lead to reptiles and birds. Timelines place the first sauropsids around 320 Ma and the first synapsids around 318 Ma, though the oldest fossils of both are about 313 million years old. Pelycosaurs, the early synapsids, appeared in the Late Carboniferous and went on to dominate the land for some 40 million years. By the period's end, amniotes had branched into pelycosaur families, protorothyridids, captorhinids, saurians and araeoscelids.

carb-057.title: Glaciers start filling the Karoo Basin
carb-057.text: Subduction and the rising Gondwanide mountains made room for the Karoo Basin across southern Africa, which then lay inside the Antarctic Circle. Ice sheets buried the surrounding highlands and floating glaciers filled its lowlands, leaving the Dwyka Group, about 800 m thick in the south.

carb-060.title: Joggins yields Hylonomus, one of the oldest reptiles
carb-060.text: The Joggins Fossil Cliffs of Nova Scotia preserve a diverse land ecosystem of lycopsids, giant arthropods and fish. Among its creatures is Hylonomus, the oldest known sauropsid and one of the oldest reptiles in the fossil record.

carb-062.title: The Kiaman superchron: a magnetic field stuck in reverse
carb-062.text: From about 312 to 262 Ma, Earth's magnetic field held reversed polarity, its poles swapped from today's, without a single flip for more than 50 million years. Geologists call such a long spell a superchron, and the Kiaman ran from the late Carboniferous into the late Permian. Comparable spells are the Cretaceous Normal Superchron and a possible one in the Ordovician.

carb-065.title: Mazon Creek seals a delta's life in ironstone
carb-065.text: Near Morris, Illinois, a large delta sealed fossils in ironstone nodules in exceptional detail, including the enigmatic Tullimonstrum, known from nowhere else. Its roughly 200 insect species, some gigantic, show that insects already filled their main modern roles as plant-eaters, scavengers and insect-eaters.

carb-067.title: A brief, fierce glaciation strikes in the Kasimovian
carb-067.text: Early in the Kasimovian, a short but intense glaciation, lasting less than a million years, drove carbon dioxide as low as 180 ppm. It ended abruptly as carbon dioxide climbed again, but only after the wetland forests had been reshaped and the tree lycopsids lost.

carb-066.title: The Alykaevo Climatic Optimum brings a warm reprieve
carb-066.text: A relatively warm interglacial, the Alykaevo Climatic Optimum, spanned the Kasimovian and Gzhelian. It separated the ice age's first and second major glacial periods.

carb-071.title: The Carboniferous rainforests collapse
carb-071.text: Around 305 Ma, a cooler, drier climate broke the coal-forest rainforests into fragments and then collapsed them. Tree lycopsids largely vanished from North America and Europe, replaced by tree-fern forests, though they held on in Cathaysia. Amphibians and amniotes were both hit, and the collapse may have let amniotes overtake amphibians, and seed plants overtake ferns and lycophytes. Only a minor extinction on land and at sea, it nonetheless left vast deserts across the continental interior.

carb-072.title: Petrolacosaurus and the first diapsid reptiles
carb-072.text: The first diapsids, reptiles with two openings in the skull behind each eye, appear around 305 Ma, among them Petrolacosaurus. By the end of the Carboniferous, saurians and araeoscelids were among several new amniote groups.

carb-074.title: The Ancestral Rocky Mountains rise and wear away
carb-074.text: Around 300 Ma, mountain building raised the Ancestral Rocky Mountains across what are now Colorado and New Mexico, with a prong reaching into Wyoming. The same Colorado orogeny began the Denver Basin, but the range itself later eroded away.

carb-075.title: Hamilton Quarry mixes sea, river and land life
carb-075.text: Hamilton Quarry in Kansas preserves a probable estuary, where a river met the sea. Its well-preserved fossils mix marine, brackish, freshwater, flying and land animals and plants.

carb-076.title: The ice age reaches its frozen peak
carb-076.text: Around 300 Ma, an exceptionally intense cooling put a very large part of Gondwana under glacial conditions. A second major glacial period began in the late Gzhelian, with ice sheets spreading from cores in Australia and India into the early Permian. The ice age peaked across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, and during the glacial maximum, 299–293 Ma, global average temperature stood at about 13 °C. Brazil's Paraná Basin, by contrast, saw its last glaciation in the early Gzhelian.

carb-077.title: Montceau-les-Mines, France's answer to Mazon Creek
carb-077.text: This French site preserves late Carboniferous vertebrates, arthropods and plants in exceptional detail, much like Mazon Creek, from temnospondyls to velvet worms and arachnids.

perm-005.title: Glossopteris forests spread across Gondwana
perm-005.text: Glossopteridales, an extinct order of seed plants, came to dominate large parts of the south once Gondwana had fused into Pangaea, led by the tree Glossopteris. As glaciation waned in the Middle Permian, the Glossopteris flora flourished and laid down huge coal deposits, as in southern Brazil and Uruguay. These forests collapsed in the end-Permian mass extinction.

perm-006.title: The Gondwanide orogeny crumples southern Gondwana
perm-006.text: Mountain building in the Permian deformed southern Gondwana, across what are now southern South America, South Africa, Antarctica, Australia and New Guinea. Its folds survive in Argentina's Sierra de la Ventana and South Africa's Cape Fold Belt. Uplift linked to it split Brazil's Paraná Basin in two. In South Africa, folding entered a new phase from about 260 Ma, after the ice sheets had melted and a great lake, the Karoo Sea, had spread.

perm-008.title: The lizard lineage goes its own way
perm-008.text: Sometime in the Permian, the lepidosauromorphs, the line of lizards and their kin, are thought to have split from their sister group. That sister group, the archelosaurs, would lead to turtles, crocodiles and birds.

perm-013.title: Pangaea stands complete, from equator to poles
perm-013.text: During the Permian, almost every major landmass gathered into Pangaea, a single supercontinent that stretched from the equator to both polar regions. Gondwana's collision with the northern continents completed its bulk, leaving the Appalachian–Ouachita mountains near its center. Kazakhstania struck Baltica in the Cisuralian, Siberia joined in the late Permian, and North China, South China and Indochina fused on by the period's end. The supercontinent was complete roughly 20 million years before the end-Permian extinction.

perm-014.title: A megamonsoon grips the supercontinent
perm-014.text: Permian climate was fiercely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons, monsoons on a continental scale, that brought harsh seasons and deep aridity to Pangaea's interior. Early Permian wind directions preserved in the rocks record a summer wet season. As the continents drifted north and spread more evenly across the equator, the megamonsoon grew stronger. Dryness broken by seasonal rain became the normal climate across much of the continent.

perm-001.title: A Kazakh river valley marks the Permian's start
perm-001.text: The Permian begins with the first appearance of the conodont Streptognathodus isolatus. Its reference section lies in the Aidaralash River valley near Aqtöbe, Kazakhstan.

perm-007.title: Insects diversify and modern orders appear
perm-007.text: Insects diversified dramatically in the Early Permian, and most living insect orders arose during the period. Insects with complete metamorphosis radiated, and scorpionflies, true dragonflies and barklice made their first appearance. The old dominant groups, the palaeodictyopterans and giant griffinflies, declined, a fall linked to a change in plant life. Insects and plants were already locked in an arms race of chewed leaves and plant defenses.

perm-012.title: Cimmeria breaks away and the Neo-Tethys opens
perm-012.text: In the Early Permian, rifting along northern Gondwana broke off the Cimmerian blocks, including Sibumasu, Qiantang and Lhasa. As they drifted toward Laurasia, the Neo-Tethys Ocean opened behind them and the Paleo-Tethys closed ahead. The new ocean began as a rift in what is now the Himalayan region and would dominate much of the Mesozoic.

perm-015.title: Patagonia completes its collision with Gondwana
perm-015.text: The Patagonian landmass, which first touched southwestern Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous, collided more broadly in the early Permian. Deformation and metamorphism, the remaking of rock by heat and pressure, continued through the Permian.

perm-017.title: Pelycosaurs rule the Early Permian land
perm-017.text: Pelycosaurs peaked in the Cisuralian and were the dominant land animals for some 40 million years. Plant-eating edaphosaurids and meat-eating sphenacodontids led the faunas of North America and Europe, alongside diadectids and amphibians. Synapsids, the group that later gave rise to mammals, diversified greatly and quickly grew large. A few pelycosaurs lingered long after their heyday; the youngest known, from South Africa, is about 260 million years old.

perm-018.title: The Urals rise as Kazakhstania meets Baltica
perm-018.text: During the Cisuralian, the Kazakhstania block collided with Baltica. The Uralian orogeny built the Ural Mountains through the Permian, continuing deformation that had begun in the Carboniferous. Molten rock rose and cooled into granites across the region.

perm-019.title: Carbon dioxide quadruples after a record low
perm-019.text: Atmospheric carbon dioxide hit a record low about 298 Ma, then quadrupled by 294 Ma. Stunted plants and oxygen-fed fires returned carbon dioxide to the air, while rising seas drowned the carbon-burying coal swamps, so more stayed aloft and warmed the planet.

perm-021.title: The Skagerrak volcanic province floods northern Europe
perm-021.text: At 297 ± 4 Ma, a large igneous province, a vast outpouring of volcanic rock, erupted around today's Skagerrak strait. It covered at least 0.5 million km², including the Oslo and Skagerrak rift valleys, southwestern Sweden, Scotland, northern England and the central North Sea. It was the oldest province tied to the African superplume, a hot mantle upwelling, followed by Bachu, Emeishan, the Siberian Traps and the Central Atlantic. Together with Siberia's Barguzin-Vitim province, it is linked to the Moscovian and Kasimovian stages of the rainforest collapse, about 310–296 Ma.

perm-022.title: The Central Pangean Mountains rival the Himalayas
perm-022.text: Raised where Euramerica collided with northern Gondwana, the Central Pangean Mountains reached their greatest height in the early Permian, rivaling today's Himalayas. Lying along the equator, the range cast a rain shadow that turned northern coal swamps into seasonally dry land and later helped Europe's Zechstein salt deposits form. Weathering cut the peaks to about half their height by the Late Permian, spreading their debris across Europe as sandstone and conglomerate, a rock of cemented pebbles. Their worn-down remnants include the Appalachian and Ouachita Mountains, the Atlas and the Bohemian Massif.

perm-023.title: Dimetrodon appears among the pelycosaurs
perm-023.text: The pelycosaur Dimetrodon evolved about 295 Ma, as its group diversified. Its remains turn up at Bromacker in Germany and in the Red Beds of Texas.

perm-024.title: The first beetles appear
perm-024.text: The first beetles appeared near the start of the Permian, about 295 Ma, beginning one of the four great insect radiations. By the Late Permian, Archostemata, Adephaga and probably Polyphaga, today's most diverse beetle group, were all present.

perm-028.title: An impact scars Latvia at Dobele
perm-028.text: An impact blasted a 4.5 km crater at Dobele, Latvia, about 290 ± 35 million years ago, in the Cisuralian.

perm-029.title: The Panjal Traps flood northwest India with lava
perm-029.text: The Panjal Traps, a large igneous province, erupted in what is now northwestern India; zircon crystals date them to 289 ± 2 Ma. Their lavas, up to 2,500 m thick in Ladakh and Kashmir, may once have covered over 200,000 square km, comparable to the Emeishan Traps. The eruptions are tied to the opening of the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which carried the Cimmerian blocks away from Gondwana's northeastern margin. Some sources once placed them at the Capitanian or end-Permian extinctions, but the zircon age makes them far older; the Siberian Traps are the better suspect.

perm-030.title: The Artinskian warming drives back the polar ice
perm-030.text: By 287 Ma, the Artinskian Warming Event had pushed the south polar ice cap back, leaving glaciers only in the uplands of eastern Australia. Around 285.1 Ma, orbital cycles stopped driving glacial growth and began driving oxygen-starved seas and drought instead, the turning point from icehouse to greenhouse.

perm-031.title: An impact gouges the Clearwater West crater in Quebec
perm-031.text: In the Early Permian, an impact in Quebec, Canada, blasted the 36 km Clearwater West crater, whose central peak rose when the walls collapsed and the floor rebounded. Its neighbor, Clearwater East, is far older at about 460–470 Ma, proof that adjacent craters need not be twins.

perm-032.title: The Choiyoi volcanoes blanket western Gondwana
perm-032.text: From about 286 to 247 Ma, volcanoes fed by subduction along Gondwana's western margin built the Choiyoi province in today's Argentina and Chile. Its lavas and volcanic ash deposits cover at least 200,000 and probably 500,000 square km, stacked 2–4 km thick. During the Permian, the line of volcanoes migrated 350 km inland, reaching San Rafael about 280 Ma. Some researchers suggest it was an added cause of the end-Permian extinction.

perm-034.title: Mesosaurs leave the oldest amniote embryos
perm-034.text: The Mangrullo Formation of Brazil and Uruguay is rich in mesosaurs, small swimming reptiles, and holds the earliest known amniote embryos. Mesosaurus also turns up in Permian black shales of Brazil's Paraná Basin, alongside coals made by Glossopteris forests.

perm-035.title: Cooling returns in the late Kungurian
perm-035.text: Cooling returned in the late Kungurian, as weathering of freshly erupted volcanic provinces drew down carbon dioxide. The resulting cool interval lasted into the early Capitanian, though temperatures stayed far above those of the early Cisuralian and Australia's P3 glaciation was largely alpine.

perm-038.title: The first Bennettitales sprout in northern China
perm-038.text: The oldest confirmed fossils of the Bennettitales, an extinct group of seed plants, are leaves from Shanxi, China, about 281 million years old. Their oldest reproductive structures, the flower-like Williamsonia, come from the Early Triassic of Australia, and the group became prominent only in the Late Triassic.

perm-039.title: The Ternovka impact leaves a buried crater in Ukraine
perm-039.text: About 280 ± 10 Ma, in the Early or Middle Permian, an impact left the Ternovka crater, 11 km across and now buried, at Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine.

perm-040.title: Sand dunes march across the Grand Canyon region
perm-040.text: About 275 Ma, the Grand Canyon region dried out and wind piled quartz sand into large dunes, now the Coconino Sandstone. Its layers are famous for trackways of scorpion-like arthropods and early tetrapods crossing a desert typical of Pangaea's interior.

perm-041.title: Therapsids split off on the road to mammals
perm-041.text: Around 275 million years ago, therapsids, the synapsid line that leads to mammals, split from the pelycosaurs. No confirmed therapsid fossils come from the Early Permian, so the group's early history is a long ghost lineage, inferred but unseen. Raranimus, from the early Middle Permian of China, is probably the earliest-branching therapsid known. Accounts differ on when all the major therapsid groups had appeared: by 275 million years ago, or only by 265 million.

perm-043.title: Ceratitid ammonoids emerge and ride out a crisis
perm-043.text: Ceratitid ammonoids, coiled-shell relatives of squid, arose in the Middle Permian and passed through the Capitanian extinction little harmed. They went on to dominate Late Permian ammonoids as goniatitids declined, and would include almost all Triassic ammonoid genera.

perm-045.title: The Capitan Reef crowns the age of Permian reefs
perm-045.text: Reef building peaked in the Guadalupian, with reefs from the Delaware and Zechstein basins to the Tethys and the cool shelves of Panthalassa. Texas's Capitan Reef, the best-known, was built mainly by calcareous sponges and encrusting algae rather than corals. Curving around the Delaware Basin and perhaps rising 61–91 m above the seafloor, it is called the world's best-preserved Paleozoic reef complex. Later, as tectonics restricted the Hovey Channel, rising heat and salinity killed the reef.

perm-047.title: Therapsids take over from the pelycosaurs
perm-047.text: In the Guadalupian, therapsids, the advanced synapsids on the line toward mammals, replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large land animals, a role they kept into the Early Triassic. The takeover came as the world grew drier, though a poor fossil record across 'Olson's Gap' hides how it unfolded. Giant dinocephalians, both plant- and meat-eaters, dominated Middle Permian South Africa and Russia, regions linked by coastal swamp corridors along East Pangaea. Therocephalians arose too and took over the saber-toothed predator niche.

perm-046.title: Sea level sinks to a Paleozoic low
perm-046.text: After standing several tens of meters above today's level through the Early Permian, the sea began a sharp fall in the Roadian. By the Wuchiapingian it had reached the lowest level of the whole Paleozoic, near today's, a retreat that may be tied to the formation of Pangaea.

perm-048.title: Olson's Extinction thins out the pelycosaurs
perm-048.text: Around 273 Ma, long before the end-Permian crisis, most pelycosaur lineages vanished in a proposed event called Olson's Extinction. Edaphosaurids and ophiacodontids died out while caseids and therapsids diversified, and afterward temnospondyl amphibians declined sharply. Extreme heat and acidic waters in Kansas coincide with it, pointing to climate change as a possible cause. Some authors call it an artifact of poor sampling or gradual change, though one review found the turnover real, and the timing of 'Olson's Gap' is still contested.

perm-050.title: Saber-toothed gorgonopsians appear
perm-050.text: Saber-toothed gorgonopsians first evolved about 270 Ma and lasted until about 252 Ma. The oldest identifiable one, Phorcys, dates to about the Wordian–Capitanian boundary, but other finds show the group already diversifying by the early Wordian. Small at first, with skulls 10–15 cm long, they grew to bear-like sizes; Inostrancevia reached 3.5 m and about 300 kg. Once the Capitanian extinction removed the dinocephalians, gorgonopsians became the top predators.

perm-051.title: The Hunter–Bowen orogeny squeezes eastern Australia
perm-051.text: In the Permian and Triassic, volcanic island arcs were welded onto about 2,500 km of eastern Australia's continental margin. Pangaea's counterclockwise rotation drove squeezing and sideways shearing along the subduction zone there. Major contraction came about 270–260 Ma and around 253 Ma, with a later phase about 235–230 Ma. In front of the rising belt, the Sydney–Bowen basins filled with sediment that built vast coal deposits.

perm-055.title: Carbon isotopes record a Capitanian chill
perm-055.text: Capitanian limestones record a rise in carbon-13, a heavier form of carbon, that reflects a cooling of global climate.
