The cooling may have caused the end-Capitanian extinction of warm-water species such as large fusulinids, alatoconchid bivalves and waagenophyllids, a family of rugose corals.

perm-056.title: The Capitanian extinction hits reefs and dinocephalians
perm-056.text: An extinction began around 262 Ma and peaked around 259 Ma, closing the Capitanian and the Middle Permian. It wiped out about 33–35% of marine genera and 60–63% of marine species, hitting ammonoids, corals, reef algae, foraminifera, bryozoans and brachiopods hardest. On land the dinocephalians and the last varanopids vanished, and the diversity of plant-eating anomodonts halved. Scientists link it to the Emeishan eruptions and a falling sea, but its severity is still debated: some see only a regional crisis or a gradual decline.

perm-057.title: The Emeishan Traps pour lava across southwest China
perm-057.text: Flood basalts, lava erupted in vast sheets, began pouring out in southwestern China 265 Ma or earlier, peaked between 262 and 261 Ma and ended about 259 Ma. The Emeishan basalts cover more than 250,000 km², up to 5.5 km thick, with a volume of about 300,000 km³, yet the later Siberian Traps dwarfed them. The eruptions had global ecological impact and are tied to the Capitanian mass extinction. Around 260 Ma a warming spike, the Emeishan Thermal Excursion, interrupted a cool spell; afterward, weathering of the basalt drew down carbon dioxide and cooled the early Wuchiapingian.

perm-060.title: Cynodonts, the ancestors of mammals, appear
perm-060.text: Cynodonts, the therapsid group ancestral to mammals, first appeared about 260 Ma, in the Late Permian, and spread worldwide. The earliest known, Charassognathus, comes from the Wuchiapingian, and cynodonts are the only major therapsid group with no Middle Permian record. They diversified rapidly after the end-Permian extinction.

perm-064.title: The sea retreats and the age of reefs ends
perm-064.text: The Guadalupian–Lopingian boundary, dated by volcanic ash to 259.857 ± 0.084 Ma, coincided with one of the Phanerozoic's most prominent falls in sea level. Across the boundary, salt beds and land deposits lie over marine carbonate rocks, and a vast unconformity marks it in strata worldwide. Falling seas and swinging salinity ended the golden age of reef building in the end-Guadalupian reef crisis. Disaster taxa, opportunists that flourish after a crisis, had rebuilt global diversity late in the Guadalupian, but it dropped again in the Wuchiapingian.

perm-067.title: The last callistophytalean seed ferns vanish
perm-067.text: Callistophytales, seed ferns whose coal forests had once covered South China, make their last appearance in the Wuchiapingian.

perm-063.title: Beaked dicynodonts and hulking pareiasaurs flourish
perm-063.text: Late Permian lands belonged to advanced therapsids, the saber-toothed gorgonopsians and beaked, plant-eating dicynodonts, alongside large herbivorous reptiles called pareiasaurs. Dicynodonts flourished after the Capitanian extinction and became among the most successful therapsids, surviving almost to the end of the Triassic. South Africa's Beaufort Group was then a semi-arid cold steppe, crossed by seasonal rivers draining into the Karoo Sea.

perm-065.title: Archosauromorphs, the future dinosaur line, appear
perm-065.text: Archosauromorphs, the reptile line that would later produce crocodile relatives, dinosaurs and pterosaurs, first appeared and diversified in the Late Permian. A molecular estimate, based on DNA differences, puts the split between turtles and the line of birds and crocodilians at about 255 Ma. A marine group of ichthyosauromorphs, sauropterygians and thalattosaurs, all later sea reptiles, may also have sprung from archosauromorphs at this time. After the end-Permian extinction, archosauromorphs exploded in diversity.

perm-066.title: Weigeltisaurids glide between Late Permian trees
perm-066.text: Weigeltisaurids, lizard-like reptiles with extendable wings like those of modern gliding lizards, are the oldest known gliding vertebrates. Their worldwide spread shows that tall, thin forests had become widespread by the Late Permian.

perm-069.title: Pangaea's first cracks open along the future Atlantic
perm-069.text: From the latest Permian, the crust began stretching along the line of the future Central Atlantic, opening north–south rift valleys from central Europe to eastern Canada. Pangaea's breakup can loosely be traced back to this time, about 252 Ma.

perm-071.title: The Kupferschiefer: a black shale rich in copper
perm-071.text: About 257 Ma, oxygen-starved water in the enclosed Zechstein basin laid down the Kupferschiefer, a black shale with up to 30% organic matter. Though usually only 30–60 cm thick, it spans 600,000 square km and holds one of the world's most important copper deposits, mined since at least 1199.

perm-072.title: The Zechstein Sea bakes into thick salt
perm-072.text: A rising sea, probably tied to melting ice, flooded a basin over today's North Sea, lowland Britain, Germany and Poland, creating the hypersaline, or extremely salty, Zechstein Sea. In the rain shadow of the Central Pangean Mountains, at least five cycles of evaporation piled up salt, anhydrite and dolomite about 1,000 m thick.

perm-074.title: The last glaciers melt and the great icehouse ends
perm-074.text: The Late Paleozoic icehouse, the longest and most extensive of the Phanerozoic, had gripped Earth since the Late Devonian. Its last regional glaciation, called P4, lingered in Australia from the middle Capitanian to the late Wuchiapingian. Around 255 million years ago, the final alpine glaciers melted in what is now eastern Australia. By one account, Earth's last greenhouse period began in the late Permian as the ice age ended.

perm-076.title: An impact punches Brazil's Araguainha crater
perm-076.text: An impact blasted a 40 km crater on the border of Mato Grosso and Goiás, Brazil, probably into a shallow sea. Its age, 254.7 ± 2.5 Ma, lies close to the Permian–Triassic boundary, and some researchers suggest the warming it caused helped trigger the extinction.

perm-077.title: Salt and gypsum fill the Delaware Basin
perm-077.text: Cut off from the sea as tectonics choked the Hovey Channel, the deep Delaware Basin of Texas and New Mexico filled with ever saltier brine. Up to 91 m of gypsum and anhydrite, the Castile Formation, settled in water over 500 m deep before salt made the basin mostly dry land.

perm-078.title: The Siberian Traps bury Siberia in lava
perm-078.text: Lava flooded Siberia for roughly two million years across the Permian–Triassic boundary, in one of the largest volcanic events of the last 500 million years. About 7 million km² of basalt survives; its magma baked the coal- and salt-rich Tungus basin, which can release vast amounts of toxic and greenhouse gases. The eruptions' carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, halogens and metals drove warming, acidic and oxygen-starved oceans, ozone loss, acid rain and repeated mercury poisoning. Zircon dating ties the eruptions to the end-Permian extinction, and the traps are believed to be its primary cause.

perm-079.title: The Glossopteris forests collapse
perm-079.text: Glossopteris trees had dominated much of southern Gondwana through the Permian, until the end-Permian extinction brought their ecosystems down. In Australia the flora collapsed around 370,000 years before the boundary, and in western Gondwana probably a few hundred thousand years before it. Just above the boundary, a conifer flora largely replaced it right across Australia. Most or all members of the glossopterid order, which had arisen at the start of the Permian, died out in the extinction.

perm-081.title: A plunge in carbon isotopes marks the boundary
perm-081.text: A large, abrupt global fall in carbon-13 coincides with the extinction and helps geologists find the boundary in rocks that cannot be dated by radioactive decay. Seafloor methane ice was once the favored source of the light carbon, but isotopes now point mainly to volcanic carbon dioxide and heat-generated methane from the Siberian Traps.

perm-082.title: Carbon dioxide soars and the planet overheats
perm-082.text: The Siberian Traps released more than 5 teratonnes, or trillion tonnes, of carbon dioxide, more than doubling the amount in the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide rose from around 400 to 2,500 ppm as some 3,900–12,000 gigatonnes of carbon flooded into the oceans and air. Average surface temperature leaped from about 18 °C to as much as 35 °C, and tropical seas off Iran topped 35 °C. This rapid greenhouse release caused the extinction and launched an extreme hothouse that lasted several million years into the Triassic.

perm-084.title: The Great Dying: Earth's worst mass extinction
perm-084.text: Earth's most severe known extinction ended the Paleozoic Era, wiping out about 62% of genera, 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrate species. The main marine pulse took just 60,000–100,000 years; ash beds at Meishan, China, pin it between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago. The consensus cause is the Siberian Traps, whose carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide brought global warming, sulfurous oxygen-starved seas and acidified oceans. Shell-building sea creatures fared worst, insects endured their largest mass extinction, plants were equally devastated, and land ecosystems took some 30 million years to rebuild.

perm-085.title: Acid seas and acid rain
perm-085.text: Rising carbon dioxide made the oceans more acidic by up to 0.7 units on the pH scale, matching the selective loss of animals with heavy shells and skeletons. On land, acid rain lowered soil pH and sped erosion, washing organic matter from the land into the sea.

perm-086.title: Poisonous, oxygen-starved waters fill the oceans
perm-086.text: From the Late Permian into the Early Triassic, oxygen-starved waters spread through the oceans, many of them euxinic, or laced with hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg gas. Across most of the Tethys and Panthalassa, this anoxia appears at the extinction itself, though at some sites it began earlier. Sulfate-reducing bacteria thrived and filled the sea with hydrogen sulfide, even in the sunlit shallows. The poisonous gas escaping from the sea may have killed life both on land and in the water.

perm-088.title: Sea level lurches as the extinction unfolds
perm-088.text: Global sea level is reported to have fallen 250 m during the extinction, shrinking shallow shelves and hastening the final decline of trilobites. Other work, however, links the main warming to a rising sea, which joined anoxia in ravaging shallow shelf life.

perm-089.title: The last spiny sharks disappear
perm-089.text: The acanthodians, or 'spiny sharks', an early class of jawed fish, died out in the Permian–Triassic extinction. Their diversity had been low but stable through the Carboniferous and slipped further in the Permian.

perm-090.title: Fusulinid foraminifera meet their end
perm-090.text: The Capitanian crisis had already shrunk fusulinid foraminifera to dwarf forms, and they were nearly gone when the end-Permian extinction finished them off. Lagenid forams survived, probably thanks to their wider tolerance of conditions and broader range.

perm-091.title: The saber-toothed gorgonopsians die out
perm-091.text: Gorgonopsians, the Late Permian's top land predators, began disappearing from Africa and Eastern Europe just before the extinction and died out in its final phase. Biarmosuchians vanished with them, while dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts shrank to a handful of species each.

perm-092.title: Giant griffinflies vanish in the worst insect extinction
perm-092.text: By the end of the Permian, several Paleozoic insect groups, including the giant griffinflies and the palaeodictyopteroids, were extinct. Only three Paleozoic insect groups are known from after the extinction, the largest known mass extinction of insects.

perm-093.title: The last progymnosperms fade out
perm-093.text: The Noeggerathiales, the last surviving progymnosperms, persisted until the end of the Permian. Progymnosperms were woody, spore-bearing plants thought to have given rise to the seed plants.

perm-094.title: The Paleozoic reef corals die out
perm-094.text: Rugose and tabulate corals, the reef-building corals of the Paleozoic, died out in the Permian–Triassic extinction. About 96% of the genera of corals and other anthozoans, the group that also includes sea anemones, vanished with them.

perm-095.title: The last scale-tree swamps hang on in Cathaysia
perm-095.text: Carboniferous-style swamps of lycopsids and horsetails survived to the end of the Permian only in Cathaysia, equatorial islands that became South China. By then tree lycopsids were rare, marginal plants there, no longer the main coal formers.

perm-096.title: Trilobites vanish after nearly 300 million years
perm-096.text: Trilobites, armored sea arthropods that had thrived since the Cambrian, vanished at the end of the Permian after nearly 300 million years. Their last order, the Proetida, had been the only one left since the Devonian. By the Changhsingian only a handful of genera remained, by one count just two. Falling sea level shrank their shallow-shelf homes, so their final decline came shortly before the main extinction.

perm-097.title: Pangaea parches as the Permian ends
perm-097.text: Pangaea grew drier near the end of the Permian as the supercontinent coalesced, and the terminal Permian volcanism and global warming made it sharply worse. In Siberia's Kuznetsk Basin, drying killed humid-adapted Cordaites forests a few hundred thousand years before the boundary.

perm-098.title: An asteroid trigger is proposed but largely rejected
perm-098.text: Contentious candidate craters for an end-Permian impact include the 250 km Bedout structure off northwest Australia and a hypothesized 480 km crater in Antarctica's Wilkes Land. Despite reported shocked quartz and meteorite fragments, iridium shows no spike and many boundary sites lack impact evidence, so the idea is now largely rejected.

perm-100.title: The sea scorpions bow out, at a disputed date
perm-100.text: Eurypterids, the 'sea scorpions', dwindled through the Permian, but when they finally died out is contentious: either early in the Middle Permian or in the end-Permian extinction. A fragment from the very end of the Permian in Australia, once called the youngest eurypterid, may instead belong to a scorpion.

tria-018.title: Pangaea's megamonsoon blows at full strength
tria-018.text: The Pangean megamonsoon, a vast seasonal swing of wind and rain, reached its greatest strength in the Triassic. It peaked when Pangaea itself was largest, after the ancient continental cores of Siberia and China had joined it. Its circulation may have turned part of the global easterly winds around, sending westerlies onto Pangaea's west coast and moisture onto the once-dry Colorado Plateau. In this greenhouse world, the continents stayed free of ice, even at the poles.

tria-019.title: A buried crater scars North Dakota
tria-019.text: An impact in what is now McKenzie County, North Dakota, left the Red Wing Creek structure, about 9 km across and now buried some 2,000 m deep. Thick Jurassic rocks fill the shattered crater, suggesting a Triassic strike, though its estimated age of 200 ± 25 million years straddles the Triassic–Jurassic boundary.

tria-014.title: Shell-crushers launch the Mesozoic marine revolution
tria-014.text: As the Mesozoic began, the seas entered a long arms race known as the Mesozoic marine revolution. Predators that crushed or bored through shells grew steadily more capable, and more animals bulldozed the seafloor. Creatures fixed in place felt the pressure most, and the balance shifted as some prey adapted faster than others. Stalked crinoids, sea lilies anchored to the bottom, made easy targets for shell-crushers from the Triassic on.

tria-009.title: Beaked rhynchosaurs appear in the aftermath
tria-009.text: Rhynchosaurs, beaked plant-eating reptiles, appeared in the Induan, the first age of the Triassic, as reptiles diversified in the wake of the extinction. Early forms such as Noteosuchus lived in what is now South Africa's Eastern Cape.

tria-002.title: Stifling, acidic seas stall the ocean's recovery
tria-002.text: Oxygen-poor water lingered through the Early Triassic, which may explain why sea life, especially on the seafloor, recovered so slowly. Chemical fossils of green sulfur bacteria, microbes that need both light and hydrogen sulfide, show that the gas reached sunlit shallow water. Persistently high carbon dioxide in air and sea also hampered the comeback of shell builders. Seafloors flipping between oxygen-rich and oxygen-free states may explain the period's carbon-isotope swings, shifts in the mix of heavy and light carbon.

tria-004.title: Desert playas lay down the red Buntsandstein
tria-004.text: From England to Poland, desert playas, or dry lake beds, laid down the Buntsandstein of the Germanic Basin, red sandstones holding small reptiles and Chirotherium tracks. Late in the Anisian, the first age of the Middle Triassic, a global sea-level rise drowned the basin under a tropical sea, starting the Muschelkalk.

tria-005.title: Coelacanths and lungfishes enjoy their heyday
tria-005.text: Coelacanths, a group of lobe-finned fishes, had their greatest burst of diversity in the Early Triassic, just after the end-Permian extinction known as the Great Dying. Lungfishes reached their peak variety during the Triassic; only three genera survive today.

tria-007.title: Pangaea bakes in the Phanerozoic's fiercest heat
tria-007.text: The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, during and just after the Siberian Traps' huge release of greenhouse gases. Equatorial temperatures may have jumped 8–10 °C at the start of the Triassic, to averages of 32–35 °C. The heat came in waves: a peak at the boundary, a brief Dienerian cooling from 251 to 249 million years ago, then the Latest Smithian Thermal Maximum. Between about 30°N and 40°S, the heat may have left the land without four-limbed animals from the Induan until the early Spathian.

tria-008.title: New-finned fishes arrive as ray-fins boom
tria-008.text: The earliest unmistakable neopterygians, the 'new-finned' fishes, appear near the start of the Triassic, though the group is suspected to have Permian roots. Ray-finned fishes peaked in the Middle Triassic, and later in the period neopterygians became leading fishes of both fresh and salt water.

tria-013.title: Lystrosaurus spreads to every corner of Pangaea
tria-013.text: The pig-sized Lystrosaurus, a plant-eating dicynodont from the mammal-relative line, made up as much as 90% of some earliest Triassic land faunas. It was the most common land vertebrate, and trackways in South Africa's Karoo Basin show dicynodonts thronging right after the crisis. Herding, tolerance of extreme and changeable climates, very fast growth and early sexual maturity probably explain its success. Some recent evidence questions its usual label as a disaster taxon, a species that booms in the wreckage of an extinction.

tria-015.title: Microbes build reefs in the extinction's wake
tria-015.text: In the earliest Triassic, reefs built by microbes, sometimes helped by sponges, briefly spread across shallow seas and steadied the damaged ecosystems. Microbial mats, thin carpets of microbes, left wrinkled surfaces at sea and on land, and their later disappearance marks burrowing animals returning as life recovered.

tria-022.title: The Siberian Traps erupt again and again
tria-022.text: Swings in carbon isotopes and spikes of mercury suggest that massive Siberian Traps activity returned several times during the Early Triassic. These pulses caused further extinctions and may have kept the climate hot. Later bursts are linked to crises at the Smithian–Spathian and Olenekian–Anisian boundaries and in the Anisian. A release of methane cannot explain such large, repeated carbon-isotope shifts.

tria-023.title: Life crawls back from the worst extinction ever
tria-023.text: Life took millions of years to recover from the largest mass extinction, held back by repeated extinction waves and a harsh climate. Early Triassic faunas were poor in species and much alike worldwide, and seafloor communities stayed sparse for about 4 million years. On land, recovery took about 30 million years, as bouts of acidity stunted ecosystems well into the Triassic. In the sea, the pace finally exploded in the Anisian, as crowded niches sharpened competition.

tria-024.title: Temnospondyl amphibians bounce back first
tria-024.text: Temnospondyls, a large group of extinct amphibians, recovered first and peaked in diversity early in the Triassic, when capitosaurs, trematosaurs and other major subgroups appeared. They shrank in the Induan but regained their old sizes in the Olenekian, the second age of the Early Triassic, then declined through the Middle and Late Triassic.

tria-017.title: Moenkopi tidal flats redden the American Southwest
tria-017.text: Rivers, tidal flats and brief marine floods laid down the red Moenkopi Formation across the American Southwest, up to about 550 m thick. Its 27 species of Early Triassic bivalves, clams and their kin, cast doubt on the idea that bivalves recovered only in the Middle Triassic.

tria-021.title: Seas creep up from a Permian–Triassic low
tria-021.text: Sea level bottomed out at the Permian–Triassic boundary and stayed low through the Triassic compared with other periods. It rose from near today's level to 10–20 m higher, then sped up to peak at up to 50 m above present in the Carnian.

tria-025.title: Guiyang fossils capture an entire marine food web
tria-025.text: In China's Daye Formation, the Guiyang biota preserves a late Induan sea community in exceptional detail, about 250.8 million years ago. It holds every trophic level, or rung of the food chain, from the first consumers to the apex predators.

tria-027.title: Cynodonts and dicynodonts rise among the survivors
tria-027.text: Only three lines of therapsids, the mammal-relative group, survived: dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts, the branch that would lead to mammals. Cynodonts and stocky kannemeyeriiform dicynodonts soon dominated, and Cynognathus became a top predator in Olenekian and Anisian Gondwana.

tria-029.title: Dinosaur cousins leave their first footprints
tria-029.text: Footprints from the Olenekian are the first traces of dinosauromorphs, the group that holds dinosaurs and their closest relatives. Fossils of early dinosaur-like animals, such as Lagosuchus and Lagerpeton, come from Argentina's Chañares Formation. Their wider group, the avemetatarsalians, played only a minor part in Triassic ecosystems, yet it eventually produced the first dinosaurs and flying pterosaurs.

tria-028.title: Dicroidium seed ferns take over Gondwana
tria-028.text: Around the Induan–Olenekian boundary, forests of Dicroidium, a seed-bearing tree with fern-like leaves, spread across large parts of Gondwana. They peaked in diversity in the Anisian and lasted until the end-Triassic extinction, which left only a relict in Antarctica.

tria-031.title: Triadobatrachus, the oldest known frog, appears
tria-031.text: Triadobatrachus massinoti, the earliest known frog, dates from about 250 million years ago. It belongs with the lissamphibians, the modern amphibians, which first appeared in the Triassic. Stem relatives of salamanders and of legless caecilians also arose, but modern amphibians became common only in the Jurassic, as the temnospondyls waned.

tria-032.title: Ichthyosaurs carry reptiles back to the sea
tria-032.text: Ichthyosaurs, the 'fish lizards', evolved from land reptiles that returned to the sea, much as the ancestors of whales and dolphins later did. They appeared around 250 million years ago, just two million years after the end-Permian extinction, among the very first marine reptiles. The oldest remains of their wider group come from Olenekian rocks on Spitsbergen, and early forms lined northern Pangaea's coasts from Japan and China to Canada. By the Middle Triassic some were very large, and the line endured until about 94 million years ago.

tria-033.title: South China docks as Pangaea reaches its peak
tria-033.text: Pangaea reached its greatest extent about 250 million years ago, at the start of the Triassic. Around then, South China collided with the Qinling complex and North China, joining the supercontinent and creating the Sichuan Basin. The single world ocean, Panthalassa, now covered almost 70% of Earth's surface.

tria-034.title: Mountain building strikes western North America
tria-034.text: Around the Permian–Triassic transition, the Sonoma orogeny, a mountain-building episode, struck western North America, long after the earlier Antler orogeny. It is linked to Sonomia, a volcanic island chain or small continental fragment, joining the continent's western edge, but some geologists dispute whether converging plates produced it.

tria-030.title: Colliding blocks piece together East Asia
tria-030.text: Between about 250 and 230 million years ago, the crustal blocks of Annamia, Sibumasu, Qiangtang and Lhasa crashed into South China and each other, raising the Indosinian orogeny. This new southern Asian landmass then hit North China, Tarim and other blocks about 240–220 million years ago, closing the Qinling ocean. Final closure of the Paleoasian Ocean, around 240–230 million years ago, stitched Tarim and North China to Kazakhstan and Siberia. These additions gave Pangaea its greatest land area just as climate shifted sharply and the megamonsoon developed, though any link is still being studied.

tria-035.title: A second blow: the Smithian–Spathian extinction
tria-035.text: During the Olenekian, a second extinction followed the end-Permian disaster, at the boundary between the Smithian and Spathian subdivisions. The late Smithian crisis was a widespread ocean anoxic event, a spell when much of the sea lost its oxygen. Renewed Siberian Traps volcanism has been linked to it, and the Smithian closed with a heat peak around 249–248 million years ago. Episodes like this kept setting back life's recovery, and Idaho's Paris biota is the first diverse fossil community known afterward.

tria-036.title: Idaho's Paris biota marks a fresh start
tria-036.text: In a shallow sea near the equator, off Pangaea's west coast, Idaho's Paris biota preserves an exceptionally diverse community from the earliest Spathian, about 249 million years ago. It is the first rich assemblage after the Smithian–Spathian extinction, roughly 3 million years after the end-Permian one.

tria-037.title: Flipper-limbed sauropterygians take to the water
tria-037.text: Sauropterygians, marine reptiles with flippers for limbs, evolved from land ancestors soon after the end-Permian extinction. The earliest appeared about 248–247 million years ago, in the Spathian at the close of the Early Triassic, and were already notably diverse. With hupehsuchians and ichthyopterygians, they were among the first reptiles to colonize the sea. They flourished through the Triassic, but only one branch, the plesiosaurs, survived the period's end.

tria-039.title: A sharp cooling ends the Early Triassic heat
tria-039.text: From 248 to 247 million years ago, the Latest Olenekian Cooling dropped temperatures by about 6 °C. The Middle Triassic stayed cooler, and the chillier Anisian oceans let animal-built reefs become common again.

tria-048.title: A third extinction closes the Early Triassic
tria-048.text: A third extinction since the Permian struck at the Olenekian–Anisian boundary, ending the Early Triassic. Siberian Traps activity has been linked to it, and to later crises in the Anisian and at the Anisian–Ladinian boundary.

tria-049.title: Pangaea starts to tear along the future Atlantic
tria-049.text: Soon after the Siberian Traps fell quiet, around 247 million years ago, the crust began to pull apart into rift valleys in the Fundy and Argana basins. From about 227 to 202 million years ago, deep rift lakes between New Jersey and Morocco filled with the red beds and shales of the Newark Supergroup. The rifts linked into the future Mid-Atlantic Ridge, yet Laurasia, Pangaea's northern half, parted from Gondwana only between 215 and 175 million years ago. Other sources put the start of the breakup later, at about 220 or 215 million years ago.

tria-045.title: Luoping fossils track the seas' revival
tria-045.text: In Yunnan, China, the Luoping biota preserves a varied community of sea animals that records the recovery of marine life. It belongs to a series of Triassic marine fossil sites in China that also includes the older Guiyang biota.

tria-043.title: The first stony corals, tomorrow's reef builders
tria-043.text: Scleractinians, the stony corals behind every Mesozoic and modern reef, first appeared late in the Anisian. They diversified rapidly in the Carnian pluvial episode, a long wet spell. That burst is linked to single-celled algae called dinoflagellates, which settled in the corals' tissues as partners. Modern-type coral reefs first became fairly common in the Carnian, but stony corals did not dominate reef building until the Triassic's end.

tria-040.title: Archosaurs push the mammal relatives aside
tria-040.text: Archosaurs, the reptile group of crocodiles and dinosaurs, started out rarer than therapsids but ruled the land by the Middle Triassic. Over 35 million years they came to include crocodylomorphs, the branch leading to crocodiles, as well as pterosaurs and dinosaurs. Crocodile-line pseudosuchians dominated, from plant-eating aetosaurs to big 'rauisuchian' predators, while dinosaurs and their nearest kin, the dinosauromorphs, shared the land. Large cynodonts such as traversodontids still held some of the big herbivore and predator roles.

tria-042.title: Dinoflagellates leave their first fossil cysts
tria-042.text: Dinoflagellates, single-celled plankton, leave their first fossils in the mid-Triassic, mostly as tough resting cysts. Chemical markers hint they existed as far back as the Early Cambrian, and by the Middle Jurassic they were prominent among the ocean's drifting algae.

tria-044.title: Turtles start out without a shell
tria-044.text: The turtle story began in the Middle Triassic with stem turtles, early members of the turtle line. Pappochelys had no shell at all, only a short torso, broad ribs and long back vertebrae. By the Late Triassic, Odontochelys carried a complete bony plastron, or belly shell, but only part of a carapace, the upper shell. The traits that built the shell may first have helped these animals dig.

tria-046.title: Placodonts, nothosaurs and kin crowd Triassic seas
tria-046.text: In the Middle Triassic, placodonts, thalattosaurs, Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined the ichthyosaurs and sauropterygians. Pachypleurosaurs and nothosaurs were common, especially around the Tethys, and some nothosaurs grew 5–7 m long. Atopodentatus is the earliest known plant-eating marine reptile, while some ichthyopterygians reached very large body masses. South China has yielded almost every known clade, or branch, of Triassic marine reptile.

tria-047.title: Seas and lakes rebuild complex food webs
tria-047.text: Some 4–6 million years after the extinction, complex ecosystems full of specialized animals began to re-form. Carbon-isotope swings abruptly calmed, and soon marine reptiles, fishes, ammonoids, bivalves and snails all grew more diverse. By the early Ladinian, the second age of the Middle Triassic, fossil dung from Chinese lakes records freshwater food webs six or more levels deep. Even so, full recovery took about 30 million years, and global marine diversity regained its old level only in the Middle Jurassic.

tria-050.title: The Tethys pushes west and floods central Europe
tria-050.text: In the Middle Triassic the Tethys, a vast gulf on Pangaea's eastern side, opened farther west as the older Paleo-Tethys shrank. Rising seas spread the shallow Muschelkalk Sea across central Europe, as far as the North Pyrenean Zone.

tria-051.title: France's Grès à Voltzia keeps the first aphids
tria-051.text: France's Grès à Voltzia, about 245 million years old, is a Lagerstätte, a site of exceptional fossil preservation. Its arthropods include the earliest known aphids and finely detailed myriapods, the many-legged group of centipedes and millipedes.

tria-052.title: Agriodontosaurus, the oldest sure lepidosaur
tria-052.text: The oldest definite lepidosaur is Agriodontosaurus, a tuatara relative from England about 244–241.5 million years old. Its group, ancestral to lizards, snakes and the tuatara, later diversified in the Carnian pluvial episode, a long wet spell early in the Late Triassic.

tria-054.title: Monte San Giorgio's lagoon preserves sea reptiles
tria-054.text: At Monte San Giorgio on Lake Lugano, a Middle Triassic lagoon sat behind reefs, its oxygen-free bottom ideal for fossilization. Its Besano Formation, about 242 million years old and now a World Heritage Site, preserves fish and marine reptiles such as Neusticosaurus and Tanystropheus.

tria-053.title: A long cooling settles over the Ladinian and Carnian
tria-053.text: From 242 to 233 million years ago, the Ladinian–Carnian Cooling kept global temperatures relatively low into the early Carnian. Abrupt warming from the Wrangellia eruptions around 234 million years ago ended the trend.

tria-057.title: True flies take wing
tria-057.text: The first true flies, or Diptera, appeared around 240 million years ago and spread widely through the Middle and Late Triassic. Flies became one of the four great insect radiations, or evolutionary bursts, and many new species of lower flies arose around 220 million years ago.

tria-055.title: Cimmerian blocks drift north and close the Paleo-Tethys
tria-055.text: A string of continental fragments, the Cimmerian blocks, drifted north across the Paleo-Tethys Ocean, closing it ahead of them and opening the Neo-Tethys behind. The Cimmerian orogeny began about 240–200 million years ago as these blocks collided with Kazakhstania and North and South China. The Paleo-Tethys, open for about 400 million years, had shrunk to a narrow seaway by the Late Triassic. Its western arm survived until about 205 million years ago, when Iranian blocks struck Eurasia's Turan platform, completing a belt from Anatolia east to the Indosinian orogen.

tria-058.title: Marine reptiles suffer their steepest extinction rates
tria-058.text: At the end of the Ladinian, which closed the Middle Triassic, Mesozoic marine reptiles suffered their highest extinction rates. Like fishes, they lost much of their diversity between the Middle Triassic and the Jurassic.

tria-062.title: Specialist rhynchosaurs spread across the globe
tria-062.text: Rhynchosaurs diversified around 240 million years ago, but the lines common in the Middle Triassic died out in the Carnian pluvial episode, leaving the specialized hyperodapedontines. These became widespread and abundant in the late Carnian, giving rhynchosaurs their broadest, truly global range.

tria-064.title: A giant delta plain fills the Boreal Ocean
tria-064.text: From 237 to 227 million years ago, a vast river delta plain spread across northern Pangaea's Triassic Boreal Ocean, in today's Barents Sea. Rapid sedimentation after the extinction had built a shallow basin there, and in the Ladinian deltas advanced more than 500 km across it.

tria-060.title: Chalk-plated coccolithophores join the plankton
tria-060.text: Coccolithophores, tiny algae armored with chalky plates called coccoliths, leave their oldest known fossils around the Norian–Rhaetian boundary, late in the Triassic. Calcareous nannofossils, microscopic chalky remains like theirs, form an unbroken record from about 220 million years ago to the present. One source places the first coccoliths, with dinoflagellates, in the Carnian pluvial episode, while a time-scale table lists the first coccolithophores in the Jurassic. They radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic, becoming prominent among the ocean's drifting algae.

tria-065.title: Moth scales turn up in fossil dung
tria-065.text: The earliest probable fossils of moths and butterflies are scales about 236 million years old, found in a plant-eater's dung in Argentina and likely swallowed by accident. Wing scales of several moth groups occur as rare microfossils at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary near Braunschweig, Germany.

tria-067.title: Wrangellia floods the land with basalt
tria-067.text: For about 5 million years, the Wrangellia flood basalts, vast sheets of lava, poured onto land and built a large igneous province, a huge pile of volcanic rock. The eruption around 234 million years ago caused abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian Cooling. Carbon and osmium isotopes tie it to the Carnian climate upheaval, with a shift in seawater osmium at the Ladinian–Carnian boundary. Its rocks, now exposed in a belt 2,500 km long, belong to the Wrangellia terrane, a crustal fragment later added to western North America.

tria-066.title: The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green
tria-066.text: Around 234–232 million years ago, the Carnian pluvial episode jolted the climate into a hotter, wetter state for perhaps 1–2 million years. Wrangellia's eruptions set off the warming, and surging rain and runoff turned Pangaea's dry interior into lush forests along rivers. At sea, shallow limestone shelves called carbonate platforms shrank, and many invertebrates died out, especially ammonoids, crinoids and colonial bryozoans. Early dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and possibly mammaliaforms, mammals and their closest kin, diversified during the event, while coccoliths and dinoflagellates joined the plankton.

tria-068.title: The first true dinosaurs appear
tria-068.text: The earliest true dinosaurs probably appeared in the Carnian, around the time of the Carnian pluvial episode, and diversified rapidly. Some of the oldest come from Brazil's Santa Maria Formation, dated to 233.23 million years ago, though Tanzania's Nyasasaurus hints at roots near 243 million years ago. They sprang from avemetatarsalians, the bird-line archosaurs, a minor part of Triassic ecosystems, and dominated only in the Jurassic. Whether the rains drove their rise is doubtful, because avemetatarsalian diversity grew faster in the Ladinian and Norian.

tria-069.title: Brazil yields the first sauropodomorphs
tria-069.text: Buriolestes and Saturnalia, from Brazil's 233.23-million-year-old Santa Maria Formation, are early sauropodomorphs, the dinosaur branch that includes the sauropods. Eoraptor, once grouped with herrerasaurids, now counts as an early sauropodomorph too, and four-legged forms appeared later in the Triassic.

tria-070.title: Ischigualasto's ash and mud bury early dinosaurs
tria-070.text: In a reactivated rift basin in northwestern Argentina, rivers from volcanic highlands laid down sandstones, mudstones and ash beds up to about 1 km thick. Packed with fossils, the Ischigualasto Formation holds some of the earliest unambiguous dinosaurs, such as Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor, among abundant rhynchosaurs and cynodonts.

tria-071.title: Theropods, the meat-eating dinosaurs, arrive
tria-071.text: Theropods, the meat-eating dinosaur line, appeared about 231 million years ago, joining sauropodomorphs among the Carnian dinosaurs. Their more advanced members, the neotheropods, arrived later in the Late Triassic.

tria-072.title: Virginia's Cow Branch Formation keeps fish and insects
tria-072.text: Virginia's Cow Branch Formation, another Lagerstätte about 230 million years old, preserves a wide range of fish, reptiles, arachnids and insects.

tria-073.title: Madygen yields over 20,000 fossil insects
tria-073.text: Kyrgyzstan's Madygen Formation, about 230 million years old, has yielded over 20,000 fossil insects, making it one of the richest Triassic Lagerstätten. Fish, amphibians, reptiles and synapsids, the mammal line, turn up too, including Kyrgyzsaurus, the earliest known drepanosaurid.

tria-074.title: Pterosaurs take to the Triassic skies
tria-074.text: Pterosaurs, the flying reptiles, evolved about 228 million years ago, a little after the first true dinosaurs. Like dinosaurs, they sprang from the avemetatarsalians, and feathers may already have been present in the two groups' common ancestor in the Early Triassic. Early long-tailed pterosaurs appeared in the Norian and quickly spread worldwide. Norian lagoon deposits in northern Italy, such as the Calcare di Zorzino, preserve them alongside other reptiles.

tria-075.title: An impact carves Manitoba's Saint Martin crater
tria-075.text: An impact in what is now Manitoba, Canada, left the Saint Martin structure, about 40 km across. Geologists once linked it with Manicouagan and Rochechouart as one multiple impact, but its age of 227.8 ± 1.1 million years shows they formed millions of years apart.

tria-078.title: A disputed end-Carnian crisis drowns a delta
tria-078.text: Near the end of the Carnian, repeated floods drowned the vast Boreal delta plain, several plant-eating archosaur relatives died out, and big therapsid herbivores dwindled. Sources hedge on whether this was a distinct extinction, partly because the age of the Carnian–Norian boundary is itself disputed.

tria-081.title: Tuatara relatives spread around the world
tria-081.text: By the end of the Carnian, rhynchocephalians, relatives of the living tuatara, had spread worldwide. They went on to become the dominant small reptiles of the Jurassic.

tria-076.title: Rivers and ash build the colorful Chinle Formation
tria-076.text: Rivers, lakes and floodplains, with plenty of volcanic ash, laid down the colorful Chinle Formation across the American Southwest. Exposed in Petrified Forest National Park and the Painted Desert, it holds a unique record of life on land from the late Carnian to the early Norian.

tria-077.title: Plant-eating dinosaurs spread through the Norian
tria-077.text: In the Norian, plant-eating sauropodomorphs diversified and began to displace large herbivorous therapsids, perhaps because they coped better with growing aridity. Plateosaurus, an early sauropodomorph, evolved around 214 million years ago and lived in Europe, Greenland and North America. Most Triassic dinosaurs, though, were small predators, and Coelophysis, 1–2 m long, was one of the few common ones. Even now, crocodile-line archosaurs filled more ecological niches than the dinosaurs did.

tria-079.title: The last rhynchosaurs vanish
tria-079.text: Hyperodapedontine rhynchosaurs, once abundant beaked plant-eaters, died out around the early Norian, and Brazil's Teyumbaita is the only one confidently known from that age. Their exact end is uncertain, and one suggestion places it in an end-Carnian extinction instead.

tria-080.title: A mid-Norian die-off strikes the seas
tria-080.text: In the middle of the Norian, a marine extinction struck single-celled radiolarians, sponges, eel-like conodonts and Triassic ammonoids. Some blame the Manicouagan impact, which may also have hastened the slide of conodonts and ammonoids toward their end-Triassic extinction.

tria-082.title: Sea level sinks to a Rhaetian low
tria-082.text: After a Carnian high of up to 50 m above today's level, sea level fell from the Norian onward. It bottomed out about 50 m below present in the mid-Rhaetian and stayed low into the earliest Jurassic. No evidence points to Triassic ice sheets, so glaciation probably does not explain these swings. At the very end of the Triassic, the sea flooded most of central and western Europe, turning it into an archipelago.

tria-084.title: Mammaliaforms, the closest kin of mammals, appear
tria-084.text: Mammaliaforms, the group of mammals and their closest extinct kin, arose from advanced cynodonts in the Late Triassic, but scientists still argue about exactly when. Some studies place their origin in the Carnian pluvial episode, others in the Norian or at the very end of the period. Unambiguous forms such as morganucodonts and haramiyids appear in the Norian of Europe and Greenland. These were small, mostly nocturnal, warm-blooded insect-eaters living in the shadow of dinosaurs, and bones from their old jaw were moving into the middle ear.

tria-083.title: A cooler spell follows the Carnian heat
tria-083.text: A relatively cool spell, the Early Norian Cool Interval, lasted from about 227 to 217 million years ago, after the warmth of the Carnian pluvial episode. At the Carnian–Norian boundary, a shift toward heavier carbon in the rocks suggests more organic carbon was being buried.

tria-085.title: Teleosts, today's dominant fishes, first appear
tria-085.text: Teleosts, the group that now makes up over 99% of living ray-finned fishes, first appear around 225 million years ago. Early stem teleosts such as Prohalecites swam in the western Tethys.

tria-089.title: Warmth returns, and Pangaea turns swampy
tria-089.text: Warmth returned in the Mid-Norian Warm Interval, about 217 to 209 million years ago, apart from a brief cooling around 214 million years ago. Around 212 million years ago, Earth's orbit grew unusually stretched, which made much of Pangaea swampy and shrank its arid zones.

tria-090.title: An asteroid 5 km wide blasts out Manicouagan
tria-090.text: An asteroid about 5 km wide struck what is now Quebec, excavating a multiple-ring crater about 100 km across, one of the largest on Earth. It was the second-largest impact of the Mesozoic, after Chicxulub, and flung shocked quartz, grains scarred by the blast, as far as England and Japan. It may have caused a brief cooling, a mid-Norian marine extinction and a turnover of land animals, but direct evidence is lacking. Some 13 million years older than the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, it is no longer thought to have caused the end-Triassic extinction.

tria-091.title: A turnover reshapes Southwest faunas
tria-091.text: Around 215 million years ago, Trilophosaurus, Desmatosuchus, dicynodonts and many phytosaurs vanished from the American Southwest as new aetosaurs and phytosaurs took their place. Pollen shifted to dry-adapted plants, but the cause and importance of this turnover are debated, and it may have been only a small, local event.

tria-092.title: Argoland begins to splinter off Australia
tria-092.text: Around 215 million years ago, Argoland, on Australia's northern margin, began breaking into small continental fragments as Late Triassic rifting pulled the Lhasa terrane away from Gondwana. A major Norian rifting episode, about 210 million years ago, split Gondwana in two.

tria-093.title: Proganochelys completes the turtle shell
tria-093.text: The earliest true turtles, such as Proganochelys and Proterochersis, appeared in the Norian. Proganochelys finished what Pappochelys and Odontochelys had begun, with a fully developed carapace and plastron. Side-necked and hidden-necked turtles, the two lines that include all living turtles, are estimated to have split about 210 million years ago.

tria-094.title: Early dinosaur rivals vanish in the mid-Norian
tria-094.text: About 215 million years ago, a range of early-branching archosaur relatives, including the protorosaurs, died out. It was the first of two Triassic extinctions that removed most of the early dinosaurs' competitors, perhaps leaving niches for dinosaurs to fill.

tria-095.title: A cool Rhaetian ends in extreme heat
tria-095.text: A cooler phase, the Rhaetian Cool Interval, lasted from about 209 to 201 million years ago. Then an extreme warming, the End-Triassic Thermal Event, closed the period and is blamed for the mass extinction.

tria-096.title: An asteroid strikes an island in western France
tria-096.text: An asteroid struck an island near Limoges, on the edge of the Massif Central, leaving the Rochechouart structure about 23 km across and probably raising a large tsunami. Its age has long been debated, with estimates from under 150 to over 240 million years, though recent dates converge on 203–207 million years ago.

tria-097.title: The giant shastasaurs vanish from the seas
tria-097.text: Shastasaurian ichthyosaurs grew huge in the Carnian and Norian, with Shonisaurus reaching 15 m, but these giants seem to have vanished at the end of the Norian. Rising competition from sharks, teleost fishes and the first plesiosaurs may explain the wider decline of ichthyosaurs.

tria-099.title: A disputed die-off at the Norian–Rhaetian boundary
tria-099.text: Near the Norian–Rhaetian boundary, losses struck ammonoids, bivalves, conodonts and radiolarians, and the once worldwide bivalve Monotis almost vanished. Alaska's Angayucham volcanic province or the Rochechouart impact may be to blame, but some sources call it a much smaller, alleged event of uncertain date and effect.

tria-098.title: Marine life falters before the final crisis
tria-098.text: Through the late Norian and Rhaetian, gastropods, or snails, suffered steady losses, offshore bryozoans kept declining, and anoxia spread across northeastern Panthalassa. Mean annual temperatures rose 7–9 °C from the late Norian into the Rhaetian, and the carbon cycle was already disturbed before the main crisis.

tria-100.title: The Karoo igneous province stirs
tria-100.text: About 204 million years ago, igneous activity began on the northern margin of the Karoo large igneous province. Its Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts would later be tied to the Toarcian extinction of the Early Jurassic.

tria-101.title: Plesiosaurs appear at the end of the Triassic
tria-101.text: Plesiosaurs first appeared in the latest Triassic, possibly in the Rhaetian, about 203 million years ago. One timeline puts their debut much earlier, at about 227 million years ago. At least six plesiosaur lineages crossed into the Jurassic, the only sauropterygians to survive. They became especially common in the Jurassic and lasted until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

tria-102.title: The Central Atlantic magmatic province erupts
tria-102.text: As central Pangaea rifted apart, vast eruptions built the Central Atlantic magmatic province, or CAMP, Earth's largest continental igneous province. It covers about 11 million km² across four continents, with 2–6 million km³ of lava. The lava came in four main pulses, each lasting no more than about 100 years, spread over some 600,000 years. The eruptions capped the long rifting of the Central Atlantic, and they are widely blamed for the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, a link that grew firmer in 2013.

tria-103.title: Volcanic carbon drives an extreme end-Triassic warming
tria-103.text: At the very end of the Triassic, an extreme warming called the End-Triassic Thermal Event drove the mass extinction. Bubbles of carbon dioxide trapped in CAMP basalts show that the volcanism helped trigger it. The pulses released their carbon over mere centuries, a pace that invites comparison with today's human-caused warming. Longer-term warming and ocean acidification followed, and a spike of heat marks the start of the Jurassic.

tria-104.title: The end-Triassic extinction hands the land to dinosaurs
tria-104.text: One of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions ended the Triassic 201.4 million years ago, erasing about 46–72% of marine genera. On land, most archosaurs except crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs perished, along with most therapsids and large amphibians. Ammonites were nearly wiped out, conodonts vanished and reefs collapsed. Driven by CAMP volcanism and the warming it caused, the crisis removed the crurotarsans, the dinosaurs' main rivals, and let dinosaurs dominate the Jurassic.

tria-105.title: Oceans lose their oxygen and turn acidic
tria-105.text: Black shales and a sharp shift in uranium isotopes show that ocean oxygen plunged during the extinction, from the Tethys to Panthalassa. Anoxia lasted into the Hettangian, the first age of the Jurassic, as nutrients from the land fed the seas. Misshapen nannoplankton and a worldwide pause in carbonate deposition point to severe acidification, while green sulfur bacteria flourished. It is the best-established case of acidification causing a marine mass extinction, selectively killing organisms with thick skeletons of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.

tria-108.title: The last dicynodonts disappear
tria-108.text: Dicynodonts, the group of Lystrosaurus, were among the most successful Permian therapsids and stayed large plant-eaters until the end of the Triassic. Their last appearance is uncertain, but they survived at least into the late Norian or earliest Rhaetian.

tria-110.title: Phytosaurs, aetosaurs and rauisuchians die out
tria-110.text: Phytosaurs and aetosaurs, common members of Late Triassic faunas, were completely wiped out by the end-Triassic extinction. Among the pseudosuchians, only small crocodylomorphs survived, and the meat-eating rauisuchids died out as well. The exact timing is hard to pin down, because the Rhaetian and Hettangian hold few large land animals and some groups may have vanished earlier.

jura-019.title: Modern amphibians branch out: the first frogs and salamanders
jura-019.text: Lissamphibians, the group that holds every living amphibian, began to diversify in the Jurassic, producing the first modern frogs and salamanders. Eocaecilia, an early relative of today's limbless caecilians, already lived in Early Jurassic Arizona, and early frog relatives and the extinct albanerpetontids followed in the Middle Jurassic. The old guard, meanwhile, faded away. Of the once-diverse temnospondyls, an ancient amphibian group, only the brachyopoids survived into the Jurassic.

jura-026.title: Pangaea's great monsoon starts to fail
jura-026.text: The Pangean megamonsoon, a vast seasonal swing of wind and rain across the supercontinent, began to fall apart as the Jurassic opened. Gondwana, the southern half of Pangaea, dried out, and so did the southern part of Laurasia, the northern half. As the continents drifted apart, the monsoon kept weakening for the rest of the period.

jura-028.title: Plesiosaurs crowd the earliest Jurassic seas
jura-028.text: Plesiosaurs, four-flippered marine reptiles, were already richly varied in the Hettangian, so the group must have diversified in the Late Triassic. Most in the Blue Lias rocks of that first Jurassic age were short-necked rhomaleosaurids. Ichthyosaurs, fish-shaped marine reptiles, now faced large plesiosaurs as well as sharks and even other ichthyosaurs. Small plesiosaurs invaded fresh water in Jurassic China and Australia, and by the Toarcian, about 180 million years ago, longer-necked plesiosaurids reached 10 meters.

jura-006.title: Conifers reclaim the fernlands of Sichuan
jura-006.text: Ferns and other plants with finely divided leaves fared better than most in the end-Triassic crisis, and hot, arid fernlands then covered China's Sichuan Basin. In the Hettangian and Sinemurian they gave way to cheirolepid conifers, an extinct family whose Classopollis pollen stays abundant through the Jurassic.

jura-018.title: Seafloor life recovers in fits and starts
jura-018.text: In Britain, seafloor communities began to recover almost at once after the end-Triassic extinction, despite repeated relapses into anoxia, when the water lost its oxygen. Lingering oxygen loss and nutrient runoff may have slowed the rebound; in Argentina's Neuquén Basin, diversity found a new balance by the late Hettangian. The carbon cycle settled down only in the Sinemurian, when brachiopods and dasycladacean green algae rediversified. Tropical reefs had collapsed outright, and they did not fully recover until much later in the Jurassic.

jura-001.title: Ammonites rebound from near-extinction
jura-001.text: Ammonoids, coil-shelled relatives of squid, had nearly vanished at the end of the Triassic. The survivors radiated into a host of new forms, the ammonites proper, with intricately folded sutures, the seams where inner walls meet the shell. Six orders appeared during the Jurassic, and their faunas formed about 20 provinces in a northern Pan-Boreal and a southern Pan-Tethyan realm. Serpenticones, ammonites coiled like snakes, are abundant in Europe's Jurassic rocks.

jura-003.title: The last coelophysoids and massospondylids disappear
jura-003.text: Early predatory dinosaurs such as coelophysoids and dilophosaurs survived into the Early Jurassic but were gone by its end. Two-legged massospondylids, early cousins of the long-necked sauropods, died out by the same time.

jura-008.title: Crocodile relatives multiply, and some go to sea
jura-008.text: Crocodylomorphs, the lineage that includes crocodiles, radiated rapidly in the Early Jurassic, filling niches quite unlike those of their Triassic relatives. One branch, the mostly marine Thalattosuchia, first appeared now and became a prominent part of ocean ecosystems. Among the oldest is a basal teleosauroid from Morocco of Hettangian–Sinemurian age. On land, a protosuchid from Arizona became the earliest known plant-eating crocodylomorph.

jura-009.title: Dinosaurs take over the land
jura-009.text: With rival reptile groups wiped out by the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs surged in diversity and numbers. In the Triassic, dinosaurs and their close kin had shared the land with pseudosuchians, the crocodile-line reptiles; now dinosaurs held it alone. Dinosaurs and pterosaurs, the flying reptiles, became the commonest land reptiles, while lizards and tuatara relatives filled the small-reptile roles. Dinosaurs reached every continent by the Early Jurassic at the latest and stayed dominant through the Cretaceous, until 66 million years ago.

jura-010.title: The first certain ornithischians appear
jura-010.text: The earliest definitive ornithischians, the ‘bird-hipped’ dinosaurs, appeared and diversified in the Early Jurassic. They included small, basal forms such as Lesothosaurus, the heterodontosaurids and early thyreophorans, the beginnings of the armored-dinosaur line.

jura-011.title: The Farallon plate dives beneath North America
jura-011.text: As Pangaea broke apart, the Farallon plate began sinking beneath western North America, a process geologists call subduction. Mountains in Nevada and California kept rising as plate motions pushed the continent northward.

jura-017.title: Dicroidium makes a last stand in Antarctica
jura-017.text: Dicroidium, a seed fern that had dominated Triassic Gondwanan floras, survived into the Early Jurassic only as a relict in Antarctica. Its relative Lepidopteris, another seed-bearing plant, likewise lingered in Patagonia.

jura-021.title: Modern sharks and the first rays appear
jura-021.text: Neoselachians, the group that holds all living sharks and rays, radiated from the Early Jurassic onward. The oldest confirmed ray, Antiquaobatis, comes from Pliensbachian rocks in Germany, and the oldest six-gilled and carpet sharks from the Pliensbachian and Toarcian of Europe. By the Late Jurassic these newcomers had largely replaced the hybodonts, the dominant sharks of the Triassic. Timelines of Earth and of life date the first rays later, to about 165 million years ago.

jura-024.title: Seawater flips from aragonite to calcite
jura-024.text: Early in the Jurassic, the oceans switched from aragonite seas to calcite seas, two chemical states that favor different crystal forms of calcium carbonate. The new chemistry tended to dissolve aragonite and to precipitate calcite.

jura-025.title: Cimmeria closes the Paleo-Tethys Ocean
jura-025.text: In the Early Jurassic, the floor of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean slid beneath the Cimmerian plate, closing the ocean from west to east. The closure was part of the Cimmerian orogeny, a slow collision that pushed up mountains. Around 200 million years ago, as the Cimmerian plate itself sank beneath eastern Laurasia, the Tethyan Trench formed.

jura-029.title: The Viking Corridor links two oceans
jura-029.text: From the Early Jurassic, a seaway several hundred kilometers wide ran between the Baltic Shield and Greenland. It linked the Boreal Ocean in the north to the proto-Atlantic.

jura-005.title: Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates fill the plankton
jura-005.text: Two kinds of microscopic plankton, coccolithophores and dinoflagellates, had first appeared in the Triassic. In the Early to Middle Jurassic they radiated and became prominent phytoplankton, the drifting, plant-like life of the sunlit sea. Coccolithophores, armored in chalky plates, have been a fixture of marine plankton ever since. Their rise altered ocean chemistry, because their seafloor deposits buffered the oceans against large bursts of carbon dioxide.

jura-030.title: Blue Lias layers keep time with Earth's orbit
jura-030.text: From the latest Triassic into the early Sinemurian, beds of limestone and shale piled up in turn, forming the fossil-rich Blue Lias. The rhythm records short climate swings driven by Milankovitch cycles, regular wobbles in Earth's orbit that shift how sunlight falls.

jura-031.title: The Andes begin to rise
jura-031.text: The Andean orogeny, the mountain building that raised the Andes, began about 200 million years ago and is still going. Volcanoes fed by subduction have erupted along western South America ever since. Its first phases actually stretched the crust, opening rifts and basins behind the volcanic arc and emplacing large batholiths, great bodies of magma that cooled underground. Early subduction also built the La Negra volcanic arc in northern Chile, and the Atacama Fault is thought to have formed as the orogeny began.

jura-033.title: Conodonts vanish after more than 300 million years
jura-033.text: Conodonts, jawless fish whose tooth-like parts help geologists date rocks, finally died out around 200 million years ago. They had lasted more than 300 million years, since the Cambrian, but only a handful of species reached the end of the Triassic. A mid-Norian marine crisis, possibly linked to the Manicouagan impact, may have hastened their decline. They vanished first from the Tethys and eastern Panthalassa, the vast ocean around Pangaea, lingering into the earliest Hettangian in Hungary and central Panthalassa.

jura-034.title: The Navajo sand sea buries western North America
jura-034.text: As the Colorado Plateau grew ever drier, some 388,000 km² of western North America became an erg, a Sahara-like sea of dunes swept by winter monsoon winds. Those dunes hardened into the Navajo Sandstone, which reaches 670 meters thick at Zion Canyon and now forms towering cliffs.

jura-035.title: Pangaea tears into Laurasia and Gondwana
jura-035.text: Around 200 million years ago, Pangaea, the supercontinent that held all the major landmasses, began to rift apart. Through the Early Jurassic it split into Laurasia, made of North America and Eurasia, in the north and Gondwana in the south. The Tethys opened between them, the water cycle grew far stronger, and by about 160 million years ago the breakup was complete. Some sources date the start of rifting to about 175 million years ago, or the final split to the Late Jurassic.

jura-032.title: A seaway opens between the Americas
jura-032.text: North and South America were still joined when the Jurassic began, but they rifted apart as Pangaea broke up. Between them formed the Central American Seaway, also called the Hispanic Corridor, which linked the North Atlantic and the Tethys with eastern Panthalassa. Fossils suggest it was already open in the Early Jurassic, and the two continents had fully parted by the start of the Late Jurassic. The seaway closed only when the Isthmus of Panama formed.

jura-038.title: Vulcanodon and the first true sauropods
jura-038.text: Gravisaurians, the core sauropod lineage, first appeared in the Early Jurassic, and the oldest definite one, Vulcanodon of Zimbabwe, probably lived in the Sinemurian. Even earlier, the four-legged Ledumahadi of South Africa reached about 12 tonnes, far heavier than other early relatives of the sauropods. By the end of the Early Jurassic, possibly after a global warming event, sauropods had become the dominant large plant-eaters on land.

jura-039.title: Sea level climbs, then falls back
jura-039.text: Sea level sat near today's mark through the Hettangian and Sinemurian, then rose several tens of meters in the late Sinemurian and Pliensbachian. By the late Pliensbachian it had fallen back to near present levels.

jura-040.title: Saltriovenator, the oldest known ceratosaur
jura-040.text: The first averostrans, an advanced branch of the theropods, or predatory dinosaurs, appeared in the Early Jurassic. The oldest known ceratosaur among them, Saltriovenator, lived in Italy in the early Sinemurian.

jura-041.title: A long cool spell chills the Early Jurassic
jura-041.text: The Jurassic opened with a cool interval that lasted from about 199 to 183 million years ago. In northeastern Siberia, ice-rafted dropstones and glendonites, crystals that form in near-freezing water, record cold winters in the Early to Middle Jurassic. The late Pliensbachian may even have been an icehouse, a world cold enough for ice sheets, perhaps with Northern Hemisphere glaciers early and late in the stage. The chill ended with a sudden warming of 4–8 °C in the early Toarcian.

jura-044.title: Lyme Regis mudstones yield the armored Scelidosaurus
jura-044.text: At Lyme Regis and Charmouth in England, the Charmouth Mudstone yields complete skeletons of the armored dinosaur Scelidosaurus, along with plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs. The same rocks also hold large numbers of exceptionally preserved fish and a diverse fauna of insects.

jura-046.title: The Puchezh-Katunki impact scars western Russia
jura-046.text: About 196 million years ago, in the Sinemurian, an impact struck what is now Nizhny Novgorod Oblast in western Russia. Argon–argon dating, a method based on the slow radioactive decay of potassium into argon, fixes the age at 195.9 ± 1.0 million years. The buried crater measures 40 km from rim to rim and about 80 km including its ring terrace, making it one of the Jurassic's major impact structures.

jura-049.title: Eocarcinus, the first true crab
jura-049.text: Eocarcinus praecursor, the earliest true crab, lived in what is now England in the early Pliensbachian. It still lacked the familiar crab-like body of modern crabs; true crabs and shrimp both make their entrance in the Jurassic.

jura-051.title: Volcanoes erupt across southern Sweden
jura-051.text: Volcanoes in central Skåne, southern Sweden, had their first and main phase from about 191 to 178 million years ago. At Korsaröd, a lahar, or volcanic mudflow, buried Early Jurassic wood, pollen and spores and preserved them exceptionally well.

jura-053.title: The first pliosaurs enter the seas
jura-053.text: Pliosaurs, short-necked plesiosaurs, entered the fossil record about 190 million years ago. Many groups of primitive sea invertebrates appeared around the same time, and sponge reefs spread widely.

jura-054.title: The Pacific plate is born as a microplate
jura-054.text: Around 190 million years ago, the Pacific plate began as a microplate where three plates met: the Farallon, Phoenix and Izanagi. A kink in one plate boundary turned this stable triple junction into an unstable one, ringed by transform faults where plates slide past each other. The new plate formed at the center of that ring, in central Panthalassa, far from the margins of the Paleo-Pacific Ocean.

jura-055.title: A small impact leaves the Viewfield crater
jura-055.text: A small impact blasted the 2.5 km Viewfield crater in Saskatchewan, Canada, about 190 ± 20 million years ago. That uncertainty places it in either the Late Triassic or the Early Jurassic.

jura-056.title: Dilophosaurus, the double-crested hunter of Arizona
jura-056.text: Two thin, arched crests crowned the skull of Dilophosaurus, a theropod from Arizona's Kayenta Formation, and Eubrontes footprints are widely credited to an animal like it. At about 7 meters and 400 kilograms, it was one of the earliest large predatory dinosaurs and North America's largest known land animal of its time.

jura-059.title: Eutriconodont mammals make their debut
jura-059.text: The earliest eutriconodonts, an extinct order of early mammals, date from the Toarcian and already include several groups, such as Argentoconodon. Through the rest of the Jurassic and the Cretaceous they spread across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas.

jura-065.title: The Toarcian extinction wipes out most Tethyan corals
jura-065.text: About 183 million years ago, the Toarcian extinction struck in two pulses and wiped out 90.9% of Tethyan coral species and 49% of their genera. Ammonoids suffered further losses, seed ferns and spore plants declined, possibly from mercury poisoning, and megalosaurid dinosaurs may later have filled the emptied niches.

jura-067.title: Karoo-Ferrar lavas flood southern Gondwana
jura-067.text: About 183 million years ago, just before Gondwana began to break apart, the Karoo and Ferrar provinces erupted across southern Africa and Antarctica. With about 2.5 million cubic kilometers of magma, they form one of Earth's most extensive large igneous provinces, regions built by colossal outpourings of molten rock. As southern Africa passed over the Bouvet hotspot, a hot plume rising from deep in the mantle, basalt flooded the Clarens desert and buried nearly the whole region. Their timing matches the Toarcian anoxic event, when the oceans lost their oxygen, and the Pliensbachian–Toarcian extinction.

jura-069.title: Holzmaden's Posidonia Shale preserves skin and blood cells
jura-069.text: At Holzmaden in Germany, the Posidonia Shale settled in a stagnant basin as the Toarcian seas lost their oxygen. It holds superb, complete skeletons of fish and marine reptiles, and its preservation became a benchmark for other fossil sites. One ichthyosaur, 182.7 million years old, still contained collagen and blood cells, and a plesiosaur kept traces of its skin.

jura-071.title: Oxygen drains from the Toarcian oceans
jura-071.text: About 183 million years ago, early in the Toarcian, oxygen vanished from wide stretches of the ocean. It is the Jurassic's only documented oceanic anoxic event, and possibly the most extreme loss of ocean oxygen since animals became abundant. Carbon dioxide from the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions warmed the climate, acidified the oceans and sped up the weathering of rock. The resulting flood of nutrients overfed the seas and stripped their oxygen, leaving organic-rich black shales, including oil shales mined commercially in China.

jura-072.title: A Toarcian heat spike pushes seas past 30 °C
jura-072.text: Early in the Toarcian, global temperatures jumped by about 4–8 °C, and the warmth lasted until about 174 million years ago. Sea surfaces likely topped 30 °C, and the interior of Pangaea probably exceeded 40 °C. Tropical storms intensified worldwide, a stronger water cycle swelled the lakes, and sea level rose gradually to a peak about 75 meters above today's. Oddly, a brief cold snap interrupted the warming just before the anoxic event.

jura-075.title: The Central Atlantic begins to open
jura-075.text: Rifting between North America and Africa came first, in the Early Jurassic, tearing open basins such as the Newark Basin from Mexico to Nova Scotia. About 180 million years ago, seafloor spreading, the growth of new ocean crust between parting plates, began to open a narrow ocean between northern and southern Pangaea. This young North Atlantic stayed narrow through the Jurassic, and the South Atlantic would not open until the Cretaceous. Its exact timing is still debated, with estimates running from 200 to 170 million years ago.

jura-076.title: Gondwana starts to come apart
jura-076.text: Around 180 million years ago, soon after the Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts poured out, the southern supercontinent Gondwana began to fragment. Madagascar and Antarctica started rifting away from Africa, opening the western Indian Ocean. The oldest magnetic stripes in the seafloor place the first break in today's southern Weddell Sea, between about 180 and 160 million years ago. The breakup sped up in the Cretaceous and was largely complete by that period's end.

jura-083.title: Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs reshuffle their ranks
jura-083.text: Between the end of the Toarcian and the start of the Bajocian, most ichthyosaur lineages appear to have died out. The ophthalmosaurids took their place, appearing in the early Bajocian and from then on making up almost all ichthyosaurs. Plesiosaurs changed too: microcleidids vanished, rhomaleosaurids nearly did, and cryptoclidids arrived in the Bajocian to dominate the rest of the Jurassic.

jura-079.title: The first true Ginkgo trees appear
jura-079.text: In the Middle Jurassic of the Northern Hemisphere, the first members of the genus Ginkgo appear, with seed-bearing and pollen organs like those of the living species. Their wider order, the Ginkgoales, was among the most important parts of Eurasia's Jurassic floras.

jura-081.title: The first octopuses appear
jura-081.text: Octopuses first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, after their lineage split from the vampyromorphs, the vampire squid line, in the Triassic to Early Jurassic. Molecular evidence suggests the wider squid-and-octopus branch had split from the belemnoids, extinct squid-like animals, back in the Permian.

jura-085.title: The Sundance Sea floods northwestern North America
jura-085.text: From the Middle Jurassic, the shallow Sundance Sea flooded much of northwest North America five times, and dinosaurs left tracks on its shores at Red Gulch, Wyoming. Late in the Jurassic it retreated for the last time, buried beneath river sediments of the Morrison Formation.

jura-086.title: Long-isolated terranes dock with North America
jura-086.text: The Alexander and Wrangellia terranes, slabs of crust with their own separate histories, joined western North America in the Middle Jurassic after long isolation in Panthalassa. The Cache Creek Ocean probably closed at the same time, and the Stikinia terrane was also added during the Jurassic.

jura-087.title: Theropods split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs
jura-087.text: By the Middle Jurassic, tetanurans, the stiff-tailed branch of the theropods, had reached every continent and split into two great lines. Allosauroids became the first giant theropods, topping 2 tonnes, and Asfaltovenator of South America may be the oldest of them. Coelurosaurs, the line that would later give rise to birds, appeared too, including early tyrannosauroids such as Proceratosaurus from Bathonian Britain.

jura-084.title: Seas rise toward a Late Jurassic high
jura-084.text: Sea level rose steadily from the Aalenian, apart from dips in the Bajocian and near the Callovian–Oxfordian boundary, and deepened the seaways between continents. It peaked possibly 140 meters above today's at the Kimmeridgian–Tithonian boundary, probably because seafloor spreading sped up.

jura-089.title: Carnosaurs join the ranks of predators
jura-089.text: Carnosaurs, a group of predatory theropods, first appeared in the Middle Jurassic around 174 million years ago. Their line endured until about 90 million years ago, when the carcharodontosaurids, its last definite family, died out.

jura-091.title: Dinosaur tracks and bones on the Isle of Skye
jura-091.text: Bones and footprints of dinosaurs both survive in Middle Jurassic rocks on Skye's Trotternish peninsula. Large theropods, sauropods and armored thyreophorans left bones there, and all three left tracks at Staffin Bay, Duntulm and Brother's Point.

jura-090.title: Toarcian warmth gives way to a cool spell
jura-090.text: When the Toarcian Warm Interval ended around 174 million years ago, the Middle Jurassic Cool Interval took over and lasted until about 164 million years ago. Brief icehouse episodes may have interrupted it, including a possible short-lived ice age in the late Bajocian. Europe turned noticeably wetter at the Aalenian–Bajocian boundary, then drier during the middle Bajocian. The interval closed with especially sharp global cooling at the Callovian–Oxfordian boundary, possibly even an ice age.

jura-093.title: The first unmistakable stegosaurs appear
jura-093.text: Plated plant-eaters such as Adratiklit, Bashanosaurus and Thyreosaurus, the earliest unequivocal stegosaurs, come from Bajocian–Bathonian rocks. Footprints called Deltapodus, left in England during the Aalenian, are the oldest probable stegosaur record.

jura-097.title: Long-necked cryptoclidids and elasmosaurids appear
jura-097.text: Cryptoclidid and elasmosaurid plesiosaurs first appeared around 170 million years ago; cryptoclidids were fairly short animals with long necks and small heads. Elasmosaurids grew up to 15 meters long, with as many as 76 neck vertebrae, more than any other known vertebrate.

jura-098.title: Megalosaurids appear in Europe
jura-098.text: Megalosaurids, the oldest radiation of tetanuran theropods, first appeared in Europe during the Bajocian, around 170 million years ago. By the late Middle Jurassic, megalosaurines were already among the largest predators on land.

jura-099.title: Salamanders and newts emerge
jura-099.text: The first salamanders and newts appeared around 170 million years ago; early modern salamanders such as Chunerpeton and Pangerpeton lived in China's Yanliao Biota. By the end of the Jurassic salamanders had reached North America, as Iridotriton from the Morrison Formation shows.

jura-096.title: The young Atlantic becomes a seaway
jura-096.text: As Pangaea broke up between about 170 and 150 million years ago, the young Atlantic began to form a seaway, the Atlantic Gateway. By the Late Jurassic, this still-narrow ocean had just separated Europe from North America. A rift spread from the Central Atlantic along the margin of northwestern France toward Aquitaine. In the Oxfordian, the same rift system opened deep basins that would later hold the Paratethys.

jura-102.title: A weak magnetic field leaves faint seafloor stripes
jura-102.text: From about 170 to 130 million years ago, Earth's magnetic field was weak, so the seafloor formed then carries only faint magnetic stripes. These stripes were once read as a ‘Jurassic Quiet Zone’, a long spell without magnetic reversals, but rocks on land record the field still flipping.

jura-100.title: Iberia slides away from Europe
jura-100.text: Between 170 and 120 million years ago, Iberia slid more than 200 km sideways past Europe as it rifted away from the Grand Banks. In the Late Jurassic the Iberian microcontinent broke from the European plate, and the Valais Ocean opened between them.

jura-103.title: The Obolon' impact strikes Ukraine
jura-103.text: An impact in what is now Poltava Oblast, Ukraine, left the Obolon' crater, a confirmed buried structure about 20 km across. One estimate puts its age at 169 ± 7 million years, in the Middle Jurassic.

jura-106.title: Lizards and snakes enter the fossil record
jura-106.text: The oldest unambiguous squamates, the lizards and snakes, come from Bathonian rocks of the Northern Hemisphere, when many modern groups, snakes included, first appear. Their common ancestor probably lived earlier, in the Early Jurassic, about 190 million years ago. A fossil called Cryptovaranoides was claimed as a Late Triassic squamate, which would push the origin back further, but its identity has been disputed since 2023. Snakes probably evolved from burrowing or aquatic lizards, and their earliest fossils date to between 167 and 143 million years ago.

jura-108.title: Choristoderes, puzzling freshwater reptiles, appear
