jura-108.text: The oldest unequivocal choristodere, the small, lizard-like Cteniogenys, lived in Britain about 168–166 million years ago. Choristoderes were freshwater reptiles of uncertain ancestry, and their order survived all the way to the Miocene.

jura-109.title: Multituberculates begin a 100-million-year run
jura-109.text: England and Russia have yielded the earliest known multituberculates, such as Hahnotherium and Kermackodon, from rocks about 168–166 million years old. One of the most successful mammal orders, they lasted over 100 million years, longer than any other order of mammals and their close kin, until the Oligocene.

jura-110.title: The mammal family tree forks into modern branches
jura-110.text: Fossils about 167 million years old, among them Ambondro, Amphilestes and Amphitherium, show that the mammal family tree had already forked. One branch led to the egg-laying monotremes, the other to the therians, the marsupials and placentals. That fork marks the origin of crown-group mammals, the group that includes every living species, though some sources place it earlier, late in the Early Jurassic. Most Jurassic mammals stayed under 10 kilograms, yet the docodont Castorocauda already had fur, and the chipmunk-sized Fruitafossor probably dug into termite nests.

jura-114.title: The Turgai Sea parts Europe from Asia
jura-114.text: In the Callovian, the Turgai Epicontinental Sea, a sea that flooded the continent itself, formed a marine barrier between Europe and Asia.

jura-113.title: Liopleurodon's sea: the Oxford Clay
jura-113.text: Over much of southeast England, from Dorset to Yorkshire, the Oxford Clay preserves a sea where the plesiosaurs Liopleurodon and Cryptoclidus swam with the ichthyosaur Ophthalmosaurus. At Christian Malford in Wiltshire, the clay even preserves coleoids, the squid and octopus group, in exceptional detail.

jura-115.title: The Gulf of Mexico opens
jura-115.text: North America began pulling away from South America in the Early Jurassic, opening a new rift beside what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Seafloor spreading in the gulf itself began about 165 million years ago, carrying the Maya Block away from the Laurentian craton, the ancient core of North America. The Florida Platform, once part of Africa, stayed with North America and gathered carbonate, evaporite salts, sand and mud as the gulf opened. How the crustal blocks of Middle America moved after 170 million years ago is still not widely agreed.

jura-119.title: A small crater forms at Zapadnaya, Ukraine
jura-119.text: The Zapadnaya crater in Ukraine's Zhytomyr Oblast, about 3.2 km across, formed some 165 ± 5 million years ago, in the Middle Jurassic.

jura-117.title: Rocky Mountain building begins in western North America
jura-117.text: Between 165 and 155 million years ago, an exotic terrane called the Mezcalera promontory began to subduct, and Rocky Mountain building got under way. Volcanoes flared in the Sierra Nevada arc from 170 to 150 million years ago, and the southern Sevier belt began to crumple around 160 million years ago.

jura-118.title: Layers of ash save China's Yanliao Biota
jura-118.text: In northeastern China, beds of volcanic tuff, or hardened ash, alternated with ordinary sediment from about 165 to 150 million years ago. Known as the Yanliao Biota, they hold some of the world's best Jurassic fossils, from dinosaurs and mammals to lizards, insects and plants. Among them, the Daohugou beds formed between 164 and 158 million years ago. The Haifanggou Formation adds pterosaurs, amphibians, arthropods and mammaliaforms, the wider group that includes mammals and their closest extinct kin.

jura-122.title: The Kimmeridgian Warm Interval brings heat and rain
jura-122.text: After the Middle Jurassic cool spell, a warm phase called the Kimmeridgian Warm Interval held from about 164 to 150 million years ago. Very high carbon dioxide levels drove high temperatures around the globe through the greenhouse effect. Fossil wood suggests it was one of the Jurassic's wettest stretches, as the widening Central Atlantic and western Indian Ocean fed moisture inland and softened the seasons. Europe, by contrast, grew steadily more arid through the Late Jurassic.

jura-123.title: The first pterodactyloid pterosaurs appear
jura-123.text: Pterodactyloid pterosaurs first appeared around 163 million years ago. Pterosaurs as a whole went on to reach their peak diversity in the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.

jura-124.title: Lhasa begins docking with Qiangtang
jura-124.text: About 163–145 million years ago, the Lhasa terrane, a crustal slice that had rifted from northern Gondwana, began colliding with the Qiangtang terrane along the Bangong suture. The collision lasted into the early Late Cretaceous, and the joined Lhasa terrane now forms southern Tibet.

jura-135.title: The two living turtle lineages part ways
jura-135.text: By the start of the Late Jurassic, the two living turtle groups had already diverged: the side-necked pleurodires and the hidden-necked cryptodires. The oldest pleurodires, the Platychelyidae, and the oldest unambiguous cryptodire, Sinaspideretes from China, are both Late Jurassic.

jura-134.title: Kimmeridge Clay: the mud that became North Sea oil
jura-134.text: The Kimmeridge Clay, a fossil-rich marine clay holding ichthyosaurs and pliosaurs, built up from Dorset to Lincolnshire and beneath the North Sea. Algae and bacteria buried in its mud turned into North Sea oil and gas, making the clay and its equivalents the region's main source rock.

jura-137.title: The Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean snaps shut
jura-137.text: Closing from west to east since the Late Triassic, the Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean finally shut in a rapid, scissor-like collision between Siberia and the North China–Amuria and Erguna blocks. The collision raised the Verkhoyansk–Kolyma mountain belt of Siberia.

jura-138.title: Reefs return, and crabs move in
jura-138.text: Reefs had withered at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, but in the Late Jurassic they expanded greatly, built both by sponges and by scleractinian, or stony, corals. They resembled modern reefs, though microbes and heavily calcified sponges built more of their rock, and living binders held it together less firmly. Crabs, rare until then, moved into the reefs and became abundant, sheltering from predators in their crevices.

jura-139.title: Teleost fishes begin their great radiation
jura-139.text: Teleosts, which now make up over 99% of living ray-finned fish, began a major diversification in the Late Jurassic. Early members of modern groups appeared, such as the Elopomorpha, the group that includes eels, and the Osteoglossoidei. Late Jurassic rocks in Peru hold the earliest known ellimmichthyiforms and the oldest clupeomorphs, the herring group. The oldest anatomically modern gars also appeared at this time.

jura-140.title: Tanzania's Tendaguru beds and the towering Giraffatitan
jura-140.text: Africa's richest Late Jurassic rocks, the Tendaguru Beds of southeastern Tanzania, record semi-arid coastal plains whose dinosaurs resembled those of North America's Morrison Formation. Their bonebeds hold Giraffatitan, the tallest and heaviest dinosaur known from good skeletons, and over a thousand bones of the stegosaur Kentrosaurus.

jura-141.title: The Zuñi transgression begins
jura-141.text: In the latest Jurassic, the sea began a long advance across North America, recorded in the rocks of the Zuñi sequence. This cratonic sequence, a vast layer of sediment left by flooding of the continent's interior, followed the Absaroka, peaked in the Late Cretaceous and ended by the Paleocene.

jura-142.title: Yinlong, the earliest ceratopsian
jura-142.text: Ceratopsians, the lineage that later produced the horned dinosaurs, appear in the fossil record around 161 million years ago with Yinlong. These first ceratopsians, members of the Chaoyangsauridae, lived in Late Jurassic China.

jura-144.title: Juramaia, a shrew-like start to the placental line
jura-144.text: Small and shrew-like, Juramaia sinensis lived in China about 160 million years ago and is the oldest known eutherian. Eutherians form the branch of mammals that includes the placentals, and Juramaia sits closer to their ancestry than to the marsupials.

jura-145.title: New ocean floor splits East and West Gondwana
jura-145.text: Around 160 million years ago, Africa separated from Antarctica as new oceanic crust began forming between East and West Gondwana. East Gondwana held Antarctica, Australia, India and Madagascar, while West Gondwana held Africa, Arabia and South America. East Antarctica moved south faster than Africa and South America, opening the Weddell, Riiser-Larsen, Mozambique and Somali basins. Australia and Antarctica also began pulling apart, and magmatism from the Australia–India breakup, 158–136 million years ago, built the Wallaby Plateau.

jura-147.title: Vepriai, Lithuania's largest impact crater
jura-147.text: An impact carved the Vepriai crater, 8 km across and the largest in Lithuania, at least 160 ± 10 million years ago, in the Middle or Late Jurassic.

jura-148.title: The Morrison floodplains teem with giant sauropods
jura-148.text: Between about 156.3 and 146.8 million years ago, rivers spread sediment across western North America as the Sundance Sea retreated before highlands rising to the west. The resulting Morrison Formation holds one of the best-known sauropod faunas, 24 recognized species, among them Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Camarasaurus and Diplodocus. Predators such as Allosaurus, Ceratosaurus and Torvosaurus left bite marks on bones at the Mygatt-Moore Quarry. At Cleveland-Lloyd, the densest known concentration of Jurassic dinosaurs, animals died around a drought-stricken pond.

jura-150.title: Argoland: a disputed landmass off Australia
jura-150.text: A hypothetical landmass called Argoland may have rifted off northwestern Australia about 155 million years ago, though its form and fate are still debated. A 2023 reconstruction treats it as an archipelago of microcontinental fragments, now in and around southwest Borneo, rather than one continent.

jura-152.title: Stegosaurs reach their peak
jura-152.text: After early forms such as China's Huayangosaurus, about 166 million years ago, came much larger stegosaurs such as Tuojiangosaurus by the Callovian–Oxfordian. Stegosaurids had their greatest radiation in the Late Jurassic, and Stegosaurus itself lived in Wyoming in the Kimmeridgian, recorded in the upper Morrison Formation.

jura-151.title: The Nevadan orogeny raises the ancestral Sierra Nevada
jura-151.text: From about 155 to 145 million years ago, the Nevadan orogeny built mountains along the western margin of North America. It began as an Andean-type volcanic arc above the sinking Farallon plate. Arc magma and accreted ocean island arcs built the ancestral Sierra Nevada and Klamath Mountains, while terranes such as Tuolumne River and Slate Creek joined the continent. One source starts its massive batholiths in the mid-Jurassic, and mountain building carried on in the Cretaceous Sevier and Laramide orogenies.

jura-156.title: Eathiestrobus and the first pines
jura-156.text: The oldest unambiguous member of the pine family is Eathiestrobus, a cone from Kimmeridgian Scotland and the group's only certain fossil older than the Cretaceous. The earliest pine trees are dated to about 153 million years ago, and by the end of the Jurassic most modern conifer groups had appeared.

jura-158.title: Archaeopteryx and the first birds
jura-158.text: Around 150 million years ago, Archaeopteryx lived in southern Germany, then a warm tropical archipelago. It has long been considered the earliest bird, though the boundary between birds and their non-bird relatives is unclear. Birds evolved from small predatory coelurosaurian theropods of the clade Paraves, and the earliest avialans, the bird lineage, appear in the Middle to Late Jurassic. Archaeopteryx already carried advanced flight feathers, so feathers must have begun evolving before the Late Jurassic.

jura-160.title: Cimmeria finally docks against Laurasia
jura-160.text: About 150 million years ago, Cimmeria collided with Laurasia and stalled, and the ocean floor behind it buckled under to form the Tethys Trench. Greece's Hellenic orogeny records Late Jurassic collisions of Cimmerian fragments with Eurasia.

jura-163.title: A cool interval closes the Jurassic
jura-163.text: Around 150 million years ago, the Jurassic began to wind down with a cooler phase, the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval, which lasted into the Early Cretaceous. During the Tithonian, a marked temperature drop known as the Early Tithonian Cooling Event deepened the chill.

jura-167.title: Solnhofen's lagoons preserve feathers and jellyfish
jura-167.text: About 149–148 million years ago, fine limestones settled in the salty lagoons of the Solnhofen archipelago in Bavaria, at the edge of the Tethys. Oxygen-free bottom waters kept scavengers away, so animals and plants washed in were buried in soft carbonate mud, down to jellyfish, dragonfly wings and stray feathers. This Konservat-Lagerstätte, a site of exceptional preservation, has yielded over 600 species, including 29 kinds of pterosaur and the famous early bird Archaeopteryx. Nearby sites such as Ettling add fish, horseshoe crabs, beetles, crustaceans and turtles.

jura-168.title: The Arctic Ocean begins to open
jura-168.text: As Pangaea's breakup continued across the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, the Amerasian Basin and the Arctic Ocean opened, from about 148 to 70 million years ago. The opening came with the High Arctic Large Igneous Province, another vast outpouring of magma.

jura-170.title: The Morokweng asteroid strikes South Africa
jura-170.text: About 146 million years ago, in the Tithonian, an asteroid 5–10 km wide struck what is now South Africa's North West province. It was an L-chondrite, a type of stony asteroid, and it hit several million years before the end of the Jurassic. The buried crater's size is debated, with estimates from 75–80 km to 240 km; the latest is about 190 km. Tithonian rocks in Brazil's Araripe basin hold a layer of iridium, a metal common in asteroids, that may be linked to the impact.

jura-172.title: The last Karoo eruptions flicker out
jura-172.text: The Karoo province ended about 145 million years ago with scattered eruptions on its fringes: Patagonia, the Antarctic Peninsula, northern South Africa, Kerala and southeast Australia.

jura-173.title: Tamu Massif, perhaps Earth's largest volcano, erupts
jura-173.text: In the northwest Pacific, lava erupting where the Pacific, Farallon and Izanagi plates met built the Shatsky Rise, Earth's third-largest oceanic plateau. Tamu Massif, its oldest and largest peak, grew in a few million years into a basalt dome about 450 by 650 kilometers, roughly New Mexico's size. Its slopes never exceed one degree, and it is likely the largest volcano yet found, though it may turn out to be several volcanoes. Its origin is still debated: a mantle plume, melting beneath a mid-ocean ridge, or a recycled slab of sunken plate.

jura-174.title: Extinction or turnover? The Jurassic draws to a close
jura-174.text: The end of the Jurassic was once counted among eight mass extinctions, but many now see a complex turnover instead, with some groups rising as others declined. Scientists still disagree about which picture fits, partly because the evidence comes mainly from Europe. Sea level probably drove the change, falling in the late Tithonian and rising at the boundary, while sharp reef losses cut crab and shrimp diversity. Most life was not strongly affected, and several ichthyosaur and pliosaur lineages crossed into the Cretaceous.

cret-003.title: Tiny algae build the chalk of Dover's cliffs
cret-003.text: More chalk formed in the Cretaceous than in any other period of the Phanerozoic, the eon of abundant animal life, and the period takes its name from it. Chalk is made of coccoliths, the microscopic calcite plates of coccolithophore algae that thrived in Cretaceous seas. Their diversity, along with that of other calcareous nannoplankton, tiny drifting organisms with chalky shells, climbed through the Mesozoic to about 150 species in the Late Cretaceous. Upper Cretaceous chalk now forms the white cliffs of Dover and similar cliffs on the Normandy coast of France.

cret-006.title: Rising seas drown a third of the land
cret-006.text: Sea level rose in earnest from the early Cretaceous, and by the Cenomanian it stood roughly 250 meters above today's, perhaps even 300. Many small, fast-recycled ocean plates made the basins shallower, pushing the water up onto the continents. At the peak of this transgression, the sea's advance over the land, one-third of Earth's present land area lay underwater. The Mid-Cretaceous Superplume, a vast upwelling of hot mantle rock, may have driven North America's flooding, the Zuñi sequence, which ebbed late in the period.

cret-013.title: Gondwana shatters into the southern continents
cret-013.text: Gondwana, the great southern landmass, had begun to crack in the Jurassic, but in the Cretaceous its breakup sped up and was largely finished by the period's end. The split began near Tasmania, and South America, Antarctica and Australia rifted away from Africa while India and Madagascar stayed joined. Two new oceans were born, the South Atlantic and the Indian. As the land divided, so did its animals: by the Early Cretaceous, dinosaurs on each landmass had grown strongly distinct.

cret-016.title: Strange bivalves called rudists build the Tethys reefs
cret-016.text: Rudists were bivalves shaped like boxes, tubes or rings, and after arising in the Late Jurassic they became the main reef builders of the Tethys. Their reefs may have pushed scleractinian corals, the stony corals of modern reefs, off many tropical shelves, including today's Caribbean and Mediterranean. The rudists had collapsed by the K–Pg extinction, the great die-off that ended the Cretaceous, and the last of them vanished with it.

cret-001.title: The Cretaceous begins without an agreed starting line
cret-001.text: The Cretaceous and its first stage, the Berriasian, begin 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years. Yet this is the only period boundary still lacking a GSSP, an agreed reference layer of rock, so its base remains formally undefined. One proposal uses the first appearance of Calpionella alpina, one of the calpionellids: enigmatic single-celled plankton with urn-shaped calcite shells. These creatures were abundant only briefly, from the latest Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous.

cret-011.title: Raptors appear: the first dromaeosaurs
cret-011.text: The first dromaeosaurs, the 'raptors', are placed at the start of the Cretaceous. Teeth that may be theirs turn up in Jurassic rocks, but no dromaeosaur bodies are known until the Cretaceous.

cret-015.title: Purbeck's lagoons hold insects, mammals and footprints
cret-015.text: Straddling the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, the Purbeck Group of southern England formed in a semi-arid land of freshwater lakes, lagoons, tidal flats and brackish water. It holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Cretaceous faunas, with hundreds of insect species, reptiles, early mammals from its 'Mammal Bed' and dinosaur footprints.

cret-002.title: Shark-toothed giants spread across the globe
cret-002.text: Large carcharodontosaurid predators, whose name means 'shark-toothed lizards', spread worldwide in the Early Cretaceous, reaching Africa, North America and South America. Dinosaur footprints suggest they may have crossed through Apulia in Italy, then joined to Africa by a land bridge.

cret-007.title: Early birds branch out, and enantiornithines take over
cret-007.text: Birds diversified into a wide variety of forms in the Early Cretaceous, and some already had a pygostyle, a short tail of fused bones. The enantiornithines became the dominant birds of the Cretaceous and held on until the end of the Mesozoic, when they died out with other dinosaur groups. China's Jehol Biota preserves a great diversity of birds, including the earliest advanced ones, and Las Hoyas in Spain holds many enantiornithines. Archaic birds had appeared in the Jurassic, but true toothless birds arose from toothed ancestors only in the Cretaceous.

cret-008.title: The Eromanga Sea floods inland Australia
cret-008.text: During the Early Cretaceous, an inland sea called the Eromanga Sea spread across a large part of Australia. Its waters were home to the giant pliosaur Kronosaurus, a short-necked marine reptile.

cret-010.title: Social ants and termites make their debut
cret-010.text: Insects diversified through the Cretaceous, and in the Early Cretaceous the oldest known ants and termites appeared, both already social. Stem-group ants, early relatives outside the modern family, such as Gerontoformica, are preserved in Albian–Cenomanian amber, fossilized tree resin, from France. Many ant groups lived in the Cretaceous, but ants only became dominant, with larger colonies, in the Eocene.

cret-012.title: The first sea turtles take to the oceans
cret-012.text: The oldest known sea turtles and soft-shelled turtles appeared in the Early Cretaceous, and the first freshwater pelomedusid turtles appeared around 135 million years ago. Turtles grew highly diverse in the Cretaceous, as the climate favored their spread around the globe.

cret-019.title: A comet or asteroid strikes central Australia
cret-019.text: About 142.5 million years ago, close to the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, an asteroid or comet hit central Australia and blasted a crater about 22 km across. Erosion has removed the rim, leaving a 5-km ring of uplifted rock; its shatter cones, fractures formed by shock waves, are the strongest evidence of impact.

cret-020.title: Mjølnir: a bolide hammers the Barents Sea floor
cret-020.text: A bolide, a large rock from space about 2 km wide, slammed into the floor of what is now the Barents Sea off Norway. It left a crater 40 km across, dated to 142.0 ± 2.6 million years ago.

cret-022.title: Orb-weaver spiders appear, spinning wheel-shaped webs
cret-022.text: Orb-weaver spiders, the builders of wheel-shaped webs, appeared around 140 million years ago.

cret-024.title: Europe pulls away from North America
cret-024.text: Between 140 and 120 million years ago, Europe rifted away from North America in the second major phase of the North Atlantic's breakup. The opening seaway let cool water flow from the Boreal Ocean into the Tethys. Around 140 million years ago a rift also began forming along the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay, a first stage in Greenland's separation. The new ocean ignored the line where an older ocean, the Iapetus, had closed, stranding ancient North American rocks in north-west Europe and Avalonian rocks in Newfoundland.

cret-023.title: Volcanic plateaus rise where Gondwana split three ways
cret-023.text: From 140 to 95 million years ago, a large igneous province, a vast pile of volcanic rock, grew where Gondwana split into Antarctica, South America and Africa. The Mozambique Ridge peaked about 120 million years ago, and a later pulse, 100–94 million years ago, built the Agulhas Plateau.

cret-021.title: The Eastern Alps begin to stack up
cret-021.text: Between 140 and 84 million years ago, the first, Eo-Alpine phase of mountain building stacked the Austroalpine nappes, sheets of rock shoved over one another. It began as Africa moved toward Europe again and the floor of the Piemont-Liguria Ocean was subducted, or dragged down, beneath the Apulian plate.

cret-025.title: The Sevier orogeny raises the western mountains
cret-025.text: From 140 to 50 million years ago, the Sevier orogeny, a mountain-building episode tied to a collision with island arcs, raised ranges in western North America. As its mountains rose, the Western Interior Basin to their east widened.

cret-026.title: Cold spells bring ice to the Early Cretaceous
cret-026.text: The cooling of the latest Jurassic lingered into the Berriasian, when snow fell often at high latitudes. Though the Mesozoic was long thought ice-free, records suggest glacial periods in the Valanginian, Hauterivian and Aptian. Dropstones, pebbles rafted out on ice and dropped into seafloor mud, hint that northern ice sheets may have reached as far south as Iberia. Rocks laid down directly by glaciers, however, are known only from the Eromanga Basin of southern Australia.

cret-027.title: Titanosaurs, the last great sauropods, appear
cret-027.text: Titanosaurs, the last great group of long-necked sauropods, lived from about 136 to 66 million years ago and were the dominant plant-eaters of their time. An early subadult, not yet fully grown, from Paraíba in Brazil is about 136 million years old. They spread almost worldwide, and their fossils turn up on every continent, Antarctica included. On the islands of Cretaceous Europe, some, like Magyarosaurus, were likely dwarfs, shrunk by island life.

cret-028.title: Paraná–Etendeka flood basalts pour out as Gondwana splits
cret-028.text: As Gondwana rifted over the Tristan hotspot, a plume of hot mantle rock, flood basalts poured out in vast sheets where the South Atlantic was opening. Their lavas covered about 1,000,000 square kilometers when the eruptions ended, and the original volume is projected at over 2.3 million cubic kilometers. The rift has since split the province in two: the Paraná Basin in South America and the Etendeka traps of Namibia and Angola. Its activity has been blamed for a warming event in the middle Valanginian, the Weissert Thermal Excursion.

cret-030.title: Jehol: volcanic ash buries feathered dinosaurs
cret-030.text: Between 135 and 121 million years ago, lake beds and volcanic ash in north-eastern China entombed a whole ecosystem, the Jehol Biota. It holds the first known feathered dinosaurs that were not birds, along with many birds and the largest known Mesozoic mammals. The beds also yield the earliest known flowering plants, with insects, fish, amphibians and pterosaurs, the flying reptiles, in huge numbers. Here, too, are the earliest neoceratopsians, therizinosaurs, tyrannosaurs and oviraptorids, groups that later spread worldwide.

cret-031.title: The Weissert Event: a sudden heat spike
cret-031.text: Around 134.5 million years ago, a hyperthermal, a rapid burst of global warming, broke into the otherwise mild Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval. Carbon dioxide from the Paraná–Etendeka eruptions is the leading suspect, though their drawn-out pace leads some scientists to doubt it. The warming robbed the oceans of oxygen but, unlike other such events, left no widespread black shales, the dark, organic-rich mud they usually lay down. When it ended, perhaps 1.4 to 2.08 million years later, temperatures fell sharply, by up to 4 °C around the Boreal Ocean.

cret-032.title: The first flowering plants leave their pollen
cret-032.text: The earliest widely accepted trace of flowering plants is single-grooved pollen about 134 million years old, from late Valanginian rocks in Israel and Italy. Within the Early Cretaceous they began to diversify rapidly, one of the major changes of the epoch. Among the oldest fossils of the plants themselves are Montsechia from Spain and Archaefructus, 124.6 million years old, from China's Yixian Formation. They radiated first in the tropics, then spread toward the poles, helped by the gentle temperature difference between the two.

cret-033.title: The Faraoni Event brings another warm pulse
cret-033.text: In the middle Hauterivian, the Faraoni Thermal Excursion came next in a series of Early Cretaceous warmings after the Weissert Event. A minor oceanic anoxic event, a spell of oxygen-starved seas, has been proposed for the Hauterivian, recorded mostly around the Atlantic.

cret-034.title: Australia begins its slow parting from Antarctica
cret-034.text: Australia and East Antarctica began to separate about 132 million years ago, and by 96 million years ago they were rifting, with seafloor spreading to follow. By then a shallow seaway was forming between them, leaving only a narrow link along the South Tasman Rise and Wilkes Land. Full separation came much later, and a narrow land connection among South America, Antarctica and Australia survived until about 50 million years ago. One timeline dates the split to about 80 million years ago, probably a later stage of the process.

cret-035.title: The first anglerfish appear
cret-035.text: The earliest anglerfish, fish that dangle a lure to attract prey, appeared about 130 million years ago.

cret-041.title: The South Atlantic begins to open
cret-041.text: About 130 million years ago the South Atlantic began to open, as the Falkland Plateau, broken from southern Africa at 132 million years ago, moved west. South America started drifting west away from Africa, while Laurasia, the northern landmass, rotated clockwise and moved north. The same stretching opened the West and Central African Rift System, including the Benue Trough, which had begun rifting at the start of the Cretaceous. By the Aptian–Albian, Africa was cut off from the rest of Gondwana and from Laurasia, and it stayed an island continent through most of the Cenozoic.

cret-038.title: India breaks loose from Australia and Antarctica
cret-038.text: Between 130 and 125 million years ago, the Indian plate broke away from Australia and Antarctica, opening a 'South Indian Ocean'. The new ocean's spreading ridge, where fresh seafloor forms, lay near the Kerguelen hotspot. Rifts along East Africa, Antarctica and Madagascar shaped the southwestern Indian Ocean, and Madagascar stopped moving on its own around 120 million years ago. Another source puts India's break from Australia later, about 100 million years ago.

cret-039.title: North China's craton loses its deep root
cret-039.text: Around 130–120 million years ago, the crust of North China switched to stretching, and its mountain belts and plateau collapsed. Its craton, an ancient continental core, lost its deep mantle root, perhaps thinned as subduction of the Paleo-Pacific plate retreated.

cret-040.title: Colombia's Paja shales preserve sea reptiles
cret-040.text: Between 130 and 113 million years ago, a warm, shallow, oxygen-starved sea over much of present-day Colombia laid down the shales and mudstones of the Paja Formation. The International Union of Geological Sciences lists it as a geological heritage site for the world's most complete record of Early Cretaceous marine reptiles.

cret-037.title: High Arctic magma helps open the Arctic Ocean
cret-037.text: Starting about 130 million years ago, the High Arctic Large Igneous Province broke up part of an old continent called Arctica and opened the Arctic Ocean. Crust in the Canadian Arctic began to stretch then, and sills and dikes, sheets of magma forced into the rock, spread widely 129–127 million years ago. The first phase lasted until 80 million years ago, and its rocks still cover over 1,000,000 square kilometers despite heavy erosion. The Iceland hotspot may have begun as a plume under the Alpha Ridge around 130–120 million years ago.

cret-042.title: Tookoonooka: a crater buried deep in Australia
cret-042.text: An impact about 128 million years ago left a crater 55–66 km across, now buried deep in Australia's Eromanga Basin. Shocked quartz, grains scarred by extreme pressure, turned up in drill core and proved its origin, and the nearby Talundilly structure may be its twin.

cret-043.title: A Belgian coal mine full of Iguanodon
cret-043.text: Deep in a coal mine at Bernissart, Belgium, lay at least 38 individuals of Iguanodon bernissartensis, a dinosaur that grew to about 9 meters long. Once read as a herd that died together, the bones now seem to record at least three separate die-offs, probably caused by flash floods.

cret-045.title: Earliest marsupial and placental relatives appear in China
cret-045.text: Sinodelphys, from 125-million-year-old shale in Liaoning, China, is the earliest known metatherian, a member of the marsupial line, and it had climbing feet. Eomaia, a eutherian of the same age on the placental line, still shared features with marsupials that placentals later lost. Both already held their limbs upright beneath the body rather than sprawling. The finds suggest early mammals began to diversify from Asia.

cret-047.title: Las Hoyas preserves a Spanish wetland in stone
cret-047.text: About 125 million years ago, freshwater wetland limestones at Las Hoyas, Spain, captured dinosaurs and many enantiornithine birds in exquisite detail. The site also yields Montsechia, one of the oldest known fossils of a flowering plant.

cret-046.title: Flowers and pollinators remake life on land
cret-046.text: From around 125 to 80 million years ago, in the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution, flowering plants diversified intensely alongside the insects that pollinated them. By the mid-Cretaceous, species diversity on land had overtaken that of the sea, reversing a pattern held for nearly all of Earth's history. Flowering plants dominated forest trees by 110–90 million years ago and displaced conifers, cycads and bennettitaleans by the period's end. Full dominance came only in the early Cenozoic; a longer view, Benton's 'Angiosperm Terrestrial Revolution', runs from 100 to 50 million years ago.

cret-044.title: Stressed forests pour out resin, and amber piles up
cret-044.text: From 125 to 75 million years ago, heat-driven storms, hurricanes, wildfires and insect attacks drove trees to produce huge amounts of resin. By the Early Cretaceous, amber was forming in concentrations matching or exceeding those of the Triassic's Carnian stage.

cret-049.title: Koolasuchus, the last temnospondyl amphibian
cret-049.text: Koolasuchus, a chigutisaurid from the Aptian of Australia, is the latest known temnospondyl, a group of early amphibians whose last members had survived from the Triassic. By the Late Cretaceous all were gone, leaving frogs, salamanders and their kin, the lissamphibians, as the only amphibians.

cret-050.title: Thalattosuchian sea crocodiles fade away
cret-050.text: Thalattosuchians, marine relatives of crocodiles that had been abundant in the Jurassic, grew scarce and mostly tropical in the Early Cretaceous. Their last records come from the Aptian.

cret-051.title: The plated stegosaurs make their last stand
cret-051.text: As seaways expanded, stegosaurs and other high-browsing plant-eaters declined; the youngest definite ones, Mongolostegus and Yanbeilong, date to the Aptian–Albian. Reported later finds have mostly proved misidentified, so the group appears to have died out in the late Early or early Late Cretaceous.

cret-052.title: Earth's magnetic field stops flipping for 37 million years
cret-052.text: From the Aptian through the Santonian, Earth's magnetic field held normal polarity, the same orientation as today, with no reversals for about 37 million years. Reversals had grown steadily rarer in the run-up, and this superchron, a long stretch without them, began 120.964 million years ago as chron C34n. It is one of only two well-established superchrons, the other being the Permian Kiaman. All the lavas of the Ontong Java Plateau are normally magnetized, so they presumably erupted after it began.

cret-053.title: The Selli Event chokes the oceans of oxygen
cret-053.text: At the start of the Aptian, the world's oceans lost their oxygen in a global anoxic event, the Selli Event, or OAE1a. It was tied to volcanism, and carbon released by magma intruding beneath the Barents Sea, perhaps 9,000 gigatonnes, may have set it off. Warming, acidifying water and oxygen loss killed marine life; the event lasted about 1.1–1.3 million years, and recovery took over a million more. With OAE2, it was one of the two Cretaceous anoxic events that most changed ocean chemistry, leaving black shales worldwide.

cret-055.title: Egg-laying monotremes appear in Australia
cret-055.text: Teinolophos, which lived in Australia about 120 million years ago, is one of the earliest known monotremes, the egg-laying mammals. Steropodon, another Australian about 105 million years old, has also been called the oldest monotreme.

cret-057.title: The last mammal-like tritylodontids vanish
cret-057.text: Tritylodontids, extremely mammal-like plant-eaters, were the last surviving cynodonts outside the mammal family tree. Fossiomanus from China shows they persisted in Asia until at least around 120 million years ago, so they died out no earlier than that, in the Early Cretaceous.

cret-059.title: A small impact scars Ukraine
cret-059.text: An impact in what is now Ukraine left a crater 2.7 km wide, dated to 120 ± 10 million years ago. A lens of broken granite and impact glass fills it, buried under Early Cretaceous sediments.

cret-056.title: The Kerguelen hotspot piles up a giant plateau
cret-056.text: The Kerguelen hotspot hit peak output 120–95 million years ago, building the Southern and Central Kerguelen Plateau and Broken Ridge. Together they cover 2,300,000 square kilometers, and the province holds about 25 million cubic kilometers of lava. Its earlier eruptions include Australia's Bunbury Basalt and India's Rajmahal and Sylhet Traps, linked to the opening of the eastern Indian Ocean. Growth of the Southern Kerguelen Plateau 118–119 million years ago contributed to oceanic anoxic event 1, and the Kerguelen microcontinent may have carried dense conifer forest.

cret-060.title: The Aptian–Albian Cold Snap chills the planet
cret-060.text: About 118 million years ago, after a warm interval, the Aptian–Albian Cold Snap set in and dragged global mean surface temperature down to about 20.7 °C. It ended around 111 million years ago, and glacial dropstones in western Tethys sediments hint at an ice age.

cret-061.title: A minor extinction strikes the Aptian seas
cret-061.text: Around 116 or 117 million years ago, a minor extinction event struck, seen mostly in marine deposits and possibly linked to the Rajmahal Traps eruptions in India. For the history of plants, though, it was an important episode.

cret-062.title: Ontong Java: the greatest eruption in 200 million years
cret-062.text: In the south-west Pacific, the Ontong Java, Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus probably formed as one vast province, by far the largest on Earth. When the eruptions ended, it covered 1% of Earth's surface with 80 million cubic kilometers of basalt, several times the volume of the Deccan Traps. The main event, around 116 million years ago, poured out up to 22 cubic kilometers of magma a year for 3 million years. Its eruptions were long thought to coincide with the Selli Event, but basalt ages of 117–108 million years and normal magnetization make that unlikely.

cret-064.title: Subduction zones begin to ring the Pacific
cret-064.text: By about 115 million years ago, today's subduction zones had begun to ring the Pacific around South America, North America and Asia. The Farallon plate was diving beneath the Americas and north-east Asia, and the Izanagi plate beneath east Asia.

cret-065.title: Vista Alegre crater scars Brazil's basalts
cret-065.text: An impact crater in the volcanic basalts of southern Brazil, near the Vargeão Dome, has recently been dated to about 115 million years ago.

cret-063.title: Deinonychus: the sickle claw that remade dinosaur science
cret-063.text: Described in 1969, Deinonychus, a sickle-clawed dromaeosaurid up to 3.4 meters long, emerged as an active, agile predator and launched the 'dinosaur renaissance'. It also stirred debate over warm-blooded dinosaurs, and its bird-like forelimbs led Ostrom to revive the now near-universal view that birds descend from dinosaurs.

cret-067.title: The first grasses take root
cret-067.text: The oldest known fossils of grasses, the family Poaceae, come from Albian rocks near the end of the Early Cretaceous. By the time the Cretaceous closed, grasses had already diversified into modern groups.

cret-068.title: Brazil's Crato lake preserves soft parts in stone
cret-068.text: The Crato and Romualdo formations of north-east Brazil, laid down near the ancient equator, preserve pterosaurs, fish, insects and plants exceptionally well. In the semi-arid Crato lake wetland, about 113 million years ago, limestone nodules formed around carcasses, saving soft parts and even fish stomach contents.

cret-070.title: Borealopelta, an armored dinosaur 'mummy' from Alberta
cret-070.text: Washed out to sea after death, the 5.5-meter armored dinosaur Borealopelta was buried in Alberta's Clearwater Formation with its skin, armor and stomach contents intact. Pigments suggest a reddish-brown hide, darker on top than below, and such camouflage implies that even this large armored animal had predators to fear.

cret-069.title: More anoxic events strike the Albian seas
cret-069.text: Further oceanic anoxic events, OAE1b, 1c and 1d, struck in the Albian, around 112–100 million years ago, within one of the longest anoxic intervals in geologic history. Their black shales lie mostly in the Atlantic region, and some researchers blame local conditions rather than global change.

cret-071.title: Snakes emerge from their lizard ancestors
cret-071.text: The oldest true snakes are marine simoliophiids such as Haasiophis from the West Bank, dated 112–94 million years ago. Snakes evolved from lizards, perhaps burrowers or mosasaur relatives, and in the Late Cretaceous they recolonized land and kept diversifying.

cret-073.title: The Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse switches on
cret-073.text: Temperatures rose sharply after the cold snap ended around 111 million years ago, opening a hothouse that lasted until the early Campanian. A string of hyperthermals followed through the Albian, from the Leenhardt Event around 110 million years ago to the Breistroffer around 101 million years ago. Late Albian tropical seas averaged about 30 °C, while dry belts on land repeatedly pushed north. From the Albian, the oceans kept warming gradually toward a peak in the Turonian.

cret-072.title: Giganotosaurus prowls Patagonia
cret-072.text: Giganotosaurus, a huge carcharodontosaurid that rivaled Tyrannosaurus among the largest predators, lived in Argentina about 111–106 million years ago. A 2026 study re-dated its rocks from the Cenomanian to the early Albian, and its lineage may have split from African relatives as Gondwana broke apart.

cret-075.title: South America and Africa finally let go
cret-075.text: Identical dinosaur footprints in Brazil and Cameroon suggest the two continents were still linked by land around 120 million years ago, in the early Aptian. By 110 million years ago the Mid-Atlantic Ridge reached the Proto-Caribbean, splitting South America from Africa and completing the Atlantic's length. The breakup may have cut off South America's carcharodontosaurids from their African relatives. Around 100 million years ago, spreading sped up sharply, the ridge grew from 1,200 to 7,000 km long, and Africa began moving north-east.

cret-076.title: Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan, the titanosaur giants
cret-076.text: At about 30–35 meters long and 65–80 tonnes, Argentinosaurus of Argentina's Huincul Formation was among the largest land animals ever. A 2026 study placed its rocks in the Albian, about 106 million years ago, though earlier work had suggested a younger Cenomanian–Turonian age. Its close relative Patagotitan, from Patagonian rocks about 101.62 million years old, was first billed as the largest land animal: 37 meters and 69 tonnes. Later estimates cut it to about 31 meters and 50–60 tonnes, still a giant among titanosaurs, the dominant sauropods of the Cretaceous.

cret-077.title: Dinosaurs endure the polar night at Dinosaur Cove
cret-077.text: Dinosaur Cove's fossils come from a rift-valley floodplain inside the Antarctic Circle, where some dinosaurs lived year-round as Australia began pulling away from Antarctica. Its 'polar dinosaurs' include small plant-eaters such as Leaellynasaura and Atlascopcosaurus, and one fossil hints at adaptations to the dim light of polar winter.

cret-078.title: The granite of Half Dome and El Capitan forms
cret-078.text: As the Farallon plate sank beneath North America, rising magma cooled underground into plutons, the bodies of granite that make up the Sierra Nevada Batholith. Uplift and erosion later exposed that granite as the peaks of the High Sierra, including Mount Whitney, Half Dome and El Capitan.

cret-079.title: Burmese amber traps a lost island world
cret-079.text: Amber from Myanmar's Hukawng Valley, 101–99 million years old, has yielded over 1,000 species, mostly insects, from a Tethys island near the equator. Its finds include Chimerarachne, an arachnid with silk spinnerets and a tail, though the amber trade is ethically controversial.

cret-080.title: Antarctica bridges South America and Australia
cret-080.text: In the Late Cretaceous and early Paleogene, Antarctica linked South America and Australia by land, and marsupials appear to have crossed it to reach Australia. Platypus-like monotremes went the other way, reaching southern South America in the latest Cretaceous.

cret-082.title: Mysterious thylacocephalan crustaceans die out
cret-082.text: Thylacocephala, an enigmatic class of crustaceans, went extinct in the Late Cretaceous.

cret-083.title: Meridiolestidans rule South America's mammal world
cret-083.text: Meridiolestidans were the dominant mammals of Late Cretaceous South America, ranging from saber-toothed Cronopio to plant-eating mesungulatids. The group outlived the dinosaurs, lingering in Patagonia until the Miocene.

cret-084.title: Shell-crushers perfect their craft in Late Cretaceous seas
cret-084.text: In the Late Cretaceous, marine reptiles and other predators perfected shell-crushing, the driver of the Mesozoic marine revolution. Sea urchins radiated into predatory niches, and faster weathering from the flowering-plant boom may have fed the change with nutrients.

cret-087.title: The Mississippi embayment takes shape
cret-087.text: The Mississippi River Delta traces its roots to about 100 million years ago, when the Mississippi embayment, a broad bay-shaped basin, formed.

cret-088.title: Modern birds arise, though rocks and clocks disagree
cret-088.text: Modern birds probably arose around 100 million years ago, near the boundary of the Early and Late Cretaceous, and diversified dramatically around the K–Pg extinction. The timing is disputed: molecular clocks, which date splits from genetic differences, favor a Cretaceous radiation, while fossils point to a Paleogene one. A 2024 genomic study pushed the split between ostrich-like birds and all others back to around 130 million years ago. On the fossil side, only waterfowl and shorebirds have an established Late Cretaceous record.

cret-086.title: Giant predators crowd North Africa's tidal coast
cret-086.text: Around 100–94 million years ago, abelisauroids, spinosaurids and carcharodontosaurids, including Carcharodontosaurus and Spinosaurus, ruled North Africa together. Their home on the Tethys shore was a mangrove coast of vast tidal flats and waterways, preserved in the Kem Kem and Bahariya beds.

cret-090.title: Zealandia tears away from West Antarctica
cret-090.text: Around 100 million years ago, magma in the region switched abruptly from the kind fed by a sinking plate to the kind fed by crust pulling apart. That shift began separating Zealandia, the continent that includes New Zealand, the Campbell Plateau and New Caledonia, from West Antarctica, a split completed about 84 million years ago. At about the same time, the Hikurangi Plateau first slid beneath New Zealand as it collided with Gondwana. The West Antarctic Rift System began stretching in the Late Cretaceous, before the Campbell Plateau broke away.

cret-089.title: A seaway cuts North America in two
cret-089.text: For 34 million years, from about 100 to 66 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean. It began as an Arctic arm pushing south, the Mowry Sea, which later merged with a southern embayment to complete the link. The seaway split the continent into western and eastern landmasses, isolating their plants and animals. Repeated spells without oxygen in its bottom waters left organic-rich shales, now a major source of oil, before it narrowed and vanished in the early Cenozoic.

cret-091.title: Sauropods vanish from western North America
cret-091.text: Around 98 million years ago, sauropods disappeared from western North America, opening a gap through most of the Late Cretaceous called the 'sauropod hiatus'. Suggested causes range from competition to habitat lost under the Western Interior Seaway, and the gap ended near the period's close, when Alamosaurus arrived, probably from South America.

cret-093.title: True crocodilians appear
cret-093.text: The first true crocodilians, the group that includes today's crocodiles, alligators and gharials, evolved around 95 million years ago.

cret-094.title: Lebanon's Sannine beds preserve rare fossil octopuses
cret-094.text: At Haqel, Hjoula and al-Nammoura, Lebanon's Sannine Formation holds famous Cenomanian Lagerstätten, sites where fossils are exceptionally well preserved. Shrimp, stingrays, bony fish and even octopuses turn up, and fossil octopuses are among the rarest of finds.

cret-095.title: A shallow sea slices Africa in two
cret-095.text: Around 95–90 million years ago, a seaway linking the Mediterranean and the proto-Atlantic partly flooded the Tuareg Shield, and rising seas drowned the Kem Kem ecosystem. Later, in the Coniacian and Santonian, bivalves show a shallow sea splitting Africa in half, linking the Tethys to the South Atlantic, probably via the Benue Trough.

cret-092.title: The Galápagos hotspot builds the Caribbean plateau
cret-092.text: Starting about 95–90 million years ago, the Galápagos hotspot built the Caribbean–Colombian oceanic plateau in the eastern Pacific, whose crust now makes up most of the Caribbean plate. Most of its roughly 4.4 million cubic kilometers of rock erupted 95–83 million years ago, with a second pulse at 81–69 million years ago. One table, though, dates the province to about 75–72 million years ago. Its main phase coincides with the Cenomanian–Turonian oceanic anoxic event, suggesting the eruptions helped cause it.

cret-096.title: Mosasaurs, the sea lizards, make their entrance
cret-096.text: The first mosasaurs, marine lizards, appear around 94 million years ago. They went on to rule the Late Cretaceous oceans, taking over the role left by the ichthyosaurs.

cret-097.title: Warming seas bring the Cenomanian–Turonian extinction
cret-097.text: Recent work confirms real extinctions of vertebrates, invertebrates and microbes at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition, not an artifact of how fossils were preserved. Planktic foraminifera, tiny shelled organisms drifting in the sea, died out in five phases. The variety of trace fossils, the burrows and tracks of animals, plummeted as the event began. Warming from the High Arctic and other large igneous provinces is thought to have driven this lesser extinction, one tied to oxygen-starved seas that struck mostly marine life.

cret-098.title: OAE2: oxygen-free water reaches the sunlit sea
cret-098.text: OAE2 is considered the most recent truly global oceanic anoxic event, striking in one of the Phanerozoic's hottest intervals, when carbon dioxide hit its Cretaceous high. Oxygen-free, sulfidic water, laced with toxic hydrogen sulfide, spread up into the sunlit surface ocean. Black shale such as the Livello Bonarelli at Gubbio built up below, and the balance of carbon isotopes, atoms of different weights, swung sharply. Osmium isotopes and trace metals point to underwater eruptions from large igneous provinces as the likely trigger.

cret-099.title: Peak heat: the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum
cret-099.text: Warming that began at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition peaked about 90 million years ago, in one of the Phanerozoic's hottest intervals. Carbon dioxide rose above 1,000 parts per million, against a pre-industrial 280, and tropical seas reached at least 30 °C, perhaps 33–42 °C. With an unusually gentle gradient from equator to pole, crocodile-like champsosaurs lived in the Canadian Arctic, where yearly temperatures averaged above 14 °C. The warmth lasted to the Turonian–Coniacian boundary, broken by brief cool spells, and claims of Turonian ice on Antarctica are disputed.

cret-100.title: The last ichthyosaurs vanish from the seas
cret-100.text: Ichthyosaurs, dolphin-shaped marine reptiles present since about 250 million years ago, were more diverse in the Cretaceous than once thought. A first extinction pulse at the start of the Cenomanian wiped out two of their three remaining feeding guilds, leaving only unspecialized top predators. After the Cenomanian–Turonian anoxic event only Platypterygius hercynicus survived, and it disappeared about 93 million years ago. Their end came in two abrupt blows, not a long decline, and mosasaurs took over their role as rulers of the oceans.

cret-101.title: Flood basalts spread across Madagascar
cret-101.text: Between about 92 and 85 million years ago, flood basalts erupted across Madagascar. The lavas are older in the north, 88–92 million years, than in the south, 85–88 million years.

cret-102.title: The Andes switch from stretching to squeezing
cret-102.text: Around 90 million years ago, faster ocean spreading and stronger subduction turned western South America from stretching to squeezing, changing the character of the Andean orogeny. Basins behind the volcanic arc in central Chile and Mendoza were squeezed upward, and western Peru's marine basins rose to become land.

cret-103.title: Ticks make their first appearance
cret-103.text: The earliest examples of ticks appear around 90 million years ago.

cret-104.title: The last carnosaurs die out
cret-104.text: Carcharodontosaurids, the last definite family of carnosaurs, went extinct in the Turonian, around 90 million years ago. Their wider group had first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, around 174 million years ago.

cret-105.title: Black shales hint at another oxygen crisis
cret-105.text: Black, organic-rich shales from the Coniacian and Santonian, found mainly in and around the Atlantic, have prompted proposals of a minor oceanic anoxic event. They are patchier than the shales of the major Cretaceous events, and some researchers think local conditions, not a global change, laid them down.

cret-106.title: A second heat peak in the Coniacian
cret-106.text: After a slight cooling, temperatures climbed again to a second peak, the Coniacian Thermal Maximum, around 87 million years ago.

cret-107.title: Niobrara Chalk preserves Pteranodon and mosasaurs
cret-107.text: Coccoliths settling in the Western Interior Seaway built the Niobrara Chalk, now beneath much of the Great Plains and rich in plesiosaurs and mosasaurs. Pteranodon, a pterosaur with wings spanning over 6 meters, occurs in most of its layers and is known from about 1,200 specimens.

cret-108.title: Maiasaura nests reveal dinosaur parents at work
cret-108.text: In what is now Montana and Alberta, the duck-billed Maiasaura raised its young in colonies of closely packed earthen nests, each holding 30 to 40 eggs. Hatchlings with weak legs and worn teeth show that adults brought food to the nest, the first evidence of parental care in dinosaurs.

cret-109.title: Duck-billed hadrosaurids appear
cret-109.text: The first hadrosaurids, the duck-billed dinosaurs, appear around 86 million years ago.

cret-111.title: An impact crater hides under Brazil's Santos Basin
cret-111.text: In the Santonian, an impact blasted the Praia Grande crater, about 20 km across, into what is now Brazil's Santos Basin. It remains well preserved, buried beneath 4 km of younger rock.

cret-112.title: The long Late Cretaceous cooling begins
cret-112.text: From the Santonian, as the mid-Cretaceous hothouse drew to a close, global climate began to cool, and the trend continued through the Campanian. Tropical sea surfaces fell from about 35 °C in the early Campanian to about 28 °C in the Maastrichtian. Turtles declined during one Campanian cooling event, yet the Late Cretaceous stayed warmer than today even as its cooling carried on into the Cenozoic. Whether continental ice sheets formed is unclear, because estimates of ocean temperatures conflict.

cret-114.title: Zealandia drifts off and the Tasman Sea opens
cret-114.text: About 85 million years ago, Zealandia, a continent stretching from New Caledonia to New Zealand's subantarctic islands, separated from Australia. About 83 million years ago, a rift running into eastern Tasmania split the Lord Howe Rise from the South Tasman Rise. The Lord Howe Rise, a 3,000 km ribbon of continent, drifted away as the Tasman Sea opened and new crust formed in the deep Tasman Basin.

cret-113.title: The High Arctic province erupts again
cret-113.text: About 85 million years ago, the High Arctic Large Igneous Province entered a second phase, erupting mildly alkaline flood basalts until about 60 million years ago. The province as a whole was active from about 130 to 60 million years ago.

cret-115.title: The magnetic field starts flipping again
cret-115.text: About 83.65 million years ago, Earth's magnetic field reversed for the first time in 37 million years, ending the Cretaceous Normal Superchron. Calibrated ages place the superchron, chron C34n, from 120.964 million years ago to the start of the reversed chron C33r. Since then, reversals have generally grown more frequent, though only slowly.

cret-117.title: India breaks from Madagascar and races north
cret-117.text: About 83 million years ago India rifted from Madagascar and began a rapid run north toward Eurasia. The Indian plate's drift would cover about 6,000 km, reaching about 18 cm per year in the Paleocene. By about 83.5 million years ago seafloor was spreading between India and Antarctica, unevenly near the Kerguelen Plateau. Some sources put the split from Madagascar earlier, at 100–90 million years ago.

cret-118.title: The northern North Atlantic begins to spread open
cret-118.text: By about 83 million years ago, seafloor spreading had begun in the North Atlantic between the Rockall Basin and North America. The ocean started opening between Ireland and Greenland after 85 million years ago. Rifting among the Eurasian, Greenland and North American plates may have begun around 81 million years ago. One source dates the division of Laurasia into Eurasia and North America much earlier, about 94 million years ago.

cret-116.title: Iberia begins pushing into Europe
cret-116.text: From about 83 million years ago Iberia converged on Europe, until it stopped moving relative to Europe 67.7 million years ago. In the Pyrenees, compression had replaced extension by about 90 million years ago, and the Bay of Biscay had become ocean by about 84 million.

cret-119.title: The Kerguelen hotspot draws the Ninety East Ridge
cret-119.text: Between 82 and 38 million years ago, the Kerguelen hotspot built the Ninety East Ridge, a volcanic chain 5,000 km long, at or near a spreading ridge.

cret-120.title: The Hawaiian chain's oldest surviving volcano forms
cret-120.text: The oldest dated volcano of the Hawaiian hotspot chain, at its northern end, is 81 million years old. The Emperor seamounts, the chain's oldest and most eroded part, range from 39 to 85 million years old.

cret-121.title: The first palm trees rise
cret-121.text: The first palm trees appear around 80 million years ago.

cret-123.title: A small impact marks Ukraine at Zeleny Gai
cret-123.text: A small impact made the 3.5 km Zeleny Gai crater in Ukraine, dated only loosely to 80 ± 20 million years ago.

cret-122.title: The Laramide orogeny begins raising the Rockies
cret-122.text: Mountain building began in western North America 80 to 70 million years ago, in the Laramide orogeny. It unfolded as buoyant slices of crust, called terranes, were added to the continent while the Farallon plate dived beneath it. The orogeny raised the Rocky Mountains and, around 75 million years ago, began lifting the region that holds the Grand Canyon. Some sources place it later, around 70 million years ago or between 70 and 40 million years ago.

cret-124.title: An asteroid carves Finland's Lake Lappajärvi
cret-124.text: About 77.85 million years ago, in the Campanian, an asteroid about 1.6 km across struck what is now Finland. It left a crater about 22–23 km wide and 750 m deep, now filled by Lake Lappajärvi, one of Finland's largest lakes.

cret-125.title: Rivers entomb the dinosaurs of Dinosaur Park
cret-125.text: Rivers flowing to the Western Interior Seaway laid down Alberta's Dinosaur Park Formation, burying many dinosaurs as articulated skeletons, their bones still joined. With 58 dinosaur species among nearly 500 species of fossil life, Dinosaur Provincial Park is one of the world's richest dinosaur sites.

cret-128.title: Velociraptor enters the fossil record
cret-128.text: Velociraptor, one of the dromaeosaurs, first appears around 75 million years ago.

cret-127.title: Velociraptor and Protoceratops, frozen mid-fight
cret-127.text: Locked in combat, a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops were buried together in Mongolia's Djadokhta Formation, direct evidence of predatory or aggressive behavior in non-avian dinosaurs. How they were buried is still debated, with drowning, a collapsing dune and a sandstorm all proposed.

cret-129.title: A space rock strikes Iowa at Manson
cret-129.text: About 74 million years ago, an asteroid or comet nucleus struck near present-day Manson, Iowa. It left an impact structure about 35 km across, now buried.

cret-130.title: The Atlantic floods Patagonia to the Andes
cret-130.text: In the Maastrichtian, foreland basins, troughs that sink beside a rising mountain range, subsided east of the early Andes and let Atlantic waters reach the mountain front. The sea laid down the marine Jagüel and Roca formations, which span the Maastrichtian into the Danian.

cret-131.title: Flowering plants crowd out the last bennettitaleans
cret-131.text: Bennettitales, or cycadeoids, seed plants present since the Permian, were widespread in the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous but declined severely as flowering plants rose. They died out in most areas toward the end of the Cretaceous, and their last northern records come from polar latitudes.

cret-133.title: The seas drain away in the Maastrichtian
cret-133.text: In the final stage of the Cretaceous, sea level fell further than at any other time in the Mesozoic. This Maastrichtian regression, the sea's retreat from the land, is one of the proposed contributors to the K–Pg extinction.

cret-136.title: A sharp Maastrichtian chill reshapes ocean life
cret-136.text: About 70.5 million years ago, surface and bottom waters cooled sharply, and marine species richness rose by 43%. Cooling peaked about 67.5 million years ago, with surface waters at 13 °C, and richness and productivity began to fall. The Western Interior Seaway was coldest early in the Maastrichtian, at about 16 °C, before warming to about 22 °C. Near the very end, ice sheets and sea ice appear to have returned briefly to Antarctica.

cret-138.title: Mosasaurus joins the giants of the Tethys
cret-138.text: The mosasaur Mosasaurus evolved around 70 million years ago. By the Maastrichtian, several large mosasaurs shared the Tethys Sea and competed within it.

cret-139.title: Multituberculate mammals branch out
cret-139.text: Multituberculates, an extinct group of mammals named for the many cusps on their teeth, grew more diverse around 70 million years ago. In the Late Cretaceous they radiated as plant-eaters and into new forms, such as squirrel-like tree dwellers, reaching their peak diversity.

cret-140.title: The Labrador Sea begins to open
cret-140.text: The Labrador Sea started opening 69 million years ago, in the Maastrichtian, as seafloor spreading in its south moved Greenland north relative to North America. The 1989 paper cited for this date, however, puts the initial opening much earlier, at 92 million years ago.

cret-141.title: Vegavis preserves the oldest known bird voice box
cret-141.text: Vegavis, from the Maastrichtian, shows that modern birds had begun diversifying before the Cenozoic, and Asteriornis, of the same age, sits close to the fowl-and-waterfowl lineage. A Vegavis specimen dated 69–66 million years ago holds the oldest known syrinx, the voice organ of birds.

cret-143.title: Quetzalcoatlus takes to the skies
cret-143.text: Quetzalcoatlus, a pterosaur and one of the largest flying animals ever, first appears around 68 million years ago.

cret-144.title: Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops arrive for the final act
cret-144.text: Tyrannosaurus, the largest land predator of western North America, enters the fossil record 68–66 million years ago. The first species of Triceratops appears at the same time. Ankylosaurus, an armored plant-eater living 68–66 million years ago, was among the very last dinosaurs other than birds.

cret-142.title: Hell Creek preserves dinosaurs to the very end
cret-142.text: Montana's Hell Creek Formation records rivers, deltas and swamps on a low eastern coast facing the Western Interior Seaway, with Tyrannosaurus and Ankylosaurus among its fossils. This Lancian fauna, a key record of dinosaurs right up to the K–Pg boundary, is closer to East Asian and Canadian–Alaskan faunas than most earlier North American ones.

cret-145.title: The Deccan Traps flood western India with lava
cret-145.text: The Deccan Traps began erupting in western India 66.25 million years ago, fed largely by the Réunion hotspot; the bulk erupted 66–65 million years ago. Three phases, two before the K–Pg boundary and one after, left about 1.5 million cubic kilometers of lava. They warmed the climate about 3 °C in the Cretaceous's last 100,000 years, and plant fossils suggest they raised carbon dioxide by 250 parts per million. Most scientists now give them a minor role in the extinction at most, though some still argue for a joint cause with the impact.

cret-147.title: A 10 km asteroid blasts out the Chicxulub crater
cret-147.text: Around 66 million years ago, an asteroid about 10 km wide struck just off the Yucatán Peninsula, leaving the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across. Megatsunamis swept the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean, while a clay layer rich in the rare metal iridium, shocked quartz and glass beads settled worldwide. A lingering impact winter halted photosynthesis and the oceans rapidly acidified, in the only mass extinction firmly tied to an impact. Dated to 66.043 million years ago, at the K–Pg boundary, the impact is widely accepted as the extinction's main cause.

cret-148.title: The end-Cretaceous extinction erases three-quarters of species
cret-148.text: In the fifth and latest great mass extinction, about 76% of species and 47% of genera vanished, among them all the non-avian dinosaurs. On land no animal over 25 kg survived, and at sea plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, ammonites and rudists died, along with over 90% of coccolithophore species. The killing was rapid, perhaps under 10,000 years, and ocean productivity and circulation collapsed for at least tens of thousands of years. All major mammal lineages and most turtles came through, and mammals then spread into the large-animal niches the dinosaurs had left.

cret-149.title: The ammonites disappear from the oceans
cret-149.text: Ammonoids, shelled cephalopods present since about 410 million years ago, vanished during or soon after the K–Pg extinction as their drifting eggs and larvae were devastated. Of all cephalopods, only nautiloids and coleoids, the squid and octopus line, survived, though a few ammonite genera such as Baculites may have lingered into the earliest Danian.

cret-150.title: The last belemnites die out
cret-150.text: Belemnites, already declining and confined to a few high-latitude regions, died out in the K–Pg extinction, probably because their embryos could not survive the acidifying oceans. Sea butterflies, tiny swimming snails, took over their larvae's place in the food chain.

cret-152.title: The last pterosaurs vanish from the skies
cret-152.text: Azhdarchid and nyctosaurid pterosaurs still flew in the Maastrichtian, and they likely died out at the K–Pg boundary. With them, every pterosaur perished in the K–Pg extinction.

cret-153.title: A New Jersey bone bed captures the mass death
cret-153.text: In New Jersey's Hornerstown Formation, the Main Fossiliferous Layer is one of the few sites that record mass death at the K–Pg boundary. Rich in marine life from a shallow sea, the 66-million-year-old layer holds iridium and shocked quartz, suggesting it formed as the ecosystem collapsed.

cret-154.title: Every non-bird dinosaur dies, but birds fly on
cret-154.text: Scientists agree that all non-avian dinosaurs, then an estimated 628 to 1,078 species, died out at the K–Pg boundary. They turn up in Maastrichtian rocks on every continent and in Cenozoic rocks nowhere, and birds are their only surviving lineage. Their large size, few small species and no known ability to burrow, swim or dive may have left them exposed. Whether they were already declining is uncertain, but 2025 dates on New Mexico beds show diverse faunas into the latest Maastrichtian.

cret-155.title: Shiva, a proposed second impact, remains unconfirmed
cret-155.text: Sankar Chatterjee and colleagues have proposed Shiva, a crater 450–600 km across and far larger than Chicxulub, dated to about 66 million years ago. They argue it helped cause the extinction, but the structure remains only a proposal, not a confirmed impact.

cret-156.title: The last rudists and giant inoceramids die
cret-156.text: Once thought to have vanished half a million years early, the reef-building rudists apparently fell to the K–Pg event itself. Giant inoceramid bivalves, most of them long in decline, died out too; Inoceramus shells exceeded 1 meter, and one from Greenland reached 1.87 meters.

cret-157.title: At Tanis, waves fling fish inland within minutes
cret-157.text: At Tanis, North Dakota, seismic waves from the impact 3,000 km away raised seiche waves, sloshing surges 10–100 m high, in the Western Interior Seaway within minutes. They flung marine, freshwater and land life inland under a rain of glass beads from Yucatán, and fossil fish there suggest the impact struck in Northern Hemisphere spring.

pale-007.title: Mammals inherit a world emptied of dinosaurs
pale-007.text: The K–Pg extinction, the catastrophe that ended the Cretaceous, killed every land animal heavier than about 25 kg. Mammals poured into the empty niches, quickly growing larger and more varied, though most stayed under about 20 kg until late in the Paleocene. Placental mammals, which nourish unborn young through a placenta, branched rapidly, producing the earliest rodents, carnivorans and plesiadapiforms, the forerunners of primates. Mammals have ruled the land ever since, a shift that would one day lead to humans.

pale-009.title: Surviving birds burst into modern lineages
pale-009.text: Only four bird lineages made it through the K–Pg extinction: the ostrich group, waterfowl, ground fowl and Neoaves, ancestors of most living birds. They filled the niches of extinct Mesozoic birds in one of the fastest diversifications of any group, likely splitting into modern lineages within about four million years. DNA studies trace nearly every living bird lineage except fowl and the ostrich group to the Paleocene. Fossils are scarce, though, and mostly waterbirds; the oldest known tree-dwelling modern bird, the mousebird Tsidiiyazhi, lived about 62 million years ago.

pale-012.title: A smaller asteroid strikes off West Africa
pale-012.text: At or near the time of Chicxulub, the giant K–Pg impact, an asteroid at least 400 m wide struck the Guinea Plateau off Guinea-Bissau. It left the Nadir crater, about 9.2 km across, and would have raised tsunamis up to 1 km high; its age is uncertain by about a million years.

pale-013.title: Pantodonts, early heavyweight plant-eaters, appear
pale-013.text: Pantodonts, plant-eating mammals, were among the first large mammals to evolve after the Cretaceous, beginning with dog-sized Bemalambda in China's early Paleocene Shanghuan Formation. They reached North America in the middle Paleocene and grew bigger through the epoch, peaking with Barylambda, the largest Paleocene form.

pale-002.title: Colorado's Corral Bluffs catch mammals bouncing back
pale-002.text: Colorado's Denver Formation holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Paleocene mammal communities, a record of how mammals diversified right after the K–Pg extinction. Its rocks run from before the catastrophe to after it, and its Corral Bluffs site also yields new species such as Mandrasuchus, an alligator relative.

pale-003.title: The oldest undisputed placental mammals appear
pale-003.text: The oldest fossils that are undisputedly placental come from the early Paleocene, just after the non-avian dinosaurs vanished. The lineages themselves are older: placentals, pouched marsupials and egg-laying monotremes all arose in the Cretaceous, before their fossils become common. In the first Paleocene land-mammal age, the Puercan, newcomers included taeniodonts, early hoofed 'condylarths' and Purgatorius, a possible relative of primates. Most Paleocene mammals, however, have uncertain family ties.

pale-011.title: Multituberculates hit their peak, then start to fade
pale-011.text: Multituberculates, rodent-like animals that were the Mesozoic's most successful mammals, peaked in the early Paleocene; European and North American forms rebounded fast, but Asian ones were devastated. From the middle Paleocene they declined, probably outcompeted by placental mammals such as rodents and ungulates, the hoofed mammals.

pale-001.title: Apulia meets Europe, and the Alps begin
pale-001.text: By the Paleocene the Piemont-Liguria Ocean had sunk entirely beneath the Apulian plate, a process called subduction, and Apulia began colliding with Europe. The Briançonnais microcontinent, a small sliver of continental crust, then arrived at the subduction zone. Africa, Arabia and India had long been closing on Eurasia, but the major phases of Alpine mountain building began only in the Paleocene to Eocene. The collision would raise the Alps and the Apennines, and its stresses lifted the Sudetes and may have faulted rocks as far away as Öland in Sweden.

pale-005.title: Paleocene swamps lay down vast coal beds
pale-005.text: Several great coal deposits formed in the Paleocene, including the Fort Union Formation, source of 43% of American coal, Texas's Wilcox Group and Colombia's Cerrejón. Powder River Basin coal began forming about 60 million years ago, as the land rose from a shallow sea and eroding highlands buried plant matter.

pale-006.title: The Laramide orogeny keeps pushing up the Rockies
pale-006.text: The Laramide orogeny, an episode of mountain building that began in the Late Cretaceous, kept raising the Rocky Mountains through the Paleocene. It buckled the crust deeply from Canada to northern Mexico, in pulses separated by quiet spells. As the Colorado Rockies rose, the Denver Basin sank deeper between 66 and 45 million years ago, and the upheaval helped reverse the flow of the California River. One account ends the orogeny with the Paleocene, but others place its end between 55 and 35 million years ago and call the timing disputed.

pale-016.title: The Boltysh impact scars Ukraine
pale-016.text: Dating published in 2021 places the impact that left Ukraine's Boltysh crater, 24 km across, about 650,000 years after Chicxulub. The study suggested the blow may have disrupted recovery from the K–Pg extinction and could explain a fern spike, a layer unusually rich in fern spores.

pale-017.title: Dan-C2: the first Paleogene heat pulse
pale-017.text: The Dan-C2 event, the first early Paleogene hyperthermal or brief burst of warming, brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon, felt most in the deep sea. Deep water warming past a threshold may have freed carbon stored there since the mid-Maastrichtian, or a pulse of India's Deccan volcanism may have set it off.

pale-019.title: South America grows its own hoofed mammals
pale-019.text: South America's native hoofed mammals, including notoungulates and litopterns, appeared around 65–63 million years ago, probably from North American 'condylarth' ancestors, and lasted until about 12,000 years ago. Ancient proteins show the litopterns were true ungulates, related to today's horses, rhinos and tapirs.

pale-018.title: Plesiadapiforms, early cousins of primates, spread
pale-018.text: Plesiadapiforms, early relatives or forerunners of primates, first appear between 65 and 55 million years ago, diversifying in North America from about 65.1 million years ago. They may have been the first mammals with fingernails instead of claws. Purgatorius, one of the new mammals of the first Paleocene mammal age, is a possible primate relative, though it may sit outside the primate line. Timelines place the first true primates around 60 million years ago, and many plesiadapiforms were gone by the Eocene.

pale-021.title: Denmark's Faxe rocks keep cold-water coral mounds intact
pale-021.text: In Denmark's Faxe Formation, a rock unit called the Baunekule facies preserves a cold-water coral mound ecosystem in exceptional detail. Dendrophyllia corals dominated the mounds, which also held snails, tubeworms, bivalve shellfish and bryozoans, tiny animals that grow in colonies.

pale-023.title: Creodonts, early meat-eating mammals, evolve
pale-023.text: Creodonts, an important group of meat-eating mammals, evolved about 63 million years ago, and their oxyaenid branch appears in North America from about 62.3 million years ago. Another branch, the hyainailouroid hyaenodonts, probably arose in Afro-Arabia late in the Paleocene.

pale-024.title: India's Deccan eruptions wind down
pale-024.text: Most of the Deccan lavas poured from fissures in India's Western Ghats between 66 and 65 million years ago, perhaps two-thirds within a million years. By about 63 million years ago, as India's plate slowed, the main phase of eruptions was over.

pale-025.title: The Latest Danian Event warms the whole ocean
pale-025.text: The Latest Danian Event warmed the ocean from surface to floor by 1.6–2.8 °C for about 200,000 years, as carbon rose and the seas turned more acidic. It struck as the Atlantic seafloor spread apart and volcanoes erupted off southeast Greenland; afterward, oxygen-starved Egyptian seas buried over 500 intact fish skeletons at Qreiya 3.

pale-026.title: Penguins take to the water
pale-026.text: The first penguins, Crossvallia and Kupoupou, appear around 62 million years ago in Antarctica and New Zealand, the earliest known birds built for life in water. Their kind would grow huge: penguins about 2 m tall lived from roughly 60 to 30 million years ago.

pale-027.title: North America's inland sea drains away
pale-027.text: The Western Interior Seaway, which had joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean since about 100 million years ago, lingered into the earliest Paleocene. A remnant still flooded the site of Memphis, but around 62 million years ago falling sea level completed North America's emergence from the water.

pale-028.title: The Labrador Sea opens and Greenland drifts free
pale-028.text: Seafloor spreading, the growth of new ocean crust along a rift, pushed north from the Central Atlantic.
