It opened the Labrador Sea around 62 million years ago and Baffin Bay around 57 million. The rift split the North Atlantic Craton, a block of ancient crust that Labrador and Greenland had shared. By 56 million years ago Greenland had become a separate plate, cut off from North America by the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift.

pale-029.title: Oxygen-starved water spreads into coastal seas
pale-029.text: In another early Paleogene hyperthermal, oxygen-poor water crept into coastal seas around the boundary between the Danian and Selandian ages. Sea level fell, most likely because warming evaporated water, since no polar ice existed to lock it up.

pale-030.title: A mantle plume floods the North Atlantic with lava
pale-030.text: Around 65 million years ago a mantle plume, a column of hot rock rising from deep inside Earth, welled up beneath Greenland. This ancestor of the volcanic hotspot beneath today's Iceland was most active from about 60.5 to 54.5 million years ago, before and during the continents' break-up. The resulting North Atlantic Igneous Province was the third-largest outpouring of molten rock in 150 million years, about 5 million cubic km from Canada to Britain. It built Baffin Island's flood basalts, vast stacked sheets of lava, and the last volcanic rocks of the British Isles.

pale-032.title: The carnivore lineage takes its first steps
pale-032.text: Carnivoramorphs, the group that includes today's carnivorans, first appeared in North America about 60 million years ago, 6 million years after the K–Pg extinction. Early members included the carnivorans Ravenictis and Pristinictis, along with the miacids, ancestors of later carnivores.

pale-033.title: The elephant order begins with tiny Eritherium
pale-033.text: Proboscideans, the order that includes elephants, first evolved in Africa around 60 million years ago, during the Selandian age. The earliest known, Eritherium, weighed only about 3–8 kg.

pale-034.title: The High Arctic lava province falls silent
pale-034.text: The High Arctic Large Igneous Province, one of Earth's largest magmatic complexes at over 1,000,000 km², went quiet around 60 million years ago. Active since 130 million years ago, it closed with a second phase of flood basalts and mildly alkaline magma, from about 85 to 60 million years ago.

pale-035.title: India closes on Asia, and collision may begin
pale-035.text: India had been racing north since the Late Cretaceous, and one account dates its first collision with Asia to about 60 million years ago, starting the Himalayan orogeny. As India approached, the Gangdese batholith, a vast underground mass of magma in southern Tibet, reawakened around 65 million years ago for 20 million years. Between about 60 and 50 million years ago, the leading edge of Greater India, the plate's now-vanished northern extension, struck the West Burma block. But the size of Greater India and the date of collision are debated, with models ranging from late Paleocene contact to collision in the middle Eocene.

pale-037.title: Titanoboa haunts the oldest known Neotropical rainforest
pale-037.text: On a wet coastal plain near 5°N, Colombia's Cerrejón Formation preserves the earliest known Neotropical rainforest, the rainforest of the American tropics. Titanoboa lived there, a snake over 13 m long and the longest ever recorded, while Carbonemys, a 60-million-year-old Colombian turtle, had a 1.7 m shell. A snake that size implies mean annual temperatures of 30–34 °C, though estimates from fossil leaves run 6–8 °C cooler. Its plants already belonged to modern families like palms and legumes, but low diversity shows a forest still recovering 7 million years after the K–Pg extinction.

pale-036.title: The Izanagi–Pacific ridge sinks beneath East Asia
pale-036.text: Between 60 and 50 million years ago, the Izanagi–Pacific spreading ridge, the seam where those two ocean plates pulled apart, began to slide beneath East Asia. So little Izanagi seafloor survives that the history of that margin remains poorly known.

pale-038.title: Buried carbon cools the late Paleocene
pale-038.text: From 59.7 to 58.1 million years ago, the burial of organic carbon cooled the climate, lowered sea level and allowed ice to grow briefly. Antarctica may have begun icing over as early as the late Paleocene, though other evidence finds no significant ice from then into the early Eocene.

pale-040.title: Horned, tusked dinoceratans appear
pale-040.text: Dinoceratans, large hoofed plant-eaters with horns and tusk-like canines, appear in the late Paleocene, almost at once in both North America and Asia. That implies a land link, probably Beringia, the land bridge across today's Bering Strait, and late in the Tiffanian age uintatheres crossed from Asia into North America.

pale-041.title: Rodents and rabbits enter the record
pale-041.text: Lagomorphs, the rabbit order, appear in the late Paleocene and may have evolved on India while it was an island continent. The earliest rodents, such as Tribosphenomys and Paramys, are also Paleocene, and rodents spread from Asia into North America from about 57.5 million years ago.

pale-042.title: The Thulean land bridge joins Europe to North America
pale-042.text: In the late Paleocene a land bridge, now sunk beneath the Atlantic, linked the British Isles to Greenland, and so Europe to North America. This Thulean route was open around 57 and 55.8 million years ago but disappeared in the early Eocene.

pale-044.title: Methane bursts heat the mid-Paleocene
pale-044.text: Temperatures spiked around 59 million years ago, probably as methane hydrate, an ice-like solid of methane and water buried in deep-sea sediments, broke down en masse. That pulse and a second one 300,000 years later released about 83 and 132 billion tonnes of methane-derived carbon, suggesting 2–3 °C of warming.

pale-046.title: Earth begins a long climb toward the Eocene hothouse
pale-046.text: From about 58 to 50 million years ago, Earth's surface warmed gradually by about 6 °C, with sharp hyperthermal spikes along the way. In the latest Paleocene, about 57 million years ago, global mean surface temperature is estimated at 22.3–28.3 °C. The relatively cool late Paleocene ended with two jolts, the Thanetian Thermal Event and then the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, or PETM. As the world warmed, plant diversity rose at both poles, especially at the very end of the epoch.

pale-047.title: A metallic asteroid leaves a crater beneath Greenland's ice
pale-047.text: About 57.99 million years ago, a metallic asteroid about 1.5 km wide gouged a 31 km crater, now buried under Greenland's Hiawatha Glacier. It left no clear mark on climate, and its age rules out any link to the Younger Dryas, a far more recent cold spell.

pale-048.title: The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum scorches the planet
pale-048.text: At the end of the Paleocene, some 2,500–4,500 billion tonnes of carbon poured into the air and oceans, perhaps within decades, perhaps over several thousand years. Global temperature jumped about 5–8 °C during the roughly 200,000-year event, and mid-latitude and polar regions may have grown hotter than today's tropics. Suspects include magma baking organic-rich sediments in the North Atlantic Igneous Province, seafloor methane ice and kimberlite volcanoes, fed from deep in the mantle, in Canada. As the oceans acidified, the event wiped out 30–50% of benthic foraminifera, shelled single-celled creatures of the deep seafloor that had come through the K–Pg extinction unscathed.

eoce-003.title: Oxygen in the air roughly doubles
eoce-003.text: At about the start of the Eocene, the amount of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere more or less doubled.

eoce-011.title: Modern mammal orders burst onto the scene
eoce-011.text: As the PETM heat arrived, more modern mammal groups spread into North America and many Paleocene forms declined. Most modern mammal orders make their fossil debut in one brief early Eocene window, including artiodactyls and perissodactyls, the even- and odd-toed hoofed mammals. The odd-toed line seems to have arisen in Asia, where Cambaytherium lived in western India roughly 54.5 million years ago. All the newcomers were small, under 10 kg, and Eocene mammals were only about 60% the size of the Paleocene mammals before them.

eoce-009.title: Denmark's Fur Formation buries a tropical world in diatoms
eoce-009.text: Just after the PETM, northern Denmark's seafloor gathered about 60 m of clay rich in diatoms, tiny glass-shelled algae, with up to 180 volcanic ash layers. It preserves abundant fish, insects, reptiles, birds and plants; its tropical to subtropical flora points to a climate about 4–8 °C warmer than today.

eoce-004.title: The last champsosaurs die out
eoce-004.text: Champsosaurus and its crocodile-like neochoristodere relatives, survivors of the K–Pg extinction, died out in the early Eocene, during the mammal turnover linked to the PETM warmth. Only the small, lizard-like Lazarussuchus carried the choristodere line on, in Europe, until the Miocene.

eoce-010.title: Gastornis, a huge flightless bird, appears
eoce-010.text: Gastornis, a large flightless bird, appears in the fossil record about 56 million years ago and survived until about 40 million years ago.

eoce-014.title: Archicebus and the first true primates
eoce-014.text: Archicebus achilles, which lived about 55 million years ago, is the earliest known ancestor of primates. At the start of the Eocene, tarsier-like omomyids and lemur-like strepsirrhines replaced the archaic plesiadapiforms in North America. Primates crossed between North America and Asia around 55.8 million years ago. By about 50 million years ago they had diversified and split into strepsirrhines, such as lemurs and lorises, and haplorhines, such as tarsiers, monkeys and apes.

eoce-017.title: Songbirds, parrots and loons join the bird world
eoce-017.text: Many modern bird orders first appear in the Eocene, among them the earliest songbirds, parrots, loons, swifts and woodpeckers. The oldest known stem loon, an early offshoot of the loon line, is Nasidytes from England's London Clay, about 55 million years old. The first perching birds, or passerines, appear around 52.5 million years ago, and the kingfisher order follows in the middle Eocene.

eoce-015.title: India meets Asia and the Himalayas start to rise
eoce-015.text: India's collision with Eurasia is most often dated to 55–50 million years ago, beginning when its northwestern corner touched first. Around 55 million years ago India's plate also slowed from about 18–19.5 cm a year to about 4.5 cm, circumstantial evidence of the crash. The collision closed that stretch of the Tethys Ocean, the sea between them, and began thrusting up the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau. The timing and nature are debated: rival models have a microcontinent collide first and India arrive around 40 million years ago or at the Oligocene's end.

eoce-016.title: Iberia presses into Europe and the Pyrenees take shape
eoce-016.text: Iberia and Europe, converging since about 100 million years ago, collided in the Eocene and Oligocene. From about 55 to 47 million years ago, compression shortened the crust by about 4 mm a year and stacked great slabs of rock into today's Pyrenees.

eoce-021.title: The North Atlantic opens and Laurasia splits in two
eoce-021.text: Seafloor spreading crept north from the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay and, by about 54 million years ago, split Greenland from Eurasia. The opening of the North Atlantic finally broke Laurasia, the old northern continent, in two. From about 56 to 54 million years ago, break-up volcanism built the Iceland Plateau and Greenland's Skaergaard intrusion, a mass of magma that cooled underground. Extension between North America and Eurasia also tore open the Eurasian Basin across the Arctic.

eoce-020.title: The London Clay preserves tropical fruits in England
eoce-020.text: Shallow seas over southeast England laid down the London Clay, packed with fossil seeds and fruits from some 350 plant species. Its flora includes tropical plants now found in Asia, a sign of the far warmer early Eocene climate.

eoce-018.title: The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum: the Cenozoic's hottest stretch
eoce-018.text: A string of intense hyperthermals, including ETM-2 and ETM-3, tipped Earth into the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, or EECO, the Cenozoic's warmest sustained interval. Global mean surface temperature reached about 23–30 °C, and the whole hothouse from 56 to 47 million years ago ran about 14 °C warmer than today. Antarctic summers hit about 25 °C, alligators and amphibians lived north of the Arctic Circle, and palms grew in Alaska. Climate models still struggle to reproduce such warm poles and mild polar winters, a puzzle known as the equable climate problem.

eoce-022.title: Elmo: a second, smaller heat spike
eoce-022.text: Eocene Thermal Maximum 2, also called H-1 or Elmo, was a brief burst of global warming, the second major hyperthermal after the PETM. It was less severe and left a smaller drop in carbon-13, a heavier form of carbon, in the rocks. It struck exactly 4.5 long eccentricity cycles, slow swings in the shape of Earth's orbit, after the PETM, and that orbital rhythm may have triggered it. Smaller hyperthermals followed within about a million years, and together they carried Earth into the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

eoce-023.title: Green River lakes entomb fish, leaves and insects
eoce-023.text: Mountain building in the Rockies created basins where three great lakes, Gosiute, Uinta and Fossil Lake, laid down the oil shales of the Green River Formation. Their oxygen-poor bottom muds slowed decay and kept scavengers away, preserving fish, leaves and even the soft parts of insects. The formation is perhaps the best record of Cenozoic freshwater life, with fish, crocodilians, birds and mammals. Frost-free weather let crocodiles live among sycamore forests, even as the moist early Eocene turned slightly drier.

eoce-024.title: Pakicetids: the first whales walk on land
eoce-024.text: The earliest whales were the pakicetids, a family of hoofed land mammals that lived about 53 million years ago. Their closest known relative was Indohyus, of the family Raoellidae. Pakicetids could already hear under water, picking up sound as vibrations through bone rather than through eardrums. Over the Eocene whales grew very diverse as they made the full transition from land to sea.

eoce-025.title: ETM-3 opens the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum
eoce-025.text: Eocene Thermal Maximum 3, informally the K or X event, was another early Eocene hyperthermal, marked by a pulse of isotopically light carbon. Its carbon-isotope excursion, a sharp swing in the mix of carbon types preserved in the rocks, marks the onset of the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

eoce-027.title: Eohippus and the first horses
eoce-027.text: The first equids, members of the horse family, lived in North America by the earliest Eocene. Eohippus appeared about 52 million years ago, and thousands of complete skeletons of these early horses survive, mostly from Wyoming's Wind River basin. One of its species branched into new kinds of horse, and about 50 million years ago Eohippus graded into Orohippus. Orohippus in turn gave rise to Epihippus, with better grinding teeth, about 47 million years ago.

eoce-028.title: Bats take mammals into the air
eoce-028.text: The earliest known bats, such as Onychonycteris, appear about 52 million years ago, only about 16 million years after the non-avian dinosaurs died out. With them, mammals had colonized the air. During the Eocene, bat lineages also crossed from Africa to South America, possibly by way of Antarctica.

eoce-026.title: Cambay amber traps India's early Eocene insects
eoce-026.text: Amber from Gujarat, in India, seals an important early Eocene community of arthropods, the jointed-legged animals, in fossilized tree resin; most are insects.

eoce-029.title: Okanagan upland lakes capture a warm world
eoce-029.text: During the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, upland lakes in British Columbia and Washington finely preserved plants, insects and fish, including palm beetles showing palms grew there. The 48.7-million-year-old Princeton Chert preserves plants down to their anatomy, with the oldest known ectomycorrhizal fungi, which live in partnership with tree roots.

eoce-032.title: The cat and dog lineages part ways
eoce-032.text: The ancestors of cats and of dogs went separate ways about 50 million years ago, among the first true carnivorans. For now these carnivorans stayed small, while oxyaenids and mesonychians, older lines of meat-eating mammals, held the top-predator roles of the Eocene. Crown-group carnivorans, the branch descended from the last common ancestor of all living carnivorans, first appeared around 42 million years ago.

eoce-035.title: The Sevier thrust belt falls quiet
eoce-035.text: The Sevier fold-and-thrust belt, which had crumpled and stacked western North America's crust since about 160 million years ago, fell quiet around 50 million years ago. In southwestern Utah, though, some Sevier thrusts may have stayed active until later in the Eocene.

eoce-034.title: Monte Bolca's fishbowl preserves fish down to their organs
eoce-034.text: Near Verona, Italy, low-oxygen mud preserved fish so well that their organs are often intact and their skin color can sometimes be made out. The site's Pesciara, or 'fishbowl', is famous for these extraordinary Eocene fish.

eoce-036.title: Ambulocetus brings whales back to the water
eoce-036.text: By about 49 million years ago whales had returned to the water, among them Ambulocetus, a crocodile-like early whale that was probably amphibious. Its family lived in the bays and estuaries of the Tethys Ocean, in what is now northern Pakistan.

eoce-037.title: The long Eocene cooling begins
eoce-037.text: Warmth peaked around 49 million years ago, and a slow cooling followed until about 34 million years ago, ultimately leading to the Quaternary ice ages. Changing geography and ocean circulation helped drive the drop, as Australia and South America drew away from Antarctica. Falling carbon dioxide, drawn down by biological productivity and the weathering of new mountains, kept it going; models suggest it mattered more than the ocean's isolation. Cold-water diatoms hint at winter sea ice in the Arctic, and Antarctica had glaciers by about 37 million years ago.

eoce-038.title: Floating ferns blanket the Arctic and bury carbon
eoce-038.text: The Arctic Ocean was almost cut off from the wider seas, and its warm water and high carbon dioxide let the floating fern Azolla spread across it. Under 20 hours of polar summer daylight, the fern can double its mass in two to three days. For about 800,000 years dead ferns sank to the stagnant seafloor and were buried, locking their carbon away in thick deposits. Carbon dioxide plunged from about 3,500 parts per million in the early Eocene to 650 during the event, a drawdown believed to have ended the early Eocene warmth.

eoce-041.title: A sea lays down the stone that built Paris
eoce-041.text: A sea over the Paris Basin laid down the limestone that gave the Lutetian age its name, taken from Lutetia, the ancient name of Paris. Quarried since Roman times, this 'Paris stone' built many of the city's grandest buildings, including parts of the Louvre and the Arc de Triomphe.

eoce-039.title: Rifts split open across western Europe
eoce-039.text: The ongoing Alpine collision opened a north–south system of rifts, long cracks where the crust pulls apart, across western Europe from the Eocene onward. In the middle Eocene the Limagne Graben, a sunken block of crust, formed and held a lake, and rifting also began in the Bresse Graben.

eoce-040.title: Grasses spread and the first savannas appear
eoce-040.text: As the climate cooled and dried after the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, grasses began to spread, moving out from riverbanks into open tracts. By the middle Eocene, subhumid savannas, fairly dry grasslands dotted with trees, had appeared in South America. One timeline puts the first grasslands later, around 35 million years ago.

eoce-044.title: The Kula plate vanishes beneath Alaska
eoce-044.text: The Kula plate, which had been diving beneath Alaska and the Yukon since the early Eocene, was entirely consumed around 48 million years ago. Only a slab of it survives, deep in the mantle beneath the Bering Sea.

eoce-043.title: Geiseltal's coastal moorland fills with fossils
eoce-043.text: A coastal moorland of lakes and tidal bays in central Germany preserved more than 50,000 fossil vertebrates, plus insects and plants. Its soft tissues were among the very first found from the Eocene, and its mammals define a European land-mammal stage.

eoce-045.title: Forests grow close to the poles
eoce-045.text: In Nunavut, high-Arctic river deposits preserve old-growth conifer forests where they stood, their leaf litter intact down to the molecular level. Swamp cypress and dawn redwood grew on Ellesmere Island and subtropical plants in Greenland and Alaska, while pollen from Prydz Bay shows taiga, or conifer forest, in Antarctica.

eoce-047.title: Messel Pit preserves animals down to fur and feathers
eoce-047.text: About 47 million years ago a lake at Messel, Germany, entombed over 1,400 kinds of plants and animals, from pygmy horses to early primates and bats. The Hesse site then lay 10° farther south, its maar lakes, craters left by volcanic blasts, ringed by lush subtropical forest averaging 22 °C. Animals sank into deep, oxygen-poor water free of scavengers, so whole skeletons survive, some with fur, feathers and 'skin shadows'. What killed them is debated: bursts of toxic volcanic gas, as at Lake Nyos in 1986, or poisonous blooms of cyanobacteria, the blue-green microbes.

eoce-048.title: The Pacific plate swerves and the Hawaiian–Emperor chain bends
eoce-048.text: A kink in the Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain, a line of undersea volcanoes, marks the Pacific plate's sudden swing from northward to northwestward motion about 47 million years ago. The turn followed the start of subduction along the plate's western edge, part of a wider reorganization that began the Izu-Bonin-Mariana and Tonga-Kermadec subduction zones. The end of a northward pull, the new western trenches and the Hawaiian hotspot's own southward drift from about 50 million years ago may together explain the bend.

eoce-046.title: Baltic amber entombs a subtropical forest
eoce-046.text: Baltic amber, the largest amber deposit on Earth and the biggest single store of fossil insects, preserves invertebrates, plants and small vertebrates of subtropical eastern Europe. Its exact age is controversial, with estimates including 47–40 and 43–35 million years ago.

eoce-050.title: Montana oil shale keeps a mosquito's blood meal
eoce-050.text: Oil shale in Montana preserves exquisitely detailed insects, including a blood-filled mosquito with traces of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying molecule of blood.

eoce-052.title: Silverpit, a possible impact crater beneath the North Sea
eoce-052.text: A 2025 study argues that Silverpit, a buried structure under the North Sea about 130 km off the Humber estuary, is an impact crater about 3.2 km wide. Others blame slowly moving salt underground, an explanation favored in a 2009 debate, so the origin remains disputed.

eoce-054.title: The Andes climb and the Altiplano begins to rise
eoce-054.text: The Altiplano, the high plateau of the central Andes, began to form in the Eocene as subduction beneath South America squeezed the plate's edge. From about 45 million years ago the high Central Andes and the Bolivian orocline, a great bend in the range, took shape, and southern Peru began rising. In northern Peru the Incaic phase of Andean mountain building struck in the middle and late Eocene. The region around the Altiplano and Puna plateaus has been squeezed horizontally ever since.

eoce-057.title: Australia pulls away from Antarctica, opening the Tasmanian Passage
eoce-057.text: In one account, Australia split from Antarctica around 45 million years ago, diverting warm equatorial currents and opening a cold-water channel, the Tasmanian Passage, between them. When oceanic crust began separating the two continents about 35.5 million years ago, global ocean temperatures dropped significantly. The timing is disputed, though: the general consensus has the continents fully separated by 60 million years ago, making 45 million a minority estimate. A 2013 paper dates the earliest flow through the Tasmanian Gateway, and the cooling it brought, to about 49–50 million years ago.

eoce-056.title: Quercy's fissures hold 'natural mummies'
eoce-056.text: Fissures in the karst of southern France, limestone country riddled with caves, filled with the remains of mammals, birds, turtles, crocodiles, plants and insects. Some amphibians and lizards survive as articulated 'natural mummies', complete with soft tissue.

eoce-058.title: India and Australia fuse into one plate
eoce-058.text: The Indian and Australian plates fused about 43 million years ago, forming a single Indo-Australian plate.

eoce-059.title: A buried crater marks an impact in Belarus
eoce-059.text: A meteorite struck near Lahoysk, Belarus, about 42.3 million years ago, leaving a crater 15 km wide that now lies buried.

eoce-060.title: Earth's magnetic field flips again and again
eoce-060.text: Earth's magnetic field reversed 17 times in just 3 million years around 42 million years ago, each time swapping its north and south magnetic poles. Earlier, a 4-million-year window centered on 54 million years ago had seen 10 reversals.

eoce-061.title: Basilosaurus, a giant whale, rules the shallow seas
eoce-061.text: Basilosaurus, a large predatory archaeocete, one of the ancient early whales, lived from about 41.3 to 33.9 million years ago. At 17–20 m long and up to 15 tonnes, it was one of the largest animals of the Paleogene. A top predator of shallow seas, it ate sharks, large fish and other marine mammals, especially the smaller whale Dorudon. By the Eocene's end whales like it had become fully aquatic, yet its extinction coincided with the Eocene–Oligocene extinction, which ended almost all other archaeocetes.

eoce-062.title: The Drake Passage may begin to open
eoce-062.text: In the early Eocene the Drake Passage, between South America and Antarctica, was only a small opening with limited circulation. Its opening date is uncertain: sediments suggest about 41 million years ago, tectonic evidence about 32 million, and estimates range from 49 to 17 million. About 40 million years ago the Scotia plate began forming, breaking up a continuous landmass from Patagonia to the Antarctic Peninsula. The cooling during the passage's first opening, about 38.5 million years ago, was not global, since the North Atlantic did not cool.

eoce-063.title: The Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum briefly reverses the cooling
eoce-063.text: From about 40.5 to 40.0 million years ago, a spell of intense warmth briefly reversed the long Middle–Late Eocene cooling. The warming struck the whole globe at once, lifting mean surface temperature to about 23 °C and Tethys sea surfaces to 32–36 °C. Carbon dioxide, not methane, drove it; one estimate puts the level at 4,000 parts per million, though other studies find a smaller rise. Among the plankton, acarinid foraminifera dwindled and the morozovellids went extinct.

eoce-064.title: Balkanatolia docks with Asia
eoce-064.text: Balkanatolia, one of three landmasses into which Eurasia was split, joined Asia about 40 million years ago, while Europe connected only about 34 million years ago. Invading Asian mammals may have driven its island-like native fauna extinct.

eoce-065.title: Eridanos, a lost Baltic river, takes shape
eoce-065.text: The Eridanos, an ancient river that flowed through what is now the Baltic Sea, began to form about 40 million years ago.

eoce-067.title: Mesohippus: horses step out into open country
eoce-067.text: Mesohippus appeared suddenly about 40 million years ago, shaped by strong new pressures of natural selection. Late Eocene horses grew larger and leggier, with tougher teeth, able to outrun predators in open country; Miohippus followed around 36 million years ago.

eoce-071.title: Castaway rodents and monkeys drift to South America
eoce-071.text: About 40 million years ago, caviomorph rodents reached South America, most likely from Africa, and primates followed the same way by 36 million years ago. The ocean gap was narrower then, and the animals floated over on driftwood or mangrove rafts, perhaps hopping between islands. The rodents gave rise to capybaras, chinchillas and New World porcupines, pushing out some small marsupials. Today the rafters' descendants make up more than twice as many South American species as the heirs of older native mammals.

eoce-070.title: Rifting cracks open northern Kenya
eoce-070.text: Between 40 and 35 million years ago, volcanism and rifting began around Turkana in northern Kenya, then spread north and south along the Gregory Rift.

eoce-068.title: A storm of eruptions sweeps the American West
eoce-068.text: From about 40 to 25 million years ago, a dramatic burst of volcanic eruptions swept the western United States. It produced about 500,000 km³ of rock in explosive blasts and 5 million km³ in gentler outpourings. The flare-up followed the end of Laramide compression, as the Farallon slab, the ocean plate sinking beneath the continent, steepened and plate motion changed. Colorado's San Juan volcanic field came alive 40–35 million years ago, and New Mexico's Mogollon-Datil field began erupting about 36.2 million years ago.

eoce-076.title: The last multituberculates die out
eoce-076.text: Multituberculates, the rodent-like mammals that had been declining since the mid-Paleocene, finally died out in the late Eocene. The last species, Ectypodus childei, vanished in North America near the Eocene's end, possibly outcompeted by rodents. So ended a lineage that dated back to the Jurassic and had dominated most mammal communities for at least 88 million years; only the gondwanatheres outlived it. One account has them lasting into the early Oligocene.

eoce-078.title: An impact carves the basin of Lake Wanapitei
eoce-078.text: Lake Wanapitei fills an 8.4 km crater blasted out by an impact about 37.2 million years ago.

eoce-079.title: The Cascade volcanoes awaken
eoce-079.text: Volcanoes of the Cascade arc in the Pacific Northwest came to life about 37 million years ago. The West Cascades period that followed, from 37 to 17 million years ago, was a time of exceptionally active eruptions.

eoce-080.title: Ice sheets begin to grow on Antarctica
eoce-080.text: By about 37 million years ago, temperatures had fallen far enough for ice sheets to start forming on Antarctica. Oxygen isotopes, the mix of heavier and lighter oxygen atoms preserved in sediments, show ice building from about 36 million years ago. Ice became permanent from about 35 million years ago, as glaciers merged into the East Antarctic Ice Sheet and buried the Gamburtsev Mountains. A brief glaciation, the Late Eocene Event, followed about 34.4 million years ago.

eoce-082.title: Beavers, squirrels and gophers take over North America
eoce-082.text: In North America's Chadronian age, from 37 million years ago, the White River fauna was in full swing. Modern rodent families such as beavers, squirrels and gophers replaced older tropical ones, alongside early relatives of bears, peccaries and rabbits, the last newly arrived from East Asia.

eoce-083.title: The Mistastin impact strikes Labrador
eoce-083.text: An impact in Labrador, Canada, about 36.6 million years ago left a crater originally about 28 km across.

eoce-084.title: Popigai: a giant impact blasts Siberia
eoce-084.text: Late in the Eocene, a large bolide, a rock from space, blasted a crater 100 km wide in northern Siberia. Popigai is tied as the fourth-largest verified impact structure on Earth. It may have struck at the same time as the Chesapeake Bay and Toms Canyon impacts, and it may be linked to the Eocene–Oligocene extinction.

eoce-085.title: A bolide gouges the future Chesapeake Bay
eoce-085.text: A bolide about 3 km wide slammed into the eastern edge of North America, then lined with rainforest and shallow limy seas. It left a crater about 85 km wide, now buried beneath the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. It is one of the best-preserved craters made by an impact into the sea, and sediment slumping over its rubble later helped shape the bay. The nearby Toms Canyon crater, and possibly Siberia's Popigai, may have formed in the same event.

eoce-087.title: The Laramide squeeze fades and the West stretches
eoce-087.text: The Laramide orogeny, which had raised mountains across western North America since the Late Cretaceous, ended sometime between 55 and 35 million years ago. Compression gave way to stretching of the crust, which ultimately formed the Basin and Range Province, a land of alternating ranges and valleys. As convergence slowed, the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion turned oblique, and volcanism flared across the Basin and Range. Its exact timing is disputed, and in New Mexico, Laramide deformation lasted until about 40 million years ago.

eoce-088.title: The Dinarides, Hellenides and Taurides begin to rise
eoce-088.text: About 35 million years ago the Anatolide–Tauride platform of Adria, a small plate, entered the subduction trench, beginning the Dinarides, Hellenides and Taurides. Between about 40 and 30 million years ago, subduction also began along the western Mediterranean arc of the Tell, Rif, Betic and Apennine chains. At the end of the Eocene, 35 million years ago, a second phase of mountain building began raising the Central and Western Alps.

eoce-089.title: The Ring of Fire reaches its modern form
eoce-089.text: By about 35 million years ago the Kula and Farallon plates had been subducted, and subduction zones ringed the Pacific plate like today's Ring of Fire. The last of its present segments, the New Zealand subduction zone, formed at about the same time.

eoce-086.title: Arabia rams Eurasia and the Zagros rise
eoce-086.text: Arabia began colliding with Eurasia about 35 million years ago, a crunch that continued into the Oligocene until about 26 million years ago. It closed that arm of the Tethys Ocean and pushed up the Zagros Mountains. Earlier in the Eocene, a sinking slab of seafloor from the Neotethys, the younger branch of the Tethys, had broken off near the Arabian margin. One timeline instead has Africa colliding with Eurasia and closing the Tethys around 50 million years ago.

eoce-090.title: EOT-1: the first step of Antarctica's big freeze
eoce-090.text: Around 34 million years ago the long cooling crossed a threshold, and as carbon dioxide fell a large ice sheet formed in East Antarctica. The ice came in two steps, and the first and smaller, EOT-1, struck about 34.1–33.9 million years ago, at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary itself. By the boundary, ice in western Antarctica reached the ocean and glaciers had appeared in Greenland. As the Arctic–Atlantic gateway closed, the ocean's deep overturning circulation, its slow conveyor of sinking water, shifted from the Pacific to the Atlantic.

eoce-092.title: Florissant's lake preserves insects and giant stumps
eoce-092.text: In Colorado, diatom blooms in a lake dammed by volcanic mudflows buried late Eocene plants and insects in fine detail. The site is also known for petrified stumps of giant sequoia relatives.

eoce-094.title: Whales divide into toothed and baleen lines
eoce-094.text: The ancestors of toothed and baleen whales split around 34 million years ago, as the opening Drake Passage changed the southern oceans' climate. The earliest known baleen whale, Mystacodon, still had teeth, but later forms lost them and strained their food through comb-like baleen. Toothed whales are defined by features for echolocation, sensing their surroundings by echoes, and Oligocene Squalodon skulls may show its first traces. Molecular studies put the split later, between 26 and 17 million years ago, but baleen whale fossils are at least 34 million years old.

eoce-095.title: Greenhouse turns to icehouse in the Eocene–Oligocene extinction
eoce-095.text: The Eocene closed with a major extinction and turnover of life, called the Grande Coupure, or 'great break', in Europe, spanning about 33.9 to 33.4 million years ago. Earth was shifting from greenhouse to icehouse: carbon dioxide fell to about 750–800 parts per million, temperatures plunged, sea level dropped and Antarctic ice spread fast. Hantkeninid foraminifera vanished at the boundary, Basilosaurus and nearly all other archaic whales died out, and snails, amphibians and reptiles turned over in central North America. The causes are debated and not fully understood, and the large Popigai and Chesapeake Bay impacts may also have played a part.

olig-012.title: Ice takes hold of Antarctica and the icehouse begins
olig-012.text: About 33.9 million years ago, ice began piling up on Antarctica, opening the Late Cenozoic Ice Age that continues today. Falling carbon dioxide was the main driver, and once it slipped past a tipping point of about 600 parts per million, the ice could grow. Earth switched from its last greenhouse climate to the present icehouse, and for the first time in the Phanerozoic both poles fell well below freezing. Ice-rafted debris, rock dropped on the seafloor by drifting ice, shows that glaciers had also reached Greenland by the start of the Oligocene.

olig-008.title: Ground sloths appear and reach the Caribbean
olig-008.text: The earliest unambiguous ground-sloth fossils come from the early Oligocene, and a femur from Puerto Rico shows these animals had reached the Caribbean by 31 million years ago. Megatheriids, the family of the later giant ground sloths, appeared in South America about 30 million years ago.

olig-001.title: Africa pushes into Eurasia and the Alps soar
olig-001.text: As Africa pushed north into Eurasia, the Alps rose rapidly, cutting off what remained of the Tethys Sea. Most of the mountain building that raised the Alps took place in the Oligocene and the Miocene that followed. From about 30 to 10 million years ago, sediment laid down in shallow seas and on land filled the Molasse basin north of the Alps.

olig-002.title: The Andes rise into a major mountain chain
olig-002.text: During the Oligocene the Andes first became a major mountain chain. The rise came as subduction, the sinking of an ocean plate beneath the continent, turned to strike the coast more directly. About 30 million years ago, the Andean orogeny, the long episode of mountain building there, was reorganized on a continental scale. The shifting subduction boosted volcanism, and the Western Cordillera of the Central Andes began to grow.

olig-004.title: Rifting resumes in the Baikal Rift Zone
olig-004.text: Rifting, the slow pulling apart of the crust, resumed in the Baikal Rift Zone during the Oligocene. The stretching later formed graben basins, long troughs dropped down between faults.

olig-005.title: Carnivorans seize the top-predator roles
olig-005.text: Led by the cat-like nimravids, carnivorans, the mammal order of cats, dogs and their kin, took over the top-predator roles held in the Eocene by oxyaenids and mesonychians. In the Old World, dogs, bears, weasels and raccoons joined the nimravids in replacing the creodonts, an older group of predatory mammals.

olig-006.title: Desmostylians, an order of marine mammals, appear
olig-006.text: Early desmostylians, an order of marine mammals that includes Behemotops, are known from the Oligocene. The group reached its peak in the Late Oligocene, with about nine species.

olig-010.title: Grasslands spread as the tropical forests retreat
olig-010.text: Grasslands expanded around the world while tropical broadleaf forests shrank back to the equatorial belt. By the early Oligocene, dry woodland and wide grasslands had replaced the tropical forests of North America and Eurasia, and savanna spread across a cooler South America. Grasses left their wetland-edge habitats for open country, helped by falling carbon dioxide, which favored C4 photosynthesis, a type of photosynthesis typical of grasses. The cooling and the spreading grass favored larger mammals, though even by the epoch's end grass was too scarce to form modern savannas.

olig-013.title: The Obik Sea drains and Europe joins Asia
olig-013.text: Early in the Oligocene, the Obik Sea, which had separated Europe from Asia, retreated and left a lasting land connection. Falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait across it. The new land route opened Europe to Asian mammals, and their arrival set off the great turnover known as the Grande Coupure.

olig-014.title: Oi-2 ice pulses drop the sea 75 meters
olig-014.text: In the middle Oligocene, pulses of glaciation built up Antarctic ice and lowered the sea about 75 meters, the largest drop in 100 million years. Rivers cut into the exposed continental shelves, leaving gaps in marine rock records around the world.

olig-015.title: The Paratethys becomes a vast oxygen-starved sea
olig-015.text: In the Oligocene, the Paratethys, a northern arm of the Tethys Ocean, covered much of central and eastern Europe. Falling sea level and rising Alpine mountains partly cut it off, so its water settled into unmixed layers and its depths turned anoxic, or oxygen-free. Sand shed by the rising mountains buried organic matter in the Maykop Suite, now a source of oil and gas around the Black Sea. The Menilite Formation preserves the sea's deep-sea fish and its microbial mats.

olig-020.title: Grande Coupure: Asian invaders remake Europe's mammals
olig-020.text: Around 33.5 million years ago, Asian species swept into Europe and replaced most of its mammals, a turnover called the Grande Coupure, French for 'great break'. Until then, native hoofed mammals such as artiodactyls and palaeotheres had dominated Europe, along with adapid and omomyid primates. Falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait, and Asian rhinos and ruminants crossed over and drove native species extinct, sparing only some endemic rodent and marsupial families. The break began with widespread extinction, and the first Asian immigrants turn up in northwest European records about 350,000 years later.

olig-022.title: The Atacama, perhaps Earth's oldest desert, dries out
olig-022.text: About 33 million years ago, the opening of the Tasmania–Antarctic passage set up a proto-Humboldt Current, which began drying out the Atacama. Humid air has generally been lacking there since then, apart from brief wetter spells, and the Atacama may be Earth's oldest desert.

olig-025.title: Greenland stops drifting and rejoins North America
olig-025.text: Until about 33 million years ago, Greenland moved as a separate plate, drifting north and rotating counterclockwise. Then seafloor spreading, the making of new ocean floor between plates, ceased in the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay and shifted to the northeast Atlantic. The halt brought the Eurekan orogeny, a mountain-building episode in the Arctic, to a close. By the late Oligocene, Greenland had rejoined North America, and the boundary between North America and Eurasia ran along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

olig-026.title: The Tasmanian Gateway opens south of Australia
olig-026.text: About 33 million years ago, at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, the Tasman Gateway between Australia and Antarctica opened, bringing abrupt cooling. Australia had been drifting slowly away from Antarctica since the Jurassic, and shallow channels south of Tasmania had opened in the Eocene. Deep-ocean routes followed from the mid Oligocene, and one estimate puts a deep channel in place by the end of the early Oligocene. Southeastern Australia, meanwhile, became a land of high rainfall and swamps.

olig-028.title: An asteroid strikes Devon Island in the Arctic
olig-028.text: An impactor about 2 km wide struck Arctic Canada's Devon Island, leaving the roughly 23-km Haughton crater, which exposes rock from as deep as 1,700 meters. Its age, revised several times, remains unsettled: one estimate gives 31–32 million years, but other analyses put it in the Eocene, about 39 million years ago.

olig-030.title: Aegyptopithecus lives before apes and monkeys part ways
olig-030.text: Aegyptopithecus, a howler-monkey-sized primate from the line of apes and Old World monkeys, lived in Egypt's Fayum before those two groups split. The Fayum's Jebel Qatrani Formation records tropical forests, swamps and rivers, home to over a dozen kinds of primates and early elephants such as Phiomia.

olig-032.title: A current begins to circle Antarctica
olig-032.text: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, a steady flow circling Antarctica, probably did not form until about 30 million years ago, though a shallow proto-current may have begun earlier. Once the gateways opened, it kept cold water circling the continent and strengthened the formation of Antarctic Bottom Water, the cold, dense water of the deep seafloor. Its timing hinges on the disputed opening of the Drake Passage, and fossil evidence puts its full establishment as late as about 23 million years ago. Scientists also still debate how much the current drove Oligocene cooling.

olig-033.title: Brontotheres, big hoofed mammals, die out
olig-033.text: The brontotheres, large hoofed mammals, went extinct about 30 million years ago, though some accounts place their end earlier, in the earliest Oligocene.

olig-034.title: The Caspian Sea basin takes shape
olig-034.text: The Caspian Sea is estimated to be about 30 million years old, which makes its basin a product of the Oligocene.

olig-036.title: Flood basalts bury Ethiopia under lava
olig-036.text: Around 30 million years ago, the Afar mantle plume, a rising column of hot rock, hit the base of Africa's lithosphere, the planet's rigid outer shell. About 350,000 cubic kilometers of lava poured from fissures across Ethiopia, northeast Sudan and southwest Yemen, stacking up into the flood-basalt plateau of the Ethiopian Highlands. The outpouring coincided with the start of rifting along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Shield volcanoes then added another 1,000–2,000 meters on top between 30 and 10 million years ago.

olig-041.title: Arabia begins to tear away from Africa
olig-041.text: For most of the Phanerozoic, the Arabian plate had been part of the African plate. Around 30 million years ago, as flood basalts poured across Ethiopia, rifts began tearing it away along the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The split opened first in the southern Red Sea and, by the late Oligocene, ran the length of the Red Sea and Gulf of Suez. Another source dates the separation of Africa and Arabia to about 25 million years ago.

olig-042.title: The Rio Grande rift begins to stretch open
olig-042.text: The crust along the Rio Grande rift began pulling apart about 30 million years ago. The most intense rifting, on low-angle faults, lasted from 30 to 20 million years ago.

olig-043.title: A spreading ridge arrives and the San Andreas forms
olig-043.text: About 30 million years ago, the Pacific–Farallon spreading ridge reached North America's subduction zone, and the San Andreas Fault began to form. The arrival of the Murray and Mendocino fracture zones started strike-slip motion, with plates grinding sideways past each other, and set off Basin and Range extension. The change also ended volcanism south of the Cascades and turned many western North American terranes, crustal blocks added to the continent, clockwise. The first ridge segment slid into the subduction zone near Baja California about 28 million years ago.

olig-035.title: Dominican amber traps a vanished tropical forest
olig-035.text: Dominican amber, 30–10 million years old, is nearly always clear and rich in trapped remains, so scientists can reconstruct a vanished tropical forest in fine detail.

olig-046.title: La Garita blasts out the Fish Canyon Tuff
olig-046.text: Some 28 million years ago, the eruption that formed La Garita Caldera in Colorado ranked among the largest and most powerful known in Earth's history. It blasted out the Fish Canyon Tuff, about 5,000 cubic kilometers of ash-flow rock, and the ground collapsed into a caldera, a vast volcanic crater. La Garita was one of many calderas in a huge flare-up of ignimbrites, or ash-flow deposits, across Colorado, Utah and Nevada from 40 to 18 million years ago. Sanidine crystals from the tuff, astronomically dated to 28.175 million years, now serve as a reference standard for argon–argon dating.

olig-048.title: The Drake Passage opens and South America breaks free
olig-048.text: Seafloor spreading along the Scotia Ridge finally parted South America from Antarctica by about 28 million years ago, opening the Drake Passage. South America became an island continent and drifted north toward North America. With the Tasmanian Gateway, the new passage reshaped ocean currents, and it may have helped trigger Antarctic glaciation, though models suggest falling carbon dioxide mattered more. The timing is hotly disputed: published estimates run from 49 to 17 million years ago, and one study finds deep-water flow possible by about 31 million.

olig-049.title: Pelicans enter the fossil record
olig-049.text: The first pelicans appear in the fossil record about 28 million years ago.

olig-050.title: Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal ever, appears
olig-050.text: Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal that ever lived, appears in the fossil record about 28 million years ago. This hornless relative of rhinos weighed up to 15–20 metric tons, and giant indricotheres like it stood up to 6 meters tall at the shoulder in Eurasia. Such giants bucked the general trend of the Oligocene, when mammals were much smaller than their Eocene predecessors.

olig-052.title: Caviomorph rodents branch out in South America
olig-052.text: Caviomorph rodents reached Patagonia by the early Oligocene and by the Late Oligocene had split into all four of their main lineages. Some grew large and competed with native hoofed mammals, perhaps helping drive those mammals' slow decline after the early Oligocene.

olig-053.title: The last embrithopods vanish from Afro-Arabia
olig-053.text: Embrithopods, an order of mammals from Afro-Arabia, make their last appearance in the fossil record in the latest Oligocene.

olig-054.title: Proailurus, the first cat, arises in Asia
olig-054.text: The first member of the cat family, Proailurus, arose in Asia in the late Oligocene and spread to Europe. Its fossils from Oligocene Europe are among the earliest of any cat, and timelines date the first cats to about 30 or 25 million years ago. Saber-tooth features came later, first showing up in the Miocene cat Pseudaelurus.

olig-056.title: The forerunners of mastodons and elephants appear
olig-056.text: Elephantimorphs first appeared in the Late Oligocene. They are the branch of proboscideans, the trunked mammals, that includes mastodons and modern elephants. One timeline dates the first true elephants to about 26 million years ago.

olig-058.title: Notoungulates evolve teeth that never stop growing
olig-058.text: Several families of notoungulates, native South American hoofed mammals, separately evolved high-crowned cheek teeth that never stopped growing. From the Late Oligocene, such species made up most of the group.

olig-060.title: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first forms
olig-060.text: About 27 million years ago, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet first formed, probably fed partly by glaciers flowing from the older East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It is a marine ice sheet: most of its ice rests on rock and sediment far below sea level, on what would be ocean floor without the ice.

olig-061.title: A mild warming lets lanternfish into the open ocean
olig-061.text: The late Oligocene probably warmed slightly despite low carbon dioxide, though the change varied by region and Antarctica stayed heavily glaciated. In the warmth, lanternfish, until then confined to shallow shelf seas, spread into the open ocean.

olig-062.title: The Farallon Plate splits into Cocos and Nazca
olig-062.text: About 26 million years ago, the Farallon Plate broke up into the Cocos and Nazca plates. Subduction sped up, reviving volcanism in the Central Andes and widening the volcanic arc to about 250 kilometers. Volcanic activity rose sharply along the Andes as the modern volcanic arc and tectonic regime took shape. Other sources describe a second split about 23 million years ago, at the Paleogene–Neogene boundary, when Pacific–Farallon spreading stopped and today's Nazca and Cocos plates formed.

olig-063.title: The South Asian monsoon strengthens as Tibet rises
olig-063.text: Around 25.8 million years ago, the South Asian monsoon, a seasonal shift of winds that brings heavy summer rain, intensified sharply as the Tibetan Plateau rose. Fossil pollen from Tibet shows the monsoon had already developed by the late Oligocene.

olig-064.title: The oldest known ape turns up in Tanzania
olig-064.text: Rukwapithecus, interpreted as the earliest known ape, comes from the Nsungwe Formation in Tanzania's Rukwa Rift, about 25.2 million years old. The same beds hold Nsungwepithecus, an early Old World monkey, so the two groups had already split by then. That fits molecular estimates of a split about 25–30 million years ago, though the family ties of these early primates remain uncertain. The finds reach into a poorly sampled stretch of time, when tectonic changes in East Africa may have shaped how both groups diversified.

olig-065.title: Central America's volcanic arc starts closing the seaway
olig-065.text: By the Oligocene, the Central American volcanic arc, a chain of volcanoes, had begun colliding with northwestern South America. The collision that would eventually close the Central American Seaway, the waterway between the Pacific and the Caribbean, started about 25 million years ago. The closing took a very long time, and deep-water links through Central America were not cut until much later in the Miocene.

olig-068.title: Riversleigh starts recording an Australian rainforest
olig-068.text: Riversleigh in Queensland, Australia's most famous fossil site, preserves remains from the late Oligocene onward, and some of its fossils are 25 million years old. Its limestones formed in what was once a very wet rainforest. Its oldest beds, Faunal Zone A, span the Late Oligocene, from 28.4 to 23.03 million years ago.

olig-069.title: The Sea of Japan begins to open
olig-069.text: Around 25 million years ago, the Sea of Japan began to open, separating Japan from the mainland and shaping today's island arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands.

olig-066.title: Africa begins to split along the East African Rift
olig-066.text: The East African Rift, a long zone where the continent is slowly pulling apart, began to develop 25–22 million years ago, around the Miocene's start. Volcanoes came first in places: around 30 million years ago, volcanism started on the central Ethiopian plateau, long before rifting. Some studies put the first rifting and volcanism in northern Kenya then too, reaching southern Kenya by 12 and northern Tanzania by 8 million years ago. Mount Elgon, at least 24 million years old, is East Africa's oldest known extinct volcano.

olig-074.title: Seals and their kin first appear
olig-074.text: The earliest pinnipeds, the group that includes seals, appeared about 24 million years ago, near the end of the Oligocene. From the Oligocene on, nautiloids, shelled relatives of squid, vanished from each region as pinnipeds arrived there.

olig-076.title: Creodonts die out beyond Africa
olig-076.text: At the end of the Oligocene, the creodonts died out everywhere except Africa and the Middle East, where a few hung on until the Middle Miocene.

olig-077.title: A 400,000-year deep freeze closes the Oligocene
olig-077.text: Rocks at McMurdo Sound and King George Island in Antarctica record a deep glaciation that lasted 400,000 years at the Oligocene–Miocene boundary. The Miocene opened with the Mi-1 cool event during a major expansion of Antarctica's ice, though no single global event defines the boundary.

olig-078.title: The pyrotheres of South America disappear
olig-078.text: The pyrotheres, a South American mammal order known since the Early Eocene, make their last appearance at the end of the Oligocene. They had been among the continent's distinctive native mammals, alongside astrapotheres, litopterns and notoungulates.

mioc-001.title: Africa's plant life thins as seasons sharpen
mioc-001.text: At the start of the Miocene, Africa's plant diversity fell sharply, probably because the seasons became more pronounced. Through the rest of the epoch, the continent's equatorial forest belt broke apart and rejoined again and again.

mioc-003.title: Apes diversify and spread across the Old World
mioc-003.text: Apes diversified in the early Miocene, though the oldest known ape, Rukwapithecus, lived a little earlier, in the late Oligocene. After Afro-Arabia met Eurasia, apes and proboscideans spread out of Africa, and apes became widespread across the Old World. Morotopithecus, about 21.6 million years old, has the earliest claimed upright spine and vertical body plan. Later waves reached Eurasia, with Griphopithecus in Turkey and Slovakia 15–13.5 million years ago and Dryopithecus in Europe by 12.5 million years ago.

mioc-004.title: Himalayan sediment builds Earth's largest undersea fan
mioc-004.text: The Ganges and Brahmaputra carried most of the sediment worn off the rising Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, building the Bengal Fan. It is Earth's largest submarine fan, an apron of seafloor sediment about 3,000 km long, 1,430 km wide and up to 16.5 km thick. Its oldest sediments recovered so far date from the Early Miocene, so the fan is at least that old. Their minerals and chemistry point to a Himalayan source, so the range was already a major mountain chain 20 million years ago.

mioc-006.title: Daisies diversify, and rodents, snakes and songbirds follow
mioc-006.text: The daisy family diversified rapidly in the Early Miocene, setting off bursts of new species among rodents, snakes and songbirds. The family itself is older, since its oldest fossil pollen, found in Antarctica, is 76–66 million years old.

mioc-007.title: The East Asian summer monsoon takes modern shape
mioc-007.text: As the globe cooled in the Early Miocene, the East Asian Summer Monsoon began to take its modern form. Major phases in the Himalayas' geological history during the Miocene affected Asian monsoon patterns, which were linked to glacial periods in the north.

mioc-018.title: India's collision raises the Tian Shan and Altai
mioc-018.text: The Central Asian Tian Shan and Altai rose in the Early Miocene, as India's collision with Eurasia crumpled crust as far north as Siberia. The Tian Shan rose sharply again in the Late Miocene, blocking westerly winds from the Tarim Basin and turning it dry.

mioc-002.title: The Andes surge upward and the Altiplano rises
mioc-002.text: Head-on subduction of the new Nazca Plate beneath South America lifted the Andes, with the greatest effect in the Miocene. The Altiplano began rising, and one account has it a high plateau, second in size only to Tibet, by about 13–11 million years ago. Another has the region climbing from low elevations to over 3,000 meters only from the Late Miocene. The Principal Cordillera east of Santiago rose about 20–8 million years ago, and Peru's Western Cordillera, quiet since the Oligocene, rose sharply after about 10 million.

mioc-005.title: Whales and dolphins reach their peak diversity
mioc-005.text: Whales and dolphins were at their most diverse in the Miocene, with over 20 genera of filter-feeding baleen whales against just six living today. During this baleen boom, raptorial sperm whales, built to seize large prey, appeared, apparently evolving to hunt the baleen whales themselves. From around 15 million years ago, modern cetaceans began to reach enormous sizes.

mioc-008.title: The Fram Strait opens a door to the Arctic
mioc-008.text: The Fram Strait opened in the Miocene and became the only route for Atlantic water into the Arctic Ocean until the Quaternary. The other path, the Barents Seaway, stayed shut to that water because the continental shelf there had been uplifted.

mioc-009.title: Diatoms finally colonize fresh water
mioc-009.text: Diatoms, single-celled algae with glassy shells, had radiated in the seas during the Cretaceous, but freshwater diatoms did not appear until the Miocene. Diatom diversity climbed through the epoch as carbon dioxide and global temperatures fell.

mioc-010.title: Grass conquers the continents and grazers multiply
mioc-010.text: Grasses kept spreading through the Miocene, and as forests dwindled they came to dominate much of the world. Tough, fire-tolerant grasses evolved alongside herds of grazers with high-crowned teeth, which pushed back the woodland and the browsers that fed in it. By the Hemingfordian, a North American land-mammal age, savanna dominated North America and grazing horses outnumbered browsers. Deep grassland soils buried carbon and held water, and grass made the land more reflective, helping turn the climate cooler and drier.

mioc-011.title: Kelp forests rise in Miocene seas
mioc-011.text: Kelp forests first appeared in Miocene seas and soon became one of Earth's most productive ecosystems. Together with grasslands on land, they were one of two new biomes, or major living communities, that supported much of Miocene life.

mioc-012.title: Necrolestes, the last meridiolestidan, burrows in Patagonia
mioc-012.text: Meridiolestidans, mammals that had dominated Late Cretaceous South America, make their last appearance in the Miocene of Patagonia. The final one, the mole-like burrowing insect-eater Necrolestes, turns up 50 million years after the previous known member.

mioc-013.title: Ducks, owls, cockatoos and crows take modern form
mioc-013.text: Clearly recognizable dabbling ducks, plovers, typical owls, cockatoos and crows all appear in the Miocene. Crows of the genus Corvus are first recorded about 17 million years ago. By the epoch's end, all or nearly all modern bird groups are thought to have been present.

mioc-015.title: Sloth families multiply across the Miocene
mioc-015.text: The major sloth families appeared in the Miocene, and sloth diversity waxed and waned before declining at the epoch's end. One basal sloth group, an early branch of the family tree, had already colonized the Antilles, the islands of the Caribbean, by the early Miocene.

mioc-016.title: Snakes boom across North America
mioc-016.text: Snakes, once a minor part of North American wildlife, rose sharply in number and diversity during the Miocene. Vipers and elapids, the cobra family, appeared there for the first time, and colubrids diversified into many modern genera.

mioc-017.title: South America's native hoofed mammals lose ground
mioc-017.text: Notoungulates lost 45% of their families during the Miocene, although their number of species held steady. By the late Miocene, litopterns and notoungulates were the only South American native hoofed groups left.

mioc-014.title: Rocky Mountain debris builds the Ogallala and its aquifer
mioc-014.text: As the Rockies rose, rivers carried eroded rock east and spread it over the plains in overlapping fans of sand and gravel: the Ogallala Formation. It now holds the Ogallala Aquifer, an underground reservoir beneath eight states that supplies about 30% of US irrigation groundwater.

mioc-019.title: Riversleigh's rainforest teems with Early Miocene life
mioc-019.text: Riversleigh's Faunal Zone B dates to the Early Miocene, when the area was very wet rainforest, and its uncompacted limestone keeps bones in three dimensions. Later Middle Miocene layers hold a 15-million-year-old platypus relative, Obdurodon, and the oldest modern bandicoots and bilbies.

mioc-021.title: Ignimbrite eruptions begin in the Central Andes
mioc-021.text: About 23 million years ago, large-scale ignimbrite volcanism began in the Central Andes, and it continues today. North of 21 degrees south, the Oxaya Formation erupted between 23 and 18 million years ago. Calderas of the Altiplano-Puna complex have since poured out about 15,000 cubic kilometers of ignimbrite. In southern Peru, the Chuquibamba Ignimbrite came from a super-eruption rated VEI 7 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, sometime between 14.3 and 13.2 million years ago.

mioc-025.title: Foulden Maar entombs a subtropical forest
mioc-025.text: Foulden Maar, a crater lake in New Zealand, laid down layers of diatomite, a rock made of diatom shells. The layers preserved fish, plants, spiders, insects and pollen from the subtropical forest around the lake.

mioc-026.title: An impact gouges the Karakul crater in Tajikistan
mioc-026.text: A large impact blasted out the 52-kilometer Karakul crater in Tajikistan no earlier than 23 million years ago, and perhaps no earlier than 5 million. That leaves its age somewhere in the Miocene or the Pliocene.

mioc-027.title: Megalodon, the giant shark, first appears
mioc-027.text: The giant shark megalodon evolved around 23 million years ago and became one of the great predators of Neogene oceans, alongside the sperm whale Livyatan. Its first appearance is disputed, though: some remains are reported from about 28 million years ago, while other estimates are as young as 16 million years.

mioc-024.title: Austria's Ebelsberg beds capture Paratethys sea life
mioc-024.text: The Ebelsberg Formation of Upper Austria was laid down in the Aquitanian, the first stage of the Miocene. It preserves huge numbers of plants, fish, marine mammals and invertebrates from the central Paratethys Sea.

mioc-020.title: The Alboran Basin opens and a strait links two seas
mioc-020.text: Between 23 and 20 million years ago, spreading thinned the crust south of Spain to just 12–15 kilometers, forming the Alboran Basin. In the early Miocene, the rotation of Iberia opened the Betic Corridor, a strait joining the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.

mioc-022.title: Chiapas amber traps insects and fungi
mioc-022.text: Amber from Chiapas, Mexico, holds insects and other arthropods, fragments of plants, and fungi that grew on leaf surfaces.

mioc-023.title: East Antarctic glaciers advance and retreat
mioc-023.text: East Antarctica probably held some glaciers through the early to mid Miocene, 23 to 15 million years ago. Along the Ross Sea, the edge of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet advanced and retreated often during the Early Miocene.

mioc-028.title: Pale granite invades the Himalaya's backbone
mioc-028.text: About 22 million years ago, granite rose into the Himalaya's backbone in many places, invading a 30-km-thick body of rock remade by heat and pressure. The Himalayan collision is one of those that made leucogranites, pale granites melted from sediment-derived rock in thickened crust.

mioc-029.title: New Zealand nearly drowns beneath the sea
mioc-029.text: About 22 million years ago, only 18% of present-day New Zealand stood above sea level. This drowning played a very important part in the radiation of the moa, New Zealand's flightless birds.

mioc-030.title: The Tibetan Plateau sinks, then rises again
mioc-030.text: The Tibetan Plateau sank about 900 meters between 25.5 and 21.6 million years ago. It then rose again by 500 to 1,000 meters between 21.6 and 20.4 million years ago.

mioc-031.title: Death at a Nebraska watering hole
mioc-031.text: At Agate Fossil Beds, watering-hole deposits in Nebraska hold mass-death assemblages of small rhinos mixed with bear dogs, entelodonts, camels and chalicotheres.

mioc-032.title: A vast wetland floods western Amazonia
mioc-032.text: From about 21 to 8 million years ago, western Amazonia held a vast wetland called the Pebas Mega-Wetland, or Lake Pebas. Its deposits, the Pebas Formation, cover about 1,000,000 square kilometers. The animals preserved there match those of La Venta in Colombia and Urumaco in Venezuela.

mioc-033.title: Conifers and cycads branch out
mioc-033.text: About 20 million years ago, some groups of conifers and cycads, the palm-like seed plants, began to diversify as conditions changed.

mioc-034.title: The rift's rising flank cuts off the Congo basin
mioc-034.text: Around 20 million years ago, the western flank of the East African Rift rose and cut the Great Lakes region off from the Congo basin. Lake Victoria did not yet exist, and rivers from Ethiopia and Uganda did not yet feed the Egyptian Nile.

mioc-035.title: Giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters appear
mioc-035.text: The first giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters appear around 20 million years ago, while bird diversity also climbs.

mioc-036.title: Arabia meets Eurasia and the Tethys seaway narrows
mioc-036.text: In the Early Miocene, the Arabian part of Africa collided with Eurasia and began cutting the Mediterranean off from the Indian Ocean. The first step, about 20 million years ago, cut water exchange through the seaway by 90%. By the middle of the Burdigalian, the Miocene's second stage, the collision had built a land bridge joining the two landmasses. This two-step story is not settled, and other sources date the closure anywhere from about 35 million years ago to 19–12 million years ago.

mioc-037.title: Animals pour across a new Afro-Eurasian land bridge
mioc-037.text: Around 20 million years ago, a land bridge between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia set off the Great Old World Biotic Interchange. Until then the open Tethyan seaway had kept most animals from crossing, but now traffic flowed both ways. Gomphotheres and deinotheres, both proboscideans, led the way out of Africa, reaching India by about 18.3 million years ago and Iberia by 18 million. At least 37 Eurasian lineages entered Afro-Arabia during the Burdigalian, and perissodactyls, the odd-toed hoofed mammals, reached Africa for the first time.

mioc-038.title: A gravity hole forms in the Indian Ocean
mioc-038.text: Around 20 million years ago, Earth's largest gravity anomaly formed south of India: a dip in sea level covering about 3 million square kilometers. Models link it to plumes from a sinking slab of old Tethys seafloor, which spread low-density material beneath the Indian Ocean.

mioc-040.title: Southern Africa lifts and erosion strips it down
mioc-040.text: About 20 million years ago, southern Africa was uplifted again, starting a long spell of erosion that stripped away kilometers of rock.

mioc-042.title: Open-ocean sharks suffer a mass extinction
mioc-042.text: About 19 million years ago, roughly 70% of all open-ocean shark species disappeared. Afterward, Neogene oceans came to be ruled by large predators such as megalodon and the sperm whale Livyatan.

mioc-043.title: St Bathans preserves New Zealand's lost subtropical fauna
mioc-043.text: The St Bathans fauna of Central Otago, about 19 to 16 million years old, is New Zealand's only Cenozoic fossil record from land. It includes early moa, kiwi and adzebills, tuatara relatives, crocodiles, turtles and many bats, though later cooling and drying wiped out its subtropical members.

mioc-041.title: Barstow's river beds fill with bones and tracks
mioc-041.text: In California's Barstow Formation, river and lake sediments layered with rhyolite tuff, ash from sticky, silica-rich eruptions, hold abundant vertebrate bones, teeth and footprints.

mioc-044.title: Overlapping volcanoes build Germany's Vogelsberg
mioc-044.text: In Hesse, Germany, many overlapping volcanoes built the Vogelsberg, Central Europe's largest basalt formation, spread over about 2,500 square kilometers. Eruptions ran from 18.5 to 10 million years ago and peaked 17–15 million years ago, linked to blocks of crust shifting along faults.

mioc-045.title: The Ethiopian rift begins to open
mioc-045.text: As the Nubian and Somali plates began to separate, rifting in Ethiopia started about 18 million years ago in the south and about 11 million near the Afar. A primary study, though, puts the southern onset earlier, at 20–21 million years ago, while agreeing on the 11-million-year northern start.

mioc-047.title: The sea floods the Gulf of Suez rift
mioc-047.text: The sea flooded the young Gulf of Suez rift in the early Miocene, and rifting there peaked in the Burdigalian, around 18 million years ago. In the Middle Miocene the Red Sea rift broke apart along its length, motion shifted to the Dead Sea Transform, and seafloor spreading followed.

mioc-050.title: Shanwang's lake beds keep insects' colors
mioc-050.text: The Shanwang Formation in Shandong, China, has yielded over 600 species, from insects with intact wing veins and colors to birds and mammals.

mioc-048.title: Iceland rises out of the ocean
mioc-048.text: Iceland, thought to be the work of a mantle plume, first rose above the ocean about 18–16 million years ago. The island sits above the plume where the Eurasian and North American plates pull apart, which gives it repeated eruptions and geysers.

mioc-046.title: Great apes part ways with gibbons
mioc-046.text: Great apes and gibbons are estimated to have split about 18 to 12 million years ago. Molecular evidence, read from the genes of living species, places the ape that gave rise to today's great ape family at 18 to 13 million years ago. Fossils from that time are too scarce to name it.

mioc-051.title: The crust stretches into the Basin and Range
mioc-051.text: By the Early Miocene, most of the Farallon plate had been consumed, and the Pacific-Farallon Ridge was nearing North America. About 17 million years ago, the crust began to stretch, and the tension thinned and dropped the land west of the Grand Canyon region. The result was the Basin and Range Province, a landscape of alternating mountain ranges and basins. Since stretching began, parts of the province have shifted 60 to 300 kilometers sideways, more in the south than the north.

mioc-052.title: Randeck Maar's crater lake captures a warm interlude
mioc-052.text: Randeck Maar, a crater lake in southwest Germany, preserved plants, insects, fish and amphibians. It sat barely above sea level during the warm climatic optimum of the Middle Miocene.

mioc-053.title: The Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum warms the planet
mioc-053.text: Between roughly 17 and 14 million years ago, Earth's climate grew about 3 °C warmer than today's. Benthic foraminifera, tiny shelled single-celled creatures of the seafloor, date the onset to 16.9 million years ago, the peak to 15.3 million and the end to 13.8 million. Around 15 million years ago, in the warmest stretch of the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, global temperature averaged about 18.4 °C and the Antarctic ice cap shrank. Many blame the Columbia River flood basalts, but that link is debated: warming began before their main pulse, and they cannot explain it before 16.3 million years ago.

mioc-055.title: Steens Mountain lavas catch the magnetic field flipping
mioc-055.text: About 16.7 million years ago, lava flows at Steens Mountain, Oregon, recorded a magnetic reversal, suggesting the field can swing up to 6 degrees a day. The reversal, which ended the magnetic interval called Chron C5Cr, was really a series of reversals and excursions, brief wanderings of the field.

mioc-054.title: Lava floods the Columbia Plateau
mioc-054.text: In the mid-Miocene, lava linked to the Yellowstone hotspot flooded the Columbia Plateau and Oregon, with 95% erupting between 16.7 and 15.9 million years ago. This large igneous province, a huge pile of volcanic rock, totals about 210,000 cubic kilometers, and its Roza Member alone held at least 1,500. A mantle plume is the most widely accepted cause, though the question is still open. The eruptions are often blamed for the Middle Miocene warming, but scientists still argue the point, because the warming began earlier, around 16.9 million years ago.

mioc-056.title: The Yellowstone hotspot blasts its first calderas
mioc-056.text: The Yellowstone hotspot, a long-lived plume of heat rising from the mantle, is thought to have arrived beneath North America in the Miocene and is still active. As the Steens flood basalts waned 16.5 to 15.5 million years ago, calderas including McDermitt and Virgin Valley formed. McDermitt Caldera, made by the hotspot about 16.4 million years ago, formed when a rhyolite lava dome collapsed. Eruptions such as Longridge Caldera's, 15.6 million years ago, produced up to 400 cubic kilometers of tuff.

mioc-058.title: Clarkia's fossil leaves still show autumn color
mioc-058.text: Idaho's Clarkia beds, within Wanapum Basalt flows 16.1 to 15.9 million years old, preserve leaves so well that some show autumn colors on exposure, before oxidizing. Small amounts of ancient DNA have reportedly been isolated from them.

mioc-059.title: The hippopotamus evolves
mioc-059.text: The hippopotamus evolved around 16 million years ago.

mioc-060.title: McGraths Flat preserves microscopic soft tissue
mioc-060.text: At McGraths Flat in New South Wales, unusual conditions preserved microscopic soft-tissue detail, rare in Australia, and revealed invertebrate species unknown to science.

mioc-062.title: Australia runs into Southeast Asia
mioc-062.text: In the Middle Miocene, Australia began to collide with Southeast Asia. The collision blocked the equatorial flow of ocean water between the western Pacific and the Indian Ocean.

mioc-063.title: The last creodonts die out
mioc-063.text: The last creodonts, early predatory mammals that had survived only in Africa and the Middle East, died out in the Middle Miocene.

mioc-064.title: Most of today's seed plants evolve
mioc-064.text: Many new plants evolved in the mid-Miocene, including 95% of modern seed plants.

mioc-065.title: The Badenian Flooding refreshes the Paratethys
mioc-065.text: About 15 million years ago, a widespread marine transgression, the sea's advance over the land, reconnected the Paratethys with the global ocean. This Badenian Flooding sent fresh ocean water into the deep basins, ending the long anoxia that had gripped the sea since the Oligocene. The Paratethys then held a tropical to subtropical ecosystem with coral reefs, high biodiversity and many species found nowhere else.

mioc-066.title: Mastodons, bovids and kangaroos appear
mioc-066.text: Around 15 million years ago, the first mastodons of the genus Mammut appear, along with the first bovids, the cattle family, and the first kangaroos. Australia's megafauna, its giant animals, diversified at the same time.

mioc-067.title: The magnetic field flips again and again
mioc-067.text: At least 51 reversals of Earth's magnetic field took place in a 12-million-year span centered on 15 million years ago.

mioc-068.title: Lake Vostok is sealed beneath the ice
mioc-068.text: Lake Vostok's water is estimated to have been sealed beneath thick East Antarctic ice about 15 million years ago, when the ice sheet formed.

mioc-071.title: Steinheim crater forms near the Ries
mioc-071.text: The 3.8-kilometer Steinheim crater lies about 40 kilometers southwest of the Ries and is also roughly 15 million years old. Whether one binary asteroid made both 14.8 million years ago, as once thought, is in question: a 2020 study suggests Steinheim is about 500,000 years younger.

mioc-070.title: Peru's Pisco Formation fills with marine giants
mioc-070.text: Peru's Pisco Formation ranks among the most important Lagerstätten, sites of exceptional fossil preservation, with superbly preserved megalodon, penguins, whales, marine crocodiles and aquatic sloths.

mioc-072.title: An asteroid blasts out the Ries crater in Germany
