mioc-072.text: An asteroid struck what is now southern Germany 14.808 ± 0.038 million years ago, gouging out the 24-kilometer Nördlinger Ries crater. The blast released about 2.4×10^21 joules, the power of 40 million Hiroshima bombs. Melted surface sand flew up to 450 kilometers and is thought to be the source of the moldavite tektites, natural glass found in the Czech Republic.

mioc-074.title: Cooling brings a wave of extinctions
mioc-074.text: About 14.8 to 14.5 million years ago, a wave of extinctions on land and in the sea, the Middle Miocene disruption, followed the warm optimum. During that warmth, monitor lizards, chameleons, cordylid lizards, alligators and giant turtles had lived in central Europe. Cooling wiped out the coral reefs of the Paratethys Sea, and the crocodilians Gavialosuchus and Diplocynodon vanished from northern latitudes between 14 and 13.5 million years ago. Desmostylians, the marine mammals that had first appeared in the Oligocene, began a terminal decline.

mioc-073.title: A permanent chill grows the East Antarctic Ice Sheet
mioc-073.text: Between 14.8 and 14.1 million years ago, a major and permanent cooling step, the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, ended the warm optimum. Cold Antarctic deep water increased, and the East Antarctic Ice Sheet expanded to roughly its present size by 14 million years ago. Antarctic summers cooled by at least 8 °C, and around 13.94 million years ago Transantarctic glaciers froze to their beds as annual temperatures fell 25–30 °C. The changed ocean circulation is thought to have caused the Miocene Carbonate Crash, a sharp fall in carbonate sediment on the seafloor, early in the Tortonian.

mioc-076.title: The Chile Ridge meets South America
mioc-076.text: About 14 million years ago, the Chile Ridge collided with South America near Tierra del Fuego, and the Antarctic Plate began sinking beneath the continent. The result was the Chile Triple Junction, a point where three plates meet.

mioc-077.title: Antarctic tundra lake preserves tiny crustaceans' soft bodies
mioc-077.text: On Antarctica's treeless tundra, a lake now called Paleolake Boreas preserved ostracods, tiny shelled crustaceans, right down to their soft anatomy.

mioc-079.title: The Sea of Japan opens at both ends
mioc-079.text: By 14 million years ago, the Sea of Japan was open to both the northeast and the southwest. This back-arc basin, a sea spreading open behind a volcanic island arc, cut Japan off further as sea levels rose.

mioc-078.title: The rising Andes cast a desert shadow
mioc-078.text: The southern Andes rose 14 to 12 million years ago. Their rain shadow, the dry zone downwind of a mountain range, created the Patagonian Desert to the east.

mioc-080.title: The Tibetan Plateau nears its modern height
mioc-080.text: East–west rift valleys in the Lhasa and Himalaya terranes suggest the plateau was close to its modern altitude by about 14 to 8 million years ago. Sudden eruptions of dark, iron-rich lava and faster uplift 14 to 11 million years ago point to delamination, the peeling away of the lithosphere's lower part. All the while, India kept pushing into Asia and building the Himalayas, whose growth affected Asian monsoon patterns. Accounts differ: the plateau may have neared its present height by the late Oligocene, yet some seams between blocks stayed tropical lowlands into the early Miocene.

mioc-082.title: The Tethys seaway closes for good
mioc-082.text: Around 13.8 million years ago, as Antarctic glaciers expanded sharply, the Tethys seaway closed in a second and final step. A link between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean had briefly reopened in the Langhian, the first stage of the Middle Miocene, before closing for good. The seaway vanished as Africa collided with Eurasia in the Turkish–Arabian region. This two-step timeline is far from settled, as other sources date the closure anywhere from about 50 or 35 million years ago to 19–12 million years ago.

mioc-081.title: Salt builds up in the stranded Paratethys
mioc-081.text: Midway through the Middle Miocene, rising central European mountains and falling sea level cut the Paratethys off from the ocean. Around 13.8 million years ago, the closing of the Bârlad Strait turned the Eastern Paratethys into a saltwater lake. Starved of fresh water, the Central Paratethys laid down evaporites, salts left behind as seawater dries, until about 13.4 million years ago, much like the later Messinian crisis. The growing isolation wiped out most of its small and mid-sized deepwater and open-ocean sharks.

mioc-083.title: La Venta preserves a rich neotropical fauna
mioc-083.text: La Venta in Colombia is a Lagerstätte holding glyptodonts, notoungulates and ground sloths that lived about 13.8 to 12 million years ago. It gives its name to the Laventan age, the only South American land-mammal age defined north of the equator.

mioc-084.title: Mount Ōkueyama unleashes a supereruption in Japan
mioc-084.text: Mount Ōkueyama erupted massively about 13.7 million years ago, possibly at VEI 8, bigger than any eruption in recorded history. It was one of several huge eruptions across southwest Japan between 15 and 13 million years ago.

mioc-086.title: Ash falls suffocate Ngorora's lake fish
mioc-086.text: In the alkaline lake beds of the Ngorora Formation, articulated fish skeletons record mass deaths by suffocation during ash falls or rapid acidification.

mioc-089.title: Brackish water brings the Badenian–Sarmatian extinction
mioc-089.text: After open-marine conditions from 13.36 to 12.65 million years ago, the Bârlad Strait reopened and the Central Paratethys turned brackish, less salty than the sea. That change caused the Badenian–Sarmatian extinction event.

mioc-090.title: China's Qaidam Basin dries out
mioc-090.text: Around 12.6 million years ago, silicate weathering in China's Qaidam Basin, the chemical breakdown of rock by water, fell sharply, marking a major drying event.

mioc-091.title: Sivapithecus, an ape with an orangutan's face
mioc-091.text: Sivapithecus, a chimpanzee-sized ape of the Indian subcontinent, had an orangutan-like face, with a concave profile, large cheekbones and close-set eyes. One of its species may have been the orangutans' ancestor, on a line probably already separate from that of chimpanzees, gorillas and humans.

mioc-092.title: Volcanic ash buries a Nebraska waterhole
mioc-092.text: Ash from the Bruneau-Jarbidge supereruption on the Yellowstone hotspot in Idaho drifted about 1,600 kilometers east and buried animals at a Nebraska waterhole. Rhino-like Teleoceras, horses, camels and birds lie articulated, one rhino with an unborn fetus, all killed by lung failure after breathing the ash.

mioc-093.title: Bullock Creek keeps marsupial skulls whole
mioc-093.text: Bullock Creek in Australia's Northern Territory preserves complete marsupial skulls, along with the crocodile Baru, an early kangaroo and the horned tortoise Meiolania.

mioc-095.title: The Eridanos river builds a giant North Sea delta
mioc-095.text: By about 12 million years ago, the Eridanos river, flowing from Lapland across the Baltic region, had reached the North Sea area. Its sediments built an immense delta, reckoned comparable in size to the modern Amazon's.

mioc-097.title: The Paratethys shrinks into a brackish megalake
mioc-097.text: Around 12 million years ago, the Paratethys became a megalake of over 2.8 million square kilometers, stretching from the eastern Alps to Kazakhstan. Its water was brackish, with salinity mostly 12–14 parts per thousand. Trapped by tectonics and cut off from the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, it became an isolated inland sea that gradually disappeared.

mioc-098.title: Pliohippus arises as grazing horses radiate
mioc-098.text: Pliohippus arose from Calippus around 12 million years ago, and like Hipparion and Protohippus it descended from Merychippus. Around 10 million years ago horses grew larger and developed high-crowned teeth, the mark of the grazers spreading across the new grasslands. Hipparion and its relatives proliferated in North America, and at least one crossed to Asia and Europe.

mioc-096.title: Hotspot supereruptions build the Snake River Plain
mioc-096.text: Around 12–11 million years ago, eruptions of rhyolite lava and ignimbrite began building the western Snake River Plain. The Yellowstone hotspot's Picabo caldera erupted the Arbon Valley Tuff about 10.2 million years ago; the Twin Falls field was active from 10 to 8.6 million. Two VEI 8 supereruptions followed: McMullen at 8.99 million years ago, with at least 1,700 km³, and Grey's Landing at 8.72 million, with at least 2,800. From 6.6 million years ago, eastern Idaho's Heise field produced four big caldera eruptions, starting with 1,500 km³ of Blacktail Tuff at 6.62 million.

mioc-094.title: Deep water stops flowing between the Americas
mioc-094.text: Deep-ocean links through Central America closed by 12–9.2 million years ago, though a shallow Pacific–Caribbean link lasted until 2.45 million years ago at the latest. The Isthmus of Panama's first uplift is dated to around 12 million years ago, though some experts propose 15 million for the first closure. In the Late Miocene, islands began forming between the Americas, and ground sloths such as Thinobadistes island-hopped north. Zircon crystals in northern Colombia's middle Miocene bedrock even suggest a full isthmus, not a string of islands, may have formed by 10 million years ago.

mioc-099.title: The Amazon begins to flow across a continent
mioc-099.text: Between 11.8 and 11.3 million years ago, the Amazon began flowing as a single river across the whole continent. Long before, in the Cretaceous, a proto-Amazon had flowed west as part of a river system draining from Africa.

mioc-100.title: Cold Benguela Upwelling begins off southwestern Africa
mioc-100.text: In the late Miocene, the Benguela Upwelling began to bring cold, nutrient-rich water up to the surface off southwestern Africa. It likely fed the phytoplankton, drifting microscopic algae, behind Hondeklip Bay's rich marine fossils, and the cold Benguela Current still helps keep the Namib Desert arid.

mioc-102.title: Europe loses much of its large-mammal variety
mioc-102.text: Europe's large mammals lost much of their diversity during the Late Miocene. In Iberia, as the climate dried, grazing animals diversified while browsers, which feed on leaves and shoots, declined.

mioc-103.title: South America's giant caimans and gharials vanish
mioc-103.text: Northern South America's giant crocodilians died out in the late Miocene, probably because the wetlands they lived in disappeared. The losses included the gharial Gryposuchus and the caiman Purussaurus, the largest of them all.

mioc-104.title: The last sebecosuchians hold out in the Caribbean
mioc-104.text: Sebecids, the final branch of the sebecosuchians, a group of crocodile relatives, apparently survived on the Greater Antilles until the late Miocene or early Pliocene. When they vanished, the whole sebecosuchian lineage went with them.

mioc-106.title: South America's sparassodont predators begin to fade
mioc-106.text: Sparassodonts, meat-eating relatives of marsupials, began a long decline across South America in the Late Miocene, possibly because of cooling. One of their families, the borhyaenids, is last known from the latest Miocene.

mioc-108.title: A German ape stirs debate over upright walking
mioc-108.text: The discoverer of Danuvius, a great ape from southern Germany, argues that it walked upright along branches, perhaps a forerunner of human two-legged walking. The claim is disputed: other researchers say its fragmentary bones differ too little from other fossil apes to show how two-legged walking began.

mioc-109.title: The last choristodere reptiles disappear
mioc-109.text: Choristoderes, semiaquatic reptiles dating back to the Middle Jurassic, had survived the K–Pg extinction that ended the Cretaceous, yet they died out in the Miocene for unclear reasons. The last was the European genus Lazarussuchus, known for certain from the Early Miocene and possibly from southern German fossils about 11.6 million years old.

mioc-110.title: Earth slides into the Late Miocene Cool Interval
mioc-110.text: About 11 million years ago, the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began. From then on, Earth's climate grew steadily more like today's. The chill may have been harsher than earlier cold spells, and desmostylians, cold-adapted marine mammals, declined through it.

mioc-111.title: The modern Yangtze River takes shape
mioc-111.text: The modern Yangtze River is estimated to have originated around 11 million years ago. Rates of sediment buildup suggest its present outlet is no older than that.

mioc-112.title: A brief, sharp warming breaks the chill
mioc-112.text: Early in the Late Miocene, around 10.8 to 10.7 million years ago, a major but short-lived warming briefly interrupted the cooling.

mioc-113.title: Aguas Calientes caldera erupts the Tajamar ignimbrite
mioc-113.text: Aguas Calientes caldera, a huge volcanic crater in the Andes, erupted the Tajamar ignimbrite between 10.5 and 10.1 million years ago. An ignimbrite is a rock sheet laid down by searing flows of volcanic ash and gas, and this one holds about 350 km³ of rock.

mioc-114.title: Ancient Lake Idaho fills for the first time
mioc-114.text: Lake Idaho first existed from about 10.1 to 6.4 million years ago. After a long absence, it returned from 4.3 to 2.5 million years ago.

mioc-116.title: True elephants arise from gomphotheres in Africa
mioc-116.text: Around 10 million years ago, the first members of the elephant family, Elephantidae, arose in Africa from gomphotheres. From the Late Miocene, many proboscideans, elephants and their trunked relatives, evolved ever larger tusks and shorter lower jaws. Late Miocene climate change drove other groups, such as the amebelodontids and choerolophodontids, into decline and extinction. The first members of today's elephant genera appeared around 6 to 5 million years ago, as the Miocene gave way to the Pliocene.

mioc-117.title: Greenland's edges rise, making room for an ice sheet
mioc-117.text: Around 10 million years ago, Greenland's western margin began to rise, eventually forming plateaus 2,000 to 3,000 meters high. The eastern uplands followed about 5 million years ago. This high ground made a single, connected ice sheet possible. Large glaciers may have formed by 8 to 7 million years ago, though forests survived on Greenland into the Pliocene.

mioc-118.title: Ground sloths island-hop to North America
mioc-118.text: By about 10 to 9 million years ago, megalonychid and mylodontid ground sloths had reached North America by hopping across new islands between the Americas. The earliest known North American megalonychid, Pliometanastes, lived in the southern United States about 9 million years ago. Some large North American plant-eaters may have gone south at the same time over an incomplete land bridge. These crossings were an early phase of the Great American Biotic Interchange, the swap of animals between the two continents.

mioc-120.title: Early great apes live along East Africa's rift
mioc-120.text: Ten-million-year-old fossils of hominids, the great-ape family that includes humans, come from East Africa, among them Chororapithecus from Ethiopia's Afar rift and Nakalipithecus. Around the same time, the gorilla branch split from the line leading to chimpanzees and humans.

mioc-122.title: Rising Carpathians wall off the Pannonian Sea
mioc-122.text: Around 10 million years ago, the rising Carpathian Mountains cut the Pannonian Sea off from the rest of the Paratethys.

mioc-124.title: The Rivera plate breaks away off western Mexico
mioc-124.text: Around 10 million years ago, the Rivera plate broke away from the Cocos plate off western Mexico. It became a microplate, a small, independent slab of Earth's outer shell.

mioc-119.title: The Gulf of California opens as Baja tears away
mioc-119.text: Rifting, the slow tearing of Earth's crust, began opening the Gulf of California 10 to 6 million years ago, dragging Baja California northwest from mainland Mexico. The East Pacific Rise, a seafloor spreading ridge, pushed up the middle of the gulf to form the Gulf of California Rift Zone. The opening gulf let a large river cut northeast around 6 million years ago; by 5.5 to 5 million, streams had merged into one major river. Many geologists date the gulf itself to about 5.3 million years ago, when rifting tore Baja California off the North American plate.

mioc-115.title: The Altiplano–Puna flare-up floods the Andes with ignimbrite
mioc-115.text: From about 10 million years ago, calderas of the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex erupted in four great pulses, separated by quieter spells. Between 10 and 1 million years ago they poured out about 10,000 km³ of felsic, or silica-rich, ignimbrite over crust 70 km thick. Mafic magma, rich in iron and magnesium, had invaded the lower crust; before 10.6 million years ago an overturn melted that crust, starting the eruptions. Volcanism peaked between 8 and 4 million years ago, with huge eruptions at Cerro Panizos, Coranzulí, Vilama, Cerro Guacha and La Pacana.

mioc-125.title: Livyatan, the sperm whale with record-sized biting teeth
mioc-125.text: Livyatan, a sperm whale 13.5 to 17.5 meters long with the largest biting teeth known, hunted off Peru between 9.9 and 8.9 million years ago. Teeth from Chile to Australia suggest it or a close relative ranged widely until about 5 million years ago, when end-Miocene cooling probably shrank its food.

mioc-126.title: Oreodonts fade as deer and bovids reach North America
mioc-126.text: North America's Hemphillian age began about 9.4 million years ago, and during it the last oreodonts, hoofed plant-eaters, died out along with mylagaulids and dromomerycids. Newcomers arrived from Asia: deer, bovids such as antelope and cattle, saber-toothed cats and skunks. Meanwhile, rabbits and short-faced bears diversified.

mioc-127.title: Asia's winter monsoons blow harder
mioc-127.text: Monsoons, seasonal winds that reverse direction through the year, grew stronger over Asia in the Late Miocene. The South Asian winter monsoon strengthened first, about 9.2 to 8.5 million years ago. From 7.9 to 5.8 million years ago, the East Asian winter monsoon followed as the subarctic front, the edge of the cold north, shifted south. Around 5.5 million years ago, that monsoon intensified rapidly.

mioc-129.title: Toxic blooms fill Cerro Ballena with stranded whales
mioc-129.text: At Cerro Ballena in Chile's Atacama Desert, more than 40 whales, along with seals, sailfish, swordfish, sharks and aquatic sloths, were buried in four separate mass deaths. Toxic algal blooms fed by high iron levels likely poisoned them, and waves then washed the carcasses ashore.

mioc-131.title: Gargano's rock fissures become animal traps
mioc-131.text: On Gargano in Italy, Miocene mammals and birds fell into fissures in much older Jurassic rock. Over time, they built up large deposits of well-preserved animals.

mioc-133.title: The Lake Malawi basin starts to form
mioc-133.text: The Lake Malawi basin began forming about 8.6 million years ago, far earlier than once thought. Deep water first appeared there only 4.5 million years ago.

mioc-134.title: Vilama caldera unleashes a VEI 8 eruption
mioc-134.text: Vilama caldera in the Andes erupted the enormous Vilama ignimbrite about 8.5–8.4 million years ago, in a VEI 8 blast, the top of the explosivity scale. The 1,000 km³ Sifon ignimbrite, erupted 8.33 million years ago, may have come from Vilama too.

mioc-136.title: Apes in Greece and Anatolia stir an out-of-Africa debate
mioc-136.text: Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus, apes from Greece and Anatolia about 8 million years old, have been read as signs that hominins, the human lineage, left Africa early. More probably, they belong to Homininae, the subfamily of African apes and humans, but not to Hominini, the human tribe itself.

mioc-137.title: The human and chimpanzee lineages part ways
mioc-137.text: Gibbons, orangutans and gorillas branched off in turn; then the lines leading to chimpanzees and humans separated, probably from a small African ape. Exactly when is still debated, with molecular and fossil estimates spanning about 13 to 4.7 million years ago. A 2026 meta-analysis of genome-based estimates that match the fossil record favors about 8 million years ago, and almost certainly more than 7. The parting may not have been clean, since the two lineages may have kept exchanging genes as late as 6.3 to 5.4 million years ago.

mioc-139.title: Rabbits and hares burst across the Northern Hemisphere
mioc-139.text: Around 8 million years ago, rabbits and hares abruptly diversified and spread across the Northern Hemisphere. Paleontologists call this sudden expansion the Leporid Datum, after leporids, the rabbit family. By 7 million years ago, they had reached South America and Africa.

mioc-138.title: A cooling world turns dry
mioc-138.text: Global cooling drained moisture from the atmosphere and pushed the whole world toward aridity, especially after 8 to 7 million years ago. Rising land in East Africa helped shrink its rainforests, and Australia dried as it moved into a low-rainfall zone. In Central Asia, the uplifted Tian Shan mountains blocked westerly winds and parched the Tarim Basin. One theory links the Sahara's drying to a monsoon that weakened when the Tethys Sea dried up around 7 million years ago.

mioc-142.title: The Banda Arc rams into Australia and Timor
mioc-142.text: In the Messinian, the last stage of the Miocene, the Banda Arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands, began colliding with Australia and Timor. Geologists use it as a standard example of an island arc striking a continent to build an orogen, a mountain belt raised by collision.

mioc-144.title: Sahelanthropus, a contested first hominin, lives in Chad
mioc-144.text: Sahelanthropus, known mainly from a partial skull nicknamed Toumaï found in northern Chad, lived about 7 million years ago. It is often listed as the first hominin, and the human line of upright-walking apes has been traced back to it. That status is contested. Some researchers see in its anatomy a match for the last common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans, while others dispute the claim.

mioc-143.title: Desmostylians, a whole order of sea mammals, vanish
mioc-143.text: Desmostylians, the only known extinct order of marine mammals, died out between 7.2 and 5.3 million years ago. Native to the North Pacific, they had declined after the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum, perhaps because Late Miocene cooling was unusually severe.

mioc-148.title: Thalassocnus, a sloth that took to the sea
mioc-148.text: The oldest fossils of Thalassocnus, a ground sloth adapted to life in the sea along South America's Pacific coast, date to roughly 7 million years ago in Peru. It is now known from many Miocene and Pliocene rock units along that coast, including Chile's Coquimbo Formation.

mioc-145.title: C4 grasses spread and remake the grasslands
mioc-145.text: Between 7 and 6 million years ago, C4 grasses became a major force in ecosystems, though not yet in the north. Their form of photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water more efficiently than the older C3 type, and as CO2 levels fell they came to dominate grasslands. These silica-rich grasses drove worldwide extinctions of plant-eaters that lacked high-crowned teeth. Proposed causes include falling CO2 or rising seasonality, drought and monsoon-fed wildfires, and the change still shows in the balance of heavy and light carbon in rocks.

mioc-147.title: A sharp chill grips the late Miocene world
mioc-147.text: Between 7 and 5.3 million years ago, temperatures fell sharply, most likely because CO2 declined and the swing in Earth's axial tilt shrank. Oceans cooled to near-modern values, with sea surfaces outside the tropics dropping by about 7 to 9 °C. Antarctic ice grew close to its present size, and a major glaciation from 6.26 to 5.50 million years ago pulsed with Earth's 41,000-year tilt cycle. A cold spell around 6 million years ago advanced glaciers and lowered sea level, helping to start the Messinian salinity crisis.

mioc-149.title: The first mammoth appears in Africa
mioc-149.text: The oldest known mammoth, Mammuthus subplanifrons, appeared in southern and eastern Africa around 6.2 to 5.3 million years ago. Mammoths went on to range across Africa, Asia, Europe and North America, surviving until about 4,000 years ago.

mioc-150.title: Orrorin, an early hominin that walked on two legs
mioc-150.text: Fossils of Orrorin tugenensis from Kenya's Lukeino Formation date from 6.1 to 5.7 million years ago. Orrorin appears to have been bipedal, walking upright on two legs, about 6 million years ago. Its bones share none of the specialized features unique to the great apes. The rise of bipedal apes like it at the end of the Miocene sped up the turnover of Africa's animal life.

mioc-151.title: Disputed hominin-like footprints on Crete
mioc-151.text: Possible footprints with hominin-like features on western Crete have been dated to about 6.05 million years ago, older than an earlier estimate of 5.7 million. They are hotly disputed: critics doubt they are footprints at all, and even if they are, an ape that evolved similar feet independently may have made them.

mioc-152.title: Argentavis soars over South America on 6-meter wings
mioc-152.text: Argentavis, a teratorn with a wingspan of 6 meters or more, soared over South America about 6 million years ago as one of the largest flying birds known. This member of an extinct family of giant birds may have fed partly on leftovers from the kills of the predator Thylacosmilus.

mioc-153.title: The Nile carves a gorge far below sea level
mioc-153.text: As the Mediterranean emptied, the ancestral Nile cut a deep gorge through Egypt, the Eonile, reaching 2,400 meters below sea level at Cairo. When the sea returned, the gorge became a gulf that slowly filled with sediment.

mioc-154.title: The Mediterranean dries out in the Messinian salinity crisis
mioc-154.text: From 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago, the Mediterranean dried out again and again, piling evaporites, salt beds left by evaporating seawater, across its floor. Plate motion at the Gibraltar Arc and mountain uplift helped close the Betic corridor and the Strait of Gibraltar's forerunner, sealing the sea from the Atlantic. After a last closure around 5.6 million years ago, the basin dried almost completely within a thousand years, and erosion cut canyons rivaling the Grand Canyon. Native sea life suffered major extinctions, and from 5.5 million years ago river water diluted the brines into brackish lakes called the 'Lago Mare'.

mioc-155.title: Cerro Guacha erupts the colossal Guacha ignimbrite
mioc-155.text: Cerro Guacha, one of the great calderas of the Altiplano–Puna flare-up, erupted the Guacha ignimbrite about 5.65 million years ago. The eruption produced roughly 1,200 to 1,300 km³ of volcanic rock.

mioc-156.title: Ardipithecus joins Africa's earliest hominins
mioc-156.text: The genus Ardipithecus appeared around 5.5 million years ago, probably after the human–chimpanzee split, though the two lines may still have been exchanging genes. Its early species A. kadabba, known from Middle Awash fossils 6.5 to 5.5 million years old, joined Sahelanthropus and Orrorin among Africa's first hominins.

mioc-157.title: The Caspian Sea becomes landlocked
mioc-157.text: About 5.5 million years ago, tectonic uplift and a fall in sea level cut off the Caspian Sea, then some 30 million years old, and left it landlocked.

mioc-158.title: Pastos Grandes caldera's first great eruption
mioc-158.text: Pastos Grandes caldera in the Andes went through its first caldera-forming cycle 5.45 million years ago. That eruption produced the Chuhuilla ignimbrite, some 1,200 km³ of volcanic rock.

mioc-159.title: The Dead Sea Transform forms as Suez rifting stops
mioc-159.text: Near the end of the Miocene, the Arabian plate began colliding with Eurasia, rifting in the Gulf of Suez stopped, and the Dead Sea Transform developed. This transform fault, where two plates slide past each other, is now the boundary between the Arabian and African plates.

mioc-160.title: Europe's apes die out
mioc-160.text: During the Miocene, about 100 species of apes lived across Africa, Asia and Europe. Among them were Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus in Greece and Anatolia. At the end of the epoch, Europe's apes died out as its habitats became more uniform.

mioc-161.title: Swinging lake levels wipe out Paratethys fish
mioc-161.text: Near the end of the Miocene, the water level and conditions of the Paratethys megalake swung rapidly in an upheaval called the Khersonian crisis. The turmoil wiped out much of the lake's unique fish life.

mioc-162.title: Warmth returns as the Miocene closes
mioc-162.text: At the end of the Miocene, global temperatures rose again as the swing in Earth's axial tilt grew, and Central Asia became more arid. The Pliocene began warmer than the cool Messinian before it.

plio-001.title: The sea floods the Bering land bridge
plio-001.text: Near the start of the Pliocene, the sea first flooded the land bridge between Alaska and Siberia. The new passage let marine life spread between the Arctic and the Pacific. Afterward, the bridge drowned and reemerged again and again. The Bering Strait itself is thought to have first opened sometime between 7.4 and 4.8 million years ago.

plio-003.title: The first tree sloths appear
plio-003.text: The first tree sloths appeared around the start of the Pliocene. Early megalonychid sloths were small and perhaps partly tree-dwelling, and by the Pliocene they had reached about half the size of the later Megalonyx.

plio-005.title: Cat-like nimravids die out
plio-005.text: The nimravids, cat-like carnivores that had still been diverse in the Early Miocene, died out around the start of the Pliocene.

plio-009.title: The Atlantic breaks through and refills the Mediterranean
plio-009.text: Atlantic water burst through the Strait of Gibraltar and refilled the dried-out Mediterranean, ending the Messinian salinity crisis and opening the Pliocene's first age, the Zanclean. By one estimate, about ninety percent of the basin filled within months to two years, with sea level sometimes rising over 10 meters a day. Peak flow may have reached about 100 million cubic meters per second, roughly a thousand times today's Amazon. Not everyone accepts so sudden a deluge, though: some sources favor a more gradual refilling, and the exact timing remains uncertain.

plio-006.title: The last oreodonts disappear
plio-006.text: Oreodonts, plant-eating hoofed mammals that had stayed diverse since the Oligocene, disappeared in the earliest Pliocene.

plio-007.title: More than a third of large sea animals vanish
plio-007.text: During the Pliocene, an extinction of marine megafauna, the ocean's largest animals, wiped out 36% of big marine species. Marine mammals lost 55%, sea turtles 43%, seabirds 35% and sharks 9%. Warm-blooded and partly warm-blooded animals fared worse than cold-blooded ones, which points to a shrinking food supply. Sea-level swings, the Cenozoic's largest and driven by growing polar ice, battered coastal habitats and may have helped cause the losses.

plio-008.title: A disputed young uplift for the Sierra Nevada
plio-008.text: The Sierra Nevada may have been lifted and tilted westward only two to three million years ago, and faulting still raises its steep eastern edge. Geologists disagree: some see young uplift in recently cut river valleys, while others find the northern range little changed since 30–40 million years ago.

plio-004.title: Mount Kenya grows into a towering volcano
plio-004.text: Mount Kenya grew as a large stratovolcano, a steep cone of layered lava and ash, on the shoulder of the East African Rift. Its summit probably topped 6,000 meters, higher than Kilimanjaro today, but glaciers have since cut it down to 5,199 meters, still Africa's second-highest mountain.

plio-010.title: The opening gulf speeds the Grand Canyon's carving
plio-010.text: The Gulf of California opened 5.3 million years ago, dropping the Colorado River's outlet; faster erosion cut most of the Grand Canyon's depth by 1.2 million. The canyon's age is debated: some studies date the river's course to 5–6 million years ago, while others make parts up to 70 million years old.

plio-011.title: The great white shark evolves
plio-011.text: The great white shark evolved about 5.3 million years ago. Abundant juvenile teeth show that the Pliocene coasts of Chile's Coquimbo Region served as its nurseries.

plio-012.title: The Pliocene Warm Interval interrupts the long cooling
plio-012.text: From about 5.3 to 2.7 million years ago, the Pliocene Warm Interval interrupted Earth's long cooling trend, starting warmer than the cool Messinian before it. Carbon dioxide levels were similar to today's, so scientists often treat the interval as an analogue, a natural test case, for near-future warming. Ice sheets collapsed much more often in the early to middle Pliocene, between 5 and 3 million years ago. The oceans stayed relatively warm, though they kept slowly cooling.

plio-013.title: Bluff Downs preserves a Pliocene Queensland waterside
plio-013.text: At Bluff Downs in northern Queensland, fossils accumulated 5.2 to 3.6 million years ago beside large water bodies fringed by riverside forests. Capped by a lava flow dated to 3.62 million years ago, it is one of Australia's most significant Pliocene sites, with marsupials from both living and extinct families.

plio-014.title: Kauaʻi rises over the Hawaiian hotspot
plio-014.text: Kauaʻi, the oldest of the main Hawaiian islands, formed as the Pacific Plate slid over the Hawaiʻi hotspot, an upwelling of hot mantle rock. The plate carries each volcano west-northwest away from the hotspot, so the chain's volcanoes grow younger toward the southeast.

plio-015.title: The Colorado Plateau and River reach their modern form
plio-015.text: About 5 million years ago, the Colorado Plateau reached its present height and the Colorado River took a course close to today's. Uplift and the opening Gulf of California rearranged its drainage; about 4 million years ago the river reached the Salton Trough, then linked to the gulf.

plio-016.title: The last giant-toothed sperm whales disappear
plio-016.text: Teeth from Australia and South Africa show that Livyatan or a close relative still hunted around 5 million years ago, possibly worldwide. By the early Pliocene these giant-toothed sperm whales were gone, probably because cooling made their prey, the baleen whales, larger and fewer.

plio-017.title: Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion, appears in Australia
plio-017.text: Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion, first appeared in the Pliocene, and its early species T. crassidentatus, about 5 million years ago, was the size of a large dog. Later species grew to the weight of a lioness, and the genus became Australia's apex predator, the hunter at the top of the food chain.

plio-018.title: The great Paratethys breaks up into inland seas
plio-018.text: From about 5 million years ago, the Paratethys grew steadily shallower and largely dried out, breaking into a few inland seas that were at times fully cut off. The Black, Caspian and Aral seas are its remnants, and in the Pliocene the Caspian was a small lake with no outlet.

plio-019.title: A magma pulse drives giant eruptions in the Puna
plio-019.text: Between 5 and 3.8 million years ago, large ignimbrite eruptions struck the northern Puna's volcanic arc, part of a magma pulse around 4 million years ago. The Puripicar ignimbrite of about 4.2 million years ago alone held some 1,500 km³, a volume matched later by the 2.89-million-year-old Pastos Grandes ignimbrite.

plio-020.title: A Tennessee sinkhole traps a warm forest world
plio-020.text: Between 4.9 and 4.5 million years ago, a sinkhole pond in a warm, wet Tennessee forest trapped new species of red panda, rhinoceros, pond turtle and hickory. The first site of its age known from Appalachia, it shows that eastern North America's wildlife still had close ties to Eurasia's in the Early Pliocene.

plio-022.title: The Kilgore Tuff eruption ends the Heise volcanic field
plio-022.text: In eastern Idaho, the Kilgore Tuff eruption, rated VEI 8, blasted out about 1,800 cubic kilometers of ash and left a caldera 80 by 60 kilometers across. It was the last caldera-forming eruption of the Heise volcanic field, active for over 2 million years above the Yellowstone hotspot, a deep plume of hot rock.

plio-023.title: Ardi: Ardipithecus ramidus walks and climbs in the Afar
plio-023.text: The early hominin Ardipithecus ramidus lived in Ethiopia's Afar region about 4.4 million years ago, and the older A. kadabba is considered its direct ancestor. Its most complete specimen is Ardi, a female skeleton whose pelvis shows that upright walking was well under way. Her hands and limbs, though, could still climb trees. Fossils of at least nine more individuals from As Duma in the Afar date to 4.51 to 4.32 million years ago.

plio-024.title: Australopithecus anamensis, the first australopith
plio-024.text: Australopithecus anamensis, the oldest known species of its genus, lived roughly 4.3 to 3.8 million years ago. Its first fossils came from Kanapoi and Allia Bay in northern Kenya, and the Allia Bay finds give early evidence of walking on two legs. Australopithecus probably arose in eastern Africa around 4 million years ago, later spread across the continent and died out somewhat after 2 million years ago. A nearly complete skull from Ethiopia, 3.8 million years old, shows that A. anamensis overlapped in time with A. afarensis.

plio-025.title: La Pacana unleashes the giant Atana ignimbrite
plio-025.text: Between about 4.2 and 3.8 million years ago, La Pacana caldera in the Chilean Andes erupted the giant Atana ignimbrite. At 2,500 to 3,500 cubic kilometers, it ranks as the fifth-largest explosive eruption known. The much smaller Toconao ignimbrite erupted at almost the same time, with no sign of a pause between the two.

plio-026.title: Hagerman's fossil beds preserve a trove of early horses
plio-026.text: The Hagerman fossil beds in Idaho, dating from at least 4 million to 3.07 million years ago, hold at least 200 species. Among the richest deposits of North America's Blancan land-mammal age, they contain the largest known concentration of the Hagerman horse, Equus simplicidens.

plio-028.title: Armored glyptodonts evolve in South America
plio-028.text: The giant armored glyptodonts Glyptodon and Glyptotherium evolved in South America from about 3.9 million years ago. Glyptodon, a plant-eating armadillo relative with a shell of hundreds of bony plates, reached 2 meters long and 400 kilograms, and survived until about 11,000 years ago.

plio-027.title: Australopithecus afarensis walks East Africa
plio-027.text: Australopithecus afarensis lived in East Africa from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago. The 3.58-million-year-old skeleton nicknamed Kadanuumuu suggests it already walked fully upright, though not all researchers agree. Selam, a three-year-old girl from Dikika in Ethiopia, lived 3.3 million years ago, about 100,000 years before the famous Lucy. Africa then held more large carnivores than today, including hyenas and saber-toothed cats, which likely preyed on australopithecines.

plio-029.title: A long wet spell greens North Africa
plio-029.text: From about 3.8 to 3.3 million years ago, North Africa went through an extended humid period. Tropical forests in northwestern Africa reached as far as Cape Blanc until around 3.5 million years ago. A significant river flowed across the Sahara until 3.35 million years ago, when the trade winds began to dominate.

plio-030.title: The woolly rhino's lineage begins in Tibet
plio-030.text: Coelodonta thibetana, the oldest known member of the woolly rhinoceros genus, lived in Tibet about 3.7 million years ago. The genus reached Siberia, Mongolia and China by the Early Pleistocene, though the woolly rhinoceros itself appeared only in the Middle Pleistocene.

plio-031.title: Three hominins leave footprints in Laetoli's ash
plio-031.text: At Laetoli in Tanzania, three early hominins, probably Australopithecus, crossed fresh volcanic ash about 3.7 million years ago, one walking in another's footprints. A soft rain then cemented the powdery ash into tuff, a rock made of volcanic ash, and preserved the trackways. The prints closely resemble modern human footprints, and when found they were the oldest known evidence of hominin bipedalism. Together with leg bones, they suggest A. afarensis was a competent walker on two legs, though less efficient than humans.

plio-032.title: Little Foot, the most complete early hominin skeleton
plio-032.text: Little Foot, an Australopithecus skeleton from South Africa's Sterkfontein caves, is about 90% complete, the most complete early hominin skeleton known. A 2015 date of 3.67 million years would make it South Africa's oldest australopith, but estimates span 2.2 to 3.67 million, and its species is disputed.

plio-034.title: Megatherium, the elephant-sized ground sloth, appears
plio-034.text: The oldest remains of Megatherium, South America's giant ground sloth, come from Bolivia and the Pampas and are at least 3.6 million years old. The genus lasted to the end of the Late Pleistocene, and its best-known species, M. americanum, was as big as an elephant at 3.5 to 4 tonnes.

plio-035.title: An impact blasts out El'gygytgyn crater in Siberia
plio-035.text: About 3.6 million years ago, an impact on the Chukchi Peninsula of northeast Siberia blasted out a crater 18 kilometers across. A lake about 12 kilometers wide now fills it, and its sediments record Arctic climate, including mid-Pliocene summers 8 °C warmer than today's.

plio-037.title: The giant shark megalodon vanishes
plio-037.text: Megalodon, a giant shark estimated at 14 to 24 meters long, had hunted the world's oceans since about 23 million years ago. A 2019 reanalysis of its fossil record moved its extinction back to about 3.6 million years ago, earlier than the long-assumed 2.6 million. Cooling seas, falling sea levels that shrank its warm nurseries, and the decline of small baleen whales probably combined to finish it. Its loss let great white sharks spread into its old waters, and baleen whales grew markedly larger afterward.

plio-036.title: Mammoths and Elephas walk out of Africa
plio-036.text: Around 3.6 to 3.2 million years ago, the elephant genera Elephas and Mammuthus, the mammoths, migrated out of Africa. Mammoths crossed into Eurasia by way of the Sinai Peninsula by 3.2 million years ago and entered Europe around 3 million years ago. Back in Africa, they became confined to the north of the continent by the Late Pliocene. Elephants, gomphotheres and stegodonts thrived in Asia, yet proboscidean diversity fell sharply during the Late Pliocene.

plio-038.title: Australopiths reach Central Africa at Koro Toro
plio-038.text: Jaw fossils about 3.5 million years old from Koro Toro, Chad, are Central Africa's only known australopiths, showing the group ranged beyond the east and south. They lived in lakeside grassland with sparse trees beside an expanded 'Lake Mega-Chad', and many researchers still assign them to A. afarensis.

plio-039.title: Flat-faced Kenyanthropus lives by Lake Turkana
plio-039.text: Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced, small-toothed hominin, lived in a mix of forest and grassland by Lake Turkana in Kenya from about 3.5 to 3.2 million years ago. It shows that more than one hominin lineage lived alongside A. afarensis, and it may have made the Lomekwian stone tools found at the same site.

plio-040.title: Camels live in a forested High Arctic
plio-040.text: Camels lived on Ellesmere Island, inside the Arctic Circle, when global temperatures were 2–3 °C warmer than today and northern forest covered the island. Protein sequences from bone collagen confirm that the fragmentary remains, referred to Paracamelus, came from close relatives of modern camels.

plio-041.title: Cut marks or sand scratches on Dikika's bones?
plio-041.text: At Dikika, Ethiopia, cut marks on two animal bones would be the oldest sign of butchery with sharp stone tools, if Australopithecus afarensis made them. The claim is disputed, because the bones lay in sandstone, where abrasive sand and gravel also scratched them.

plio-044.title: Hominins strike the first known stone tools at Lomekwi
plio-044.text: The oldest known stone tools, found at Lomekwi 3 in West Turkana, Kenya, date to 3.3 million years ago. They are simple flakes, struck by pounding a core on an anvil or with a hammerstone, from volcanic rock gathered within 100 meters. No one knows who made them, and cut-marked bones about 3.4 million years old from Ethiopia's Lower Awash Valley hint that tool use may be older still. With these tools begins the Paleolithic, the Old Stone Age, which covers almost all of humanity's prehistoric technology.

plio-046.title: The Phoenix plate's long descent grinds to a halt
plio-046.text: About 3.3 million years ago the Antarctic–Phoenix Ridge stopped spreading, and after over 100 million years the Phoenix plate's sinking into the mantle slowed or ceased. What remained of the plate was absorbed into the Antarctic plate.

plio-047.title: A possible impact strikes Argentina
plio-047.text: A possible cosmic impact struck Argentina about 3.3 million years ago, at the start of the Marplatan land-mammal age. Some have suggested it drove a turnover of South America's animals, but both the impact and that link remain controversial.

plio-045.title: The Mid-Piacenzian Warm Period, with CO2 near 400 ppm
plio-045.text: Between 3.3 and 3.0 million years ago, global temperatures ran 2–3 °C above today's, with carbon dioxide near 400 parts per million, as in 2000. During this peak of Pliocene warmth, also called the Pliocene Thermal Maximum, global sea level stood about 25 meters higher than today. Arctic summers were about 8 °C warmer than now, and Greenland's ice was confined to its highest eastern and southern peaks. Models suggest the Arctic above 70°N was 10 to 20 °C warmer, while the tropics barely changed.

plio-042.title: Australopithecus africanus lives in South Africa
plio-042.text: Australopithecus africanus lived in South Africa from about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago, leaving fossils at Taung, Sterkfontein, Makapansgat and Gladysvale. Its first specimen, the Taung Child, a juvenile skull about 2.8 million years old, was the first early hominin ever found. It kept a more apelike upper body than East Africa's A. afarensis and ate a highly varied diet, including C4 foods such as grasses and seeds. Strong swings in climate, and perhaps competition with Homo and Paranthropus robustus, probably drove it to extinction.

plio-048.title: Lucy walks upright at Hadar
plio-048.text: Lucy, a female Australopithecus afarensis whose skeleton is about 40% complete, lived at Hadar in Ethiopia's Afar region around 3.2 million years ago. Ash layers beneath her were argon-dated to 3.22 and 3.18 million years ago, the younger lying just one meter below the bones. Her small, apelike skull paired with an upright, two-legged gait shows that walking upright came before bigger brains. Nearby, the 'First Family' site AL 333, of about the same age, holds at least thirteen individuals of different ages.

plio-049.title: The eastern Pacific's permanent El Niño ends
plio-049.text: In the early to middle Pliocene, a permanent El Niño-like state kept the eastern equatorial Pacific warm, so the planet reflected less sunlight. Around 3 million years ago, cold surface water appeared there. The change may have aided global cooling and altered how climate responded to orbital cycles, the regular shifts in Earth's path and tilt.

plio-050.title: Savannas open up across East Africa
plio-050.text: Around 3 million years ago, savanna spread across East Africa as the climate turned cooler and drier. Global cooling may have hastened the loss of forests and the growth of grasslands. One hypothesis holds that walking upright and other hominin traits evolved as forests gave way to open savanna. Life in savanna, where wildfires were common but easier to survive than in dense forest, may also have been the first step toward early humans' control of fire.

plio-051.title: South America's native predators collapse
plio-051.text: Roughly 3 million years ago, South America's native carnivore community collapsed, taking with it the last sparassodonts, the continent's meat-eating relatives of marsupials. Thylacosmilids last appear about 3 million years ago, already rarer before the Great American Interchange, and terror birds declined after it. The collapse did not match northern carnivores' arrival: dogs and weasels reached South America about 2.9 million years ago but stayed rare until the Pleistocene. The sparassodonts' long decline, from the Late Miocene to the Pliocene's end, may be linked to cooling and the onset of the Quaternary ice ages.

plio-053.title: The South Asian summer monsoon strengthens
plio-053.text: The South Asian summer monsoon grew stronger after 2.95 million years ago, probably because the Indonesian Throughflow, the current carrying Pacific water into the Indian Ocean, was reorganized.

plio-054.title: Oldowan tools spread across Africa
plio-054.text: The Oldowan, the first widespread stone-tool industry, was used by hominins across much of Africa from about 2.9 million years ago until at least 1.7 million. The oldest examples come from Nyayanga on Kenya's Homa Peninsula, and thousands of artifacts at Gona, Ethiopia, are firmly dated to 2.6 million years ago. The tools served mainly for butchering, and 2.5-million-year-old tools lay beside cut-marked bones. Their makers are debated: early Homo and Australopithecus garhi are both candidates, and Homo habilis was making them by about 2.3 million years ago.

plio-056.title: The Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas
plio-056.text: Around 2.8 million years ago, the new Isthmus of Panama joined the two Americas and closed the last non-polar strait between the Pacific and Atlantic. Surface-water exchange through the seaway may already have been fading by 4.6–4.2 million years ago, and some studies place the isthmus as early as 4 million. The closure ended the last of a current that had circled the equator since the Cretaceous, and pushed more heat and salt toward the North Atlantic. Strengthened Gulf Stream and Humboldt currents cooled the Arctic, eventually leading to the great glaciations of the Quaternary ice age.

plio-055.title: The Ledi-Geraru jaw, the oldest known Homo
plio-055.text: The oldest known fossil of the human genus, Homo, is the jawbone LD 350-1 from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia's Afar region, dated to 2.8 to 2.75 million years ago. Its age suggests Homo may have evolved from Australopithecus afarensis around this time, most likely in East Africa's Rift Valley. Teeth from Koobi Fora in Kenya, 3 to 2.7 million years old, may belong to the same species. The origin of Homo coincided with climatic changes, but too few fossils are known to tell whether climate was the cause.

plio-057.title: The largest wave of the Great American Interchange
plio-057.text: From around 2.7 million years ago, the new land bridge set off the last and largest wave of migration between the Americas. Cats, condors, raccoons and camelids moved south, while armadillos, hummingbirds, opossums, ground sloths and glyptodonts moved north. Horses and tapirs also entered South America, where competition from northern hoofed mammals helped drive native ones toward extinction. The exchange was lopsided: extinction rates ran much higher in South America, and northern groups diversified greatly there.

plio-058.title: Ice spreads across the Northern Hemisphere
plio-058.text: Around 2.7 million years ago, temperatures dropped and glaciation began in the Northern Hemisphere. Once carbon dioxide fell to 280 to 320 parts per million, Greenland's separate ice caps merged into one sheet covering most of the island. Ice-rafted cobbles on northern Atlantic and Pacific seabeds mark the new Arctic ice, as does an abrupt shift in oxygen isotopes, oxygen's heavy and light forms. Suggested causes include falling carbon dioxide and a stronger North Atlantic circulation after Panama closed, which carried moisture north.

plio-059.title: Robust Paranthropus evolves in East Africa
plio-059.text: The robust hominin genus Paranthropus evolved around 2.7 million years ago; its earliest species, P. aethiopicus, lived in East Africa until about 2.3 million. Its oldest remains, from Ethiopia's Omo Kibish Formation, are 2.6 million years old.

plio-060.title: Nearby supernovae sprinkle iron-60 on the seafloor
plio-060.text: Ancient seabed deposits record a large influx of radioactive iron-60, which only supernovae, exploding stars, can make, about 2.6 million years ago. A scattered excess over 10 million years points to several fairly close supernovae, near enough that they could have damaged Earth's ozone layer and killed some ocean life.

gela-002.title: Earth's magnetic poles swap and the Quaternary begins
gela-002.text: About 2.58 million years ago, Earth's magnetic field flipped, ending a long spell of normal polarity called the Gauss Chron and opening the reversed Matuyama Chron. Since 2009 the flip has marked the start of the Pleistocene and the Quaternary, and its reference rocks lie at Monte San Nicola in Sicily. A minor extinction of calcareous nannofossils, microscopic chalky plankton such as Discoaster surculus, coincides with it. The weakened field may also have left the surface unshielded for about 15,000 years from the radiation of an early Pleistocene supernova.

gela-004.title: Ice sheets spread and the Quaternary ice age begins
gela-004.text: Around 2.58 million years ago, as the Arctic ice cap formed, ice sheets began spreading across the Northern Hemisphere in an ice age that is still going on. In the very first glacial, a cold phase of advancing ice, Patagonian ice reached today's Argentine coast. Glacials then alternated with warm interglacials, and the swings between them widened as mean temperatures fell. At their height, ice sheets at least 4 km thick covered parts of Europe, North America and Siberia.

gela-003.title: Mastodons and their kin vanish from the Old World
gela-003.text: Proboscideans are the trunked mammals, and during the Early Pleistocene nearly all of them outside the Americas died out, except the elephantids, the family of elephants and mammoths. The losses swept away the mammutids, or mastodons, along with the gomphotheres and the deinotheres. Of the other lineages, only Stegodon held on in the Old World, while gomphotheres survived across the Americas.

gela-005.title: The Eltanin asteroid strikes the deep South Pacific
gela-005.text: An asteroid about 1–4 km wide plunged into the deep ocean at the edge of the Bellingshausen Sea, some 1,500 km southwest of Chile. The sea there was 4–5 km deep, and the impact left no known crater. Scientists found the site instead from a telltale spike of the metal iridium in sediment cores. The blast probably vaporized about 150 km³ of seawater and raised tsunami waves hundreds of meters high.

gela-006.title: Polar ice dries the planet as grasslands spread
gela-006.text: Ice at both poles dried out the globe around 2.5 million years ago, speeding a long decline in the range of ecological roles filled by hoofed mammals. In Africa, a cooling and drying trend coincided with the rise of thick-molared hominins, Homo rudolfensis and Paranthropus. The Omo–Turkana Basin held a patchwork of forest, woodland, grassland and bushland, and grasslands kept spreading through the Early Pleistocene. Australia dried out too, in an event at 2.56 million years ago that may be linked to the onset of Arctic continental glaciation.

gela-007.title: Hominins branch out and the genus Homo appears
gela-007.text: East Africa's hominin fossils suddenly turn extraordinarily diverse about 2.5 million years ago, with robust australopithecines and early Homo appearing first in the Turkana Basin. This apparent adaptive radiation, a burst of new species from one stock, straddles the Pliocene–Pleistocene boundary. Earlier hominins had kept their tree-climbing habits, but now the first Homo species appeared and brain size began to climb quickly. Paranthropus and early Homo shared the landscape for a time, yet for much of the Pleistocene only Homo erectus would remain.

gela-009.title: Ethiopian waters join the Nile for the first time
gela-009.text: For the first time, about 2.5 million years ago, rivers from Ethiopia flowed north and joined the ancestral Egyptian Nile. Farther south, uplift of the Rwenzori Mountains turned paleolake Obweruka's drainage east and began forming Lake Victoria, which did not yet drain north.

gela-013.title: Saber-toothed Smilodon and short-faced bears appear
gela-013.text: The saber-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus both evolved about 2.5 million years ago. The first Smilodon species, S. gracilis, probably arose from Megantereon, and the genus lasted in the Americas until 8,200 years ago at the latest.

gela-011.title: Robust Paranthropus boisei shares East Africa with Homo
gela-011.text: Paranthropus boisei, a robust australopithecine, lived in East Africa from about 2.5 to 1.15 million years ago, persisting even after Homo habilis gave way to Homo erectus. One 1.7-million-year-old skull, KNM-ER 406, held a 510 cc brain and shows that several hominin species shared Africa at once.

gela-010.title: Rising ground dams the Murray into Lake Bungunnia
gela-010.text: After the Grampians of Victoria rose more than 250 m about 2.5 million years ago, earth movements blocked Australia's Murray River near Swan Reach. Vast, freshwater Lake Bungunnia filled behind the blockage and lasted until 0.5 million years ago.

gela-012.title: Pre-Illinoian ice sheets push south to Kansas
gela-012.text: North America lived through repeated glacials and interglacials between about 2.5 and 0.2 million years ago, a span grouped as the Pre-Illinoian. Researchers found 11 distinct glaciations in it, not the two once assumed, and discarded the old Nebraskan, Aftonian, Kansan and Yarmouthian stages. The Laurentide Ice Sheet pushed south into the Missouri and Ohio river valleys, reaching as far as Douglas County, Kansas. One table starts the Pre-Illinoian later, about 1,200,000 years ago.

gela-014.title: The last sea gap through Panama closes
gela-014.text: By 2.45 million years ago, the last shallow, temporary sea link through the Central American Seaway had closed. Deep-ocean connections had already shut between 12 and 9.2 million years ago, after a collision that began about 25 million years ago.

gela-015.title: The Amazon River settles into its modern form
gela-015.text: The Amazon had been a transcontinental river, flowing right across South America, since 11.8 to 11.3 million years ago. About 2.4 million years ago, it finally took its present shape.

gela-017.title: Wind-blown dust begins burying China's Loess Plateau
gela-017.text: Crustal movement and a cold climate began laying down loess, fine wind-blown silt, on China's Loess Plateau about 2.4 million years ago. Uplift of Tibet had already set up the East Asian monsoon. The drier Quaternary climate then weathered out the silt that became the loess.

gela-019.title: Sundaland rises from the sea and mammals reach Java
gela-019.text: Sundaland emerged around 2.4 million years ago as sea level fell, opening a land route from mainland Asia. Java had no mammals before then; now animals such as the dwarf elephant relative Sinomastodon bumiajuensis walked in from the mainland.

gela-018.title: Oldowan stone tools spread across Africa and beyond
gela-018.text: Between 2.4 and 1.7 million years ago, Oldowan stone tools, simple flakes knocked off cobbles, flourished in eastern Africa and spread to southern Africa. Securely dated tools 2.4 to 1.9 million years old at Ain Boucherit, Algeria, carry the industry into North Africa. The toolmakers also left Africa: by 1.8 million years ago, early Homo was using Oldowan tools at Dmanisi, Georgia. After more refined Acheulean tools appeared about 1.7 million years ago, people kept making Oldowan kits until other traditions replaced them about 0.25 million years ago.

gela-016.title: Homo habilis, the 'handy man', makes tools and eats meat
gela-016.text: Homo habilis, the 'handy man', lived in East and South Africa from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago. Its brain held about 500 to 900 cm³ and it may still have climbed trees, yet it made Oldowan tools and ate much meat, probably scavenged. Around 2 million years ago it may have built the first structures, branches propped with stones; a 1.75-million-year-old Olduvai stone circle is the oldest claimed architecture. Whether it was the direct ancestor of Homo erectus is now debated.

gela-020.title: Giant ground sloths walk into North America
gela-020.text: Eremotherium eomigrans, a megatheriid or giant ground sloth, crossed the new Panamanian land bridge about 2.2 million years ago, the first of its family in North America. Traffic ran the other way too: horses that entered South America evolved there into Hippidion around 2.5 million years ago.

gela-021.title: Stone tools at Shangchen hint at hominins in China
gela-021.text: Possible stone tools at Shangchen in central China are 2.12 million years old, judging by the magnetic record in the surrounding layers. That is about 300,000 years before Dmanisi, and if confirmed, they are the oldest known stone tools outside Africa. Other early claims include pebble tools at Yiron, Israel, 2.4 million years old, and tools perhaps 2.48 million years old in Jordan's Zarqa Valley. If such finds hold up, Homo habilis or an ancestral species may have left Africa before Homo erectus and spread across Asia.

gela-022.title: The Waiteariki supereruption shakes New Zealand
gela-022.text: One huge eruption in New Zealand's Tauranga Volcanic Centre, about 2.1 million years ago, laid down roughly 870 ± 87 km³ of dense rock as the Waiteariki ignimbrite. This ignimbrite, rock left by a racing flow of hot ash and pumice, probably came from the Omanawa Caldera, a collapsed crater detected only by a gravity anomaly.

gela-023.title: Yellowstone erupts and spreads ash to St. Louis
gela-023.text: Yellowstone's volcanism began 2.15 million years ago, and its first and largest cycle climaxed in the Huckleberry Ridge eruption. Rated VEI 8, top of the Volcanic Explosivity Index, it threw out about 2,450–2,500 km³ and left the Island Park Caldera, roughly 80 by 65 km. It made about 2,500 times as much ash as Mount St. Helens in 1980, and that ash now turns up from southern California to St. Louis. The ash hardened into the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff, part of which records a brief magnetic-field wobble dated to 2.0773 ± 0.0034 million years ago.

gela-024.title: Homo erectus arrives with a modern body plan
gela-024.text: The oldest known Homo erectus is DNH 134, a 2.04-million-year-old skull from Drimolen, South Africa, where it lived beside Paranthropus robustus. Other early fossils, such as KNM-ER 2598 at about 1.9 million years old, come from Koobi Fora, Kenya. The African form, often called Homo ergaster, was the first human with a slender, modern body plan. Its populations spread through savannas that widened as the ice age dried the planet, and the species lasted until about 0.6 million years ago.

gela-025.title: Great ash eruptions fade in the central Andes
gela-025.text: Large ignimbrite eruptions kept rocking the central Andes, including the 550 km³ Galán eruption about 2.1 million years ago. After 2 million years ago the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex quieted, and after 1 million years ago it erupted mostly andesite, with no large ignimbrites.

gela-028.title: Homo walks out of Africa for the first time
gela-028.text: Close to 2 million years ago, hominins began leaving Africa in waves of expansion led by Homo erectus, known together as Out of Africa I. Key early sites include Riwat in Pakistan at about 2 million years old, Dmanisi in the Caucasus at 1.81 million and Ubeidiya in the Levant at 1.5 million. Favorable climate swings probably opened the Levantine corridor, the land route along the eastern Mediterranean, to the adaptable Homo erectus, perhaps only at times. By 2.0–1.5 million years ago, hominins were settling southern Europe and Asia.

gela-029.title: Thick-toothed Homo rudolfensis lives in East Africa
gela-029.text: Homo rudolfensis lived in East Africa about 2 million years ago, with molar enamel almost as thick as that of Paranthropus. Fossils from Ethiopia and Malawi dated 2.5–2.4 million years ago could make it the earliest known Homo, but which specimens belong to it is disputed.

gela-030.title: Ancient DNA finds mastodons in a warm northern Greenland
gela-030.text: At least two million years ago, average minimum temperatures at the Kap København Formation in northern Greenland ran more than 10 °C above today's. Environmental DNA from its sediment records poplar, birch and willow trees, horseshoe crabs, corals and mastodons, which ranged much farther north than once thought.

gela-034.title: South America's native saber-tooths die out
gela-034.text: About 2 million years ago, the saber-toothed thylacosmilids died out, though in the Pliocene they had been among South America's only large mammal predators. Their placental rivals, carnivorans such as dogs, weasels and saber-toothed cats, entered the continent only in the early Pleistocene. The exchange cut both ways: the terror bird Titanis died out in North America about 1.8 million years ago, perhaps outcompeted by carnivorans. Bears, cats and skunks had reached South America by about 1 million years ago, when the short-faced bear Arctotherium first appears there.

gela-035.title: New Zealand's Taupō Rift tears open
gela-035.text: New Zealand's crust began pulling apart about 2 million years ago, opening the Taupō Rift along with the old Taupō Volcanic Zone. Major activity in the Coromandel Volcanic Zone ended, and the suspected Omanawa Caldera sat where the old and new rifts met.

gela-027.title: The Congo River basin takes its modern shape
gela-027.text: Between about 2.0 and 1.5 million years ago, the basin of the Congo River acquired its present shape, soon after the Amazon reached its own modern form.

gela-026.title: A swollen Colorado River cuts the Grand Canyon deeper
gela-026.text: Wetter ice-age climates from about 2 million years ago swelled the Colorado River, and it cut the Grand Canyon faster than ever before. The canyon neared today's depth by 1.2 million years ago, while nearby Zion Canyon's upper half was carved about 2 to 1 million years ago.

gela-036.title: Australopithecus sediba lies buried in Malapa Cave
gela-036.text: Malapa Cave, South Africa, perhaps a natural death trap, holds two partial Australopithecus sediba skeletons, a juvenile and an adult female, about 1.98 million years old. Once proposed as an ancestor of Homo, A. sediba may instead be a late-surviving relative of A. africanus, a question still contested.

gela-037.title: Homo erectus invents the Acheulean hand axe
gela-037.text: Around 2 million years ago, toolmakers turned the Oldowan into something new: the Acheulean, a technology built around carefully shaped hand axes. Homo erectus is credited with the invention, and finds from Ethiopia date to 1.95 million years ago, with others from West Turkana, Kenya, at about 1.76 million. Between 1.5 million and about 800,000 years ago the technology spread from Africa to Asia, the Middle East and Europe, reaching southern India by 1.51 million years ago. Its end is blurry; counting the Sangoan tradition, it lasted until as late as 130,000 years ago.

gela-038.title: Dmanisi yields the oldest human bones outside Africa
gela-038.text: Hominins lived at Dmanisi, Georgia, from about 1.8 million years ago, leaving the oldest human skeletal remains known outside Africa. Its five skulls include Skull 5, the first complete adult hominin skull from the Early Pleistocene. They resemble early African Homo so closely that all early Homo may belong to one species. One toothless, elderly skull has been read as early evidence that the group cared for its old or disabled.

gela-039.title: The Olduvai magnetic flip ends and the Calabrian begins
gela-039.text: From about 1.95 to 1.77 million years ago, Earth's magnetic field flipped back to normal polarity in a short spell called the Olduvai subchron. It interrupted the long, reversed Matuyama chron that had begun with the Pleistocene. The Calabrian Age begins just above the top of the Olduvai layers and the extinction of the nannofossil Discoaster brouweri. Before 2009 this level, then dated to 1.806 million years ago, marked the start of the Pleistocene.

gela-040.title: The wolf event spreads Canis across Eurasia
gela-040.text: Around 1.8 million years ago, in what is called the wolf event, the dog genus Canis burst into new forms across Eurasia, including the large wolf C. falconeri. Coyote and wolf lineages split about 1.5 million years ago, and the first wolves appear about 810,000 years ago.

gela-041.title: Charred bones at Wonderwerk Cave hint at early fire
gela-041.text: Charred bones deep in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, beyond the reach of wildfires, have been offered as evidence of human fire use about 1.79 million years ago. The cited study itself, however, dates the burning there to about 1.0 million years ago.

gela-042.title: Diprotodon, the largest marsupial ever, appears
gela-042.text: Diprotodon was the largest marsupial that ever lived and the biggest plant-eater in Australia. Its earliest fossils, from the Nelson Bay Formation in New South Wales, are indirectly dated to between 1.77 million and 780,000 years ago.

gela-044.title: Homo erectus reaches China and Java
gela-044.text: Homo erectus had reached Yuanmou in southern China by 1.7 million years ago and Sangiran on Java by 1.66 million. A cranium from Lantian dates to 1.63 million years ago, and stone tools in northern China's Nihewan basin to 1.7–1.6 million. By 1.3 million years ago, Oldowan tools had reached as far north as the 40th parallel at Xiaochangliang. By 1 million years ago, the species had spread across Eurasia, mostly south of the 50th parallel.

gela-045.title: The last australopithecines die out
gela-045.text: The australopithecines, a group of early hominins that had arisen in East Africa around 4 million years ago, died out about 1.7 million years ago. South Africa may have been their last refuge until about 2 million years ago, as the climate grew more volatile and Homo and Paranthropus competed with them. Around 2.07 million years ago, just before Paranthropus robustus and Homo erectus arrived, Australopithecus africanus vanished from South Africa's Cradle of Humankind.

gela-046.title: Twin eruptions build New Mexico's Valles Caldera
gela-046.text: In New Mexico's Jemez Mountains, the Toledo eruption 1.61 million years ago produced 216–550 km³ of dense rock, a supereruption at the high estimate. A second great eruption about 1.25 million years ago formed the Valles Caldera, one of the best-studied resurgent calderas, whose floor later domed back up.

gela-047.title: Turkana Boy, the most complete Homo erectus
gela-047.text: Turkana Boy, a Homo erectus youth who lived near Lake Turkana, Kenya, 1.6–1.5 million years ago, is the most complete skeleton of his species ever found. Some assign him to Homo ergaster, and his spine could not have supported the strong breathing muscles needed for speech.

gela-048.title: The first Missoula floods scour the Scablands
gela-048.text: At least 1.5 million years ago, the oldest Pleistocene Missoula floods tore through the Channeled Scablands. Their age rests on calcretes, hard limy crusts formed between flood layers in warm interglacials, along with magnetic signatures and luminescence dating.

gela-049.title: Mammoths cross into North America
gela-049.text: The steppe mammoth arose in East Asia around 1.7 million years ago and crossed the Bering Land Bridge into North America 1.5–1.3 million years ago. There it gave rise to the Columbian mammoth, and its spread south of Alaska, about 1.4 million years ago, often marks a new land-mammal age, the Irvingtonian. DNA from a Siberian tooth, 1.1–1.65 million years old, reveals the Krestovka lineage, probably the first mammoths to colonize the Americas. Gomphotheres went the other way, into South America, in the Great American Interchange, the swap of animals between the two continents.

gela-050.title: Ubeidiya: Homo erectus reaches the Jordan Rift Valley
gela-050.text: Ubeidiya, just south of the Sea of Galilee, records one of the earliest migrations of Homo erectus out of Africa. Its layers hold Oldowan and early Acheulean tools, and a hominin vertebra that seems to belong to a different species than the Dmanisi hominins.

gela-054.title: Yellowstone's Mesa Falls eruption opens Henry's Fork Caldera
gela-054.text: Yellowstone's second eruptive cycle peaked about 1.3 million years ago in an eruption of more than 280 km³ that left the Mesa Falls Tuff. It formed Henry's Fork Caldera inside the older Island Park Caldera, and precise argon dating puts it at 1.3001 ± 0.0006 million years ago.

gela-056.title: Hominins cross the sea to Flores
gela-056.text: Ancestors of Homo floresiensis probably reached Flores between about 1.27 and 1 million years ago; the island's oldest stone tools are about 1 million years old. Getting there meant crossing open sea, and Homo erectus may have built rafts by about 840,000–800,000 years ago.

gela-057.title: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition stretches the ice-age rhythm
gela-057.text: Between about 1.25 and 0.7 million years ago, the ice-age rhythm stretched from about 41,000 years to lopsided cycles of about 100,000 years. Long cold spells built thick, high ice sheets that ended in rapid jumps to warm interglacials, so climate swings grew more extreme. Around 850,000 ± 50,000 years ago, eccentricity, the slow stretching of Earth's orbit, replaced axial tilt as the main pacemaker. Models reproduce the shift with falling carbon dioxide and glaciers scraping the loose rock and soil, or regolith, off the northern continents.

gela-058.title: Africa's Gregory Rift begins to pull apart
gela-058.text: The Gregory Rift, the eastern branch of the East African Rift, began spreading about 1.2 million years ago, and it still widens by about 3 mm a year. The faulting followed big eruptions of shield volcanoes, broad and gentle cones, along the edge of a craton, a continent's old and stable core.

gela-060.title: The robust Paranthropus lineage dies out
gela-060.text: The last of Paranthropus, the robust hominins that had shared Africa with early Homo, died out about 1.2 million years ago. The youngest Paranthropus boisei fossil, OH 80 from Olduvai Gorge, is about 1.34 million years old, though the species may have lasted to 1 million years ago. One chronology suggests that Australopithecus and Paranthropus made stone tools right up to their extinction, no later than 1.1 million years ago.

gela-061.title: Toba's first known caldera erupts on Sumatra
gela-061.text: Toba on Sumatra produced the earliest known of at least four caldera-forming eruptions there about 1.2 million years ago. The same volcano would later produce the Youngest Toba eruption.

gela-059.title: Homo antecessor, the 'pioneer', settles Spain
gela-059.text: Homo antecessor, 'pioneer man', is recorded at Spain's Sierra de Atapuerca from 1.2 to 0.8 million years ago, among the first people to settle Western Europe. Once proposed as the last common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans, it is now seen as a side branch that split off just before them.

gela-064.title: An asteroid punches the Bosumtwi crater into Ghana
gela-064.text: An asteroid blasted a 10.5 km crater into lush rainforest in Ghana about 1.07 million years ago, and Lake Bosumtwi, about 8 km across, now fills it. Tektites, glassy beads of melted rock, landed in neighboring Ivory Coast, and finer microtektites settled on the seafloor west of Africa.

gela-066.title: The Kidnappers supereruption lays Earth's widest ignimbrite
gela-066.text: New Zealand's Mangakino caldera unleashed the Kidnappers eruption, rated VEI 8, about 1 million years ago. It produced about 1,200 km³ of ignimbrite and 2,760 km³ of material in all. That ignimbrite covers more than 45,000 km², the most widespread on Earth. Eruptions about 1.25 and 1.0 million years ago spread ignimbrite sheets across the North Island from Auckland to Napier.

gela-067.title: Kilimanjaro's Kibo and Mawenzi cones begin to erupt
gela-067.text: Kibo and Mawenzi, two of Kilimanjaro's three cones, began erupting about 1 million years ago; Shira, the third, had been active since 2.4 million. Kibo, the largest, formed the summit crater in its last activity, and the dormant mountain, at 5,895 m, is Africa's highest peak.

gela-068.title: Central Europe's Pannonian Sea finally disappears
gela-068.text: The Pannonian Sea, a shallow, landlocked sea in Central Europe since about 10 million years ago, finally vanished about 1 million years ago. By then 3–4 km of sediment had filled its basin.

gela-069.title: The magnetic field briefly flips back in the Jaramillo
gela-069.text: During the Jaramillo subchron, Earth's magnetic field briefly flipped back to normal polarity; some studies start it earlier, at 1.07 million years ago. What causes such short flips is still disputed, and a proposed link to the Bosumtwi impact has been called highly speculative and refuted.

gela-070.title: Hominins leave the oldest footprints outside Africa in Norfolk
gela-070.text: Hominins, perhaps Homo antecessor, pressed footprints into sediment at Happisburgh, Norfolk, the first evidence of early humans this far north. Flint tools lie in the same deposits, whose beds fall between the Jaramillo and Brunhes–Matuyama magnetic reversals.

gela-072.title: Palaeoloxodon elephants march out of Africa
gela-072.text: The elephant genus Palaeoloxodon spread out of Africa and across Eurasia about 800,000 years ago, at the end of the Early Pleistocene. Among them were the first straight-tusked elephants, Palaeoloxodon antiquus.

gela-073.title: An unseen impact scatters glass across Australasia
gela-073.text: About 790,000 years ago, a large impact scattered tektites across the enormous Australasian strewnfield, the zone where they fell. Its crater has not been found, though one about 100 km wide in Indochina, perhaps beneath Tonlé Sap in Cambodia, has been suggested. Artifacts found with the tektites tie a population of Homo erectus to the impact and its aftermath. A link to the Brunhes–Matuyama magnetic reversal is highly speculative, and the two probably just happened around the same time.

gela-074.title: Fire and cooked fish at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov
gela-074.text: Around 780,000 years ago, hominins at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in northern Israel kept fires and left the oldest likely evidence of cooking, mostly heated fish teeth. It is the oldest established site of continuous fire use outside Africa, and its people ate 55 kinds of fruits, vegetables, seeds, nuts and tubers.

chib-001.title: Earth's magnetic field flips for the last time
