chib-001.text: About 774,000 years ago, Earth's magnetic field last reversed, ending the Matuyama chron and opening the Brunhes chron that continues today. Estimates of how long the flip took range from within a single human lifetime to several thousand years, or even about 22,000 years. Part of the spread is local: at any one site, the apparent duration can vary tenfold with latitude and quirks of the field. Ratified in 2020 as the base of the Chibanian at Japan's Chiba section, the reversal is also a standard tie-point for dating ocean cores and volcanic rocks.

chib-003.title: Old mammals vanish and newcomers sweep into Eurasia
chib-003.text: When Sinomastodon died out in East Asia, the gomphotheres vanished from Africa and Eurasia, though they survived in the Americas into the Late Pleistocene. Around the same transition, many of Europe's meat-eating mammals died out, including the giant hyena Pachycrocuta. Newcomers arrived too: true horses migrated out of North America into Eurasia, and the Asian steppe mammoth replaced Mammuthus meridionalis in Europe. The elephant genus Palaeoloxodon also spread from Africa into Eurasia, bringing the first straight-tusked elephants.

chib-002.title: The last clawed chalicotheres disappear
chib-002.text: The chalicotheres, clawed relatives of horses and rhinos among the odd-toed hoofed mammals, survived from the Eocene into the Middle Pleistocene before vanishing. One account instead lists them among groups that died out in the Pliocene.

chib-004.title: The Bishop Tuff eruption opens Long Valley Caldera
chib-004.text: In eastern California, a VEI 7 eruption about 760,000 years ago released some 600 km³ of material, which cooled into the Bishop Tuff. As the magma chamber drained, the ground collapsed into Long Valley Caldera, about 32 by 18 km and one of Earth's largest calderas. Pyroclastic flows, racing avalanches of hot gas and ash, burned and buried thousands of square miles, and ash blanketed much of the western United States.

chib-005.title: Lava flows dam the Colorado in the Grand Canyon
chib-005.text: Between 725,000 and 100,000 years ago, more than 150 basalt lava flows dammed the Colorado River at least 13 times. The dams rose in weeks, up to 610 m high and 138 km long, though how long they held back lakes is still debated.

chib-007.title: The 100,000-year ice-age rhythm takes hold
chib-007.text: By about 0.7 million years ago, the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, under way since about 1.25 million years ago, was complete. Ice ages now came in lopsided, high-amplitude cycles averaging 100,000 years instead of 41,000, and climate swings grew more extreme. Interglacials after the transition held more carbon dioxide in the air than those before it. Since about 600,000 years ago, six major glacial periods have lowered sea level by up to 120 m, laying bare the edges of the continents.

chib-008.title: Acheulean hand axes arrive in Europe
chib-008.text: Typical Acheulean hand axes, stones worked on both faces, appeared suddenly in Europe about 700,000 years ago, perhaps under influence from Africa rather than by purely local invention. An older view put their arrival near 500,000 years ago, while hand axes from Spain may be more than 900,000 years old.

chib-009.title: Mata Menge yields tiny ancestors of the Flores 'hobbit'
chib-009.text: Teeth and a partial jaw from Mata Menge on Flores belong to hominins thought to be ancestors of Homo floresiensis. They were as small as the later Liang Bua fossils, or smaller, so the species stayed small for hundreds of thousands of years.

chib-010.title: A 'ghost' human lineage branches off
chib-010.text: Around 700,000 years ago, an archaic hominin population broke away from the lineage leading to modern humans, a 'ghost' known mainly from its genetic traces. Its DNA later entered some sub-Saharan hunter-gatherer groups, such as the Biaka and San, about 35,000 years ago.

chib-011.title: Ice kills the Eridanos, Europe's lost giant river
chib-011.text: At its height about 2 million years ago, the Eridanos ran some 2,700 km from Lapland across the Baltic region to a vast delta in western Europe. During the first glacial of the Cromerian Complex, a long, relatively warm stretch of time, Scandinavian ice caps wrecked its source area and the river died.

chib-012.title: MIS 16 locks up a record volume of ice
chib-012.text: Marine Isotope Stage 16 was one of the two most extreme glaciations of the Quaternary, matching MIS 12 in global ice volume. The oceans, though, were only about as cold as in the neighboring glacials MIS 14 and MIS 18. On the East European Plain, the Don ice sheet reached its greatest extent, pushing into the middle and lower Don basin at about 50° N.

chib-013.title: Neanderthal and Denisovan lineages part ways
chib-013.text: Genetic distances suggest that Denisovans and Neanderthals split from each other about 640,000 years ago, though another estimate says 744,000. Their nuclear DNA shows they were closer to each other than either was to modern humans.

chib-014.title: The Lava Creek supereruption carves today's Yellowstone Caldera
chib-014.text: About 631,000 years ago, Yellowstone's third cycle climaxed in the eruption that laid down the Lava Creek Tuff and created today's Yellowstone Caldera. Rated VEI 8, it hurled out more than 1,000 km³ of rock, dust and volcanic ash. Its ash bed spread over 3–4 million km², and debris up to two meters deep covered a large part of North America. It capped several hundred thousand years of eruptions of rhyolite, a thick, silica-rich magma, and blasts this large strike somewhere on Earth about every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

chib-015.title: The Rockland eruption blasts out of the Lassen area
chib-015.text: About 610,000 years ago, California's Lassen area erupted over 130 km³ of rhyolite magma in huge pyroclastic flows and an ash plume tens of kilometers high. Recent studies put the Rockland ash at up to 326.7 km³, over twice the Mazama ash.

chib-016.title: The Great Barrier Reef builds its first complete reefs
chib-016.text: The earliest evidence of complete reef structures on the Great Barrier Reef dates to about 600,000 years ago. Coral skeleton deposits there go back about half a million years.

chib-017.title: Homo heidelbergensis, a disputed ancestor, appears in Africa
chib-017.text: About 600,000 years ago, a new kind of human evolved from Homo erectus in Africa, and many scientists call it Homo heidelbergensis. Its fossils from the warm MIS 15 interglacial, between 621 and 563 thousand years ago, include Heidelberg Man and the Bodo cranium. It was the likely ancestor of Neanderthals and Denisovans, perhaps of modern humans too, and some scholars credit it with the first symbolic communication. Yet the species itself is controversial and poorly defined, and scientists still argue over the tangle of Middle Pleistocene humans nicknamed the 'muddle in the middle'.

chib-019.title: Today's Cascade volcanoes begin to grow
chib-019.text: An older generation of Cascade volcanoes died about half a million years ago, and many of today's stratovolcanoes, tall cones of layered lava and ash, began to grow. Glacier Peak, Mount Shasta and Newberry started about 600,000 years ago, followed by Rainier and Hood at 500,000, Adams at 450,000 and Mazama at 420,000.

chib-020.title: The woolly mammoth evolves in Siberia
chib-020.text: By around 600,000–500,000 years ago, the woolly mammoth had evolved in Siberia from the steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii. Its lineage began to diverge about 800,000 years ago, yet Siberian mammoths over a million years old already carried many of its genes for tolerating cold. Its trademark molars, with 26 ridges, appeared about 400,000 years ago. Woolly mammoth numbers crashed around 280,000 years ago, then recovered.

chib-021.title: A meteorite blasts the Lonar crater into Indian basalt
chib-021.text: A meteorite blasted a crater 1.8 km wide and 150 m deep into Maharashtra's Deccan basalt; it holds India's only crater lake of meteoritic origin. Argon–argon dating gives 570 ± 47 thousand years, far older than an earlier 52 ± 6 thousand, a disputed age, since inherited argon may inflate it.

chib-022.title: Tautavel Man shelters in France's Arago Cave
chib-022.text: Archaic humans lived in the Caune de l'Arago, a limestone cave at Tautavel in France, from about 550,000 to 400,000 years ago. Almost all their remains come from a single layer dated to 455,000 years ago, and outside, the land swung repeatedly between temperate forest and cold, dry steppe.

chib-023.title: An engraved shell on Java may be the oldest art
chib-023.text: A Pseudodon shell from Trinil on Java, engraved with geometric markings between 546,000 and 436,000 years ago, could be the earliest known art-making. The Homo erectus population at Trinil also turned such shells into scrapers, possibly prying them open with shark teeth.

chib-024.title: A warm MIS 13 interglacial puts Boxgrove on the coast
chib-024.text: MIS 13 was an interglacial covering the late Cromerian in Britain, about 524,000–474,000 years ago, and it opened with birch, pine and spruce. Boxgrove then lay on the coast below chalk cliffs, where mudflats gave way to woodland and grassland.

chib-025.title: The first brown bears appear
chib-025.text: The first brown bears appeared around 0.5 million years ago.

chib-026.title: Early humans push north into Europe and Britain
chib-026.text: Around 500,000 years ago, early humans often called Homo heidelbergensis came to Europe from Africa, and in time they evolved into the Neanderthals. Some populations had already dispersed into Europe by 700,000 years ago, carrying Late Acheulean tools, and more permanent groups settled north of 45°N. They pushed beyond the 50th parallel to Boxgrove in Sussex, about 500,000 years old and Britain's earliest site with fossils of Homo. From then on settlements grew more permanent, and occupation became much more frequent.

chib-027.title: Lake Victoria takes shape and starts feeding the Nile
chib-027.text: Around 0.5 million years ago, Lake Victoria took roughly its modern shape, and the lakes plateau tilted north. Water began draining on and off toward Egypt, roughly along the modern White Nile, and paleolakes formed where the Sudd swamps lie today.

chib-031.title: The Anglian ice sheet buries Britain and the North Sea
chib-031.text: The Elster glaciation, called the Anglian in Britain, was the first ice age to cover North Germany and much of Europe on a large scale. Globally it was MIS 12, which ranks with MIS 16 among the two largest ice volumes of the Quaternary. An ice sheet filled much of the North Sea, and to its south the Rhine, Scheldt and Thames fed a large lake dammed against the ice. Great Britain was widely glaciated, and the cold ended the long, relatively warm Cromerian Complex.

chib-032.title: The mammoth steppe spreads across the north
chib-032.text: During the MIS 12 glacial, the steppe-tundra first emerged, a new biome, or large-scale community of life. It united animals of the northern tundra with those of the Central Asian steppe. From then on it repeatedly expanded and contracted with each later glacial cycle.

chib-033.title: A megaflood breaches the Dover Strait chalk ridge
chib-033.text: During the Anglian glaciation, an ice dam to the north backed river water into a vast lake in the southern North Sea. A chalk ridge from the Weald to Artois held the lake in, until it broke through in the first of two megafloods to cut the ridge. Sonar still shows deeply gouged channels and streamlined islands on the seabed, and the flood diverted the Rhine into the English Channel. It also broke the land bridge between Britain and France, though links returned whenever the sea fell low.

chib-034.title: Early Neanderthals leave the oldest human DNA in Spain
chib-034.text: The hominins of Sima de los Huesos in Atapuerca, Spain, dated to about 430,000 years ago, were early members of the Neanderthal line. Their bones have yielded the oldest known human DNA. Their anatomy suggests that many Neanderthal traits had evolved by the middle of the Middle Pleistocene. They probably lived through one of the coldest glacial phases of the last million years, which dried out Iberia.

chib-036.title: A super-interglacial melts much of southern Greenland
chib-036.text: MIS 11 was the longest and warmest interglacial of the last 500,000 years, perhaps lasting twice as long as others. It opened with the strongest warming out of an ice age in 5 million years, and high-latitude seas ran warm as coral reefs expanded. Sea level rose above today's: southern Greenland lost nearly all its ice around 410,000–400,000 years ago, releasing enough water to raise the sea 4.5–6 m. Britain calls this interglacial the Hoxnian, Central Europe the Holsteinian and North America the Yarmouthian, and Swanscombe Man lived during it.

chib-037.title: Homo heidelbergensis develops the Clactonian toolkit
chib-037.text: From about 0.4 million years ago, humans often called Homo heidelbergensis developed a tool industry of their own, the Clactonian.

chib-038.title: The first modern gray wolves appear
chib-038.text: The earliest modern gray wolves date to around 400,000 years ago, though the species may reach back as far as 1 million years. Between 400,000 and 300,000 years ago, dholes, the wild dogs of Asia, matched wolves in size, but wolves were slowly growing larger.

chib-039.title: The first polar bears appear
chib-039.text: The first polar bears appeared about 400,000 years ago.

chib-040.title: Humans master fire, striking sparks from pyrite
chib-040.text: About 400,000 years ago, reliable evidence of regular fire use appears in the archaeological record; before that, fire use was sparse. The oldest definitive fire-making, at a Neanderthal site in eastern England, left burnt soil, fire-cracked hand axes and pyrite for striking sparks. The change may mark the true taming of fire and fire-starting technology, or simply better ways of keeping a fire alight. Fire became widespread in the Middle Paleolithic, the middle stage of the Old Stone Age, and by about 250,000 years ago humans were cooking their food.

chib-041.title: The Saale glaciations grip northern Europe
chib-041.text: The Saale complex, the middle of northern Europe's three great Scandinavian ice-sheet glaciations, spanned about 400,000 to 130,000 years ago. It held several glacial cycles separated by warmer periods, opening with the Fuhne cold phase and the Dömnitz interglacial. Britain's equivalent, the Wolstonian, lasted about 374,000–130,000 years ago, and in the Alps the Riss glaciation parallels MIS 10, 8 and 6. Its last part coincides with the Penultimate Glacial Period, the ice age before the most recent one.

chib-043.title: The Neanderthals take shape
chib-043.text: Neanderthals had evolved by about 350,000 years ago, and Middle Pleistocene Europeans such as those at Sima de los Huesos are seen as their ancestors. Their characteristic teeth had appeared by about 300,000 years ago, and from then on they lived across Europe and the Near East. Some Neanderthal traits arose only near the start of the Late Pleistocene, possibly when the species fully split off.

chib-045.title: The Whakamaru supereruption opens a New Zealand flare-up
chib-045.text: About 340,000 years ago, a VEI 8 eruption sequence lasting under a thousand years blasted 1,200–2,000 km³ of tephra, or volcanic debris, across New Zealand's North Island. It left the Whakamaru Caldera, about 30 by 40 km, just north of today's Lake Taupō. The sequence opened a burst of under 100,000 years in which the Taupō Volcanic Zone erupted more than 4,000 km³ in all. This was part of an ignimbrite flare-up that ran from about 350,000 to 240,000 years ago.

chib-046.title: The MIS 9 interglacial closes the Lower Paleolithic
chib-046.text: MIS 9, the Purfleet Interglacial in Britain, closed the Lower Paleolithic, the earliest stage of the Old Stone Age. Its carbon dioxide was probably higher than in MIS 11, and East Antarctica's Wilkes Basin lost enough ice to raise sea level by about 0.9 m.

chib-047.title: Schöningen's wooden spears reveal hunters who plan ahead
chib-047.text: Ten spruce and pine spears, found with butchered horse bones at Schöningen, Germany, are the oldest complete wooden weapons known and show forward planning. Their makers were Homo heidelbergensis or early Neanderthals, and their age is disputed: estimates run from about 400,000 to about 200,000 years.

chib-048.title: Small-brained Homo naledi lives in the Rising Star Cave
chib-048.text: Homo naledi, a small-brained archaic human, lived in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system between 335,000 and 236,000 years ago. Its brain was so small that experts first assumed the fossils were 1–2 million years old; its line had branched from other Homo by 900,000 years ago. The Dinaledi Chamber holds over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, the largest find of a single hominin species in Africa. Some researchers argue that it deliberately placed its dead in that remote chamber, a claim still debated.

chib-049.title: Olorgesailie toolmakers haul obsidian and use pigments
chib-049.text: By about 320,000 years ago, people at Olorgesailie, Kenya, moved obsidian, a volcanic glass, over long distances, used pigments and possibly made projectile points. The timing roughly matches the earliest Homo sapiens fossils, hinting that complex behavior arrived with the species itself.

chib-050.title: The Levallois prepared-core technique takes hold
chib-050.text: Middle Paleolithic toolmakers developed the Levallois, or prepared-core, technique, shaping a stone in advance so one blow could strike off a ready-made flake. In Europe the Mousterian tradition, built on this method, appeared around 320,000 years ago and displaced the Acheulean there by about 125,000 years ago.

chib-051.title: Jebel Irhoud yields the oldest known Homo sapiens
chib-051.text: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, once thought to be Neanderthal, are now assigned to Homo sapiens, with a weighted average age of 315,000 years. Burnt flint tools found with them were dated to about 315,000 years ago by thermoluminescence, which measures how long ago the flint was last heated. They are by far the oldest known members of the species, showing that modern humans lived across Africa 100,000 years earlier than once thought. Early Homo sapiens may have spread across Africa with several regions contributing, and the Florisbad skull, about 259,000 years old, also belongs to the species.

chib-052.title: The Middle Stone Age begins in Africa
chib-052.text: Around 300,000 years ago, Africa's Middle Stone Age began, linked to anatomically modern or nearly modern Homo sapiens. Its European counterpart, the Middle Paleolithic, broadly spans 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, so the Chibanian straddles the shift from the Lower to the Middle Paleolithic. Hafting, fixing stone points to handles or shafts, becomes much more common in both Europe and Africa after 300,000 years ago. By about 164,000 years ago, Middle Stone Age people at Pinnacle Point, South Africa, cooked shellfish and heated silcrete stone in fire to make better tools.

chib-053.title: Gigantopithecus, the giant ape, dies out
chib-053.text: Gigantopithecus, a giant Asian relative of the orangutan, died out about 300,000 years ago; its youngest remains, from two caves in China, are 295,000–215,000 years old. After about 400,000 years ago it survived only in Guangxi, and shrinking subtropical forest, perhaps along with archaic humans, likely drove it extinct.

chib-054.title: Denisovans leave their DNA in a Siberian cave
chib-054.text: Toolmakers left early Middle Paleolithic cores and scrapers in Denisova Cave, Siberia, about 287,000 years ago. Denisovan DNA from the cave's sediments goes back to 217,000 years ago, and these archaic humans ranged across Asia from about 200,000 to 32,000 years ago. Child hand- and footprints at Quesang in Tibet, dated 226,000–169,000 years ago, may be Denisovan and are the plateau's oldest human traces. A 200,000-year-old Denisovan molar carries about 5% of its genome from a previously unknown Neanderthal population.

chib-055.title: An early wave of Homo sapiens may leave Africa
chib-055.text: Early Homo sapiens, or a close relative, may have first left Africa as early as 270,000 years ago, the first of several waves. The idea rests on Neanderthal mitochondrial DNA, passed down only through mothers, being closer to that of Homo sapiens than to that of Denisovans.

chib-056.title: MIS 7, a cool interglacial in three warm pulses
chib-056.text: MIS 7 brought three phases of very low ice volume and high temperatures, peaking in MIS 7e about 237,000–228,000 years ago. Even so, it was the coldest interglacial since the Mid-Brunhes Event, with MIS 7e about 1.4 °C below the pre-industrial global temperature.

chib-057.title: The Mamaku eruption collapses the Rotorua Caldera
chib-057.text: About 240,000 years ago a VEI 7 eruption blasted out over 340 km³ of Mamaku ignimbrite, and the collapsing Rotorua Caldera formed Lake Rotorua's basin. Within days or weeks, a second eruption from the same magma body burst out at Ohakuri, about 30 km south.

chib-058.title: A South Dakota sinkhole traps dozens of mammoths
chib-058.text: Near Hot Springs, South Dakota, a limestone cavern collapsed about 232,000–160,000 years ago into a steep sinkhole at least 20 m deep, filled by a warm, spring-fed pond. Its sediments trapped and buried Pleistocene animals, among them 58 Columbian mammoths and 3 woolly mammoths.

chib-059.title: Mesotherium, the last typothere, disappears
chib-059.text: Mesotherium, the last of the mesotheriids and of the wider group Typotheria, has its final records around 220,000 years ago. Afterwards the Toxodontidae were the only family of notoungulates, South America's native hoofed mammals, to survive into the Late Pleistocene.

chib-060.title: Mitochondrial Eve: the oldest maternal line of Homo sapiens
chib-060.text: Mitochondrial DNA traces the earliest maternal lineage of Homo sapiens to about 200,000 years ago, though another estimate says 99,000–148,000 years. One study places this 'Mitochondrial Eve' in the Makgadikgadi lake region of southern Africa, but that homeland claim remains controversial.

chib-061.title: Woolly mammoths take over from steppe mammoths
chib-061.text: In the mid-to-late Middle Pleistocene, the woolly mammoth replaced its forerunner, the steppe mammoth Mammuthus trogontherii. By around 200,000 years ago, the takeover was complete in Europe. In North America, woolly mammoths spread south of Alaska with bison and other northern specialists during the Rancholabrean, the land-mammal age marked by bison. Neanderthals lived alongside mammoths and used their bones for tools and building, as at La Cotte de St Brelade about 200,000 years ago.

chib-062.title: Early modern humans at Omo and Herto in Ethiopia
chib-062.text: Ethiopia's Omo Kibish remains, about 195,000 years old, were long seen as the oldest Homo sapiens fossils, backing an East African origin around 200,000 years ago. Herto Man, also from Ethiopia and about 160,000 years old, adds more early evidence from the Middle Stone Age.

chib-063.title: Steppe bison cross the Bering land bridge
chib-063.text: Steppe bison, the ancestors of the American bison, crossed the Bering land bridge into North America around 195,000–135,000 years ago. Their arrival opens the Rancholabrean faunal stage, which is defined by the presence of bison. Bison first appeared in northwestern North America during the Illinoian glacial stage, then spread across the continent in the following Sangamonian. They moved south of Alaska alongside caribou, muskoxen, moose and woolly mammoths.

chib-064.title: MIS 6: the Penultimate Glacial Period freezes Eurasia
chib-064.text: The Penultimate Glacial Period, the coldest and last part of the Saale complex, ran from about 194,000 to about 135,000 years ago. At its peak, around 140,000 years ago, Eurasia saw its most extensive glaciation in 400,000 years, and a thick ice sheet over northern Europe slashed the vegetation. High latitudes were colder, and the tropics warmer, than at the Last Glacial Maximum, the peak of the most recent ice age. In North America it matches the Illinoian Stage, while the Bull Lake glaciation of the Rocky Mountains, about 200,000–130,000 years ago, ran at the same time.

chib-065.title: A Misliya jaw hints at Homo sapiens in the Levant
chib-065.text: A jawbone with eight teeth from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, possibly from Homo sapiens, was dated in 2018 to 177,000 years ago. If so, modern humans may have moved in and out of the Levant several times, perhaps even before 200,000 years ago.

chib-066.title: Karymsky volcano blankets a vast region in ash
chib-066.text: Kamchatka's Karymsky volcano has been linked to an eruption of VEI 6 or larger, about 177,000 years ago, that spread ash over more than 1.5 million km².

chib-067.title: A second megaflood makes Britain an island
chib-067.text: During the Saalian or Wolstonian glaciation, a second megaflood broke through the Weald–Artois chalk ridge. A lake held back in the Doggerland region, the now-drowned land under the southern North Sea, burst through and cut the Strait of Dover. Cohen and Hijma date the ridge's final destruction to the Saalian peak around 160,000 years ago, though other studies suggest dates as early as 350,000 years ago. From then on, Britain became an island whenever sea level was high.

chib-068.title: Megadroughts grip tropical Africa and scatter its people
chib-068.text: From 135,000 years ago, megadroughts struck tropical Africa, pushing humans toward the coasts and onto other continents. By the MIS 5 megadrought, 130,000 years ago, Africa held two ancestral human population clusters, one of them carrying the maternal lineage L0 in the south.

chib-069.title: Termination II: meltwater ends the Penultimate Glacial
chib-069.text: About 133,000 years ago, meltwater pulse 2B, a flood of water from melting ice, substantially weakened the Indian Summer Monsoon. This deglaciation, Termination II, sent Dnieper and Volga meltwater into the Black and Caspian Seas and included a cold reversal like the later Younger Dryas.

chib-070.title: The Aso-3 eruption helps carve Japan's Aso caldera
chib-070.text: Japan's Aso-3 eruption, about 130,000 years ago, produced some 96 km³ of magma, measured as dense rock. It was one of four great eruptions of hot ash flows that formed the Aso caldera between 270,000 and 90,000 years ago.

chib-071.title: Burials at Krapina hint at care for the dead
chib-071.text: Burials at Krapina, Croatia, date to about 130,000 years ago. Some anthropologists see in such burials a growing belief in an afterlife and a concern for the dead.

late-001.title: A green Sahara opens roads out of Africa
late-001.text: The Eemian brought an exceptionally intense humid period to northern Africa, greening it more strongly than the Holocene's own wet phase would. Such humid spells come with interglacials, the warm intervals between ice ages, and with precession minima, set by the slow wobble of Earth's axis; glacial stages bring drought. The green corridors opened pathways across Arabia and northern Africa, and modern humans dispersed along them at least 130,000 to 115,000 years ago. Before 140,000 and after 115,000 years ago, the Red Sea coastal route was extremely arid.

late-002.title: The Last Interglacial: forests at Norway's North Cape
late-002.text: The Last Interglacial, or Eemian, followed the Penultimate Glacial Period, and its start is the proposed beginning of the Late Pleistocene. It was one of the warmest spells of the last 800,000 years: up to about 2 °C warmer than the Holocene, with CO2 near 280 ppm. Around 125,000 years ago forests grew at North Cape, Norway, where tundra lies today, and Arctic summers ran about 2–4 °C warmer than in 2011. Shifts in the North Atlantic Current brought abrupt cold spells around 120,000 years ago, and by about 115,000 years ago the warmth was over.

late-003.title: Hippos wallow in northern England
late-003.text: Interglacial warmth let hippos range north to Stockton-on-Tees in England, sharing temperate landscapes with straight-tusked elephants, Merck's rhinos, aurochs, cave lions and cave hyenas. Warmer seas let tropical 'Senegalese' marine snails, such as cone shells, colonize the Mediterranean.

late-004.title: West Antarctica collapses and seas rise 6–9 meters
late-004.text: At the Eemian peak, sea level stood probably 6–9 m above today's, fed by Greenland, Antarctica and thermal expansion, the swelling of seawater as it warms. The West Antarctic Ice Sheet appears to have collapsed around 125,000 years ago, under temperatures like the early 21st century's. Seas may have risen as fast as 2.5 m per century, turning Fennoscandia and Jutland into islands and flooding much of northwestern Europe and the West Siberian Plain. Fossil reefs from this highstand, the sea's high-water mark, now sit stranded above the waves in the Caribbean and along the Red Sea.

late-005.title: Klasies River: shellfish and game on South Africa's coast
late-005.text: People began living in the Klasies River Caves on South Africa's coast about 125,000 years ago, during the Middle Stone Age, eating both sea life and grassland animals. Their remains include jaws about 119,000 years old and finger bones 90,000–100,000 years old.

late-006.title: Modern humans reach Arabia by two possible roads
late-006.text: Stone tools at Jebel Faya in the United Arab Emirates show that modern humans were in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago. They may have left Africa by two routes: through the Nile, Sinai and Levant, or across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait when seas were low. On a raised reef of the same age at Abdur, Eritrea, tools suggest coastal foragers were eating shellfish over 100,000 years ago. These early ventures do not seem to have founded lasting settlements, and they had faded by about 80,000 years ago.

late-007.title: Lake Ouki floods the Bolivian Altiplano
late-007.text: From about 120,000 to 98,000 years ago, the Ouki lake filled the Bolivian Altiplano, a high Andean plateau, long before the better-known Lake Tauca. Between 115,000 and 100,000 years ago its surface stood above 3,720 m, while Lake Ballivián occupied the Titicaca basin.

late-008.title: Skhul and Qafzeh: early modern humans in the Levant
late-008.text: Early Homo sapiens fossils from Israel's Qafzeh and Es-Skhul caves, about 120,000–80,000 years old, record a dispersal out of Africa into a Levant shared with Neanderthals. No later modern human fossils turn up there until Manot 1, about 54,700 years ago.

late-009.title: Giant long-horned bison arise in North America
late-009.text: Steppe bison spread from Alaska into central North America as Laurentide ice melted, and there evolved into Bison latifrons, the giant long-horned bison. First known from Colorado's Snowmass site, it gave rise by 60,000 years ago to Bison antiquus, widely considered the ancestor of the modern American bison.

late-010.title: Neanderthals hunt straight-tusked elephants at Neumark-Nord
late-010.text: At Neumark-Nord in Germany, Neanderthals left the butchered remains of at least 57 straight-tusked elephants, hunting them regularly, perhaps every 5 to 6 years. Similar butchery at Lehringen, Taubach and Gröbern shows such hunts were widespread, and the hunters may have rendered fat from the bones.

late-011.title: Denny, daughter of a Neanderthal and a Denisovan
late-011.text: A bone fragment from Denisova Cave in Russia, 118,100–79,300 years old, belonged to a 13-year-old girl with a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. The two archaic human groups mixed deeply: about 17% of the Denisova Cave Denisovan genome came from interbreeding with Altai Neanderthals.

late-012.title: Solo Man, the last Homo erectus, fades in Java
late-012.text: Solo Man, the youngest known Homo erectus population, lived beside Java's Solo River about 117,000–108,000 years ago. By then a much wetter climate had made Java an island and spread tropical rainforest, and the species probably died out as forest replaced the savannas it needed. It vanished long before modern humans arrived, roughly 55,000–50,000 years ago, and left no living descendants. Older studies dated the skulls much younger, to between roughly 70 and 40 thousand years ago.

late-014.title: Cold returns: the Last Glacial Period begins
late-014.text: About 115,000 years ago the Last Interglacial ended and the Last Glacial Period began, a cold age that lasted until 11,700 years ago. Average temperatures dropped markedly, pushing warmth-loving woodland species out of northern Europe, and kept falling gradually toward the Last Glacial Maximum. It is the Würm in the Alps, the Devensian in Britain and the Weichselian in northern Europe, broadly matched by North America's Wisconsin. Lower seas exposed much of Sundaland, the shelf joining Borneo, Java and Sumatra to Asia, and left most of the Persian Gulf dry.

late-013.title: Dansgaard–Oeschger jolts: Greenland warms 8 °C in decades
late-013.text: Twenty-five times during the Last Glacial Period, climate lurched in Dansgaard–Oeschger events, best recorded in Greenland ice cores that reach back about 115,000 years. In the sharpest cases Greenland warmed about 8 °C within 40 years, though 5 °C over 30–40 years was more typical. They struck when ice volume and CO2 sat at middle levels, letting the Atlantic overturning circulation, the ocean's heat conveyor, flip between two stable states. Each nudged CO2 up about 5 ppm and weakened the Indonesian–Australian monsoon; a proposed 1,470-year rhythm is still debated.

late-016.title: The Acheulean hand axe finally disappears
late-016.text: Acheulean hand axes vanish from the archaeological record around 100,000 years ago, replaced by more complex Middle Paleolithic tool kits such as the Mousterian and Aterian. The Mousterian displaced them in Europe and the Middle East by around 125,000 years ago; East Asia may have kept them until about 50,000 years ago.

late-017.title: Ata caldera buries southern Japan in tephra
late-017.text: About 100,000 years ago Ata caldera, a volcanic collapse crater, erupted and spread tephra, the ash and rock fragments a volcano blasts out, across southern Japan. Rated 7.5 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI), it produced over 300 km³ of tephra; most estimates date it to 100,000–109,000 years ago.

late-018.title: Blombos Cave: engraved ochre and shell beads
late-018.text: At Blombos Cave on South Africa's southern Cape coast, people of 100,000–70,000 years ago left engraved ochre, shell beads and refined bone tools. Their ochre cross-hatching is thought to be the earliest known drawing, and wind-blown sand sealed the cave about 70,000–68,000 years ago.

late-019.title: Woolly mammoths cross into North America
late-019.text: Woolly mammoths crossed the Bering Strait into North America about 100,000 years ago. Where they met Columbian mammoths they interbred: two molars from British Columbia carry 21.6% and 34.6% Columbian ancestry.

late-020.title: Los Chocoyos: Central America's greatest eruption
late-020.text: Guatemala's Atitlán caldera produced Central America's largest known eruption, about 1,220 km³ of rhyolitic ash from silica-rich magma, equal to 730 km³ of solid rock. Pyroclastic currents, racing avalanches of hot gas and ash, left deposits 6–10 m thick in Chiapas, over 130 km away, and Lake Atitlán now fills the caldera. Its date is uncertain, somewhere between 98,000 and 75,000 years ago; one recent estimate of about 79,500 years ago puts it close to Toba. Whether it disrupted the climate is disputed.

late-021.title: The last terror bird dies in South America
late-021.text: Psilopterus, a relatively small terror bird, appears to have survived in South America until about 96,000 years ago, the last of its family.

late-022.title: Kikai caldera spreads ash from Kyushu to the Pacific
late-022.text: Lake Suigetsu sediments date a VEI 7 eruption of Japan's Kikai caldera to 94,500 ± 4,800 years ago. Its rhyolitic ash layer, the K-Tz tephra, reaches from southern Kyushu to eastern Honshu and the Pacific, and possibly to the Shandong Peninsula.

late-023.title: Aso-4: Kyushu's caldera erupts on a colossal scale
late-023.text: Aso caldera on Kyushu erupted about 90,000 years ago, releasing 384 km³ of magma, measured as solid rock, for a rating of at least VEI 7. Another account rates it VEI 8, with about a trillion cubic meters of ash.

late-025.title: Bone harpoons at Katanda bring fish into the diet
late-025.text: About 90,000 years ago, Middle Stone Age people at Katanda, in Central Africa's Semliki River valley, made harpoons from bone. Harpoons, first invented about this time, brought fish into human diets as a hedge against starvation.

late-026.title: Ice dams Siberia's great rivers into a vast lake
late-026.text: When the Barents-Kara Ice Sheet blocked the Arctic outlets of the Ob and Yenisei rivers, their water ponded into a vast lake in western Siberia. Between 90,000 and 80,000 years ago it covered about 610,000 km² and held 15,000 km³; a second phase, 60,000–50,000 years ago, reached 881,000 km² and 32,000 km³.

late-024.title: The Barents–Kara Ice Sheet walls off Arctic Russia
late-024.text: During the Weichselian glaciation, the Barents–Kara Ice Sheet covered the Barents and Kara seas and Novaya Zemlya, probably reaching Svalbard and Franz Josef Land. On land it stretched from the North Russian Plain to the North Siberian Lowland. Its ice dammed the north-flowing Yenisei, Ob, Pechora and Mezen rivers, ponding them into lakes and rerouting them.

late-027.title: Taforalt's people string sea shells into necklaces
late-027.text: At Taforalt, the Grotte des Pigeons in Morocco, people strung perforated sea shells into necklaces, early North African evidence of fully modern behavior. The cave lies 40 km inland, so the shells probably traveled through an exchange network, and their use as ornaments suggests they carried meaning.

late-028.title: Modern humans in China, perhaps by 80,000 years ago
late-028.text: Modern human teeth from China are claimed to be at least 80,000 years old, and Zhirendong cave finds may belong to the same early wave. Those finds may be over 100,000 years old; Liujiang man, among East Asia's earliest modern humans, is most often dated to at least 67,000 years ago.

late-029.title: West Antarctic ice spreads to the shelf edge
late-029.text: In the Eemian the West Antarctic Ice Sheet had shrunk to minor, isolated ice caps, but by about 80,000 years ago it was roughly its present size. It then grew much larger, spreading to the edges of Antarctica's continental shelves during the Last Glacial Maximum.

late-030.title: Heinrich events: iceberg armadas cross the North Atlantic
late-030.text: In Heinrich events, great fleets of icebergs broke from the Laurentide ice sheet and drifted through Hudson Strait into the North Atlantic, especially during the Wisconsin glaciation. As they melted, the bergs dropped rock debris, now found as Heinrich layers, and poured in fresh water that likely altered ocean circulation. Discharges between 21,000 and 11,500 years ago coincided with droughts in the subtropics. Why the ice sheet became unstable is still debated.

late-031.title: Cold drives mastodons and giant beavers from the north
late-031.text: American mastodons, at home in North America's far north during the Last Interglacial, vanished there about 75,000 years ago as the Wisconsin glaciation began. This happened long before people arrived, leaving mastodons only south of the ice sheets; giant beavers likewise vanished from Alaska and the Yukon.

late-032.title: Toba's supereruption blankets India in ash
late-032.text: Around 74,000 years ago Toba in Sumatra erupted about 2,800 km³ of magma, a VEI 8 supereruption and one of the largest known in the Cenozoic. It left the caldera now filled by Lake Toba and spread about 5 cm of ash across India. The blast came during the rapid cooling into Marine Isotope Stage 4, but whether it sped that cooling is debated, and Arabian Sea records suggest it did not. The Toba catastrophe theory ties it to a human population bottleneck, a sharp crash in numbers, yet that link remains highly controversial.

late-033.title: A deep cold stage drives glaciers forward
late-033.text: Marine Isotope Stage 4 was a cold stage lasting from about 71,000 to 57,000 years ago. Southern Hemisphere glaciers reached their greatest extent as Australasia, Africa and Europe grew colder and drier. North America's Wisconsin glaciation had begun about 75,000 years ago, and in northwest Europe a very cold phase peaked around 70,000 years ago. The Sierra Nevada's Tahoe glaciation perhaps peaked about then, while glaciation became continuous on Siberia's Azas Plateau.

late-034.title: Falling seas raise the Bering land bridge again
late-034.text: Falling glacial sea levels last exposed the Bering land bridge about 70,000 years ago, joining Asia and North America by land. Through the rest of the Late Pleistocene, Beringia, as the bridge and its neighboring lands are called, formed a mosaic of biological communities spanning both continents. Some accounts date its creation much later, to a sea-level fall beginning about 30,000 years ago.

late-037.title: Yellowstone's last lava flow
late-037.text: Yellowstone's most recent known magmatic eruption, a lava flow, came about 70,000 years ago. Since its great caldera eruption, the volcano had produced basalt flows, rhyolite domes and minor explosive deposits.

late-036.title: Out of Africa along the southern coasts
late-036.text: Most people living outside Africa today descend from a single expansion of Homo sapiens about 70,000–50,000 years ago. A small group, perhaps fewer than 1,000 people carrying a maternal DNA lineage called L3, crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait into Arabia. They hugged the coasts around Arabia and Persia, reaching South Asia before 55,000 years ago and pushing on toward Southeast Asia and Oceania. Around 50,000 years ago others entered Eurasia through the Zagros Mountains, some heading for the Central Asian steppes.

late-035.title: Lake Lisan fills the Jordan Rift
late-035.text: From about 70,000 to 12,000 years ago, Lake Lisan filled the Jordan Rift Valley in West Asia, a long trough where Earth's crust is pulling apart.

late-038.title: The first people cross the sea to Sahul
late-038.text: Following the southern coast of Asia, people crossed the sea from Sunda through the islands of Wallacea to Sahul, the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea. At Madjedbebe in northern Australia they were possibly living by 65,000 ± 6,000 years ago, and they were there by at least 50,000 years ago. Some experts question the older date: a 2020 study suggested termites had disturbed the layers, and 50,000 years has long been the accepted figure. Settlement of southern Australia coincided with a wet period between 60,000 and 40,000 years ago.

late-039.title: Modern humans mix with Neanderthals and Denisovans
late-039.text: As migrants left Africa, they interbred with archaic humans already living outside it, adding archaic DNA to the modern gene pool. Genetic linkage studies date the last Neanderthal gene flow into the ancestors of Europeans to 47,000–65,000 years ago. Denisovan genes entered the ancestors of Oceanians after they split from other Eurasians about 50,000 years ago, and before 37,000 years ago. An earlier wave of modern humans had already exchanged genes with Neanderthals around 100,000 years ago.

late-040.title: Modern humans may briefly visit France's Mandrin Cave
late-040.text: Modern human teeth, including a baby's molar, lie in layer E of Mandrin Cave in France's Rhône valley, between layers of Neanderthal remains. The layer's Neronian tools resemble finds at Ksar Akil in Lebanon, hinting at a brief incursion from the Levant, an idea not yet confirmed.

late-041.title: The last trace of Denisovans in the Altai
late-041.text: Denisovans are confirmed at Denisova Cave in the Altai only until about 55,000 years ago; the Denisova 3 finger bone dates to 76,200–51,600 years ago. Elsewhere they lingered: a Denisovan rib fragment from Baishiya Cave in China is 48,000–32,000 years old.

late-043.title: The 'Hobbit' of Flores vanishes
late-043.text: Homo floresiensis, the small 'Hobbit' human of Flores, survived on the island until modern humans arrived about 50,000 years ago. Its bones at Liang Bua date from 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, and the youngest stone tools there are about 50,000 years old. Its world was already drying: a trend that intensified around 61,000 years ago shrank fresh water and the dwarf Stegodon, an elephant relative it may have hunted. Initial dating put its tools as late as 13,000 years ago, a figure since revised.

late-044.title: Homo luzonensis, a small human of Luzon
late-044.text: Homo luzonensis, a small, possibly pygmy archaic human, is known from teeth and finger bones in Luzon's Callao Cave, at least 50,000 and perhaps 67,000 years old. Hominins, members of the human family, were active on the island as early as 771,000–631,000 years ago.

late-045.title: Australia's last giant primitive snakes disappear
late-045.text: Madtsoiids, giant primitive snakes resembling pythons, such as Wonambi, survived in Australia until about 50,000 years ago, the last of their family.

late-046.title: The great megafauna die-off begins
late-046.text: From around 50,000 years ago most large land animals outside Africa died out, an extinction unprecedented in how strongly it targeted big species. About 65% of megafaunal species vanished worldwide, including 72% in North America, 83% in South America and 88% in Australia. The losses began in Sahul about 50,000 years ago and in the Americas about 13,000 years ago, each time as modern humans arrived. Scientists still argue over how much hunting and how much climate change were to blame, though most accept that people played at least some part.

late-047.title: An iron meteorite blasts out Meteor Crater
late-047.text: About 50,000 years ago a nickel-iron meteorite some 50 m across blasted out Arizona's Meteor Crater, now called the best-preserved meteorite crater on Earth. The Colorado Plateau was then cooler and damper, with open grassland and woods roamed by mammoths and giant ground sloths.

late-048.title: Rotoiti eruption rocks New Zealand's Ōkataina caldera
late-048.text: New Zealand's Ōkataina caldera erupted at Rotoiti about 50,000 years ago, leaving widespread layers of tephra and ignimbrite, rock formed from hot, fast-moving flows of volcanic debris. Paired eruptions at Rotoiti and Earthquake Flat produced about 120 km³ and 10 km³ of material.

late-042.title: Procoptodon, the largest kangaroo, disappears
late-042.text: Procoptodon goliah, the largest known kangaroo, stood about 2 m tall and weighed up to 240 kg, perhaps the largest hopping mammal ever. It vanished as people arrived, in a fairly stable climate, and scientists still argue over whether hunting, human-set fires or drought was to blame.

late-049.title: The Upper Paleolithic: tools diversify and art appears
late-049.text: The Upper Paleolithic, the later Old Stone Age, began between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago, as Africa's Middle Stone Age ended. Before then, stone tools were much alike everywhere, but around 50,000 years ago artifacts grew markedly more diverse; whether a sudden 'Great Leap Forward' occurred is debated. Art followed: Spanish cave paintings and the Lion-man figurine date to around 40,000 years ago. In Europe and southwest Asia, the Aurignacian culture flourished from 43,000 to 26,000 years ago.

late-051.title: Charcoal and chipped chert spark a dispute at Topper
late-051.text: At South Carolina's Topper quarry, charcoal beneath the Clovis layer, found beside chipped chert taken for tools, was radiocarbon dated to about 50,000 years ago. Critics call the chipping natural, blame a wildfire for the charcoal and note the date sits at radiocarbon's limit; others see a 16,000-year-old pre-Clovis site.

late-050.title: Genyornis, the last dromornithid bird, disappears
late-050.text: Genyornis newtoni, a flightless bird 2–2.5 m tall, was the last survivor of the dromornithids, a bird family once diverse in the Miocene. Eggshells 53,900–43,400 years old suggest people collected and cooked its eggs, but drying lakes, as at Lake Callabonna, are also blamed, and the cause is still debated.

late-052.title: Diprotodon and Australia's other giants vanish
late-052.text: About 46,000 years ago, all the megafauna on the Australian mainland died out in one rapid window, including every mammal over 1,000 kg. Victims included Diprotodon, the largest marsupial known, and the giant monitor lizard Megalania; the latest known survivor is a Zygomaturus from New South Wales, 33,000–37,000 years old. The losses followed human arrival, not any known climate shift, and drying is judged an unlikely cause. Most scientists see at least some human role, but how large a part people played is still argued over.

late-053.title: People wield fire to reshape Australia's landscapes
late-053.text: By 46,000 years ago people were deliberately burning Australia's landscapes, and fire became abruptly more common about 45,000 years ago. One geologist credited Aboriginal fire-stick farming, but how far it turned dense forest into open eucalyptus country, and whether it helped doom the megafauna, is debated.

late-054.title: Modern humans reach Flores after the 'Hobbit'
late-054.text: Teeth from Liang Bua cave, about 46,000 years old, probably belonged to Homo sapiens, the earliest sign of modern humans on Flores. They arrived soon after the last traces of the 'Hobbit' and dwarf Stegodon, and later stone tools, made of different materials, point to new makers.

late-055.title: Modern humans push into Europe's glacial steppe
late-055.text: Modern humans had reached northwestern Europe by 45,000 years ago; remains in Germany date to 45,000–47,000 years ago, and finds in Italy and Britain to 43,000–45,000. Coming from Central Asia and the Middle East, they were adapted to hunting big game on the glacial steppe, and some lived as far north as 61°N. Settling the continent may have taken 15,000–20,000 years, and from 40,000 to 16,000 years ago Europe held only some 4,000–6,000 people. Teeth from Mandrin Cave may push the first arrival back to 56,800–51,700 years ago.

late-056.title: Modern humans head north into Siberia
late-056.text: By about 45,000 years ago modern humans had pushed into Siberia's mammoth steppe, and Ust'-Ishim man lived as far north as 58°N. People reached Japan by about 30,000 years ago and Siberia above the Arctic Circle by about 27,000 years ago.

late-057.title: The Châtelperronian, a disputed Neanderthal tool tradition
late-057.text: The Châtelperronian, a tool tradition of central and southwestern France and northern Spain, is the earliest Upper Paleolithic industry there, known for curved-backed flint knives. Many attribute it to Neanderthals, perhaps borrowing modern human techniques, but its makers and its existence are debated; critics see mixed Mousterian and Aurignacian layers.

late-058.title: The straight-tusked elephant's final refuge in Iberia
late-058.text: Bulls of the straight-tusked elephant averaged 4 m tall and 13 tonnes, and after the Last Interglacial the species retreated from northern Europe to southern refuges. Its youngest confirmed remains, from Iberia, are about 44,000–43,000 years old, though footprints may stretch its record to 28,000 years ago.

late-059.title: Ngwenya: the world's oldest known mine
late-059.text: People at Ngwenya in Eswatini were digging out hematite, an iron-rich mineral, about 43,000 years ago to make red ochre, in the oldest mining known.

late-060.title: Laschamp: Earth's magnetic field briefly flips
late-060.text: Between 42,200 and 41,500 years ago, in the Laschamp excursion, Earth's magnetic field flipped in about 250 years and stayed reversed for about 440. During the transition it fell to 5% of today's strength, letting in more cosmic rays that boosted beryllium-10 and carbon-14 production, thinned ozone and altered atmospheric circulation. A fossil kauri tree from New Zealand, alive 42,500–41,000 years ago, recorded the event. Claimed links to megafauna and Neanderthal extinctions, and to cave art, lack corroborating evidence.

late-061.title: Lake Mungo: one of the oldest cremations
late-061.text: Human remains from Lake Mungo in southeastern Australia date to about 42,000 years ago, when the Willandra Lakes held deep fresh water. Lake Mungo 1 is among the oldest known cremations: the body was burned twice and covered with ochre carried from hundreds of kilometers away.

late-062.title: The last Neanderthals disappear
late-062.text: Neanderthals disappeared from the fossil record about 40,000 years ago, their distinctive tools vanishing with them, as modern humans spreading from Africa replaced them across Eurasia. A 2021 recalibration dates their extinction to 40,700 ± 200 years ago; they had already gone from northwestern Europe by 44,200–40,600 years ago. Possible late holdouts lived in Iberia 37,000 years ago and at Byzovaya in the Urals, near the Arctic, about 33,000–32,000 years ago. A small amount of Neanderthal DNA survives in people today.

late-063.title: People walk to Tasmania over the Bassian Plain
late-063.text: Aboriginal Tasmanians arrived about 40,000 years ago across the Bassian Plain, a land bridge that low glacial seas had exposed about 43,000 years ago. Tasmania's megafauna disappeared about 41,000 years ago, apparently through hunting.

late-064.title: Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion, dies out
late-064.text: Thylacoleo, Australia's carnivorous 'pouch lion' and the only surviving genus of its family since the Pliocene, lived until around 40,000 years ago. It vanished at essentially the same time as most Australian megafauna, and scientists still debate how much climate change or newly arrived people were to blame.

late-065.title: Campi Flegrei unleashes the Campanian Ignimbrite
late-065.text: Near Naples, the Archiflegreo volcano at the Campi Flegrei erupted 39,850 ± 140 years ago, the largest event in the area's history. It produced about 200 km³ of magma, or 500 km³ in bulk, and its ash, known as the Y-5 layer, spread over about 3,000,000 km². The eruption coincided with a suite of biological and cultural changes in and beyond the Mediterranean. One theory blamed it for the Neanderthals' extinction, but a 2021 recalibration places their disappearance at 40,700 ± 200 years ago, before the eruption.

late-066.title: Chauvet Cave: the best-preserved figurative cave art
late-066.text: Chauvet Cave in southeastern France holds some of the world's best-preserved figurative cave paintings, along with the remains and prints of animals, some now extinct. Most of its black drawings date from a first occupation 37,000–33,500 years ago, and a collapsing cliff sealed the entrance about 29,000 years ago.

late-067.title: Stegodon fades from mainland Asia
late-067.text: Gone from Africa, the elephant relative Stegodon held on across South, Southeast and East Asia, surviving in China until at least 30,000–20,000 years ago. The harsh Last Glacial Maximum may have hastened its decline, though the cause is debated; Asian elephants, with more flexible diets, survived.

late-068.title: Gravettian hunters weave cloth and carve Venus figurines
late-068.text: The Gravettian culture succeeded the Aurignacian about 33,000 years ago, reached as far as Estremadura in Portugal and is known for its Venus figurines, small sculpted female figures. At Pavlov I in Moravia, clay fragments bear impressions of woven textiles about 26,980–24,870 years old, and the culture had mostly disappeared by about 22,000 years ago.

late-069.title: Disputed early traces of people in the Americas
late-069.text: Possible stone artifacts from Mexico's Chiquihuite Cave date to 26,000 and perhaps 33,000 years ago, and Yukon's Bluefish Caves may record people 24,000 years ago. These claims are disputed: most researchers place people south of the ice only after about 20,000–15,000 years ago.

late-070.title: Wolves begin to become dogs
late-070.text: Mitochondrial DNA dates the split of dogs from wolves to 32,100–18,800 years ago, and a 2021 review places the start of domestication in Siberia 26,000–19,700 years ago. Skeletons from Siberia's Altai Mountains and a cave in Belgium, about 33,000 years old, are the oldest known dogs.

late-071.title: Ancestors of Native Americans settle Beringia
late-071.text: The ancestors of the first Americans split from Ancient East Asians about 36,000 years ago and were living in Beringia by 32,000 years ago. At most a few thousand people lived there through the Last Glacial Maximum, forming the Ancestral Native American lineage 25,000–20,000 years ago.

late-072.title: Ice bulldozes the Dogger Bank into a ridge
late-072.text: About 31,600–23,100 years ago, glacial-lake sediments built Dogger Bank, then advancing ice shoved them into a thrust moraine, a ridge of debris pushed up by a glacier.

late-073.title: Cave hyenas, hunters of bison and horses, die out
late-073.text: Cave hyenas hunted horses, bison and aurochs from Western Europe to Southeast Asia, but vanished from Europe about 31,000 years ago and northeast Asia about 20,000. The cause is unclear: climate alone seems insufficient, and human activity and shrinking prey probably contributed.

late-075.title: The Ito eruption carves out Aira Caldera
late-075.text: About 30,000 years ago the colossal Ito eruption formed Aira Caldera on Kyushu, spreading tephra and ignimbrite over the land. Seawater later filled the caldera, helping form the 200 m-deep Kagoshima Bay, where Sakurajima volcano now rises.

late-077.title: The rains fail and the Sahara turns to desert
late-077.text: Until about 30,000 years ago the Mousterian Pluvial, a long wet phase, kept northern Africa, Sahara included, well watered and cooler than today. When the pluvial ended, the Sahara became arid. Dunes of eolianite, wind-blown sand later cemented into rock, began forming in the north of the Chad Basin 40,000–20,000 years ago.

late-076.title: Lake Bonneville begins to rise
late-076.text: Lake Bonneville began rising about 30,000 years ago from levels like today's Great Salt Lake. After about 24,000 years ago it rose rapidly, reaching its highest level, the Bonneville shoreline, about 17,500 years ago.

late-079.title: Mammoth-steppe giants thrive in glacial Europe
late-079.text: Megafauna were most abundant in Europe around 27,000–21,000 years ago, thanks to the cold of a stadial, a frigid phase within the glacial. As the cold peaked during the Last Glacial Maximum around 23,000 years ago, Europe's top predators began to die out.

late-080.title: The Last Glacial Maximum: ice 3 kilometers thick
late-080.text: Ice sheets that had begun advancing about 33,000 years ago in both hemispheres reached their greatest extent of the Last Glacial Period between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Ice up to 3 km thick covered much of northern Europe, Asia and North America, along with Greenland and Antarctica. Around 21,000 years ago the global average temperature was about 6 °C colder than today. In the north, people and animals retreated to refugia, sheltered pockets where they survived until the ice withdrew.

late-081.title: Oruanui: the world's most recent supereruption
late-081.text: About 25,700 years ago, Taupō Volcano in New Zealand erupted in the world's most recent supereruption, rated VEI 8. Bursting through a lake system, it became the largest known phreatomagmatic eruption, one driven by magma meeting water, and produced about 530 km³ of magma. It destroyed Lake Huka and formed the caldera that now holds Lake Taupō, which later rose about 75 m above today's level before breaching its ignimbrite dam. The eruption may have deepened the glacial cold in New Zealand and the nearby Pacific.

late-082.title: Andean and Patagonian glaciers reach their peak
late-082.text: Glaciers peaked around 27,000 years ago in the northern Andes and 25,200–23,100 years ago around the Strait of Magellan. During the coldest period the Andean tree line stood about 1 km lower than today.

late-083.title: The Laurentide ice sheet reaches Manhattan
late-083.text: North America's ice reached its maximum about 25,000–21,000 years ago, in the Late Wisconsin. After retreating 52,000–40,000 years ago, the Laurentide Ice Sheet grew fast, covering Canada east of the Rockies and reaching south to the Missouri and Ohio rivers and Manhattan. Ice sheets extended to about the 45th parallel north. In the Rockies, the Pinedale glaciation peaked 23,500–21,000 years ago.

late-084.title: Lake Sajsi fills the Uyuni basin
late-084.text: During the Last Glacial Maximum, Lake Sajsi filled the Uyuni basin on the Bolivian Altiplano 25,000–19,000 years ago, reaching its greatest depth 23,000 years ago. It was a forerunner of the larger Lake Tauca.

late-085.title: The Mal'ta boy reveals the Ancient North Eurasians
late-085.text: About 24,000 years ago, a boy was buried with artifacts and a Venus figurine at Mal'ta, a site of bone-walled houses near Siberia's Lake Baikal. His people, the Ancient North Eurasians, were important genetic contributors to Native Americans, Siberians and Europeans.

late-086.title: The cave bear dies out
late-086.text: Ancient DNA shows cave bear numbers falling steeply from about 40,000 years ago, as modern humans arrived and the Aurignacian began. No longer abundant in Central Europe by 35,000 years ago, the bear died out about 24,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum.

late-088.title: Ohalo II: cereal harvesting beside the Sea of Galilee
late-088.text: About 23,000 years ago people near the Sea of Galilee were cultivating emmer, barley and oats, eating wild cereal grains long before farming began. Glossed flint blades from Ohalo II, their lakeshore camp, are the earliest known composite tools, made of joined parts, for harvesting cereals.

late-087.title: White Sands footprints, possibly America's oldest
late-087.text: Buried seeds date human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, to 23,000–21,000 years ago; if correct, they are possibly the oldest human traces in the Americas. The site holds perhaps hundreds of thousands of human and animal tracks, recording people alongside ice-age megafauna. Skeptics argue the seeds took up old carbon from groundwater, which would make the prints no older than 15,500–13,500 years. Pollen and quartz-grain dating in 2023, and mud dating in 2025, supported the older ages, but the debate continues.

late-089.title: Scandinavian ice spreads across northern Europe
late-089.text: The Fennoscandian Ice Sheet reached the edge of the mid-Norwegian shelf by about 26,000 years ago, then merged with ice from the Barents Sea and Britain. It buried the entire Scandinavian Mountains and spread into Denmark, Germany, Poland and the former USSR. The ice reached its maximum in Denmark, Germany and western Poland about 22,000 years ago, and in Lithuania and Belarus about 19,000 years ago. Its margin began to retreat 22,000–17,000 years ago.

late-090.title: Lascaux: generations paint the great animals
late-090.text: Lascaux Cave in France's Vézère valley holds celebrated Upper Paleolithic paintings, mainly of large animals matching the local fossil fauna, made by many generations. They are usually dated to 17,000–22,000 years ago, in the early Magdalenian culture, though their age is still debated.

late-091.title: Solutrean flintworkers ride out the glacial peak
late-091.text: The Solutrean flint industry succeeded the Gravettian in France, Spain and Portugal, where people sheltered in a glacial refuge between forest steppe and steppe tundra. Its toolmakers used techniques never seen before and not rediscovered for millennia, and together with earlier traditions it gave rise to the Magdalenian.

late-092.title: The oceans drop about 125 meters
late-092.text: Around 21,000 years ago sea level stood about 125 m below today's, with the missing water locked in ice, mostly in the Laurentide sheet. The low seas exposed the Bering land bridge between Siberia and Alaska and the Bassian Plain linking Tasmania to Australia. On the Great Barrier Reef, reef growth moved seaward, reaching farthest from today's coast around 20,700–20,500 years ago.

late-093.title: Xianren Cave foragers make the oldest known pottery
late-093.text: Pottery fragments from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, dating from the Last Glacial Maximum, are the earliest pottery yet known anywhere. Mobile foragers made them, and scorch marks suggest cooking; pottery had been thought to arrive with farming in the Neolithic, around 10,000 years ago.

late-096.title: The great thaw begins
late-096.text: Northern ice began to retreat around 19,000 years ago, and the retreat sped up around 15,000 years ago. At the onset, a meltwater pulse, a sudden surge of melt into the sea, may have lifted sea level up to 10 m within 500 years. Over the whole deglaciation, global mean temperature rose about 5 °C, high latitudes warmed over 10 °C, and sea level climbed more than 120 m. The melting was neither steady nor simultaneous: Antarctica warmed abruptly around 22,000 years ago, while ice covered most of Great Britain until about 16,000 years ago.

late-095.title: Carbon dioxide climbs as the Southern Ocean stirs
late-095.text: Ice cores show CO2 at 180–210 ppm during ice ages and 280–300 ppm in warm interglacials. At the Last Glacial Maximum, the carbon missing from the air sat in the deep ocean, trapped beneath the Southern Ocean's stable, layered waters. As the ice retreated, stronger winds and shrinking sea ice may have churned up the deep Southern Ocean and released that carbon. Rising CO2 warmed the globe out of the glacial maximum, climbing in three abrupt pulses and stalling during the Antarctic Cold Reversal.

late-097.title: Vesuvius's Basal Pumice eruption forms the Somma caldera
late-097.text: About 18,300 years ago Vesuvius, which had begun forming about 25,000 years ago, produced the VEI 6 Basal Pumice eruption, first forming the Somma caldera. From about 19,000 years ago the volcano had switched to Plinian eruptions, large explosive blasts that build calderas, the most recent in AD 79.

late-099.title: Rising seas begin to drown Sundaland
late-099.text: At the Last Glacial Maximum, with sea level about 120 m lower, the entire Sunda Shelf lay exposed, joining Borneo, Java and Sumatra to Asia. Around 18,000 years ago rising seas began to submerge parts of Sundaland, a process lasting until about 5000 BCE.

late-098.title: The Oldest Dryas stalls the retreat of the ice
late-098.text: The Oldest Dryas, a cold stadial from about 18,000 to 14,700 years ago, interrupted the retreat of the ice. Heinrich event 1 cooled the North Atlantic and weakened the overturning circulation, pushing rain belts south and drying northern Africa. Europe was a treeless, dry, grassy tundra, though brown bears and other species began returning from refuges in the Carpathians, Italy, Spain and Greece. Even so, rising CO2 warmed the planet about 2 °C, nearly half of it in the stadial's last centuries.

late-100.title: The south warms fast and Patagonia's ice retreats
late-100.text: In southern Chile, rapid warming from 17,800 years ago brought interglacial temperatures within about 1,000 years, as glaciers retreated and Valdivian rainforest spread. A 2017 study linked stratospheric ozone loss about 17,700 years ago to this abrupt acceleration of southern deglaciation. The Patagonian Ice Sheet peaked about 18,000–17,500 years ago, covering some 480,000 km², then melted rapidly along its northern edge. That melt freshened the nearby ocean and altered its circulation, while retreat also began around 18,000 years ago on Antarctica's Alexander Island and New Zealand's Tongariro.

late-101.title: Lake Tauca rises on the Altiplano
late-101.text: During the wetter first stage of the Central Andean Pluvial Event, 17,500–15,900 years ago, Lake Tauca on the Bolivian Altiplano peaked, about 16,500 years ago. Many explanations link the wet phase to Heinrich event 1, whose circulation changes carried more moisture onto the plateau.

late-102.title: The Erralla dog, the earliest widely accepted dog
late-102.text: The Erralla dog from the Basque Country in Spain, dated 17,410–17,096 years ago, is the most widely accepted earliest dog, though disputed remains go back 36,000 years. The Bonn–Oberkassel dog, about 14,500 years old, is the oldest known dog buried with people, and dogs were the Pleistocene's only domesticated animal.

late-103.title: Lake Bonneville bursts in a single great flood
late-103.text: At its highest level, about 17,400 years ago, Lake Bonneville covered about 83,000 km² of northern Utah. It breached a natural dam of alluvial fans, stream-laid sediment heaps, at Red Rock Pass, and a 120 m flood crest roared toward the Snake River. Peaking at about 930,000 m³ per second, the flood scoured the Snake River Canyon, created Shoshone Falls and drained about 5,000 km³, lowering the lake 107 m. Unlike the repeated Missoula floods, the Bonneville flood happened only once.

late-104.title: The Pacific coast opens a path south from Beringia
late-104.text: By around 17,000 years ago, retreating glaciers on the Alaska Peninsula had opened a path from Beringia to the Pacific coast. Once the coast range was ice-free, by 16,000–15,000 years ago, kelp forests, estuaries and other shoreline habitats could have formed an unobstructed migration corridor.

late-105.title: A proposed Caspian overflow into the Black Sea
late-105.text: Andrei Chepalyga proposed that Caspian meltwater overflowed through the Manych–Kerch spillway into the Black Sea basin 17,000–14,000 years ago, raising it 60–70 m. This 'Late Pleistocene Great Flood' is one researcher's hypothesis, not an established event, and differs from the disputed Holocene Black Sea deluge.

late-106.title: Vashon ice peaks in the Puget Lowland
late-106.text: The Puget Lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet passed Seattle about 17,950 years ago and reached its maximum near Tenino about 16,950 years ago. Retreating about 340 m a year, it released a major outburst flood from a breached ice dam; seawater refilled Puget Sound by about 16,000 years ago.

late-107.title: Woolly mammoths and rhinos retreat to the far north
late-107.text: Woolly rhinos vanished from Europe 17,000–15,000 years ago, and their youngest reliable bones, from the Urals and northeast Siberia, are about 14,200–14,000 years old. Mammoths disappeared from most of Europe by 14,000 years ago and from Alaska and Yukon about 13,300 years ago, roughly 1,000 years after people arrived. From about 15,000 years ago wet tundra and forest replaced most of Siberia's mammoth steppe, and DNA shows a final mammoth crash about 12,000 years ago. Whether vanishing habitat or human hunting mattered more is still debated.

late-109.title: People spread south through the Americas
late-109.text: Scholars agree the first Americans came from Siberia and spread widely after the Last Glacial Maximum, around 16,000–13,000 years ago. Ice blocked inland routes until about 16,000 years ago, though a Pacific coastal route may have opened by 17,000 years ago. Accepted pre-Clovis sites include Cooper's Ferry in Idaho, about 15,800 years old, and Oregon's Paisley Caves, about 14,200, whose dates some critics still question. People reached South America around 15,000 years ago, before its megafauna disappeared.

late-108.title: The Baltic Ice Lake fills the Baltic basin
late-108.text: Meltwater pooled along the southern Baltic as the retreating ice reached its shore about 16,000 years ago, and by 14,600 years ago a well-defined Baltic Ice Lake existed. It stretched from southern Sweden to Estonia and lasted until about 11,700 years ago, close to the start of the Holocene.

late-110.title: Meadowcroft Rockshelter's disputed pre-Clovis dates
late-110.text: Radiocarbon dates suggest people used Pennsylvania's Meadowcroft Rockshelter from 16,000 years ago, possibly 19,000, though critics suspect contamination from local coal-bearing rock. Later tests support the early dates, yet they remain controversial: in a 2013 survey, 38% of archaeologists accepted them and 20% rejected them.

late-113.title: Rising seas begin flooding the Persian Gulf
late-113.text: Rising seas from the melting ice sheets began flooding the Persian Gulf basin about 15,000 years ago. Much of the Gulf floor was still dry 12,000–9,000 years ago, and the modern marine Gulf formed in the early Holocene, by about 6,000 years ago.

late-112.title: Missoula floods tear open the Channeled Scablands
late-112.text: Glacial Lake Missoula, held back by an ice dam on the Clark Fork River, stored up to about 2,500 km³ of water. Between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago the dam failed and re-formed again and again, unleashing dozens of floods, about one every 55 years. The largest discharged about 10 km³ an hour, sweeping across eastern Washington and on into Oregon's Willamette Valley. Together the floods stripped about 210 km³ of loess, or wind-blown silt, along with sediment and basalt from the Channeled Scablands.

late-111.title: The Altai megaflood bursts down the Katun River
late-111.text: Near the end of the last glaciation, Altai glaciers dammed the Chuya River, forming a lake of up to 600 km³ in the Chuya and Kurai basins. According to some geomorphologists, the lake burst in cataclysmic floods down the Katun River, leaving giant current ripples up to 18 m high.

late-115.title: Magdalenian reindeer hunters recolonize northern Europe
late-115.text: Descended mainly from Gravettian groups who sheltered in southwestern Europe during the glacial peak, Magdalenian reindeer hunters moved north around 15,000 years ago, reaching Britain and Poland. From about 14,000 years ago, Western Hunter-Gatherers linked to the Epigravettian culture spread north across the Alps, largely replacing them.

late-114.title: The cave lion vanishes
late-114.text: Cave lions died out almost simultaneously across their range about 15,000–14,000 years ago, though they lingered roughly 1,000 years longer in North America. The cause is unknown; climate change, shrinking prey and competition with other carnivores and humans have all been suggested.

late-116.title: The Antarctic Cold Reversal chills the south
late-116.text: While the north warmed, the Southern Hemisphere cooled in the Antarctic Cold Reversal, about 14,500 to 12,900 years ago. A meltwater pulse, probably from the Antarctic or Laurentide ice sheet, is thought to have caused it. The cooling may have pushed the southern polar front north and increased Andean rain and snow.

late-117.title: The Bølling–Allerød: abrupt warmth returns to the north
late-117.text: About 14,690 years ago the Northern Hemisphere warmed abruptly, opening the Bølling–Allerød interstadial; Greenland's NorthGRIP ice core records the onset at 14,600 years ago. A stronger Atlantic overturning circulation carried heat north while the Southern Hemisphere cooled, a pattern called the 'polar seesaw'. The Allerød phase lifted northern Atlantic temperatures almost to present-day levels. The warmth let people repopulate Eurasia from glacial refuges, and in Beringia shrub tundra replaced dry steppe after 14,000 years ago.

late-118.title: Meltwater pulse 1A: seas rise up to 25 meters
late-118.text: Global sea level rose 16–25 m in about 400–500 years, roughly 40–60 mm a year, the fastest known rates of post-glacial rise. Rapid collapse of continental ice sheets is blamed, and the pulse began with, or just after, the abrupt Bølling–Allerød warming recorded in Greenland ice. West Antarctic ice shrank between 15,000 and 14,000 years ago, matching an abrupt rise around 14,500 years ago. It is the most widely recognized and least disputed of the named meltwater pulses.

late-119.title: The African humid period begins and Lake Victoria refills
late-119.text: North Africa turned wetter about 14,600–14,500 years ago, as Heinrich event 1 ended and the Bølling–Allerød warming began. Summer sunshine at least 4% stronger than today's, aided by changes in vegetation, dust and greenhouse gases, strengthened the African monsoon. Lake Victoria, dry around 15,000 years ago, refilled and overflowed, and Lakes Albert and Tana spilled into the White and Blue Nile. Lake Chad grew, glaciers grew on Kilimanjaro, and the Sahara shrank.

late-120.title: Monte Verde: a tent of wood and hides
late-120.text: Monte Verde II in southern Chile, about 14,500 years old, is one of the widely accepted sites older than Clovis. Its people built a tent-like structure of wood and animal hides and probably lived in their river basin most of the year, alongside late Pleistocene megafauna.

late-121.title: Natufian foragers settle down in the Levant
late-121.text: Natufian foragers in the Levant harvested wild cereals and hunted gazelles, yet lived in settled or semi-settled communities before agriculture. Their settlements, some with round stone buildings, hold the first evidence of food storage, but the cold, dry Younger Dryas pushed groups back toward mobility.

late-122.title: Ancient human DNA in Oregon's Paisley Caves
late-122.text: Coprolites, fossilized feces, from Oregon's Paisley Caves date to about 14,300–14,400 years ago and hold the oldest human DNA found in North America. The DNA ties these pre-Clovis people to Siberia or Asia, but critics question the dates and the coprolites' human origin, suspecting contamination by leached DNA.

late-123.title: Meltwater fills the Great Lakes basins
late-123.text: Around 14,000 years ago retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved, and meltwater began filling them to form the Great Lakes. In Wisconsin, too, the ice began to retreat about then as the climate warmed.

late-124.title: The Older Dryas: a brief cold snap
late-124.text: About 14,000 years ago the Older Dryas, a brief cold stadial lasting only a century or two, interrupted the warmth between the Bølling and Allerød phases. Ice readvanced in places, as in the Littleton–Bethlehem readvance and Canada's Shulie Lake phase.

late-127.title: The Americas lose their giant mammals
late-127.text: In North America, megafauna extinctions clustered around 13,800–11,400 years ago, alongside the onset of the Younger Dryas and the Clovis culture. About 72% of North American and 83% of South American megafaunal species died out, among them ground sloths and every mammal over 1,000 kg. Butchered bones, such as an Ohio ground sloth dated 13,738–13,435 years ago, show that people hunted these animals. Whether hunting, climate change or both caused the extinctions is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept at least a contributory human role.

late-128.title: Ice-free corridor opens, too late for the first Americans
late-128.text: By 21,000 years ago the Cordilleran and Laurentide ice sheets had merged east of the Rocky Mountains, closing a route into North America's interior. A gap opened about 13,800 ± 500 years ago by 2022 estimates, after the earliest widely accepted sites, so it could not have carried the first people south.

late-129.title: Clovis hunters spread fluted points across North America
late-129.text: The Clovis culture flourished about 13,050–12,750 years ago; at Blackwater Draw in New Mexico, the site that defines it, its tools lay alongside Columbian mammoth remains.
