Its hallmark was the fluted, or grooved, Clovis point, a large lance-shaped projectile point also used for cutting. Clovis people were mobile hunter-gatherers who relied on big game, especially mammoths, and the idea that they helped drive the megafauna extinctions remains controversial. From about 12,750–12,600 years ago Clovis gave way to regional cultures such as Folsom.

late-130.title: Laacher See erupts in the Rhineland
late-130.text: Germany's Laacher See erupted on the scale of Pinatubo in 1991, and its tephra dammed the Rhine into a 140 km² lake until the dam broke. Dated to 13,006 years ago, it came more than a century before the Younger Dryas, though 1990s research had proposed it as the trigger.

late-132.title: Lake Agassiz, larger than any lake today
late-132.text: Fed by meltwater from the retreating Laurentide Ice Sheet, Lake Agassiz spread over parts of Manitoba, Ontario, Minnesota, North Dakota and Saskatchewan around 13,000 years ago. At its greatest it may have covered 440,000 km², more than any lake today and about the area of the Black Sea. From about 13,500 years ago it overflowed south toward the Mississippi, and at times it drained east to Lake Superior or northwest to the Arctic. Its huge freshwater releases are thought to have disrupted ocean circulation, and one about 13,000 years ago may have triggered the Younger Dryas.

late-131.title: The Champlain Sea floods the St. Lawrence lowlands
late-131.text: From about 13,000 to 10,000 years ago, rising seas flooded the St. Lawrence and Ottawa valleys, still pressed down by the ice, forming the Champlain Sea. About 12,000 years ago a failed ice dam dropped Lake Vermont 91 m in hours or days, letting salt water sweep in.

late-133.title: Hunter-gatherers reach Cyprus and its dwarf beasts
late-133.text: Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 11,000–10,000 BCE, bringing wild boar, and the Aetokremnos site may record their hunting of dwarf hippos and dwarf elephants. Both later vanished, and the genet Genetta plesictoides died out after people and invasive species arrived.

late-134.title: The Irish elk returns briefly to northern Europe
late-134.text: The Irish elk's range collapsed during the Last Glacial Maximum, but it recolonized northern Europe in the Bølling–Allerød; most Irish remains date to around 13,000 years ago. Its range shrank again in the Younger Dryas, and by the end of that cold spell it had vanished from northern Europe.

late-135.title: California's island pygmy mammoths disappear
late-135.text: On California's Channel Islands, Columbian mammoths evolved into pygmy mammoths under half their mainland size, which lived there 80,000–13,000 years ago. Their end coincided with rising seas, declining conifer forests and the first people, thought to have hunted them; which mattered most is debated.

late-137.title: The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, a fringe idea
late-137.text: In 2007 Richard Firestone's team proposed that a comet or meteor impact or airburst, about 12,900 years ago, triggered the Younger Dryas and helped kill megafauna. Most relevant experts reject this fringe hypothesis for lack of clear evidence, and the Hiawatha crater, once linked to it, proved 58 million years old.

late-136.title: The Younger Dryas: a last plunge into glacial cold
late-136.text: The Younger Dryas, about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, was the last cold phase of the Last Glacial Period, a return to glacial conditions. Annual temperatures fell about 3 °C in North America, 2–6 °C in Europe and up to 10 °C in Greenland, where the cooling took 3 years or less. Scientists agree a severe weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation caused it; a Lake Agassiz meltwater flood and a volcanic trigger are among the proposed sparks. It ended as rapidly as it began, with dramatic warming over about 50 years that closed the Pleistocene.

late-138.title: North America loses its short-faced bear
late-138.text: Beringia lost Arctodus simus, a short-faced bear of up to 957 kg, about 23,000 years ago, possibly to sharp cooling tied to Heinrich event 2. Elsewhere it survived until about 12,800 years ago; shrinking food as vegetation shifted, and competition with brown bears, are among the debated causes.

late-139.title: Scimitar-toothed cats leave a last trace in Alberta
late-139.text: For some 4 million years, Homotherium, a lion-sized scimitar-toothed cat of up to about 250 kg, roamed North America, Eurasia and Africa. Its youngest well-dated remains come from southern Alberta, and its extinction, like the saber-toothed Smilodon's, has been linked to losing prey such as mammoths and horses.

late-140.title: Columbian mammoths, bigger than woolly ones, die out
late-140.text: Standing up to 4.2 m tall and weighing 12.5 tonnes, the Columbian mammoth outsized the woolly mammoth and ranged from southern Canada to Costa Rica. Its latest date, from Colorado's Dent site, falls as the Younger Dryas began; climate-driven habitat loss, Clovis hunting or both remain the rival explanations.

late-141.title: Lake Lahontan reaches its highstand
late-141.text: At its Sehoo highstand about 12,700 years ago, Lake Lahontan covered over 22,000 km² of the Great Basin and reached about 270 m deep near Pyramid Lake. One of North America's largest lakes of the last glacial period, it then began a gradual drying as the Pleistocene drew to a close.

late-142.title: The bear-sized giant beaver disappears
late-142.text: North America's biggest Pleistocene rodent was Castoroides, a bear-sized beaver of about 90–125 kg and the largest beaver known. Its last populations lived south of the Great Lakes, where its youngest bones, in New York, overlap Paleo-Indian artifacts by up to a thousand years.

late-144.title: Pica glass forms in the Atacama, origin disputed
late-144.text: Pica glass, found in the Atacama Desert, dates to about 12,000 years ago, but sources disagree on how it formed. One account attributes it to increased wildfire activity, while a list of possible impact structures counts it as an inferred impact.

late-145.title: Macrauchenia, one of South America's last litopterns, dies out
late-145.text: The long-necked, hoofed Macrauchenia was among the last litopterns, an order native to South America for over 60 million years. At Paso Otero 5 on the Argentine Pampas, its burned bones lie with Fishtail spear points, but the roles of hunting and climate remain disputed.

gree-004.title: Farmers sow the first fields in the Fertile Crescent
gree-004.text: As the world warmed at the start of the Holocene, people in the Fertile Crescent began growing crops and herding animals, opening the Neolithic. They domesticated wheat, barley and legumes, along with sheep, goats, cattle and, later, pigs. Barley was tamed around 11,000 years ago, and domesticated emmer wheat appears in Iran by 9,800 BP, or years before present. Settlers had reached Cyprus by 8800–8600 BCE, and systematic husbandry of plants and animals took hold between 8500 and 7000 BCE.

gree-005.title: The Younger Dryas breaks and the Holocene begins
gree-005.text: The Younger Dryas cold spell, which began about 12,800 years ago, ended about 11,700 years ago and took the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene with it. The change came fast: Greenland's average yearly temperature rose by about 8 °C within 40 years, in three jumps of five years each. The boundary's GSSP, the formal reference point for where a unit of geologic time begins, sits in Greenland's NGRIP2 ice core and was ratified in 2008. Warming then continued at a gentler pace, and in the American Southwest the cool, wet pluvial, or rainy, climate gave way to semi-arid conditions.

gree-006.title: Forests and wetlands swallow the mammoth steppe
gree-006.text: As the Holocene began, mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands overran the vast mammoth steppe, the cold grassland that fed the Ice Age grazers. Higher temperatures and more rain shrank the grazers' habitat, splitting their populations into fragments and then driving them extinct. By about 10,000 years ago, patches of closed larch and pine forest had grown up in northern Siberia. Only then did forbs, flowering herbs other than grasses, decline, as woody plants and grasses took over.

gree-008.title: Ice Age wolves lose most of their genetic diversity
gree-008.text: As the Holocene began, ancient wolves in Alaska, Siberia and Europe lost most of their genetic diversity, sharing little with modern wolves. In North America a bottleneck, a population crash, nearly erased the old lineages, and the Japanese wolf proved the last of Siberia's Pleistocene wolves.

gree-001.title: The Baltic Ice Lake yields to the Yoldia Sea
gree-001.text: Close to the start of the Holocene, the Baltic Ice Lake fell to sea level, and salt water flowed in to create the Yoldia Sea. Pine and birch pollen surged around the basin from 11,500 years ago, and people lived on its Estonian shores by 11,200–10,200 years ago.

gree-007.title: The die-off of giant mammals rolls on
gree-007.text: Many megafauna species died out during the Greenlandian, keeping up the pace of extinction set at the end of the Late Pleistocene. From the Late Pleistocene into the early Holocene, most animals heavier than 45 kilograms vanished, including 80% of those over a tonne. In the Colombian Andes, spores of dung fungi record a second wave of megafaunal extinction around 10,990 BP. Whether climate change or human hunting drove these losses is a long-running argument, though most scholars accept that people played at least some part.

gree-003.title: Melting ice sheets lift the sea 60 meters
gree-003.text: Between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago, world sea level jumped about 60 meters as the continental ice sheets melted. The usual pace was 6–10 millimeters a year, broken by brief bursts of 30–60 millimeters a year. The rising water drowned vast lowlands and cut off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania, while in Brazil's Bahia region mangroves pushed inland. As the ice sheets dwindled, the rise slowed from over 10 millimeters a year to under 1 millimeter a year by 4,200 years ago.

gree-009.title: The northern ice sheets begin their final retreat
gree-009.text: The abrupt warming around 9700 BCE set off rapid melting of the remaining ice sheets of North America and Europe. By about 11,000 years ago the Cordilleran ice sheet had essentially melted away in northern British Columbia, but most of the deglaciation's melting still lay ahead. The vast Laurentide ice sheet began losing more mass each year than it gained only in the early Holocene, once solar heating and summer temperatures rose. From 8,500 BP, ice pouring off the collapsing Laurentide made the climate of the North Atlantic erratic.

gree-010.title: Meltwater pulse 1B: a disputed burst of rising seas
gree-010.text: Just after the Younger Dryas, sea level may have surged in meltwater pulse 1B, read from Barbados corals as 28 meters in about 500 years. Other studies cut it to 7.5 meters or under 6, and some find no clear break from steady rise, so even its existence is debated.

gree-011.title: Hunter-gatherers raise the stone pillars of Göbekli Tepe
gree-011.text: Around 9500 BCE, hunter-gatherers in today's Turkey began raising Göbekli Tepe, rings of animal-carved stone pillars that are among the oldest known megaliths. Its builders hunted gazelle and ground much cereal, though sources differ on whether any of it was domesticated, and they used the site until about 8000 BCE.

gree-015.title: The Sahara turns green under a stronger monsoon
gree-015.text: Between 11,000 and 10,000 BP, Earth passed closest to the Sun at the June solstice; summer sunlight rose about 8%, driving the African monsoon farther north. Grasses, trees and lakes spread over much of the Sahara, deepening a humid period that had begun about 14,600 years ago. From 11,000 years ago Lake Mega-Chad covered more than 350,000 square kilometers, and lakes even formed in Arabia's Rub' al Khali 9,000–7,000 years ago. People followed the water: the Takarkori site was first occupied 10,000–9,000 years ago, and the Kiffian culture flourished 10,000–8,000 years ago.

gree-016.title: Glacial Lake Algonquin floods the upper Great Lakes
gree-016.text: Glacial Lake Algonquin, a vast lake of meltwater, first flooded about 11,000 years before present. At the time, the front of the Laurentide ice sheet lay along the northern edges of Lakes Superior and Huron.

gree-017.title: South America's notoungulates reach the end of the line
gree-017.text: Notoungulata, an order of South American hoofed mammals that included the rhinoceros-sized grazer Toxodon, died out about 11,000 years ago after some 61 million years. Toxodon remains at Itapipoca, Brazil, have given even younger dates, 7320–6099 BCE.

gree-018.title: North America loses its horses, ground sloths and short-faced bears
gree-018.text: Around 11,000 years ago, short-faced bears vanished from North America, its last giant ground sloths died out, and every native horse disappeared. In Arizona's Rampart Cave, dung from Shasta ground sloths piled up from 13,000 BP and then stopped suddenly at 11,000 BP. Horses had evolved largely in North America, yet the continent had none again until they were reintroduced in the 15th century. Of the continent's odd-toed hoofed mammals, only Baird's tapir, reaching into southern Mexico, survived, though ground sloths lingered on Caribbean islands until about 4,000 years ago.

gree-019.title: Wakamiko Caldera erupts inside Kyushu's Aira Caldera
gree-019.text: Some time between 9050 and 7050 BCE, Wakamiko Caldera, a collapsed volcanic basin inside Kyushu's larger Aira Caldera, blew out about 12 cubic kilometers of material. The eruption rates VEI 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, the standard scale of eruption size.

gree-021.title: Glyptodon dies out, but its cousins linger
gree-021.text: After about 3.2 million years in South America, Glyptodon, a giant armadillo relative, died out around 11,000 years ago as a wetter climate remade its grasslands. Human hunting may also have contributed, and its cousins Doedicurus and Panochthus lingered on the Argentine Pampas, living alongside people for at least 4,000 years.

gree-020.title: Goats, sheep, pigs and cattle become the first livestock
gree-020.text: The first livestock appear in northern Mesopotamia: goats and sheep by c. 9000 BCE, pigs by c. 8500 BCE and cattle by c. 8000 BCE. By 10,000 years ago hunters were culling young males and sparing females to breed, and domestic animals later became Eurasia's main source of new human infections.

gree-023.title: The Baltic becomes a freshwater lake
gree-023.text: As the land rose after the ice melted, the Baltic basin, once the Yoldia Sea, became the freshwater Ancylus Lake from about 10,700 to 9,800 years BP. Its spreading water pushed people near Pärnu inland, and after it drained through the Dana River, salt water began entering at 9,800 BP.

gree-031.title: The last mainland woolly mammoths die in Siberia
gree-031.text: Woolly mammoths survived in mainland Siberia until around 10,000 years ago, and the youngest mainland fossils, from the Kyttyk Peninsula, are 9,650 years old. Europe's last known mammoths lived in the Southern Urals, 9650 BCE, and at Cherepovets in Russia, 9290–9180 BCE. Cold-adapted giants like the mammoth and woolly rhinoceros were generally Eurasia's last megafauna to go, though a small population on Wrangel Island lasted much longer. In Canada, trackways at St. Mary Reservoir show a herd of adults, subadults and young still roaming there 11,300–11,000 years ago.

gree-033.title: The modern coyote appears
gree-033.text: The modern coyote appeared around 10,000 years ago, most likely descended from its Ice Age forerunner, the Pleistocene coyote.

gree-032.title: The woolly rhinoceros fades out in Siberia
gree-032.text: The youngest woolly rhinoceros bones date to 9450 BCE, but its DNA turns up in permafrost, frozen ground, near Russia's Kolyma River dated to 8050–7650 BCE. Its range had been shrinking toward Siberia since 17,000 years ago, and its loss was part of the end-Pleistocene event that wiped out most large land animals.

gree-028.title: Doggerland drowns beneath the North Sea
gree-028.text: In the early Holocene, a low land called Doggerland joined eastern Britain to northern France, the Low Countries, northwest Germany and Jutland. By 9000 BCE a large tidal bay had opened between eastern England and Dogger Bank, and rapid sea-level rise followed. Between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago the sea broke Doggerland into low islands and then swallowed it, leaving Dogger Bank itself as an island. Britain was finally cut off from mainland Europe around 6500 BCE, and most traces of the people who lived on Doggerland date to the Mesolithic.

gree-029.title: Farming takes root far beyond the Fertile Crescent
gree-029.text: Farming had more than one cradle: between 10,000 and 7,000 BP, plants and animals were rapidly domesticated in tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa and Central America. At Kuk Swamp in highland New Guinea, drainage ditches show taro and other crops in cultivation perhaps by 8000 BCE. Mehrgarh in Balochistan, South Asia's earliest Neolithic site, grew wheat and barley and kept herds, though its start is dated anywhere from 8500 to 6500 BCE. Maize was domesticated in Mesoamerica from about 7000 BCE, and rice in the Far East.

gree-035.title: The sea cuts the Bering land bridge
gree-035.text: Around 8000 BCE rising seas flooded the Beringian land bridge, closing the main migration route from Siberia. The drowning created the Bering Strait and separated Asia from the Americas. Estimates based only on the strait's depth and the global sea-level curve put the final flooding earlier, around 11,000 years BP.

gree-038.title: Scandinavia's ice sheet shrinks to a mountain remnant
gree-038.text: The Scandinavian ice sheet retreated into the mountains, clearing Russia by 10.6 ka, or 10.6 thousand years ago, and Finland by 10.1 ka. Its center over southern Norway vanished about a thousand years after the ice left Finland. By 9.7 ka, the last remnant of the great Fennoscandian ice sheet lay in the eastern Sarek Mountains.

gree-039.title: A long warm spell, the Holocene Climatic Optimum, begins
gree-039.text: The Holocene Climatic Optimum was a warm period lasting roughly from 9,500 to 5,500 years BP. Northern Hemisphere heating peaked about 9,000 years ago, when Earth's axis tilted 24° and the planet passed closest to the Sun during northern summer. The far south warmed earlier: New Zealand and Antarctica were warmest roughly 10,500 to 8,000 years ago, when Antarctica's Amery Ice Shelf retreated about 80 kilometers. North-western North America peaked 11,000–9,000 years ago, even while the Laurentide ice sheet still chilled eastern Canada.

gree-041.title: The eastern Mediterranean lays down its latest sapropel
gree-041.text: The eastern Mediterranean laid down its latest sapropel, S1, a dark, organic-rich mud that forms when bottom waters lose oxygen. The African humid period swelled the Nile and other rivers, whose fresh water layered the sea and overloaded it with nutrients.

gree-040.title: Freed of ice, Scandinavia and Canada rise
gree-040.text: Relieved of its ice, Scandinavia rose 9–13 millimeters a year, and the uplift set off large earthquakes about 9,000 years ago that formed new faults. In Canada, rising land had drained the Champlain Sea by about 10,000 years ago, and Hudson Bay, the Great Lakes and Fennoscandia are still rebounding.

gree-042.title: The last saber-toothed cats die out
gree-042.text: The youngest remains of North America's Smilodon fatalis, which ranged from Alberta to northwestern South America, date to 7615–7305 BCE. Its South American cousin Smilodon populator lasted a little longer, until 7129–6239 BCE at Itapipoca in Brazil, and with it the last Smilodon species died out.

gree-043.title: The American mastodon disappears
gree-043.text: Mastodons, mammoths and horses still roamed North America as recently as 10,000 years ago, but in Minnesota the giant animals were gone by about 9,000 years ago. The youngest American mastodon remains date to 7110–6810 BCE.

gree-044.title: Today's Great Barrier Reef starts to grow
gree-044.text: About 9,000 years ago, the living Great Barrier Reef is thought to have begun growing on top of an older platform.

gree-045.title: Lake Lahontan shrinks as the Great Basin dries
gree-045.text: By about 9,000 years ago, Lake Lahontan, a pluvial lake in the Great Basin, had largely vanished in its extended form. Farther south, tufa, a limestone crust laid down in lake water, records a wet period at Lake Cahuilla that ended 9,000 years before present.

gree-046.title: A proposed seawater flood into the Black Sea
gree-046.text: Some researchers propose that Mediterranean seawater burst into the Black Sea, then a freshwater lake, around 8,800 years ago, a date revised in 2003 from 7,600 years ago. The idea remains controversial, and other authors favor a gradual filling, citing water flowing out of the basin as late as 15,000 years ago.

gree-049.title: A VEI 7 blast carves Kamchatka's Kurile Lake caldera
gree-049.text: In 6460–6414 BCE a huge eruption in Kamchatka blasted out about 155 cubic kilometers of material and formed the caldera that now holds Kurile Lake. Rated VEI 7, it laid down an ignimbrite, a rock welded from hot flows of volcanic ash, and dropped ash up to 1,700 kilometers away. Two spikes of volcanic sulfate in Greenland's GISP2 ice core, around 6470 and 6476 BCE, may record it. It ranks with Fisher, Kikai and Mazama among the largest eruptions around the Pacific Ring of Fire, during an especially active spell from 6600 to 6400 BCE.

nort-001.title: The 8.2-kiloyear event: a sudden global chill
nort-001.text: Around 8,200 years ago global temperatures fell abruptly, and the cold, recorded in caves from Eurasia to southern Africa, lasted two to four centuries. In Greenland the temperature dropped 3.3 °C below the decadal average in under 20 years, and the coldest phase lasted about 60 years. A pulse of meltwater, probably from glacial lakes Agassiz and Ojibway, may have weakened the Atlantic overturning, the current system that carries warm water north, by 55–62%. Its signal in Greenland's NGRIP1 ice core, dated to 8,236 years before 2000, now marks the start of the Northgrippian.

nort-002.title: Lakes Agassiz and Ojibway empty into the sea
nort-002.text: As the last ice over Hudson Bay melted, glacial Lake Agassiz, a vast lake of meltwater, drained almost completely in its final major shift. Its neighbor Lake Ojibway, comparable in size, likely emptied at the same time, perhaps in two floods through a broken ice dam and beneath the ice. The water raised global sea level by an estimated 0.8 to 2.8 meters, and this freshwater flood is the leading suspect behind the 8.2-kiloyear cooling. Some researchers have proposed an earlier drainage, 9,900–10,000 years ago, as the trigger instead, but that idea is disputed.

nort-004.title: The Storegga Slides unleash a North Atlantic tsunami
nort-004.text: Off Norway, three submarine landslides moved about 3,500 cubic kilometers of debris along 290 kilometers of the continental shelf, among the largest slides known. An earthquake that destabilized methane clathrate, methane locked in ice within seabed sediments, is thought to have set off the collapse. Tsunami waves up to 20 meters high struck Scotland and the Faroe Islands, leaving sediment up to 29 kilometers inland and 4 meters above today's normal tide. The waves may have flooded Doggerland's last low-lying land, though their impact there is debated.

nort-005.title: Early farmers may have begun raising greenhouse gases
nort-005.text: Carbon dioxide began a marked climb about 8,000 years ago, and methane followed some 3,000 years later. Forest clearing by early farmers drove the rise, argues William Ruddiman, but critics dispute it, citing an earlier interglacial and noting that all interglacials differ.

nort-008.title: The Holocene reaches its warmest
nort-008.text: After the 8.2-kiloyear cold snap, the climate warmed to the Holocene's highest temperatures, peaking around 8,000 years BP as polar ice caps shrank to their smallest. One study finds the warmest 200 years, around 6,500 years ago, about 0.7 °C warmer than the 19th century. Rain belts shifted: Tibet's Yarlung Tsangpo valley got up to twice today's rainfall, and a stable climate helped farming take hold in China. A slow decline of 0.1–0.3 °C per millennium followed, lasting until about two centuries ago.

nort-009.title: The steppe bison makes its last stand in Siberia
nort-009.text: The steppe bison, a grazer of the mammoth steppe, survived in north-central eastern Siberia until about 8,000 years ago. Bison DNA in northeastern Siberian permafrost may push its survival to 5050–3800 BCE, and its youngest North American remains, from Yukon, date to 3628–3377 BCE.

nort-010.title: Menengai collapses in Kenya's Rift Valley
nort-010.text: Menengai, a broad shield volcano on the floor of Kenya's Rift Valley, erupted and collapsed into a caldera 12 by 8 kilometers across. The eruption is rated VEI 6, with about 70 cubic kilometers of material.

nort-011.title: Rising seas break up Sahul and strand Tasmania
nort-011.text: Post-glacial sea-level rise flooded the Bassian Plain and opened Bass Strait, cutting off Aboriginal Tasmanians, whose ancestors had walked across the land bridge about 40,000 years ago. About 8,000 years ago New Guinea also separated from mainland Australia, ending Sahul, the single landmass they had formed. Over the next 2,000 years, thousands of islands took shape in the Torres Strait and along the coast. Some sources date Tasmania's separation later, to about 6,000 years ago.

nort-006.title: The Laurentide ice sheet splits and collapses
nort-006.text: About 8,000 years ago the Laurentide ice sheet thinned and broke into two lobes, one over Quebec–Labrador and one over Keewatin. Central Asia stayed at near-glacial temperatures until the sheet collapsed around 8,000 BP. Ice pouring off the dying sheet kept North Atlantic climate erratic until 6,700 BP, and the last ice left Nunavik about 6,500 years ago. After the final melt, between 8 and 7 ka, global sea level rose much more slowly.

nort-012.title: Slowing seas let the Mississippi and Rhine deltas grow
nort-012.text: As sea-level rise slowed, the modern Mississippi delta plain began to build around 8,000–7,500 years ago, and the Dutch Rhine–Meuse delta began forming too. The Mississippi switched course every 1,000–1,500 years, building six delta complexes, and such deltas became major farming and population centers.

nort-013.title: The Irish elk dies out in western Russia
nort-013.text: The Irish elk, or giant deer, survived in western Russia until around 7,700 years ago, long after its range had shrunk dramatically. Its latest dated remains, from Kamyshlov and Maloarkhangelsk in Russia, belong to the 6th millennium BCE, and it probably died out soon after.

nort-014.title: Mount Mazama blows apart and leaves Crater Lake
nort-014.text: Oregon's Mount Mazama, active again after 20,000 quiet years, ended in a VEI 7 eruption and collapsed into the caldera that now holds Crater Lake. The USGS calls it the largest explosive eruption in the Cascades in the past million years, with an ash column 48 kilometers high that reached the stratosphere. Ash fell on eight western US states and three Canadian provinces, and the orange Mazama Ash, found even in Greenland's ice, became a standard dating marker. Its aerosols may have cooled mid- to high northern latitudes by 0.6–0.7 °C for one to three years, and ashfall emptied one Alberta site for about 200 years.

nort-015.title: Farming spreads from the Aegean across Europe
nort-015.text: Fast sea-level rise, the 8.2-kiloyear cooling and lost coastal land may have helped push the Neolithic Revolution, the shift to farming, into Europe. Farming appears in the Aegean by c. 6500 BCE and took about 2,500 years, 8500–6000 BP, to reach Britain, with the Baltic following around 5500 BP. La Marmotta, an Early Neolithic lakeshore village in Italy, dates to about 5700 BCE, and from about 7,500 years ago farmers crossed from Iberia into Northwest Africa. In Central Europe, pollen records first show human impact from 7,500 BP, and it becomes substantial after 6,300 BP.

nort-016.title: The sea drowns Sundaland's last lowlands
nort-016.text: Between 7,500 and 6,200 BP a marine transgression, an advance of the sea over land, drowned the Gulf of Thailand, which had been dry land. It was part of the flooding of Sundaland, Southeast Asia's exposed Sunda Shelf, a submergence under way since 18,000 years ago that continued until about 5000 BCE.

nort-017.title: The giant ground sloth Megatherium dies out
nort-017.text: Megatherium americanum, a ground sloth up to 6 meters long and 4 tonnes in weight, died out in Argentina around 5370 BCE. Its latest remains, at Campo Laborde, show signs of human hunting and butchery, while habitat models suggest its range had already shrunk and broken apart.

nort-018.title: Kikai's Akahoya super-eruption shakes southern Japan
nort-018.text: Japan's submarine Kikai Caldera produced the Akahoya eruption, a VEI 7 event and one of only six confirmed eruptions of that size in the Holocene. Pyroclastic flows, racing avalanches of hot gas and ash, crossed the sea to southern Kyushu up to 100 kilometers away, and ash fell as far as Hokkaido. A 2024 study put the ejecta at 332–457 cubic kilometers, which would make it the largest eruption of the past 11,700 years. Two large earthquakes and a megatsunami struck during the eruption, and the early Jōmon culture of southern Kyushu took nearly 1,000 years to recover.

nort-019.title: Twin craters scar southeastern Estonia
nort-019.text: Two craters about 80 meters and 50 meters wide formed together at Ilumetsa in southeastern Estonia, probably blasted out by a meteorite. No meteorite fragments or shock features, the marks an impact leaves in rock, have been found, so the impact origin is probable rather than proven.

nort-020.title: An eruption carves the caldera of Lake Mashū
nort-020.text: An eruption on Hokkaido, rated VEI 6 with about 18.6 cubic kilometers of material, created the caldera that now holds Lake Mashū. The Global Volcanism Program dates it to 5550 ± 100 BCE, about 500 years older than the rounded figure of 7,000 years ago.

nort-022.title: The long cooling of the Neoglacial begins
nort-022.text: About 6,000 years ago the post-glacial warming trend ended and a long cooling began. This Neoglaciation, a time when glaciers advanced or re-formed after the Holocene Climatic Optimum, has no single clear start. In East Asia it coincided with a major weakening of the summer monsoon, and western North America's vanished mountain glaciers re-formed shortly before 5000 BP. Orbital models suggest the cooling trend would continue for another 23,000 years.

nort-024.title: The rising sea levels off at last
nort-024.text: Global sea level, rising steadily since 20,000 years ago, leveled off about 6,000 years ago and has stayed fairly stable since. The rise slowed from over 10 millimeters a year to under 1, though one source puts the end of rapid rise at about 4,200 years ago. In places the sea overshot today's level: off Santa Catarina, Brazil, it peaked about 2.1 meters above present 5,800–5,000 BP. The final stage of the rise drowned the last land bridges, such as the southern Kuril link to Hokkaido around 6,000 BP.

nort-021.title: The green Sahara dries into desert
nort-021.text: The African humid period ended about 6,000–5,000 years ago, often put at 5,500 BP, and the green Sahara began turning into desert. North of the monsoon belt the drying came in a single step within 500 years, and dust blowing off Mauritania rose sharply within a few centuries. Shifts in Earth's orbit cut rainfall and raised temperatures, though overgrazing has also been proposed as a trigger. As lakes dried and plants vanished, North Africa's population fell within a millennium, and many inner-Arabian settlements were abandoned about 5,300 years ago.

nort-025.title: Pinatubo's Crow Valley eruptions dwarf those of 1991
nort-025.text: Mount Pinatubo's Crow Valley eruptive period produced pyroclastic flows two to three times larger than those of its 1991 eruption. It is rated VEI 6, with about 12 cubic kilometers of material.

nort-026.title: The 5.9-kiloyear drought drives herders to the Nile
nort-026.text: Around 3900 BCE an aridification event, a sharp turn to drier conditions, struck the Sahara. Pastoral herders were forced into the Nile valley to survive, and the drying may also have driven the spread of farming in the Sahel. The event matches Bond event 4, one of eight North Atlantic episodes when drifting ice carried rock far out to sea. By 3500–3000 BCE the Sahara desert had re-formed.

nort-027.title: The last mammoths of St. Paul Island run dry
nort-027.text: A small population of woolly mammoths survived on St. Paul Island, Alaska, until about 3750 BCE, long after their mainland relatives vanished. The island shows no sign of prehistoric people, and bone dates point to an end around 5,600 years ago, most likely as fresh water ran short.

nort-028.title: The Piora Oscillation chills the Alps
nort-028.text: From 5,600 to 5,000 years ago the Piora Oscillations, two cold spells named after Switzerland's Val Piora, brought cooling, erratic rainfall and spreading Arctic sea ice. Around 5,375 BP a sudden rise of Lake Constance forced people to abandon the Arbon-Bleiche 3 lakeshore village.

nort-029.title: Ötzi the Iceman dies on an Alpine pass
nort-029.text: About 5,300 years ago Ötzi was killed on the Tisenjoch pass, on today's Austrian–Italian border, carrying both a copper axe and a flint knife. Glacier ice at about 3,210 meters preserved him as the oldest known human mummy, with einkorn and barley grains beside him that reflect Neolithic farming.

nort-031.title: A meteorite fall leaves seven craters near Poznań
nort-031.text: A meteorite fall made a field of seven craters near today's Poznań, Poland, the largest about 100 meters wide.

nort-032.title: Mount Rainier's summit collapses into the Osceola Mudflow
nort-032.text: About 5,000 years ago a huge part of Mount Rainier slid away, taking about 490 meters off its summit. The debris avalanche fed the Osceola Mudflow, a flood of volcanic mud that reached the sites of today's Tacoma and south Seattle.

nort-033.title: A disputed impact crater under the Indian Ocean
nort-033.text: The Holocene Impact Working Group argues that a 29-kilometer undersea feature in the southwest Indian Ocean is an impact crater about 5,000 years old. Its backers link it to floods that affected Sumerian civilization, but other geologists dispute that it is an impact crater at all.

nort-030.title: Iron meteorites rain down on Campo del Cielo
nort-030.text: A shower of iron meteorites fell on the plains bordering Argentina's Chaco Province, scattering the field now called Campo del Cielo.

nort-034.title: A shattered meteorite blasts the Henbury craters
nort-034.text: A meteorite broke apart and blasted more than a dozen craters in central Australia no earlier than about 4,700 years ago. Among the best-preserved small crater fields, it is also one of the few impacts in a populated area.

nort-035.title: Cerro Blanco unleashes the Central Andes' largest known eruption
nort-035.text: Cerro Blanco in Argentina produced the largest known eruption of the Central Andes, a VEI 7 event that formed its youngest caldera and thick ignimbrites. It released about 110 cubic kilometers of tephra, the rock fragments and ash a volcano hurls out, comparable to the largest Holocene eruptions. Its tephra is now a regional time marker, and the ground beneath the volcano is still subsiding, or sinking, perhaps as a lasting effect.

megh-001.title: The 4.2-kiloyear drought parches three continents
megh-001.text: Around 2200 BC a severe drought set in across North Africa, the Middle East, India and midcontinental North America, and it probably lasted a century. Models tie it to a sharp weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation, which carries warm water north, and a southward lurch of the tropical rain belt. As Nile floods failed and irrigated fields salted up, it is thought to have helped topple Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Akkadian Empire and China's Liangzhu culture. A stalagmite in India's Mawmluh Cave marks it as the Meghalayan Age's base, a choice critics dispute, arguing the drought was neither global nor neatly timed.

megh-005.title: The last mammoths die out on Wrangel Island
megh-005.text: A small population of dwarf woolly mammoths clung on at Wrangel Island, in the Siberian Arctic, until about 4,000 years ago. They outlasted the mainland mammoths by some 6,000 years and were the last of their kind anywhere. The youngest remains date to 1795–1675 BCE, and their end did not coincide with human arrival, because the island had been a human-free refuge.

megh-004.title: Africa's long wet phase ends, lake by lake
megh-004.text: About 4,000 years ago a major environmental change swept the tropics, and the drying of East Africa peaked. The Blue Nile's flow fell, and its sediment load rose as plants thinned across its catchment between 4,000 and 3,600 years ago. In the Sahara, Lake Teli dried out completely about 4,200 years ago, and groundwater-fed Lake Yoa had turned hypersaline, saltier than seawater, by 4,000. Nearer the equator, Africa's humid period ended later, between 4,000 and 2,500 years ago; at Lake Malawi, drying began only about 1,000 years ago.

megh-007.title: Mount St. Helens fires off its Yn eruption
megh-007.text: Around 1860 BCE Mount St. Helens erupted at VEI 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, the standard scale of eruption size. Its roughly 15 km³ of tephra, the shattered rock and ash a volcano hurls into the air, is known as the Yn or Smith Creek layer.

megh-008.title: Vesuvius buries Bronze Age settlements in the Avellino eruption
megh-008.text: Vesuvius exploded around 1800 BCE in the VEI 6 Avellino eruption, much larger than its eruption of 79 CE. It destroyed several Bronze Age settlements, and near Nola pumice and ash buried a hastily abandoned village and thousands of footprints of fleeing people.

megh-009.title: A weakening monsoon dries the Indus Valley
megh-009.text: The Indus Valley grew markedly cooler and drier from about 1800 BCE as the monsoon weakened. The monsoon-fed Ghaggar-Hakra rivers had already turned seasonal as the Indus civilization waned, and most of its cities were abandoned by about 1700 BCE.

megh-010.title: Alaska's Aniakchak erupts and chills the globe
megh-010.text: Alaska's Mount Aniakchak blew out about 50 km³ of material in a VEI 6 eruption, which a revised Greenland ice-core chronology of 2019 dates to 1628 BC. Its ash turned up in a big Greenland spike of volcanic sulfate long blamed on Thera, and frost-scarred tree rings record extreme global cooling in 1627 BC.

megh-011.title: Thera explodes and buries Minoan Akrotiri
megh-011.text: Around 1600 BC a catastrophic Plinian eruption, one driving a tall, sustained ash column skyward, devastated the Aegean island of Thera, or Santorini. Rated VEI 7, it ejected some 28–41 km³ measured as solid rock, leaving a caldera, a vast sunken crater, that now forms the island's central bay. It destroyed the Minoan town of Akrotiri, struck Crete and nearby islands with quakes and tsunamis, and left ash layers at nearly every eastern Mediterranean site. Its date is fiercely contested: radiocarbon favors the 17th–16th century BC, while archaeology points to about 1550–1480 BC.

megh-014.title: The last ground sloths fade from the Caribbean
megh-014.text: Ground sloths had vanished from the mainland about 11,000 years ago, but they hung on in Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, possibly until 1550 BCE. Like Wrangel Island's mammoths, these island relicts were the last survivors of their group.

megh-015.title: South America's litopterns may linger into the late Holocene
megh-015.text: Litopterns, an order of native South American hoofed mammals that arose 62.5 million years ago, are usually thought to have died out about 12,000 years ago. A 2025 study dated a Xenorhinotherium specimen to 3,493–4,217 years ago by radiocarbon, a clock based on decaying carbon, but that late survival rests on a single date.

megh-016.title: A meteor blasts nine craters into Estonia
megh-016.text: A meteor of 20–80 tonnes broke up over Saaremaa, Estonia, blasting nine craters up to 110 m wide and burning vegetation 6 km away. One of the few impacts in a populated area, it struck no earlier than about 1530–1450 BC, though published ages vary by up to 6,000 years.

megh-017.title: Thylacines and devils vanish from mainland Australia
megh-017.text: Thylacines, the dog-like marsupial predators also called Tasmanian tigers, died out on mainland Australia around 1277–1229 BCE, and the latest mainland remains of Tasmanian devils share that date. Competition with human hunters and dingoes is the likely cause, perhaps aided by a warming climate, and both animals survived only in Tasmania.

megh-019.title: Iceland's Hekla 3 eruption stunts trees in Ireland
megh-019.text: Hekla's H3 eruption, one of Iceland's largest in the Holocene, hurled about 7.3 km³ of rock into the atmosphere at VEI 5. Its traces reach Scottish peat bogs, Irish tree rings show a decade of stunted growth, and it probably chilled northern lands for a few years.

megh-020.title: Mount Pinatubo erupts in its Maraunot period
megh-020.text: Around 1050 BCE Mount Pinatubo, on the Philippine island of Luzon, erupted at VEI 6 and ejected about 12.5 km³ of material during its Maraunot eruptive period.

megh-023.title: The Sun goes quiet in the Homeric Minimum
megh-023.text: From about 800 to 600 BCE the Sun sank into the Homeric Minimum, a deep, persistent lull in solar activity. It is linked to a cold spell in western North America and Europe, though whether that spell was wetter or drier is still debated.

megh-024.title: The central Sahara turns to desert for good
megh-024.text: By 2,700 years ago the central Sahara had become a desert, and it has stayed one ever since. At Libya's Wadi Tanezzuft, water stored in dunes and the Tassili mountains had kept rivers flowing until then, when they finally stopped. Arabia's long drying, under way since 7,000–5,000 years ago, also ran until 2,700 years ago. Brief humid spells still returned, as in Roman North Africa and around the Dead Sea between 500 BCE and 300 CE.

megh-025.title: Raoul Island blows open the Denham caldera
megh-025.text: About 2,200 years ago a VEI 6 blast of dacite, sticky silica-rich magma, tore open Raoul Island's 6.5 by 4 km Denham caldera, in the Kermadecs. Rivaling Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, it left the Fleetwood tephra; at one spot 40 m of pumice lies under 80 m of welded ash-flow rock.

megh-026.title: Europe basks in the Roman Warm Period
megh-026.text: Europe and the North Atlantic enjoyed unusually warm weather in the Roman Warm Period, and Alpine glaciers single out 100–400 CE as markedly warm. Yet a 2019 analysis of a much larger set of climate records found it was regional, not a globally coherent episode.

megh-027.title: Lake Chad's northern basin dries into a dust factory
megh-027.text: Lake Chad shrank to about 5% of its former size, and its deep northern Bodélé basin, cut off from the Chari River, dried out completely. That lakebed, dry since about 2,000–1,000 years ago, is now the largest single source of dust on Earth.

megh-028.title: Giant lemurs and elephant birds vanish from Madagascar
megh-028.text: At least 17 giant lemur species vanished from Madagascar, nearly all after people colonized the island about 2,000 years ago. The biggest animals went soon after people arrived, while human-set fires cleared forest and prolonged hunting finished others as settlers spread about 1,000 years ago. Malagasy hippos and the giant, flightless elephant birds probably died out in 750–1050 CE, though one hippo bone about 100 years old hints a few lingered. Some giant lemurs lasted into modern times, Palaeopropithecus until about 510 years ago, making this one of history's most recent extinctions of very large animals.

megh-029.title: Alaska's Okmok plunges the north into deep cold
megh-029.text: In 43 BCE Alaska's Okmok volcano blew out a new caldera at VEI 6, hurling 15–16 million tonnes of sulfur into the stratosphere, above the weather. Along with an earlier eruption, it made 43 BCE and the following two years among the coldest in 2,500 years, with famine and failed Nile floods.

megh-030.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum
megh-030.text: In 79 CE Vesuvius erupted at VEI 5, and collapsing ash columns sent pyroclastic currents, ground-hugging avalanches of scorching gas and rock, over Herculaneum and Pompeii. The eruption of about 3.2 km³ killed more than 2,000 people and became the benchmark for other Plinian eruptions.

megh-031.title: Taupō's Hatepe eruption scorches New Zealand
megh-031.text: In 232 CE, give or take 10 years, Taupō Volcano in New Zealand unleashed its most recent major eruption, the Hatepe. It ejected roughly 100–120 km³ of material, 30 km³ of it within a few minutes, making it one of the largest eruptions of the last 5,000 years. Its pyroclastic flow was hot enough to burn forest 160 km from Lake Taupō. It struck before people settled New Zealand, and the rings of a tree it killed now help fix its date.

megh-032.title: Kamchatka's Ksudach collapses into a new caldera
megh-032.text: Around 240 CE Ksudach volcano in Kamchatka erupted at VEI 6, ejecting 18–19 km³ of material. The volcano collapsed into a 4 by 6.5 km crater, now called Caldera V.

megh-033.title: Ilopango's Tierra Blanca Joven eruption rocks El Salvador
megh-033.text: El Salvador's Ilopango produced the Tierra Blanca Joven eruption, a VEI 6 blast of an estimated 37–82 km³, among the Holocene's most intense. Some evidence once identified it as the 539/540 eruption behind the Late Antique Little Ice Age, but a newer study dates it to 431.

megh-035.title: A mystery eruption turns summer cold across the north
megh-035.text: A large eruption of unknown source, rated VEI 6–7, brought extreme weather in 535–536 CE, and European summers fell up to 2.5 °C below normal. Krakatoa was once blamed, but drilling in the Sunda Strait ruled out an eruption there that year; the climate shock is compared with Tambora and Samalas.

megh-034.title: The Late Antique Little Ice Age chills a century
megh-034.text: Three large eruptions, growing sea ice and a deep lull in the Sun's output kept the Northern Hemisphere cold for a century, from 536 to about 660. Scandinavia may have lost up to half its people, and the cold coincided with the Plague of Justinian, which began in 541.

megh-037.title: Mount Churchill spreads the White River Ash
megh-037.text: Around 847 CE Alaska's Mount Churchill erupted at VEI 6, ejecting about 50 km³ and laying down the eastern lobe of the White River Ash. An earlier VEI 6 eruption, about 145–345 CE, spread the northern lobe, and together they blanket northwestern Canada.

megh-039.title: Paektu Mountain unleashes its Millennium eruption
megh-039.text: In late 946 CE Paektu Mountain, on the China–North Korea border, produced the VEI 6 Millennium eruption, one of the largest of the last few thousand years. Tree rings counted from the 774–775 Miyake spike, a sudden jump in radiocarbon, pin the year, and ashfall records from Nara suggest it began about 2 November.

megh-040.title: A patchy medieval warmth comes and goes
megh-040.text: From about 950 to 1250, a warm spell called the Medieval Warm Period, or Medieval Climate Anomaly, preceded the Little Ice Age. The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool, hot surface water between the two oceans, stayed warm and salty from 1000 to 1400, near today's temperatures, then cooled. Yet the warmth was not globally synchronous, and the twentieth century was warmer still, so the term is of limited use for hemispheric or global trends. The warmth may have sent extra fresh water into the North Atlantic, possibly disrupting ocean circulation ahead of the Little Ice Age.

megh-042.title: Samalas tears open Lombok and chills the world
megh-042.text: In 1257 Samalas, on the Indonesian island of Lombok, erupted at VEI 7, one of the largest eruptions of the Holocene. Columns rose 38–43 km, and pyroclastic flows buried much of Lombok, destroyed the city of Pamatan and left the 6–7 km Segara Anak caldera. Its sulfate aerosols, fine acid droplets that reflect sunlight, cooled the climate by about 0.7 °C in 1258 and 1.2 °C in 1259. Floods, crop failures and famine struck Europe and Japan, though their scale is still debated, and the eruption may have helped trigger the Little Ice Age.

megh-045.title: Quilotoa wakes after 14,000 years and collapses
megh-045.text: After 14,000 years asleep, Ecuador's Quilotoa erupted at VEI 6 in 1280, leaving a 3 km caldera and sending lahars, or volcanic mudflows, to the Pacific. Together with Samalas, it is linked to a cold, dry interval on the South American Altiplano between 1200 and 1450.

megh-046.title: The Little Ice Age grips the North Atlantic world
megh-046.text: The Little Ice Age, a regional cooling strongest around the North Atlantic, ran from about 1300 to about 1850, though it was never a true global ice age. Across the Northern Hemisphere the chill was modest, less than 1 °C below late twentieth-century levels, yet mountain glaciers advanced in Europe, Alaska, New Zealand and Patagonia. Eruptions, a weak Sun, shifting ocean currents and human depopulation have all been proposed as causes, and climate models point to volcanism as the main driver. Onset came between 1200 and 1400 in the north and two centuries later in the south; the IPCC, the UN climate panel, puts the coldest stretch at 1450–1850.

megh-048.title: The last West Indian giant tortoise vanishes
megh-048.text: Chelonoidis alburyorum, the last of the West Indian giant tortoises, vanished one island at a time. It lasted on the Abacos until 1170 CE, on Grand Turk until 1200 and on Middle Caicos until about 1400.

megh-051.title: Hunters wipe out New Zealand's moa
megh-051.text: Moa, nine species of wingless birds up to about 3.6 m tall, were New Zealand's largest land animals and its dominant plant-eaters until the Māori arrived. Hunting, and to a lesser degree forest clearance, wiped them out, probably within 100 years of human settlement. By 1445 every moa was gone, along with Haast's eagle, the giant raptor that had preyed on them. Ovens near the mouth of the Waitaki River alone held the remains of an estimated 29,000–90,000 birds.

megh-052.title: A mystery eruption deepens the Little Ice Age
megh-052.text: An undocumented eruption in 1452/1453, possibly at Kuwae in Vanuatu, is known mainly from its climate signal, and one table rates it VEI 7. It set off a second pulse of Little Ice Age cooling, giving Central Europe seven cold summers in the 1450s.

megh-056.title: Swiss glaciers surge in the Grindelwald Fluctuation
megh-056.text: From the 1560s to the 1630s, glaciers at Grindelwald, Switzerland, advanced markedly as temperatures fell 1–2 °C below twentieth-century averages, among the lowest of the Holocene. Eruptions of Colima, Nevado del Ruiz and Huaynaputina likely contributed, though the cooling began about 15 years before the first of them.

megh-057.title: Huaynaputina's blast brings frost from Sweden to Japan
megh-057.text: On 19 February 1600 Huaynaputina in southern Peru began the largest eruption ever witnessed in South America, rated VEI 6. It killed perhaps 1,000–1,500 people and buried the land around it under 2 m of volcanic rock. Its sulfur cut incoming sunlight by about 1.9 watts per square meter, making the summer of 1601 one of the Northern Hemisphere's coldest in six centuries. Frosts and failed harvests followed from Sweden to China and Japan, and the eruption may have helped bring on the coldest phase of the Little Ice Age.

megh-058.title: A dip in carbon dioxide, perhaps from regrowing forests
megh-058.text: Atmospheric CO2 fell around 1610, perhaps because conquest and disease had killed up to 90% of Indigenous Americans and forest reclaimed their fields. Critics doubt that pre-Columbian farming cleared forest on a modern scale, and Huaynaputina's eruption may also have contributed, so the cause remains debated.

megh-059.title: The last wild aurochs dies in a Polish forest
megh-059.text: The aurochs, the wild ancestor of most modern cattle, once roamed Eurasia, North Africa and India. Hunting, forest clearance, competition with livestock and cattle diseases left a single herd in Poland's Jaktorów forest, where the last animal died in 1627.

megh-060.title: Sunspots almost vanish in the Maunder Minimum
megh-060.text: From 1645 to 1715 solar activity sank very low: sunspots were minimal, and deposits of carbon-14 and beryllium-10 increased. It fell in the coldest part of the Little Ice Age, yet northern cooling began earlier, and climate models make volcanoes the bigger driver.

megh-062.title: The dodo disappears from Mauritius
megh-062.text: The dodo, a large flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius, was last seen in 1662, ravaged by hungry sailors and, probably worse, by introduced pigs. It became an early poster species for human-caused extinction, and other Mascarene birds followed, including the Réunion ibis, last recorded in 1763.

megh-063.title: Cascadia's great quake sends a tsunami to Japan
megh-063.text: Around 9 pm on 26 January 1700, a magnitude 9.0 quake ruptured 1,000 km of North America's Cascadia subduction zone, where one plate dives under another. Coasts from British Columbia to Oregon dropped up to 2 m, and tsunami sand buried 'ghost forests' of drowned red cedar with final rings from 1699. About ten hours later the tsunami struck Honshu, Japan, where it was recorded as an 'orphan tsunami', a wave with no earthquake felt locally. Coastal peoples' oral traditions recall the shaking and saltwater floods; it remains the zone's last megathrust earthquake, the giant kind that strikes where plates converge.

megh-065.title: Methane in the air rises 2.6-fold
megh-065.text: Since about 1750 atmospheric methane has climbed from 722 parts per billion to 1,936 by 2025, a 2.6-fold rise to the highest level in at least 800,000 years. Human activities caused almost all of it; methane is only 3% of greenhouse emissions by mass but about 23% of their warming effect. Growth resumed in 2007 after a flat decade and hit a record annual jump in 2021, with isotopes pointing mainly to microbial sources such as wetlands and farming. From 2010 to 2019 methane caused about 0.5 °C, roughly 30%, of observed global warming.

megh-066.title: The Great Lisbon earthquake kills about 100,000 people
megh-066.text: On 1 November 1755 the Great Lisbon earthquake struck, one of the most destructive in history, killing around 100,000 people. It heads the list of large earthquakes and tsunamis that the Azores–Gibraltar fault zone has produced since records began in the 1700s.

megh-067.title: Hunters erase Steller's sea cow in 27 years
megh-067.text: The largest known sirenian, a cousin of manatees, Steller's sea cow reached 10 m and 5–10 tonnes and survived as a relict in the Bering Sea's Commander Islands. Discovered in 1741, it was hunted for meat and hides until it was gone by 1768, just 27 years later.

megh-068.title: The Industrial Revolution starts warming the planet
megh-068.text: Around 1780, with the Industrial Revolution and the steam engine, large-scale greenhouse gas emissions began to warm Earth. Carbon dioxide had stayed near 280 ppm for 10,000 years before the mid-18th century, and it has since risen 54%. Antarctic ice cores record the highest greenhouse gas levels from this point on, and the IPCC uses 1750 as its pre-industrial baseline. It is one proposed start of the Anthropocene, a suggested new epoch defined by human impact, though people had already reshaped much of Earth's landscape.

megh-069.title: Laki's fissure floods Iceland with lava and poison
megh-069.text: From June 1783 to February 1784, a 40 km crack in Iceland called the Laki fissure poured out about 15 km³ of lava over 565 km². It was one of history's largest effusive eruptions, the kind that pours out lava rather than exploding, and it released about 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide. Fluorine and chlorine poisoning devastated farming, and about a fifth of Iceland's people died. Its sulfate signal in northern ice cores exceeds even Samalas's, its sulfur cooled the climate substantially, and famine cost Egypt a sixth of its people in 1784.

megh-071.title: Tambora unleashes the most powerful eruption on record
megh-071.text: Tambora, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, produced the most powerful eruption in recorded history in April 1815, a VEI 7 that ejected 37–45 km³ of material. At its climax on 10 April it drove a column 45 km high, and it remains the most recent confirmed VEI 7 eruption. About 10,000–11,000 people died directly, and 49,000–90,000 more died of famine and disease on Sumbawa, Lombok and Bali. Its sulfur dioxide formed a veil of sulfate in the stratosphere, seen in 1815 as a persistent 'dry fog' that dimmed the Sun.

megh-072.title: The Year Without a Summer brings June snow
megh-072.text: Tambora's aerosols lowered global temperatures by about 0.4–0.7 °C, and 1816 became the 'Year Without a Summer' across the Northern Hemisphere. Frost and snow struck New England and Quebec in June, ruining most North American crops, while Europe's harvests failed in the worst famine of the nineteenth century. India's monsoon failed, and a new strain of cholera spread from Bengal. With help from an eruption around 1809 and the Dalton Minimum, a spell of weak sunlight, the 1810s became the coldest decade on record.

megh-073.title: A mystery eruption is traced to the Kuril Islands
megh-073.text: A powerful explosive eruption in the northern summer of 1831 may have come from Zavaritski Caldera on Simushir, in the Kuril Islands. Its radiative forcing, the change it made to Earth's energy balance, matches Pinatubo's in 1991 and may explain cooling in 1831–1833, ending the volcanic cold spell of 1809–1831.

megh-075.title: Glaciers retreat as the Little Ice Age ends
megh-075.text: As the Little Ice Age ended in the late nineteenth century, glaciers began a strong retreat after about 1850. Since then Austria has lost 40% of its glacier cover and Switzerland 30%, and Alpine ice shrank from 1,817 km² in 1876 to 1,342 km² by 1973. By 1879 the ice of Alaska's Glacier Bay had pulled back 77 km. Photographs track the shrinking, and by 1993 only 27% of Glacier National Park's 1850 ice cover remained.

megh-076.title: The long-quiet seas start rising faster
megh-076.text: After 3,000 years of near stability, sea level began to rise faster, an onset variously dated between 1850 and 1900. Tide gauges, later joined by satellites, show the global mean rose 19.5 cm from 1870 to 2004, about 1.44 mm a year. Between 1901 and 2018 the seas rose 15–25 cm, faster than in any century for at least 4,000 years. Since the 1970s they have climbed 2.3 mm a year.

megh-078.title: Krakatoa's blast is heard 4,800 kilometers away
megh-078.text: On 26–27 August 1883 Krakatoa, in Indonesia's Sunda Strait, exploded at VEI 6 in one of history's most violent eruptions, ejecting about 25 km³ of rock. The blasts were heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues, and barographs worldwide, which record air pressure, logged the pressure wave seven times. Tsunamis running up to 41 m killed at least 36,417 people, and two-thirds of the island was destroyed, leaving a caldera. Ash rose 80 km, that year's northern summer cooled by 0.4 °C on average, and the sterilized islands became a classic case of life rebuilding from scratch.

megh-079.title: Extinctions soar far above the natural rate
megh-079.text: No earlier than about 1900, extinctions began running at over 1,000 times the background rate, the natural pace of loss, and that rate is still rising. Some call this Earth's sixth major extinction, though estimates of its rate range from 100 to 1,000 times background and remain disputed. Over 322 species are often cited as lost to human activity since the Industrial Revolution, perhaps 500 of them vertebrates, mostly after 1900. Islands suffer most: 95% of bird extinctions since the late 15th century struck island species.

megh-080.title: Santa María erupts for the first time on record
megh-080.text: Guatemala's Santa María had its first recorded eruption in October 1902, ejecting about 5.5 km³ of magma, or molten rock, in two days at VEI 6. It killed 7,000–13,000 people and ranks with Novarupta in 1912 and Pinatubo in 1991 among the three largest eruptions of the 20th century.

megh-081.title: An airburst flattens the Siberian forest at Tunguska
megh-081.text: On 30 June 1908 a huge explosion over the taiga, Siberia's vast northern forest, flattened about 2,150 km² of trees near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River. Scientists blame a 50–60 m space rock that burst 5–10 km up, releasing about 10–15 megatons, though whether it was an asteroid or a comet is debated. The shock wave killed at least three people and registered worldwide, and models suggest it cut ozone, the gas that screens out ultraviolet light, by 35–45%. The most violent impact event of modern times, it may have left a fragment's crater at nearby Lake Cheko, though sediment studies disagree.

megh-082.title: Novarupta fills the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes
megh-082.text: From 6 June 1912 Novarupta, on the Alaska Peninsula, produced the 20th century's largest eruption, a 60-hour VEI 6 outburst of 13–15 km³ of ash. Magma drained from beneath Mount Katmai, whose summit collapsed, and deep pyroclastic flows filled the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes.

megh-083.title: Martha dies and the passenger pigeon is gone
megh-083.text: Habitat loss and mass hunting for a meat industry destroyed the passenger pigeon, once perhaps 40% of all birds in North America. Martha, the last known bird, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, 20 years after the species had vanished from the wild.

megh-084.title: The last known thylacine dies in Hobart Zoo
megh-084.text: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, survived only in Tasmania, where the last confirmed wild one was killed in 1931. The last known animal died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936, though a 2023 analysis of sightings suggests the species lingered for decades.

megh-086.title: An iron meteorite showers the Sikhote-Alin Mountains
megh-086.text: More than 23 tonnes of meteoritic iron fell on the Sikhote-Alin Mountains of the Soviet Far East on 12 February 1947. Its fragments scattered across about 1.3 km² and blasted craters up to 26 m wide.

megh-088.title: The Atlantic's overturning current may be slowing
megh-088.text: Reconstructions suggest the Atlantic's overturning circulation weakened by roughly 15–20% after the mid-twentieth century, perhaps under ocean warming and Greenland meltwater. Other observations and analyses find no clear decline, and scientists still argue over how much of any change is climate-driven rather than natural.

megh-089.title: Carbon dioxide turns the oceans more acidic
megh-089.text: Between 1950 and 2026 the average pH of the ocean surface, a scale on which lower means more acidic, fell from about 8.15 to 8.05. That small step means roughly 26% more hydrogen ions, the particles that make water acidic. Human carbon dioxide is the main cause, and today's pH and its rate of change are unprecedented for at least 26,000 years. Falling pH speeds the dissolving of calcium carbonate, the mineral that mollusks, single-celled foraminifera and other shell-builders need.

megh-090.title: Fossil fuels drive rapid global warming
megh-090.text: Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels have warmed the whole planet: the global average rose from 14 °C in 1951–1980 to 15 °C in 2013–2017. The ocean is about 0.7 °C warmer than in 1950, a warming that has helped raise sea level by more than 15 cm. The Arctic warmed faster than most regions and land twice as fast as ocean, while after 1990 the South Pole warmed at triple the global rate. The results include more extreme weather, thawing permafrost, marine heatwaves, and oceans that are losing oxygen and growing more acidic.

megh-091.title: A magnitude 9.0 quake rocks Kamchatka
megh-091.text: On 5 November 1952 a magnitude 9.0 megathrust earthquake ruptured the Kuril–Kamchatka subduction zone, the most powerful quake ever recorded in Russia. Its tsunami struck the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka with waves 15–18 m high at Severo-Kurilsk, Russia's deadliest and most damaging tsunami.

megh-092.title: Bomb fallout marks the Great Acceleration in sediment
megh-092.text: After World War II, population, economic growth, pollution and resource use all began rising at a dramatic rate, a surge called the Great Acceleration. Since about 1950 humans have doubled Earth's fixed nitrogen, the form plants can use, and cut off almost a fifth of river sediment from the sea. Atomic-bomb tests scattered radionuclides, radioactive forms of elements such as cesium-137 and plutonium, into sediments and glacial ice worldwide, with levels peaking around 1965. In the mud of Crawford Lake, Ontario, a plutonium spike from hydrogen-bomb tests marks 1952, alongside carbon particles and nitrates from fossil fuels and fertilizers.

megh-094.title: West Antarctica warms and sheds its ice
megh-094.text: West Antarctica warmed by about 2.4 °C between 1958 and 2012, a change attributed to rising greenhouse gases, and warming seawater is melting its ice shelves. Its ice loss rose from 53 billion tonnes (Gt) a year in 1992 to 159 Gt in 2017, adding about 7.6 mm to global sea level.

megh-093.title: Mauna Loa's Keeling Curve tracks the CO2 climb
megh-093.text: From March 1958, the Keeling Curve of measurements on Mauna Loa showed carbon dioxide climbing fast, from 313 ppm to 406 ppm by November 2018. On 9 May 2013 the daily reading passed 400 ppm, a level probably not reached since the mid-Pliocene, 2 to 4 million years ago.

megh-095.title: Chile's Valdivia earthquake is the largest ever recorded
megh-095.text: The largest earthquake ever recorded, of magnitude 9.4–9.6, struck southern Chile on 22 May 1960, where the Nazca plate sinks beneath the continent. Its tsunami reached 25 m on the Chilean coast and 10.7 m at Hilo, Hawaii, 10,000 km away, and two days later the Cordón Caulle volcano began erupting.

megh-097.title: North America's mightiest quake heaves up Alaska's coast
megh-097.text: In 1964 a magnitude 9.2 megathrust earthquake shook southern Alaska for 4 minutes 38 seconds, the most powerful ever recorded in North America. Land rose across 520,000 km², by as much as 13–15 m on Montague Island, and tsunamis ran up 67 m; about 139 people died. The shaking collapsed weak clay beds left by ancient Lake Atna, setting off catastrophic landslides in Anchorage. Its seismic waves set water sloshing in seiches, standing waves in enclosed basins, as far away as Puerto Rico.

megh-098.title: Wildlife populations plunge by almost 70%
megh-098.text: After 1970, monitored populations of vertebrate wildlife fell by almost 70% on average, driven mainly by agriculture and fishing. Land-use change, overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species all played a part, and migratory freshwater fish declined by 76%. In 1987 the death of the last Kauaʻi ʻōʻō ended an entire bird family, the Hawaiian honeyeaters. In China's Yangtze River, the Chinese paddlefish was last recorded in 2003, and the baiji river dolphin was declared extinct in 2006, the loss of a whole genus.

megh-101.title: A fungal plague drives amphibians to extinction
megh-101.text: Chytridiomycosis, a fungal disease spread by travel and the wildlife trade, has driven steep declines in over 500 amphibian species and perhaps 90 extinctions. Among its victims are Australia's gastric-brooding frogs, gone by the mid-1980s, and Costa Rica's golden toad, last seen in 1989.

megh-100.title: Arctic sea ice shrinks by more than half
megh-100.text: Satellites have tracked Arctic sea ice since 1979, and it has declined by over 50%, with losses accelerating to 4.7% per decade in the early 21st century. The September minimum hit a record 3.39 million km² in 2012, smashing the 2007 record of 4.16 million km². Ice at least four years old fell from 26% of the cover in 1988 to 7% by 2013, while overall thickness dropped 66% over six decades. Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average, and its melt season has grown five days longer each decade.

megh-102.title: Mount St. Helens loses its flank
megh-102.text: On 18 May 1980 Mount St. Helens erupted at VEI 5, and its flank collapsed in a huge debris avalanche, the reference case for such collapses. Ferns were first to recolonize the devastated ground, a 'fern spike' like the one after the dinosaur extinction.

megh-103.title: Manufactured chemicals tear a hole in the ozone layer
megh-103.text: From the late 1970s the ozone layer in the stratosphere thinned worldwide, and each spring a far deeper loss opened over Antarctica, the 'ozone hole'. The main culprits were manufactured chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, along with halons and related refrigerants, solvents and propellants. Antarctic spring ozone fell by up to 70%, first reported in 1985, and Arctic losses reached 30% in the coldest years. Stronger ultraviolet-B under the thinned layer cuts plant productivity by about 6%, and the hole has at times reached parts of Australia, Chile and Argentina.

megh-104.title: El Chichón warms the northern winter
megh-104.text: In spring 1982 long-dormant El Chichón, in Chiapas, Mexico, produced three Plinian eruptions in a week, putting 7 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere. Its haze circled Earth in three weeks and brought winter warming to North America, Europe and Siberia in 1982–83, while Alaska, Greenland and China ran colder.

megh-105.title: Pinatubo's haze cools the whole planet
megh-105.text: Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines exploded on 15 June 1991 at VEI 6, the second-largest land eruption of the 20th century after Novarupta. Its ash column rose 35 km and put more particles into the stratosphere than any eruption since Krakatoa. A global haze of sulfuric acid cooled world temperatures by about 0.5 °C in 1991–1993 and briefly worsened ozone depletion. The summit collapsed into a 2.5 km caldera, later filled by Lake Pinatubo, while rain-driven lahars flooded the lowlands around it.

megh-106.title: Satellites clock the seas rising ever faster
megh-106.text: Satellites have measured the height of the sea from orbit since TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992, recording 7.5 cm of rise from 1993 to 2017. The pace kept climbing, reaching 4.62 mm a year in 2013–2022. From 1993 to 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers supplied 44% of the rise, and warming seawater, which expands as it heats, supplied 42%. In 2016 floods on Bramble Cay wiped out its melomys, a small rodent, the first mammal lost to human-caused sea-level rise.

megh-108.title: Greenland's ice sheet melts at record pace
megh-108.text: Jakobshavn Isbræ, the biggest glacier draining Greenland's ice sheet, began losing ice fast after 1997 as warming North Atlantic water melted its front from below. Ice loss from the whole sheet accelerated to about 187 Gt a year in 2000–2010 and 286 Gt a year in 2010–2018. In July 2012 melting reached 97% of the surface, unmatched since 1889, and that year's record net loss of 464 Gt was beaten by 586 Gt in 2019. During another record melt in 2021, rain fell for 13 hours on the 3,216 m Summit Station, where it had never rained before.

megh-109.title: Coral bleaching goes global for the first time
megh-109.text: In 1998 coral bleaching, in which heat-stressed corals expel the algae that feed them, became a recognized global event for the first time. A very strong 1997–98 El Niño warmed Indian Ocean waters by 2 °C and put 21% of the world's reefs under bleaching-level heat stress. Belize's barrier reef suffered its first recorded mass bleaching, and the Great Barrier Reef its first major one. That year was the warmest then on record, and since the early 1980s marine heatwaves have made mass bleaching sharply more frequent and severe.

megh-110.title: Warming slows briefly, then hits new records
megh-110.text: In 1998–2013, cool phases of Pacific and Atlantic ocean cycles briefly slowed surface warming; newer data shrink this 'hiatus', and claims that warming stopped are disputed. It ended after 2012: every year from 2015 on was warmer than any before it, and 2024 passed 1.5 °C of warming.

megh-111.title: Heatwaves bleach the Great Barrier Reef again and again
megh-111.text: Marine heatwaves bleached the Great Barrier Reef in 1998, 2002, 2006, 2016, 2017 and 2020, and another mass bleaching was confirmed in March 2022. Over half the reef's coral cover was lost between 1995 and 2017, and many breeding adults died in the 2016–17 bleaching.

megh-112.title: The Sumatra megaquake sends a tsunami across an ocean
megh-112.text: The boundary between the Indian and Burma plates slipped off Sumatra on 26 December 2004, in a megathrust earthquake of magnitude 9.1–9.3. More than 1,600 km of fault ruptured, lifting the seafloor up to 5 m and shoving it 11 m sideways within seven minutes. The tsunami reached 35 m near Banda Aceh and killed approximately 229,800 people around the Indian Ocean. Deposits on Phra Thong, Thailand, record at least three earlier major tsunamis in 2,800 years, the latest about 700 years ago.

megh-114.title: A magnitude 8.8 quake shakes central Chile
megh-114.text: Central Chile shook in a magnitude 8.8 earthquake on 27 February 2010. Its waves set off seiches as far away as Louisiana, and the Caldera del Atuel and other volcanic centers sank after the quake.

megh-115.title: The Tōhoku megaquake and tsunami strike Japan
megh-115.text: On 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9.0–9.1 megathrust earthquake struck off Honshu, as the Pacific plate drove beneath the Okhotsk microplate. Japan's most powerful recorded quake, it shook the worst-hit areas of Tōhoku for about six minutes and released about 93% of the strain built up there since 1926. Its tsunami reached up to 40.5 m at Miyako and swept up to 10 km inland, killing 19,759 people and melting down three reactors at Fukushima Daiichi. Its seismic waves crossed 8,000 km in under 30 minutes, raising seiches 1.5–1.8 m high in Norway.

megh-117.title: A meteor explodes over Chelyabinsk
megh-117.text: An asteroid about 20 m across exploded in the air over Chelyabinsk, Russia, on 15 February 2013, the largest such airburst observed with modern instruments. The roughly 500-kiloton blast shattered windows and injured over 1,000 people; its likeness to Tunguska strengthened the case for a high meteoroid airburst there too.

megh-118.title: Record ocean heat kills coral on an unprecedented scale
megh-118.text: Record ocean heat during the 2014–2017 El Niño caused the longest and most destructive coral bleaching then known. Reefs making up three-quarters of the world's reef systems were severely bleached, and coral died on an unprecedented scale. In 2016 bleaching killed 29 to 50% of the Great Barrier Reef's coral, and near Port Douglas over half the bleached corals died.

megh-119.title: Reykjanes Peninsula wakes after nearly 800 years
megh-119.text: After nearly 800 years of quiet, earthquakes and volcanic activity returned to Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula from 2020, and Fagradalsfjall erupted on 19 March 2021. In late 2023 a 15 km magma intrusion forced the town of Grindavík to evacuate, and experts suggest decades of volcanism may lie ahead.

megh-120.title: Hunga Tonga blasts seawater into the stratosphere
megh-120.text: On 15 January 2022 the undersea volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai erupted, the largest since Pinatubo, its plume reaching 58 km into the mesosphere, above the stratosphere. It lofted 146 million tons of seawater, a tenth of the stratosphere's water vapor, enough to warm the surface temporarily, and a Pacific-wide tsunami followed.

megh-121.title: The fourth global bleaching becomes the largest yet
megh-121.text: A fourth global coral bleaching event began in February 2023, and in April 2024 NOAA, the US ocean and weather agency, confirmed it as the largest yet. From January 2023 to September 2025, bleaching-level heat reached about 84% of the world's reef area, with bleaching in at least 83 countries and territories. On the Great Barrier Reef, hard-coral cover fell by up to 30.6% from 2024 to 2025, the largest single-year drops since 1986 in two regions.

megh-122.title: Record warmth pushes past the 1.5 °C mark
megh-122.text: The year 2024 was the warmest since regular tracking began in 1850, reaching 1.60 °C of warming, well above the 1.5 °C mark. It beat 2023, already 1.48 °C above the 1850–1900 average, and 2015–2025 held all eleven of the warmest years since 1850.

megh-123.title: Geologists reject the Anthropocene as a formal epoch
megh-123.text: In March 2024, after 15 years of deliberation, stratigraphers, who sort rock layers into time, voted down a formal Anthropocene epoch by a wide margin. Its shallow sediment record and very recent start weighed against it, and though the term stays in wide informal use, its scientific validity remains disputed.

megh-124.title: A magnitude 8.8 megaquake strikes Kamchatka again
megh-124.text: In 2025 another giant megathrust earthquake, of magnitude 8.8, struck the Kamchatka coast. There the Pacific plate plunges down along the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench, the same subduction zone that produced a magnitude 9.0 quake in the mid-twentieth century.

openers.hadean-eon: The Hadean is named for Hades, the Greek underworld, and the name fits a newborn planet whose surface was probably molten. Impacts hammered it throughout the eon, and the largest ones periodically disrupted the young ocean. A thick early atmosphere gave way to a superocean covering nearly the whole planet, with scarce land that may have risen and then drowned. Once oceans formed, life became possible, though it stayed vulnerable to large impacts. Almost no rock survives from this world: its record lies in zircon, a tiny and durable crystal found mostly in Western Australia's Jack Hills, and in the Moon and meteorites.
openers.archean-eon: Archean Earth was mostly a water world, its continental crust largely drowned beneath a superocean deeper than today's oceans. The air held almost no free oxygen, and the Sun gave only 75–80% of its present light, yet the surface stayed about as warm as today. Heat poured out of the interior at nearly three times today's rate as the eon began, and still twice today's rate at its end. The first cratons, old and stable blocks of continental crust with deep roots, took shape. Life stayed simple: prokaryotes, single cells without a nucleus, lived in shallow-water microbial mats, thin carpets of microbes, and in stromatolites, the layered mounds those mats built.
openers.eoarchean-era: The era opens with Canada's Acasta Gneiss, at 4,031 million years the oldest rock formation still preserved. Earth had cooled a great deal, and oceans covered much of the planet, though asteroid impacts still periodically disrupted them. The Sun shone at only about 70% of its modern brightness, yet the water cycle was already running.
