The earliest traces of weathering and the oldest sediments laid down in water date to about 3.8 billion years ago. From about 3.7 billion years ago, microbes that lived without oxygen, including early photosynthesizers, appear as continental crust grows at a quickening pace.
openers.paleoarchean-era: Little Paleoarchean rock survives, because deformation and metamorphism have wiped most of the record clean. Much continental crust existed, but it still lay underwater, and no one knows whether any land stood exposed. A hotter mantle ruled out plate tectonics in its modern form, and cratons such as the Kaapvaal and Pilbara grew by gathering terranes. By about 3.4 billion years ago, nitrogen made up most of a stable second atmosphere, and asteroids still struck often. Microbial mats and biofilms spread through shallow water, while microbes that needed no oxygen lived around hot vents and deep inside buried sediments.
openers.mesoarchean-era: The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of subduction in its modern style, along with a spread of microbial life. Low-lying cratons edged broad, shallow seas, and weathering of the land fed nutrients into the oceans. Methane and carbon dioxide kept the climate warm or temperate, yet the era also saw the oldest known glaciation. Microbes with diverse ways of making a living released gases that changed the air, and oases of relatively high oxygen formed in some nearshore seas. A supercontinent, Vaalbara, may have existed.
openers.neoarchean-era: Plate tectonics may have worked much as it does today, though sinking slabs snapped off more often in the hotter mantle. Raindrop prints in volcanic ash show air less than twice as dense as today's, and gas bubbles in lava suggest a pressure near 0.23 bar. Changing air and soils pushed microbes to diversify, and more copper in the environment favored organisms that use oxygen. Phosphorus, buried organic matter and more oxidized volcanic gases helped oxygen build up, leading toward the Great Oxygenation Event. Much of the deep rock that anchors today's continents may have formed in this era.
openers.proterozoic-eon: The Proterozoic is the longest eon of all, running from 2,500 to 538.8 million years ago, and its rocks survive far better than the Archean's. At first Earth's interior still sheds about twice today's heat, while the Sun shines 5 to 18 percent more weakly than it does now. Continents grow: about 43 percent of today's continental crust forms in this eon, and subduction, where one plate sinks beneath another, reaches levels the Archean never saw. Early on, plankton in the seas reaches roughly modern abundance, and sulfidic, oxygen-free water becomes more common. Ahead lie the Great Oxidation Event, the first eukaryotes, cells that keep their DNA in a nucleus, Snowball Earth and the Ediacaran biota, the first large complex life.
openers.paleoproterozoic-era: The Paleoproterozoic, the first era of the Proterozoic and the longest in Earth's history, runs from 2,500 to 1,600 million years ago. Its four periods are the Siderian, Rhyacian, Orosirian and Statherian. During it the continents first stabilize. Cyanobacteria, microbes that use sunlight to make food and give off oxygen, lift the oxygen in the air from almost nothing to as much as 10 percent of today's level. Rocks cooked at ultra-high temperatures in this era are taken to mark the start of modern-style plate tectonics.
openers.siderian-period: The Siderian, from 2,500 to 2,300 million years ago, takes its name from the Greek for iron, after the banded iron formations laid down in its seas. Continental plates grow, and Siberia and the Canadian Shield sit together in a continent called Arctica. Swarms of dikes, sheets of magma that fill cracks, slice through cratons, the old and stable cores of continents, in North America, South Africa and Australia. Oxygen begins an irreversible rise, and as it destroys methane, Earth slides into the Huronian glaciation from the middle of the period. Life leaves only faint traces: microfossils in Australian black chert and bacterial remains in South African iron formation.
openers.rhyacian-period: The Rhyacian, from 2,300 to 2,050 million years ago, takes its name from the Greek for lava flow. Huronian ice still grips the planet for roughly the first 40 percent of the period. Oxygen surges, life expands and buried organic matter piles up on the seafloor, while the first red beds rust on land. In South America and West Africa, colliding crust starts to build a new supercontinent, Columbia. Somewhere in these seas, scientists think, the first eukaryotes and sexual reproduction arise, though claimed signs of larger life in 2.1-billion-year-old rocks are heavily disputed.
openers.orosirian-period: The Orosirian, from 2,050 to 1,800 million years ago, is named from the Greek for mountain range, and in its later half mountains rise on virtually every continent. Collisions such as the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China orogenies crush the continents together into the supercontinent Columbia. Two of the largest impacts Earth has known strike, Vredefort early in the period and Sudbury near its end. Volcanoes pour out carbon dioxide and atmospheric oxygen falls, while banded iron formations largely stop forming after 1.85 billion years ago. Along what is now Lake Superior's north shore, microbes preserved in the Gunflint chert carry out photosynthesis, a sign the air holds enough oxygen for microbial life.
openers.statherian-period: The Statherian, from 1,800 to 1,600 million years ago, takes its name from the Greek for stable. On most continents, new flat platforms form and young fold belts harden into cratons. Columbia is already assembled and keeps growing at its edges, as subduction feeds magma and adds slices of crust. Oxygen stands at 10 to 20 percent of today's level, and fossils from North China's Changcheng Group show that eukaryotes have already diversified. In what is now Gabon, natural nuclear reactors flicker to life underground about 1.7 billion years ago.
openers.mesoproterozoic-era: The Mesoproterozoic runs from 1,600 to 1,000 million years ago, across the Calymmian, Ectasian and Stenian periods. Columbia breaks apart between 1,500 and 1,350 million years ago, and its pieces regather as Rodinia around 1,100 to 900 million years ago. The world is warm: the equator may sit at 22 to 27 °C and the global average near 19 °C, some 4 °C warmer than today. Oxygen may stay below 0.1 to 1 percent of modern levels, and old cratons such as the Yilgarn have been worn down into flattish, subdued ground. Life here was long thought purely microbial, but multicellular organisms already live in these seas.
openers.calymmian-period: The Calymmian, from 1,600 to 1,400 million years ago, takes its name from the word for cover. Blankets of sediment, called platform covers, spread across the continents. At times oxygen rises briefly to about 4 percent of present levels. In North China's seas about 1,589 million years ago, some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia, grow alongside possible fungi. Around 1,500 million years ago, the microbes of the Volyn biota are exceptionally preserved in what is now Ukraine.
openers.ectasian-period: The Ectasian, from 1,400 to 1,200 million years ago, is named for extension, the stretching of crust. A day lasts about 17 hours and 32 minutes at the start of the period and 18 hours and 28 minutes by its end. Columbia holds together until at least 1.35 billion years ago, then breaks apart amid swarms of dikes, while Rodinia begins to assemble. Across the tidal zones of oceans and seas, stromatolite colonies and reefs dominate. Acritarchs keep appearing, along with a moderate number of other eukaryotes.
openers.stenian-period: The Stenian, from 1,200 to 1,000 million years ago, takes its name from the word for narrow, after the narrow metamorphic belts left by its many orogenies. Rodinia finishes assembling, and most of the Grenville orogeny unfolds as continents grind together. Around 1,100 million years ago North America nearly tears in two along the Keweenawan Rift, the deepest failed rift on Earth. Oxygen is still low, at about 0.5 to 5 percent of present levels. Around 1.047 billion years ago the red alga Bangiomorpha appears, the oldest known organism that reproduced sexually, while stromatolites decline swiftly and eukaryotes take over fresh water.
openers.neoproterozoic-era: The Neoproterozoic, the last era of the Proterozoic, runs from 1,000 to 538.8 million years ago through the Tonian, Cryogenian and Ediacaran periods. It opens with Rodinia, holding most of Earth's land, straddling the equator. Marine algae multiply across the seas, feeding life on the seafloor and spurring the evolution of single-celled eukaryotic predators. Late in the era, a second surge of oxygen, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event, drives rapid evolution of multicellular life. Complex life finally appears: first Otavia, described as a primitive sponge, in the Tonian, then the strange organisms of the Ediacaran biota.
openers.tonian-period: The Tonian runs from 1,000 to about 720 million years ago, and its name, meaning stretch, recalls the stretching of continental crust as Rodinia broke up. Through the early part of the period, Rodinia and the superocean Mirovia hold steady, and the supercontinent reaches its greatest extent around 900 million years ago. Between 900 and 815 million years ago, oxygen climbs to over 13 percent of present levels. Acritarchs bloom in their first great radiation, and early multicellular life may diversify in oxygen oases of the deep ocean, though widespread oxygen-free water keeps eukaryote diversity low. Molecular studies place the root of the animal family tree somewhere in this period.
openers.cryogenian-period: The Cryogenian, from 720 to 635 million years ago, lives up to its name, which means cold-making. Rodinia is rifting apart, and every continent sits in the tropics, where weathering rock keeps drawing carbon dioxide from the air even as the planet cools. Twice, in the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations, ice spreads in the most severe ice ages Earth has known, with glaciers reaching the sea near the equator. Between them comes a warmer spell of rising seas and oxygen-free oceans. Life is sparse, yet testate amoebae appear and single-celled algae multiply a hundred- to a thousandfold.
openers.ediacaran-period: The Ediacaran, from 635 to 538.8 million years ago, is the last period of the Proterozoic, named for South Australia's Ediacara Hills. It opens as the last Cryogenian ice melts, and as Rodinia's pieces scatter, Gondwana gathers through a series of orogenies until most land lies near the south pole. Oxygen rises, though the deep ocean stays oxygen-free until about 580 million years ago. Microbial mats carpet the seafloor, and on them live the first widespread complex multicellular organisms, shaped like segmented worms, fronds, discs or motionless bags. Only at the very end do animals with hard shells appear.
openers.cambrian-period: Stand on a Cambrian shore and nothing green grows behind you; only slick microbial mats coat the tidal flats, helping to build the first soils. Most continental crust lies in the warm low latitudes, with Laurentia, ancient North America, straddling the equator and wide oceans keeping every major continent apart. The climate is mild, averaging about 20–25 °C, and the sea rises steadily, flooding continental interiors with shallow water. Ocean chemistry lurches at least ten times, leaving sharp swings in carbon isotopes, the heavy and light forms of carbon. All life is in the sea, and quirks of preservation make Cambrian Lagerstätten, fossil beds that keep soft tissue, unusually abundant.
openers.terreneuvian-epoch: The Terreneuvian, the first epoch of the Cambrian, begins with a burrow and ends with a trilobite. It runs from the first Treptichnus pedum burrow to the first trilobites, so it is the only Cambrian epoch without their fossils. At about 20–22 °C on global average, it is cooler than the rest of the period. Avalonia, Ganderia and other terranes, blocks of crust that later join other landmasses, lie in polar waters off Gondwana, the great southern continent. The Cambrian explosion surges on, yet deuterostomes, the branch of animals that includes vertebrates, are missing, apart from the possible Yanjiahella.
openers.cambrian-series-2-epoch: Around 514 million years ago, Laurentia sits on the equator, Siberia lies just south of it, and Gondwana spreads mostly across the Southern Hemisphere. Trilobites now crawl the seafloor, and archaeocyath reefs flourish in Stage 3 before collapsing in Stage 4. Nektaspids, a group of arthropods, reach their greatest diversity. Animals diversify fast, yet many trilobites and reef sponges stay confined to their home regions, which makes rocks hard to match across the globe. The epoch's base still lacks a formal reference section; geologists expect it to be the first trilobites in Gondwana.
openers.miaolingian-epoch: The Miaolingian, roughly the old middle Cambrian, spans about 506.5 to 497 million years ago. Laurentia drifts south and swings about 20° counterclockwise, while Avalonia and other terranes off Gondwana sit at high to middle southern latitudes. New mountains along Gondwana's Australian–Antarctic margin shed weathered rock into the sea, and the extra nutrients make the oceans more productive. Benthic graptolites, small colonial animals living on the seafloor, spread widely, and most modern mollusc groups, including snails, clams and monoplacophorans, are present. Large Paradoxides trilobites live in seas all over the world.
openers.furongian-epoch: In the Furongian, the last Cambrian epoch, Gondwana stretches from the South Pole, then in northwest Africa, to subtropical latitudes, with East Antarctica near the equator. Judging by where different trilobites lived, the temperature difference between pole and equator is only moderate. Sea level rises and falls as ice caps melt, a pattern that continues through the Ordovician. Trilobites reach their greatest diversity and dominate nearly every fossil community, while green algae are common. Along Gondwana's proto-Andean edge and in northern North China, ocean floor starts to sink beneath the land, building volcanic chains such as the Bainaimiao arc.
openers.ordovician-period: The Ordovician sea stands about 180 m above today's level, later 220 m, spreading shallow water across North America, Europe and Gondwana. Gondwana reaches from north of the equator to the South Pole, while Laurentia, Siberia and Baltica stay separate and the Panthalassic Ocean covers much of the north. Around 450 million years ago, a fainter Sun delivers about 1,312 watts per square meter, against about 1,361 today. The climate slides from greenhouse heat to an icehouse world with polar ice by the Hirnantian, the period's final age, and oxygen rises in the air. Trilobites, brachiopods, nautiloids, graptolites, corals and echinoderms crowd the seas, while on land the first simple plants, like mosses and liverworts, take hold.
openers.early-ordovician-epoch: The Early Ordovician is a hothouse, with very high carbon dioxide and sea surfaces as warm as those of the Early Eocene, a much later hot spell. The South Pole lies in what is now northern Africa, and Baltica sits near Gondwana in southern latitudes. Across the Iapetus Ocean, over 4,000 km wide, Laurentia lies in the southern tropics, and rising seas cover today's central Nevada and western Utah. Trilobites now share the water with new corals, brachiopods, colonial bryozoans, drifting graptolites, conodonts and the first true starfish.
openers.middle-ordovician-epoch: The great heat breaks, and by the end of the Middle Ordovician low-latitude seas have cooled to about today's equatorial temperatures. On the shelves, trilobites lose their dominance to mixed communities of brachiopods, bryozoans, molluscs and echinoderms, while acritarchs, tiny and mostly algal plankton, reach peak diversity. Labechiid sponges build reefs from South China to eastern North America, and animals spread widely across narrowing oceans such as the Iapetus. On Baltica, early land plants already form a diverse flora by the Darriwilian. Overhead, the debris of a shattered asteroid sends meteorites falling far more often than today.
openers.late-ordovician-epoch: Gondwana sits over the South Pole, with ice centered on what is now the Sahara, and tropical oceans run about 5 °C cooler than today's. Avalonia slows as it nears Baltica and then collides with it, and brachiopods and trilobites spread between the converging continents. On the equator, the Kazakh terranes form an archipelago of island arcs and microcontinents, and the Proto-Tethys Ocean reaches its widest. Armored jawless fish such as Arandaspis swim among drifting graptolites, and the first jawed vertebrates may be appearing. The sea rises early on, then falls for about 3 million years before the Hirnantian glaciation, and volcanic ash beds abound.
openers.silurian-period: Picture a planet of warm, shallow seas under air holding about 4,500 parts per million of carbon dioxide. Gondwana sprawls across the equator and much of the Southern Hemisphere, while the vast Panthalassa Ocean fills most of the north. High seas over flat land leave chains of islands, and violent storms smash shells into rubble beds. The climate never settles: the Silurian records more isotope excursions, abrupt shifts in the chemical signals locked in rock, than any other period. Life is still mainly marine and still recovering from the end-Ordovician extinction, but life on land is more prominent than ever before.
openers.llandovery-epoch: The Llandovery opens just after the Ordovician–Silurian extinctions, which had slashed biodiversity and left ecosystems wide open. Melting ice raises sea level, glaciers retreat toward the South Pole, and the climate turns much warmer. Black shales full of graptolites, tiny animals that lived in colonies, show oxygen-starved seafloors lingering into the earliest Rhuddanian. Reef building spreads, sea lilies called crinoids diversify, and marine faunas become some of the most cosmopolitan of the Phanerozoic, with the same kinds found far and wide. The epoch ends with the Ireviken event, which kills half of all trilobite species and 80% of conodont species.
openers.wenlock-epoch: In the Wenlock, Baltica closes in, and Laurentia stops being an independent continent. Glaciers have almost vanished, though glacial phases still return in the Sheinwoodian and Homerian. The limestone seafloors of what is now Britain teem with brachiopods, shellfish with two hinged shells, alongside corals and trilobites such as Calymene. Jawless eugaleaspids diversify, and osteostracans appear, probably in central Euramerica. Cooksonia, the oldest known vascular plant, appears, and air-breathing millipedes from Scotland may date from this epoch, though their age is disputed.
openers.ludlow-epoch: In the Ludlow, Scotland and Greenland meet Norway around 425 million years ago, closing the Iapetus Ocean in the Scandian orogeny. Near the ocean's eastern edge, a warm shallow sea lays down the Aymestry Limestone. On land, lycophytes, the clubmoss lineage, and zosterophylls join Cooksonia, while millipedes scuttle at Kerrera in Scotland. In the sea, acanthodians grow more diverse, and placoderms such as Silurolepis swim in waters that are now Yunnan. Late in the epoch, the Ludfordian brings the last major glaciation of the Early Paleozoic Ice Age, and sea level falls sharply.
openers.pridoli-epoch: The Přídolí, named for a spot near Slivenec, a suburb of Prague, closes the Silurian. The late Silurian is warm and arid, and evaporating seawater leaves salt deposits in shallow basins from Michigan to West Virginia. Warming ends the Andean-Saharan glaciation, land plants spread further, and oxygen climbs high enough for the first wildfires, which leave the oldest charcoal. In the sea, eurypterids reach their greatest diversity even as trilobites dwindle and stromatoporoid sponges suffer a second round of extinction. Scyphocrinoid loboliths, the bulb-shaped bases of certain sea lilies, appear suddenly at the very end of the period and vanish just as fast.
openers.devonian-period: For about 60.7 million years, the Devonian world runs warm, probably without glaciers for most of its length, though climates vary greatly between epochs and regions. Laurussia lies mostly south of the equator, drifting north, while Gondwana sprawls across the Southern Hemisphere with the South Pole inside it. The wide Rheic Ocean separates them, and Siberia begins the period upside down compared with today. Seas stand high but slowly fall, trilobites, brachiopods and great reefs still thrive, and fishes diversify so much that the Devonian is called the Age of Fishes. On land, rooted plants join the Silurian moss forests and microbial mats, and by the period's end trees stand up to 30 m tall.
openers.early-devonian-epoch: Through the Early Devonian, dry climates grip Siberia, Australia, North America and China, while Africa and South America stay warm and temperate. Tropical seas average about 30 °C at the surface, judging from the chemistry of conodont fossils. Oxygen remains relatively low, possibly half of modern values, and low sea levels split Laurussia's seafloor animals into separate provinces. On land, lichens such as Spongiophyton are unusually prominent, just before the first forests arrive. In the water, armored jawless fishes, thelodonts and petalichthyid placoderms all reach their peak diversity.
openers.middle-devonian-epoch: In the Middle Devonian, Laurentia lies in the Southern Hemisphere, between the equator and 30°S. Shrub-like forests of lycophytes, horsetails, ferns and progymnosperms, woody plants that still spread by spores, cover more and more ground, and the earliest trees rise among them. These new forests pull carbon from the air and bury it, perhaps cooling the climate by around 5 °C. Jawed fishes thrive in oceans and fresh water while armored jawless fishes decline, and stromatoporoid reef sponges reach their greatest diversity in the Eifelian. Shallow, warm, oxygen-poor lakes ringed by early plants favor fishes with lungs that can crawl briefly onto land.
openers.late-devonian-epoch: Gondwana still covers much of the Southern Hemisphere, and shallow seas drown much of South America. The climate warms back to Early Devonian levels and temperate climates spread, yet broad oxidized sediments in Euramerica record severe droughts. Plants and insects have colonized the land, Archaeopteris forests spread rapidly, and lycophytes become a dominant part of the flora. In Siberia, rifting and mantle plumes, columns of hot rock rising from deep inside Earth, pour out flood basalts, vast sheets of lava. Late in the epoch temperatures begin to drop, and a short-lived glaciation grips the late Famennian.
openers.carboniferous-period: The Carboniferous takes its name from the Latin for coal, and over about 60 million years its swamps laid down coal beds worldwide. Gondwana sprawls over the South Pole with Laurussia to its northwest, and the two are fusing into the supercontinent Pangaea, ringed by the vast ocean Panthalassa. The Late Paleozoic Ice Age, the longest and most extensive icehouse of the Phanerozoic, grips the planet, yet oxygen climbs from 15–20% of the air to as much as 25–30%. Across tropical Euramerica rise towering rainforests of lycopsids, tree-sized relatives of today's club mosses, where air-breathing insects, millipedes and arachnids, some of them giants, crawl and fly. Temnospondyl amphibians rule the land, the first amniotes appear, and crinoids, sharks and ray-finned fish fill the seas.
openers.mississippian-subperiod: The Mississippian, the earlier of the Carboniferous's two subperiods, runs from 358.86 to 323.4 million years ago. Shallow seas spread across the continents early on, their floors carpeted with crinoids, while sharks and ray-finned fish take over the open water after the end-Devonian crisis. A seaway through the Rheic Ocean links the Paleo-Tethys and Panthalassa, so sea creatures spread almost worldwide. The South Pole sits in southern Africa, yet the early Tournaisian is warm, with a global average near 22 °C, before short glaciations return. On land, forests are still sparse and coal is scarce, though some trees already stand 40 m tall.
openers.pennsylvanian-subperiod: The Pennsylvanian, the later Carboniferous subperiod, runs from 323.4 to 298.9 million years ago. Laurussia straddles the equator under coal forests, where Lepidodendron and Sigillaria trees tower over horsetails and seed ferns, and peat mires fill the basins beside the Central Pangean Mountains. Far to the south, Gondwana's ice sheets wax and wane, so the sea floods and drains the shallow tropical shelves again and again. Oxygen climbs above 25% of the air, cockroach relatives swarm as the most successful insects, and amniotes split into the lines leading to reptiles and to mammals. By the end, the South Pole has drifted to eastern Antarctica and the equatorial heart of Pangaea is drying out.
openers.permian-period: The Permian, the last period of the Paleozoic, lasts about 47 million years and takes its name from Russia's Perm region. Nearly all land now forms one supercontinent, Pangaea, stretching from the equator to both poles, with the microcontinents of Cathaysia off to the east. Its vast interior bakes and freezes with the seasons, drenched by megamonsoon rains in places and parched into deserts elsewhere, as the world swings from icehouse to greenhouse. Synapsids, the ancestors of mammals, dominate the land, while brachiopods help build reefs in the seas. Three or possibly four major extinctions strike, ending with the Great Dying, the largest in Earth's history.
openers.cisuralian-epoch: The Cisuralian, or Early Permian, runs from 298.9 to 274.4 million years ago and takes its name from the western slopes of the Ural Mountains. It opens with the ice age at its peak, but the glaciers soon retreat as the climate warms, and the continental interiors dry out. North of the Central Pangean Mountains, in the dry rain shadow behind the peaks, coal-swamp plants give way to seasonally dry vegetation, while wet, frost-free Cathaysia keeps its swamps of lycopsids and tree ferns. Pelycosaurs, diadectids and temnospondyls rule the land, and glossopterid trees spread across southern Gondwana. Insects diversify dramatically, even as diversity and turnover in the seas stay low.
openers.guadalupian-epoch: The Guadalupian, or Middle Permian, takes its name from the Guadalupe Mountains of New Mexico and Texas and runs from 274.4 to 259.857 million years ago. Reefs flourish from Texas to the Zechstein Basin and the Tethys, the high point of Permian reef building, and trilobites reach a final peak of diversity. Equatorial forests now follow a seasonal wet–dry rhythm, and coastal swamps along eastern Pangaea link the temperate zones. Therapsids are on the rise, giant dinocephalians among them dominate the land, and Glossopteris floras flourish in Gondwana as the ice wanes. Sea level falls sharply from the Roadian onward, and two extinctions bracket the epoch: Olson's near its start and the Capitanian at its close.
openers.lopingian-epoch: The Lopingian, the last epoch of the Permian, runs from 259.857 to 251.902 million years ago. North China, South China and Indochina fuse onto Pangaea, a great mountain barrier stands in its interior, and the supercontinent grows ever drier. Therapsids rule the land, from saber-toothed gorgonopsians to beaked, plant-eating dicynodonts, and dicynodonts and cynodonts may be evolving warm blood. Glossopterid trees dominate southern Gondwana, while the old Carboniferous-style swamps of lycopsids and horsetails survive only in Cathaysia. The seas are already under strain, as rocks in Australia's Bowen Basin record repeated stress for marine life, a prelude to the largest extinction in Earth's history.
openers.triassic-period: Nearly all the world's land is welded into one supercontinent, Pangaea, which sits astride the equator and covers about a quarter of Earth's surface. Around it spreads Panthalassa, one ocean over almost 70% of the globe, where algae with borrowed chloroplasts become the chief plankton. The interior is hot and dry, a land of deserts, red sandstone and salt beds, and even the poles carry no ice while sea level stays low. Survivors of the end-Permian extinction share this world with newcomers, among them the first dinosaurs and early mammal relatives, that will shape the rest of the Mesozoic. On land, crocodile-line and dinosaur-line archosaurs share power, while Dicroidium seed ferns rule the forests of Gondwana, Pangaea's southern half.
openers.early-triassic-epoch: In the wake of the Siberian Traps, a colossal outpouring of lava, the Early Triassic becomes the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, the eon of abundant animal life. Even the poles are merely temperate, and with so little difference between equator and pole, tropical species may spread far toward them. Life is crawling back from the end-Permian extinction, and the same few species turn up almost everywhere. On land, the plant-eater Lystrosaurus outnumbers every other backboned animal, among sparse stands of Pleuromeia, a relative of club mosses. In the shallow seas, microbial mats and reefs spread, coil-shelled ammonoids boom and crash, and the first marine reptiles, ichthyosaurs among them, slip into the water.
openers.middle-triassic-epoch: The fierce heat finally eases: the Middle Triassic runs cooler than the epoch before, and temperatures fall through most of the Anisian. Pangaea begins to crack, the Tethys Ocean opens on its eastern side, and the shallow Muschelkalk Sea spreads across central Europe. Some 4–6 million years after the extinction, complex ecosystems form again, and archosaurs push the therapsids aside to rule the land. The forests hold only seed ferns and gymnosperms, seed plants without flowers; no flowering plant has yet evolved. Offshore, ichthyosaurs, nothosaurs, pachypleurosaurs and placodonts thrive, especially around the Tethys.
openers.late-triassic-epoch: The Late Triassic opens with rain: the Carnian pluvial episode, a long wet spell, turns the arid interior into lush forests along its rivers. Pangaea now arcs almost from pole to pole, and lake-filled rift valleys open along the future Central Atlantic, from Florida to Newfoundland and across Morocco and Iberia. The hothouse swings between cooler and warmer spells, and sea level sinks from a Carnian high to about 50 m below today's. Gymnosperm forests cover the land, and crocodile-line archosaurs such as phytosaurs, aetosaurs and rauisuchians fill more niches than the young dinosaurs. At sea, neopterygian fishes spread as ceratitid ammonites decline, and shastasaurian ichthyosaurs grow to enormous size.
openers.jurassic-period: For about 58.3 million years, the Jurassic world runs hot: 5–10 °C warmer than today, with roughly four times today's carbon dioxide. Both poles lie in open ocean, free of ice, and forests grow close to them, while deserts and scrub spread across the low latitudes. Ferns, conifers, cycads, ginkgos and the extinct Bennettitales clothe the land, and there are still no widely accepted flowering plants. Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs rule the seas, pterosaurs rule the sky, and the young North Atlantic stays a narrow channel throughout. Sea level rises and falls again and again, 64 times in all, and 15 of those swings top 75 meters.
openers.early-jurassic-epoch: When the Early Jurassic begins, 201.4 million years ago, Pangaea still holds every major landmass, but it is starting to split into Laurasia and Gondwana. New seas open between the pieces, and the air turns tropical and far more humid than in the Triassic. Tropical seas wash over parts of Europe, laying down the marine rocks called the Lias that now line England's Jurassic Coast. Dinosaurs reach every continent, ichthyosaurs hit their peak diversity offshore, and the leaf-shedding conifer Podozamites dominates the forests of East Asia. A long cool spell, from about 199 to 183 million years ago, ends with a sharp Toarcian warming.
openers.middle-jurassic-epoch: Between 174.7 and 161.5 million years ago, Pangaea pulls apart into Laurasia and Gondwana as the young Central Atlantic widens. The Toarcian heat fades into a cooler interval, possibly interrupted by brief ice ages, and sea level climbs from the Aalenian onward. Ammonites, ichthyosaurs, sharks, rays and ray-finned fish swarm the seas, while dinosaurs roam forests of cycads and conifers on land. Sauropods diversify, Europe gains its first megalosaurid predators, and small mammals branch out, from furred Castorocauda and the gliding Volaticotherium to early multituberculates. In northeastern China, volcanic ash buries the dinosaurs, mammals, salamanders, insects and plants of the Yanliao Biota.
openers.late-jurassic-epoch: By 161.5 million years ago, Pangaea has split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south, with the wide Tethys Ocean between them. Europe is an archipelago in a warm, shallow tropical sea, much nearer the equator than today, fringed by spreading sponge and coral reefs. Very high carbon dioxide keeps the world hot, and across the still-narrow Atlantic a carbonate platform nearly 7,000 km long fringes eastern North America. On the Morrison floodplains of western North America, giant sauropods such as Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus feed while Allosaurus hunts. Small predatory theropods have given rise to the first birds, among them Archaeopteryx, and pterosaurs near their greatest diversity.
openers.cretaceous-period: Picture a world with no permanent ice, where lush forests grow at the poles and the seas stand around 300 meters higher than today. At the peak of the flooding, shallow, warm seas cover a third of today's land. In them, tiny coccolithophore algae thrive, and their calcite plates pile up as the chalk that gives the Cretaceous its name. Pangaea, the old supercontinent, is finishing its breakup into today's continents, though they sit in unfamiliar places, and North America is cut off from the rest. On land, flowering plants spread and insects diversify, founding many of the groups that dominate Earth today.
openers.early-cretaceous-epoch: The Early Cretaceous opens cool, with snow falling often at high latitudes and the tropics wetter than before. Conifers rule the forests, among them podocarps, pines, araucarias and cypresses, alongside ginkgos, bennettitaleans and ferns. Gondwana starts out whole, but South America, Antarctica and Australia then rift from Africa, and the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans begin to open. A proto-Amazon–Congo river flows west across western Gondwana, while the inland Eromanga Sea drowns much of Australia. As seaways spread, high-browsing sauropods and stegosaurs decline, and by the late Albian tropical seas average about 30 °C.
openers.late-cretaceous-epoch: The Late Cretaceous opens in one of the hottest spells of the Phanerozoic, with the highest carbon dioxide of the whole period. A seaway runs from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean, splitting North America into Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east. Hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs and ceratopsians thrive in western North America and eastern Asia, and tyrannosaurs rule North America as top predators. At sea, mosasaurs take over once the ichthyosaurs vanish, and the Arctic is warm enough for crocodile-like choristoderes. The world cools slowly over the epoch, yet near its end Antarctica still holds temperate rainforest and marsupials.
openers.paleogene-period: The Paleogene, first period of the Cenozoic Era, runs about 43 million years, from 66 to 23.04 million years ago. It opens in the wreckage left by the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs, and mammals step into the vacant world to rule the land from then on. Four plates floor the Pacific Ocean, the Pacific, Farallon, Kula and Izanagi, while Africa creeps toward Eurasia. The last fragments of Gondwana, the old southern supercontinent, drift apart as Antarctica pulls away from South America and Australia. Over three epochs, the Paleocene, Eocene and Oligocene, the climate swings from searing heat through a long cooling to the first permanent ice sheets on Antarctica.
openers.paleocene-epoch: Picture a greenhouse world with no ice at either pole, averaging about 24–25 °C against roughly 14 °C in recent times. Even the deep ocean is mild, at 8–12 °C, and its cold, sinking water forms in the North Pacific rather than the North Atlantic. Forests cover the land right up to the poles, dense because no large plant-eaters thin them, yet poor in plant species. Small, fast-evolving mammals scurry through this emptied world, while crocodile relatives, snakes and choristoderes, crocodile-like reptiles, are the biggest hunters on land. Offshore, ray-finned fish take over the open ocean and the recovering reefs, as the Rockies rise and India begins to press into Asia.
openers.eocene-epoch: Step into an Eocene jungle and the air is hot and heavy: Earth averages about 27 °C, its warmth held in by carbon dioxide and methane. Australia and South America still cling to an ice-free Antarctica, and Eurasia is broken into Western Europe, Balkanatolia and Asia. Small mammals of brand-new orders, none over 10 kg, pick their way through cramped jungles, while huge lakes fill the high basins of western North America. The heat peaks around 49 million years ago and then slowly drains away. By the epoch's end, continental interiors are drying, forests are thinning, open country is spreading and ice is building on Antarctica.
openers.oligocene-epoch: The Oligocene opens with a massive spread of ice across Antarctica, and both poles sit well below freezing for the first time in the Phanerozoic, the eon of abundant animal life. Antarctica grows lonelier as deep ocean channels open toward Australia and South America, while the other continents drift toward their present places. Lower seas than in the early Eocene bare wide coastal plains in Europe and along North America's Gulf and Atlantic coasts, and North American land temperatures have just dropped 7–11 °C. Forests retreat before open plains and grasses, and by the late Oligocene life on land and at sea has sunk to a low ebb in diversity. Cut off from the rest, South America and Australia keep their own native animals, and South America's top predators are still terror birds and carnivorous marsupial relatives.
openers.neogene-period: Through the Neogene, the continents sit very close to where they lie today, though India keeps shoving into Asia and the Himalayas climb higher. The climate cools markedly across the period, a long slide that ends in the continental glaciations of the Quaternary. On land, mammals and birds remain in charge and spread into many habitats, while giant predators such as the shark megalodon and the sperm whale Livyatan rule the oceans. Late in the period the Isthmus of Panama joins North and South America, and near its end the first humans, Homo habilis, appear in Africa.
openers.miocene-epoch: The Miocene world would look familiar: its plants and animals are recognizably modern, and many of today's mammal groups make their first appearance. Grasslands keep spreading and forests keep shrinking, carrying on the trend of the Oligocene. The long cooling is broken by short warm spells, and in one of them the global climate rivals the Oligocene's. In the Early Miocene, the temperature contrast between mid-latitude lands and seas is much like today's. Far northern Australia has monsoons, and pockets of rainforest still dot its center, though a drier climate will later shrink them.
openers.late-miocene: Through the Late Miocene, the warm Middle Miocene gives way to a cooler, drier world that looks more and more like today's. Only a land bridge between the Americas is missing from the modern map, and the Andes are lifting the future Altiplano from low ground to over 3,000 meters. In Eurasia, the cut-off Paratethys sprawls from the eastern Alps to Kazakhstan as a brackish megalake, a vast lake of half-salty water. On spreading grasslands, recognizable members of the dog family, bears, deer and camels live beside now-vanished three-toed horses, hornless rhinos and gomphotheres, early elephant relatives. Late in the epoch, the Mediterranean is cut off from the Atlantic and nearly evaporates.
openers.pliocene-epoch: By the Pliocene, the continents have drifted to within about 70 kilometers of where they sit today, and the map looks almost modern. The climate grows cooler, drier and more seasonal, bridging the warm Miocene and the icy Pleistocene, yet wet 'Green Sahara' phases return about every 21,000 years. Fairly warm seas teem with sea cows, seals, sea lions, sharks and whales. Grasslands and savannas spread, and in Africa hoofed animals dominate while australopithecines, early upright-walking hominins, appear alongside baboon-like monkeys. In Asia, elephants, gomphotheres and stegodonts thrive, while in Australia the dog-like thylacine and the cat-like Thylacoleo still hunt.
openers.quaternary-period: The Quaternary is the shortest period of the Phanerozoic, the eon of abundant animal life, and it has not ended yet. Its clock starts 2.58 million years ago, a date fixed in 2009 so that all the recent repeated glaciations fall inside it. This is a world that keeps freezing and thawing. Perhaps as many as 44 times, ice sheets swell during cold glacials and shrink back in warm interglacials. Through every swing, the Antarctic ice sheet never lets go.
openers.pleistocene-epoch: The Pleistocene runs from 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago, the first epoch of the Quaternary and the most recent stretch of repeated glaciations. Its first part, the Early Pleistocene, lasts until 774,000 years ago and contains two ages, the Gelasian and the Calabrian. Great Britain is still a peninsula of Europe, joined to it by a chalk ridge across the Strait of Dover, and the Rhine flows through what is now the North Sea. In Africa, archaic members of the human genus, Homo, arise and spread across Africa and Eurasia. For much of the epoch, Homo erectus is the only hominin, the group that includes humans and their extinct close relatives.
openers.gelasian-age: The Gelasian opens 2.58 million years ago with a flip of Earth's magnetic field, recorded in rocks at Monte San Nicola in Sicily, and closes 1.80 million years ago. Until 2009 it belonged to the Pliocene; geologists moved it because climate, oceans and life all shifted at its base. Ice sheets now begin to grow across the Northern Hemisphere. Deep-sea cores log about 40 marine isotope stages, numbered cold and warm phases read from ocean sediments, while the Alps endure some 20 glacial cycles of varying strength. On the coast of East Anglia, the Red, Norwich and Weybourne Crags pile up layer by layer, recording early Pleistocene environments.
openers.calabrian-age: The Calabrian runs for about a million years, from 1.80 million to 774,000 years ago, and its reference rocks lie at Vrica in Calabria, Italy. Ice comes and goes on a steady 41,000-year beat, paced by the obliquity cycle, the slow rocking of Earth's tilt. In the Alps glaciers grow during the Danube stage, while northern Europe enjoys the warm Waalian interglacial around 1.6 to 1.4 million years ago. Across Eurasia, Homo erectus is on the move, colonizing lands as far away as China and Java. Near the end of the age the rhythm of the ice begins to change, and the oldest ice now known in Greenland forms about a million years ago.
openers.chibanian-age: The Chibanian, or Middle Pleistocene, begins with the last reversal of Earth's magnetic field and ends near the close of the Penultimate Glacial Period. The continents sit essentially where they are today, having moved no more than about 100 km since the Pleistocene began. Ice now advances in long glacials about every 100,000 years, piling up 1,500 to 3,000 m thick over North America and northern Europe. At each peak the sea drops by up to 120 m, and exposed continental shelves become dry land that links one landmass to the next. Mammoths, saber-toothed cats and giant sloths roam the land, and by the age's end Neanderthals, Denisovans and early Homo sapiens all walk the Earth.
openers.late-pleistocene-age: Picture a world swinging between extremes: the Late Pleistocene opens with the brief, warm Last Interglacial, then slides into the long Last Glacial Period. At its height the Laurentide ice sheet reaches from the Rockies through the Great Lakes into New England, covering nearly all of Canada. Beyond the ice, a vast grassland called the mammoth steppe runs from Spain across Eurasia and Beringia into Alaska and the Yukon. Around 18,000 years ago the sea stands 120–130 m below today's, so Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi form a single island. Across the ice-free world, modern humans spread out of Africa, meeting and interbreeding with the archaic humans already living there.
openers.holocene-epoch: The Holocene, the current epoch, opens about 11,700 years ago as the Younger Dryas cold spell ends. It is an interglacial, a warm pause in the ongoing Quaternary cycle of ice ages, and the continents drift less than a kilometer in 10,000 years. The map is essentially today's, but the coastlines are not: melting ice lifts the sea about 35 meters early on and another 30 meters later. In 2018 geologists divided the epoch by climate into three ages: the Greenlandian, the Northgrippian and the Meghalayan. Often called the Age of Humans, it spans the first farms, the rapid spread of people and all of written history.
openers.greenlandian-age: The Greenlandian, the Holocene's first age, runs from about 11,700 to 8,200 years ago and ends in a sudden cold snap, the 8.2-kiloyear event. Warming continues at a gentler pace, and rising seas drown the Bering land bridge and cut off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania. A stronger African monsoon, the seasonal wind that brings summer rain, turns much of the Sahara into grassland, woodland and lakes. Many megafauna, the giant animals of the Ice Age, are still dying out. Eurasia enters the Mesolithic, the Middle Stone Age, while in the Near East the first farmers and herders begin the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.
openers.northgrippian-age: The Northgrippian opens with a cold snap 8,200 years ago, then warms to the Holocene's highest temperatures, so its first stretch falls within the Holocene Climatic Optimum. Polar ice caps shrink to their smallest extent of the epoch, and the rising sea floods Doggerland and Sundaland. Six thousand years ago the Sahara is only about half its present size, and Lake Mega-Chad has at times spread over some 350,000 square kilometers. Rain belts sit in different places from today: a stronger East African monsoon raises lake levels, while western North America is drier than now. Across much of the world, people move from foraging to farming and herding, entering the Neolithic.
openers.meghalayan-age: The Meghalayan, the latest age of the present Holocene epoch, opens 4,250 years before 2000 with a great drought and runs to the present day. After their long post-glacial climb, the seas hold nearly still, while in Iceland the North American and Eurasian plates keep pulling apart and feeding eruptions. Monsoonal China dries and big eruptions chill the north again and again, while El Niño, the recurring warm swing of the tropical Pacific, grows stronger. Giant flightless moa still stride across New Zealand, but people already live on every continent except Antarctica. By 2026 their fuels have pushed carbon dioxide from a steady 280 parts per million (ppm) to 432 ppm, and their farms dominate the land.

closing:
Earth began as wreckage. About 4.57 billion years ago, a collapsing cloud of hydrogen gave birth to the Sun, and the leftover disc of dust clumped into planets. Earth was largely built within 10 to 20 million years. Then a Mars-sized protoplanet called Theia slammed into it, and the debris thrown into orbit gathered into the Moon. Iron sank to the center to form the core, and its churning metal raised the magnetic field that still shields the surface. The oldest intact rock that survives from that hellish first chapter, the Acasta Gneiss of northern Canada, is 4.03 billion years old.

Life appeared early and worked quietly. By about 3.48 billion years ago, microbial mats were building layered mounds called stromatolites in what is now Western Australia. Around 3.2 billion years ago, some microbes began releasing oxygen as waste, although scientists still argue over exactly when. For ages the oceans' dissolved iron soaked that oxygen up and rusted into iron ore. Then, between about 2.46 and 2.06 billion years ago, oxygen finally built up in the air, an irreversible change called the Great Oxidation Event. Somewhere in this deep past, perhaps near 3 billion years ago, the crust broke into moving plates, though the timing is still debated.

The next stretch looks slow but changed everything. Cells with a nucleus, the eukaryotes, appeared by about 2 billion years ago, and the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction comes from a red alga 1.05 billion years old. Continents gathered into supercontinents, Columbia and then Rodinia, and broke apart again. Between 717 and 635 million years ago, glaciers reached sea level near the equator. Whether Earth froze into a full snowball or kept a slushy band of open water is still disputed. After the thaw came the Ediacaran biota, large soft-bodied creatures that are the oldest known complex multicellular life.

Animals then took over the oceans, and plants and animals took over the land. From 538.8 million years ago, the Cambrian explosion produced the first representatives of most modern animal phyla within about 20 to 25 million years. Animals grew skeletons and began burrowing into the seafloor. The first land plants left spores about 470 million years ago. Forests rose by about 390 million years ago, and limbed vertebrates were walking by 365 million years ago. Around 335 million years ago, the continents locked together into Pangaea, a supercontinent that lasted about 160 million years.

Catastrophe pruned this world again and again. The worst came 252 million years ago, when the Siberian Traps poured out lava and gas, warming the planet and souring the seas. About 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrate species vanished. Dinosaurs rose from the survivors around 233 million years ago and ruled the land for most of the next 167 million years. Their reign ended 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about 10 kilometers wide struck off the Yucatán Peninsula. About 76% of species disappeared, including every dinosaur except the birds.

Mammals inherited the emptied world, and the planet slowly cooled. About 56 million years ago, thousands of billions of tonnes of carbon flooded the air and oceans, and global temperatures jumped about 5 to 8 °C. India rammed into Asia, and the Himalayas began to rise. About 33.9 million years ago, falling carbon dioxide let ice build up on Antarctica, opening the icehouse world that continues today. Grasslands spread, the human and chimpanzee lineages split about 8 million years ago, and Panama joined the Americas. By 2.58 million years ago, ice sheets were spreading across the Northern Hemisphere.

People are newcomers to this story. Homo erectus appeared in Africa about 2 million years ago. The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 315,000 years old. Modern humans left Africa between 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, and the Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago. The last ice age peaked between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Then, 11,700 years ago, Greenland warmed by about 8 °C within 40 years, the Holocene began, and farming soon took root in the Fertile Crescent.

Now one species has become a geologic force. Carbon dioxide stayed near 280 parts per million for 10,000 years before the mid-18th century, and it has since risen 54%. The global average temperature climbed from 14 °C in 1951–1980 to 15 °C in 2013–2017. Lake mud in Ontario holds a plutonium spike from 1952 hydrogen-bomb tests. In 2024, stratigraphers voted against naming a formal Anthropocene epoch, but the debate over the term goes on. Earth's history has been written by collisions, volcanoes, ice and microbes, and its newest layer is being written by humans.
